subtopic: 1.13 Loci in the complex plane: a circle and a half-line
syllabus_ref: AHL 1.13 (modulus-argument form; loci in the complex plane, |z - z0| = r and arg z = theta)
title: 1.13 Loci in the complex plane: a circle and a half-line
q_html:
The complex number $z$ satisfies $|z-(3+2i)|=2$. The circle and the half-line $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{4}$ are drawn on the Argand diagram in the figure. Answer all parts without using a calculator and give every answer in exact form.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Show that the locus of $z$ in the complex plane is a circle, and state the centre and the radius of this circle.

    (Show that)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    The half-line $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{4}$ meets the circle at the two points $P$ and $Q$ shown in the diagram. Determine the exact value of $|z|$ at each of $P$ and $Q$.

    (Determine)
  3. [2 marks](c)

    Calculate the exact distance $PQ$ between the two points found in part (b), giving your answer in the form $\sqrt{k}$ where $k$ is an integer.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    The point $W$ lies on the circle, and $|W|$ is smaller than the modulus of every other point of the circle. Determine $W$ in the form $a+bi$ and state the exact value of $|W|$.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Put $z = x + iy$. Then $z - (3+2i) = (x-3) + i(y-2)$, and the condition $|z-(3+2i)| = 2$ says that $\sqrt{(x-3)^2 + (y-2)^2} = 2$. Squaring both sides gives $(x-3)^2 + (y-2)^2 = 4$. (M1) This is the equation of the circle with centre $3 + 2i$ and radius $2$. (A1)(AG)

(b) Every point of the half-line $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{4}$ has equal real and imaginary parts, so write $z = t(1+i)$ with $t > 0$. (M1) Substituting into the circle equation gives $(t-3)^2 + (t-2)^2 = 4$. (M1) Expanding, $2t^2 - 10t + 9 = 0$. (A1) The quadratic formula gives $t = \frac{10 \pm \sqrt{100-72}}{4} = \frac{10 \pm \sqrt{28}}{4} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{7}}{2}$. For a point $z = t(1+i)$ the modulus is $|z| = t|1+i| = t\sqrt{2}$, so the two moduli are $\frac{(5+\sqrt{7})\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{14}}{2}$ and $\frac{(5-\sqrt{7})\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{5\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{14}}{2}$. (A1)(A1) Numerically these are $5.41$ and $1.66$, and the diagram confirms that both lie in the first quadrant.

(c) The two points are $z_1 = t_1(1+i)$ and $z_2 = t_2(1+i)$, and from the quadratic $t_1 - t_2 = \sqrt{7}$. (M1) Because both points lie on the same ray, $PQ = |z_1 - z_2| = (t_1-t_2)|1+i| = \sqrt{7}\,\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{14}$. (A1)

(d) The point of a circle closest to a given point lies on the line joining that point to the centre, so $W$ lies on the line from the origin through $3+2i$. (M1) The distance from the origin to the centre is $|3+2i| = \sqrt{13}$, and the origin is outside the circle because $\sqrt{13} > 2$, so $|W| = \sqrt{13} - 2$. (A1) Since $W$ lies on that line, $W = \frac{\sqrt{13}-2}{\sqrt{13}}(3+2i) = \frac{3(\sqrt{13}-2)}{\sqrt{13}} + \frac{2(\sqrt{13}-2)}{\sqrt{13}}i \approx 1.336 + 0.891i$. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Award M1 for translating the modulus condition into an algebraic equation, either by writing $z = x+iy$ and squaring, or by quoting the circle form directly. Award A1 for centre $3+2i$ and radius $2$. Accept $(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2=4$ as an equivalent statement of the locus. (b) M1 for the parameterisation $z = t(1+i)$ or for any equivalent use of $y = x$ with $x > 0$; M1 for substituting into the circle equation; A1 for the reduced quadratic $2t^2-10t+9=0$; A1 for $t = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{7}}{2}$; A1 for both moduli in exact form. A candidate who obtains $t$ correctly but reports $\frac{5 \pm \sqrt{7}}{2}$ as $|z|$ has omitted the factor $\sqrt{2}$ and scores 4 of the 5 marks. Do not award the final A1 for decimal answers alone. (c) M1 for $PQ = (t_1-t_2)|1+i|$, A1 for $\sqrt{14}$. Follow through from the candidate's own $t_1, t_2$ provided the method is sound. (d) M1 for placing $W$ on the line joining the origin to the centre, A1 for $|W| = \sqrt{13}-2$, A1 for the exact complex form. Accept $1.34 + 0.89i$ only when the exact form is also given, since the question asks for exact values. Do not accept $W$ found by scaling the centre by any other factor.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: Exact coordinates on the unit circle for an obtuse angle, the tangent of that angle, the chord between two symmetric points and the area of the sector
syllabus_ref: SL 3.6 (the unit circle and the definition of sin, cos and tan for angles greater than 90 degrees) with SL 3.4 (the circle: radian measure and arc length) and SL 3.5 (the equation sin x = c and its solutions on a stated interval)
title: Exact coordinates on the unit circle for an obtuse angle, the tangent of that angle, the chord between two symmetric points and the area of the sector
q_html:
The diagram shows the unit circle. The point $P$ lies on the circle in the second quadrant with an angle of $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ measured from the positive $x$-axis, and the point $Q$ lies on the circle in the first quadrant with an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. The sector $POQ$ is shaded and the chord $PQ$ is drawn.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    State the exact coordinates of $P$ and of $Q$.

    (State)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Find the exact value of $\tan\left( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \right)$.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Show that the length of the chord $PQ$ is $\sqrt{3}$.

    (Show that)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Hence find the exact area of the shaded sector $POQ$.

    (Hence)
a_html:
(a) On the unit circle a point at angle $\theta$ has coordinates
$(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. The reference angle for $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is
$\pi - \dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and because $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is in the second
quadrant its cosine is negative and its sine is positive:

$$\cos\left( \frac{5\pi}{6} \right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad
\sin\left( \frac{5\pi}{6} \right) = \frac{1}{2}.$$

Hence

$$P\left( -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \; \frac{1}{2} \right).$$ (A1)

For $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, which is in the first quadrant, both coordinates are positive:

$$Q\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \; \frac{1}{2} \right).$$ (A1)

The two points have the same $y$-coordinate, so the chord $PQ$ is horizontal, and $P$ and $Q$
are mirror images of one another in the $y$-axis.

(b) The tangent of an angle is the quotient of the sine and the cosine, which on the unit
circle is the quotient of the two coordinates:

$$\tan\left( \frac{5\pi}{6} \right)
= \frac{\sin(5\pi/6)}{\cos(5\pi/6)}
= \frac{\;1/2\;}{-\sqrt{3}/2}.$$ (M1)

Dividing by the fraction $-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ multiplies by its reciprocal:

$$\tan\left( \frac{5\pi}{6} \right) = \frac{1}{2} \times \left( -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right)
= -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.$$ (A1)

The value is negative, as it must be for an angle in the second quadrant, where the sine is
positive and the cosine is negative.

(c) The chord $PQ$ joins $P\left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2} \right)$ and
$Q\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2} \right)$. Because the $y$-coordinates are equal, the
chord is horizontal and its length is the difference of the $x$-coordinates:

$$PQ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left( -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)
= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}.$$ (M1)(A1)

Alternatively, the angle $POQ$ is

$$\frac{5\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{4\pi}{6} = \frac{2\pi}{3},$$

and $OP$ and $OQ$ are both radii of the unit circle, so triangle $POQ$ is isosceles with two
sides of length $1$ and included angle $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. The chord is therefore the base of
that triangle:

$$PQ = 2(1)\sin\left( \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)
= 2\sin\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) = 2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}.$$ (M1)(A1)

Both routes give $\sqrt{3}$, as required. (AG)

(d) The sector $POQ$ has radius $r = 1$ and angle $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so its area is

$$A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta
= \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)
= \frac{\pi}{3}.$$ (M1)(A1)(A1)

The area of the shaded sector is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ square units. Note that the chord length found
in part (c) is not needed here; the area of a sector depends only on the radius and the angle
between the radii, whereas the chord depends on the angle as well but is not required once the
angle is known.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for $P\left( -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right)$, (A1) for $Q\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right)$. Accept the coordinates in either order provided the labels match. An answer of $P\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right)$ scores (A0) for the first mark: the cosine of an angle in the second quadrant is negative. (b) (M1) for forming the quotient of the coordinates, (A1) for $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ or the equivalent $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Accept $-0.577$ only if given to at least three significant figures. A positive value scores (M1)(A0). (c) (M1) for a valid method, either the horizontal difference of the two $x$-coordinates or the isosceles-triangle relation with the correct included angle, (A1) for reaching $\sqrt{3}$, (M1)(A1) for the second valid method or (AG) where the student completes the algebra to the stated result. Do not award the method mark for merely asserting that the chord is $\sqrt{3}$. (d) (M1) for using $A = \frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta$ with $r = 1$, (A1) for the correct angle $\frac{2\pi}{3}$, (A1) for $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Award follow-through from an incorrect angle in (c) only if the angle used is consistent with the coordinates given in (a).

subtopic: 3.13 The closest point of a line segment is an endpoint when the foot of the perpendicular falls outside it
syllabus_ref: SL 3.13 The definition of the scalar product of two vectors; SL 3.12 Concept of a vector, position vectors and displacement vectors; 3.1 The distance between two points in three dimensions
title: 3.13 The closest point of a line segment is an endpoint when the foot of the perpendicular falls outside it
q_html:
The points $A$, $B$ and $P$ have position vectors

$$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}, \qquad \mathbf{p} = 9\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}.$$

The figure shows the plane containing all three points, with the line through $A$ and $B$ drawn horizontally and the segment $AB$ marked on it.

(a) Show that the point of the line through $A$ and $B$ that is closest to $P$ does not lie on the segment $AB$.

(b) Find the shortest distance from $P$ to the segment $AB$.

(c) A candidate obtains $\sqrt{73/3} \approx 4.93$. State what this value is the distance from $P$ to, and explain why it is not the answer to part (b).

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Show that the point of the line through $A$ and $B$ that is closest to $P$ does not lie on the segment $AB$.

    (Show that)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Find the shortest distance from $P$ to the segment $AB$.

    (Find)
  3. [2 marks](c)

    State what the value $\sqrt{73/3} \approx 4.93$ is the distance from $P$ to, and explain why it is smaller than the answer to part (b) yet is not a possible answer to it.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) $\overrightarrow{AB} = 2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP} = 7\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 14 + 12 + 6 = 32$ and $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2} = 4 + 16 + 4 = 24$ (M1). The closest point of the line is $\mathbf{a} + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}$ with $t = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}}{|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2}} = \dfrac{32}{24} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, and since $\tfrac{4}{3} > 1$ that point lies beyond $B$ and therefore outside the segment $AB$ (A1).

(b) Because the closest point of the *line* is outside the segment, the closest point of the segment is its nearest endpoint, namely $B$ (M1), and the distance is $|\overrightarrow{BP}| = |5\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}| = \sqrt{25 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3} \approx 5.20$ (A1).

(c) $\sqrt{73/3}$ is the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the infinite line through $A$ and $B$: $|\overrightarrow{AP}|^{2} = 49 + 9 + 9 = 67$, and $67 - \dfrac{32^{2}}{24} = 67 - \dfrac{128}{3} = \dfrac{73}{3}$ (M1). It is not the answer to (b) because the foot of that perpendicular is not a point of the segment. A segment is a bounded set, and the closest point of a bounded set need not be where the perpendicular falls: it can be, and here is, an endpoint. The perpendicular distance is smaller because it is measured to a point the segment does not contain, so it is a lower bound that the segment cannot attain (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for the two ingredients of the projection, $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 32$ and $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2} = 24$, however they are obtained; (A1) for $t = \tfrac{4}{3}$ together with the observation that the point corresponding to $t > 1$ lies beyond $B$. The comparison with $1$ is the mark: a candidate who computes $t = \tfrac{4}{3}$ and says nothing about what it means has done the arithmetic and missed the part.

(b) (M1) for recognising that the endpoint is now the closest point; (A1) for $\sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}$. Accept $5.20$.

(c) (M1) for identifying the value as the distance to the line and reproducing the calculation that produces it; (A1) for the point that the segment is bounded so the minimum over the segment is attained at an endpoint. Do not credit 'it is wrong because the foot is outside' without the consequence, which is that the smaller number is unattainable.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.11 The moment of a region found from its symmetry, without ever knowing the function
syllabus_ref: SL 5.11 Definite integrals, including the analytical approach; SL 5.5 Introduction to integration as anti-differentiation; 2.14 Odd and even functions
title: 5.11 The moment of a region found from its symmetry, without ever knowing the function
q_html:
The figure shows the graph of a continuous function $f$ on the interval $0 \leq x \leq 4$. The graph is symmetrical about the line $x = 2$; that is,

$$f(2 + u) = f(2 - u) \qquad \text{for every } u \text{ with } 0 \leq u \leq 2.$$

The area of the region between the graph and the $x$-axis is $12$.

Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} x\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

(a) Use the substitution $x = 4 - u$ to show that $I = 48 - I$.

(b) Hence find the value of $I$.

(c) A second function $g$ on $0 \leq x \leq 4$ is symmetrical about the line $x = 3$ and also encloses an area of $12$. Explain why the argument used in part (a) gives no information about $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} x\,g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Using the substitution $x = 4 - u$, show that $I = 48 - I$.

    (Show that)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Hence find the exact value of the definite integral $I$ defined above.

    (Hence)
  3. [2 marks](c)

    Explain why the same argument gives no information about the corresponding integral for a function symmetrical about the line $x = 3$ on the same interval.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) With $x = 4 - u$ we have $\mathrm{d}x = -\mathrm{d}u$ and the limits swap, so $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} (4 - u)\,f(4 - u)\,\mathrm{d}u$ (M1). By the symmetry, $f(4 - u) = f(2 + (2 - u)) = f(2 - (2 - u)) = f(u)$, so

$$I = \int_{0}^{4} (4 - u)\,f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u = 4\int_{0}^{4} f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u - \int_{0}^{4} u\,f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u = 4 \times 12 - I = 48 - I \quad (A1).$$

(b) $2I = 48$, so $I = 24$ (M1) (A1). This is $2 \times 12$: the integral of $x\,f(x)$ over the region is the abscissa of the axis of symmetry multiplied by the area, which is what a centroid argument would also give, since the centroid of a region with a vertical axis of symmetry lies on that axis.

(c) The substitution $x = 4 - u$ reflects the interval $[0,\,4]$ about the line $x = 2$, and that reflection maps the interval onto itself (M1). Reflecting $[0,\,4]$ about the line $x = 3$ instead sends it to $[2,\,6]$, which is not the interval the integral runs over, so the substituted integral cannot be renamed as the original one and the symmetry of $g$ produces no relation between the integral and itself. A symmetry is only useful here if it is a symmetry of the interval as well as of the function (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for carrying out the substitution correctly, including the interchange of limits; (A1) for using $f(4 - u) = f(u)$ and separating the integral into $4\int f - I$. The separation is the mark: a candidate who writes the substituted integral and stops has not yet produced an equation in $I$.

(b) (M1) for $2I = 48$; (A1) for $I = 24$.

(c) (M1) for noticing that the reflection is of the interval and not only of the function; (A1) for the conclusion. Credit a candidate who makes the point by remarking that $x = 6 - u$ would be the substitution matching an axis at $x = 3$ and that it turns $[0,\,4]$ into $[2,\,6]$. Watch for the converse error, which is to claim the method still works; it does not, and a candidate who thinks it does has not noticed that the limits moved.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.17 The area between a sideways parabola and a chord, integrated with respect to y
syllabus_ref: AHL 5.17 Area of the region enclosed by a curve and the y-axis; SL 5.11 Definite integrals, including the analytical approach; SL 2.2 Concept of a function, domain, range and graph
title: 5.17 The area between a sideways parabola and a chord, integrated with respect to y
a_html:
(a) A point on both curves satisfies $y^{2} = 3 - 2y$, so $y^{2} + 2y - 3 = 0$ (M1). Factorising, $(y + 3)(y - 1) = 0$, so $y = -3$ or $y = 1$. Substituting back gives $x = y^{2} = 9$ when $y = -3$ and $x = 1$ when $y = 1$, so the two points are $(9,\,-3)$ and $(1,\,1)$ (A1).

(b) For every $y$ between $-3$ and $1$ the line lies to the right of the curve, because $3 - 2y - y^{2} = -(y + 3)(y - 1)$ is positive on that interval (M1). A horizontal strip at height $y$ therefore has width $(3 - 2y) - y^{2}$ and height $dy$, and the area of $R$ is the sum of those strips:

$$A = \int_{-3}^{1}\left(3 - 2y - y^{2}\right)dy = \left[3y - y^{2} - \tfrac{1}{3}y^{3}\right]_{-3}^{1} \;(M1).$$

At the upper limit, $3 - 1 - \tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{5}{3}$. At the lower limit, $-9 - 9 + 9 = -9$. Subtracting,

$$A = \tfrac{5}{3} - (-9) = \tfrac{32}{3} \approx 10.67 \;(A1).$$

So the enclosed area is $\tfrac{32}{3}$ square units, which is a little over ten and a half. Notice that the antiderivative is a cubic whose value at the lower limit is negative: the region straddles the $x$-axis, and the integral handles that without any adjustment because the strips are measured horizontally and each one keeps its own sign of $x$, not of $y$.

(c) Integrating with respect to $x$ means slicing the region vertically, and the top of a vertical slice is not the same curve all the way across (M1). To the left of the point where the two boundaries cross, the slice runs from the lower branch of the parabola to the upper branch, so its height is $2\sqrt{x}$; to the right of that point the upper branch of the parabola lies above the line, so the height becomes $\dfrac{3 - x}{2} + \sqrt{x}$ and the two curves have exchanged roles as the upper boundary. The change happens where $y^{2} = 3 - 2y$ has its positive root, that is at $y = 1$, and there $x = 1$; this is the dashed vertical line drawn in the figure, and it is the only vertical slice for which the two descriptions agree, since it runs from $y = -1$ to $y = 1$ (A1). A candidate working in $x$ must therefore write

$$A = \int_{0}^{1} 2\sqrt{x}\,dx + \int_{1}^{9}\left(\frac{3 - x}{2} + \sqrt{x}\right)dx = \tfrac{4}{3} + \tfrac{28}{3} = \tfrac{32}{3},$$

which is the same area at roughly twice the work: two integrals, two antiderivatives, and a split point that has to be found before either integral can be set up. Investing in the coordinate that matches the shape of the region is what removes the split.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for forming $y^{2} = 3 - 2y$ or the equivalent and reducing it to $y^{2} + 2y - 3 = 0$; (A1) for both points $(9,\,-3)$ and $(1,\,1)$ with the substitution shown. Accept a candidate who solves for $x$ first, provided both coordinates of both points are stated. A candidate who gives the roots $y = -3$ and $y = 1$ but never forms the coordinates scores the first mark only.

(b) (M1) for setting up the integral with the line minus the curve over $y$ from $-3$ to $1$, with the sign of $3 - 2y - y^{2}$ justified or evidently checked; (M1) for the correct antiderivative $3y - y^{2} - \tfrac{1}{3}y^{3}$; (A1) for $\tfrac{32}{3}$ or $10.7$ to three significant figures. Three fields; credit two, and the displayed integral already earns the first. Do not accept an area given as negative, and do not accept $\tfrac{27}{3}$ or $9$ from substituting the limits in the wrong order.

(c) (M1) for the observation that the upper boundary changes from the upper branch of the parabola to the straight line; (A1) for $x = 1$, correctly located as the point where the interval of $y$ is the largest. Award the second mark for $x = 1$ alone, but only if the change of upper boundary has been stated. A candidate who says the region must be split 'because it is curved' has not identified what changes and scores nothing.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.11 Two unbounded regions, one of which encloses a finite area, decided by the exponent
syllabus_ref: SL 5.11 Definite integrals, including the analytical approach; SL 5.10 Indefinite integral of x to the power n (n rational); AHL 5.13 The evaluation of limits
title: 5.11 Two unbounded regions, one of which encloses a finite area, decided by the exponent
a_html:
(a) Writing $x^{-2}$ and integrating, $$\int_{1}^{t} x^{-2}\,dx = \left[-x^{-1}\right]_{1}^{t} = -\frac{1}{t} + 1 = 1 - \frac{1}{t} \;(M1)(A1).$$

As $t$ increases without bound the term $\dfrac{1}{t}$ tends to $0$, so the partial area increases towards the value $1$. The shaded region is unbounded in extent but encloses exactly one square unit: to reach an area of $0.99$ the region must be extended to $t = 100$, to reach $0.999$ to $t = 1000$, and no finite $t$ ever achieves the full unit (A1). Each doubling of the extent adds less than half of what the previous doubling added, and the total therefore settles.

(b) Writing $x^{-1/2}$ and integrating, $$\int_{1}^{t} x^{-1/2}\,dx = \left[2x^{1/2}\right]_{1}^{t} = 2\sqrt{t} - 2 \;(M1)(A1).$$

Here the partial area increases without limit as $t$ increases, because $2\sqrt{t} - 2$ does: extending the region to $t = 100$ gives an area of $18$, to $t = 10\,000$ an area of $198$, and to pass an area of $200$ the region must be taken out to $t = 10\,201$. There is no number that the area approaches from below, so the shaded region in the right-hand panel has no finite area (A1). The distinction between the two panels is therefore not that one region is longer than the other -- both are equally long -- but that one of them has a measurable area and the other does not.

(c) Both integrands are powers, $x^{-p}$, and both antiderivatives are powers, $x^{1-p}$ divided by $1-p$ (M1). What decides the outcome is the sign of the exponent $1 - p$ in the antiderivative. When $p > 1$ that exponent is negative, so the antiderivative is a negative power of $t$ and it tends to $0$ as $t$ grows; the area then settles at the finite value $\dfrac{1}{p-1}$, which for $p = 2$ is $1$, and for $p = 1.5$ would be $2$. When $p \leq 1$ the exponent is positive or zero, so the antiderivative grows with $t$ and there is no finite limit; for $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ it grows like $\sqrt{t}$ (A1). The property that decides, then, is how fast the integrand decays: a finite tail requires the integrand to fall away faster than $\dfrac{1}{x}$, and the two panels differ only in that their exponents are $2$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$, one above the threshold and one below it.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for integrating $x^{-2}$ rather than $x^{2}$, or for any correct antiderivative of $x^{-2}$; (A1) for the evaluation $1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$ with both limits used correctly; (A1) for the limit $1$, with the behaviour of $\dfrac{1}{t}$ stated. Three fields; credit two, and a candidate who writes down $1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$ and then states the area as $1$ without a word about the limit earns two of the three.

(b) (M1) for integrating $x^{-1/2}$; (A1) for $2\sqrt{t} - 2$; (A1) for the conclusion that the area is unbounded, with the reason that the expression grows without limit rather than settling. The conclusion is the mark that matters: an answer of '$\infty$' with no statement about the growth is worth the first two fields only.

(c) (M1) for comparing the antiderivatives of $x^{-p}$ and identifying the sign of $1 - p$ as the deciding feature; (A1) for expressing the criterion as $p > 1$, equivalently that the integrand must decay faster than $\dfrac{1}{x}$, and for observing that the two panels sit on opposite sides of that threshold. Do not accept a criterion stated in terms of the curves 'getting closer to the axis', since both of them do.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.10 Indefinite integral of x^n, sin x, cos x, 1/x, e^x
syllabus_ref: SL 5.10 (indefinite integral of x^n, n in Q, sin x, cos x, 1/x, e^x)
title: The indefinite integral that needs a logarithm and a cosine
q_html:
Find the indefinite integral $\int\left(3x^{2}-\frac{2}{x}+6\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\sin x\right)\mathrm{d}x$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Find the general antiderivative, including the constant of integration.

    (Find)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the derivative of your answer and confirm that it returns the original integrand.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Find the value of the antiderivative at $x=1$, taking the constant of integration to be zero.

    (Find)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Find the constant of integration if the antiderivative takes the value $7$ when $x=1$.

    (Find)
a_html:
(a) Integrate the expression term by term, because the integral of a sum is the sum of the separate integrals. The power term gives $\int 3x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=x^{3}$ (M1). The reciprocal term gives $\int -\frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=-2\ln|x|$ (A1), where the absolute value is required so the logarithm is defined. The exponential term gives $\int 6\mathrm{e}^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and the sine term gives $\int -4\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x=4\cos x$ (A1), since the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. No term affects another, so the four rules can be applied in any order, and adding the constant of integration gives the general antiderivative $F(x)=x^{3}-2\ln|x|+6\mathrm{e}^{x}+4\cos x+C$ (A1)(AG). Each standard rule is applied to one term independently, so the final result is the sum of four antiderivatives.

(b) Differentiate the answer to check it. We have $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^{3})=3x^{2}$ (M1), $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(-2\ln|x|)=-\frac{2}{x}$ (A1), $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(6\mathrm{e}^{x})=6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(4\cos x)=-4\sin x$ (A1). Adding these derivatives gives exactly the original integrand $3x^{2}-\frac{2}{x}+6\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\sin x$ (A1)(AG). This reverse check is valuable, because it catches any single sign slip instantly, and the derivative undoes the integration term by term, which is why the check confirms the antiderivative is correct.

(c) With $C=0$ and $x=1$, substitute to obtain $F(1)=1-2\ln 1+6\mathrm{e}^{1}+4\cos 1$ (M1). Because $\ln 1=0$, this simplifies to $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1$, which evaluates to $19.470900$ to six decimal places (A1). The logarithm contributes nothing at $x=1$, so the value is dominated by the exponential and the cosine term, and those two terms together account for almost the whole magnitude of the result.

(d) The condition $F(1)=7$ gives $19.470900+C=7$ (M1), so the constant is $C=7-19.470900=-12.470900$ (A1)(AG). This constant shifts the whole antiderivative downwards so that its graph passes through the point $(1,7)$. Choosing the constant in this way fixes a unique member of the family of antiderivatives, and the negative sign is required because the value without the constant already exceeds $7$, which is why $C$ must be negative.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for integrating the power term to $x^{3}$ and (A1) for $-2\ln|x|$; the absolute value bars are required for full credit. Award (A1) for $6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and (A1) for $4\cos x$, noting the sign change that comes from integrating $-4\sin x$. The final (A1)(AG) is for the combined antiderivative $x^{3}-2\ln|x|+6\mathrm{e}^{x}+4\cos x+C$. A candidate who writes $\ln x$ without bars earns the term mark only, not full credit.

(b) Award (M1) for the derivative of the power term and (A1) for $-2/x$ from the logarithm. Award (A1) for $6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and (A1) for $-4\sin x$, with (A1)(AG) for recovery of the original integrand. The confirmation must show the derivative equals the given integrand term by term.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=1$ with $C=0$ and (A1) for the numerical value $19.470900$ to six decimal places. Accept $19.47$ if rounded, but the exact form $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1$ is preferred in the markscheme.

(d) Award (M1) for forming $19.470900+C=7$ and (A1)(AG) for $C=-12.470900$. Follow through from an incorrect part (c) value is allowed provided the subtraction is consistent with it. A candidate who misses the negative sign earns no credit for the final answer.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 2.15 The solution set of 2^x >= x^2, where the two exact intersections x = 2 and x = 4 are the only ones a natural window shows and the third intersection is at a negative value of x that the window excludes
syllabus_ref: AHL 2.15 (solutions of g(x) >= f(x), both graphically and analytically) with SL 2.9 (exponential functions and their graphs) and SL 2.10 (solving equations graphically and analytically)
title: 2.15 The solution set of 2^x >= x^2, where the two exact intersections x = 2 and x = 4 are the only ones a natural window shows and the third intersection is at a negative value of x that the window excludes
a_html:
(a) The diagram is drawn on $0 \le x \le 5$ and shows the two curves meeting at $(2,\,4)$ and $(4,\,16)$, since $2^{2} = 4 = 2^{2}$ and $2^{4} = 16 = 4^{2}$ (A1). Reading the sign of the difference between the curves off the diagram, the solid exponential curve lies above the dashed parabola from $x = 0$ up to $x = 2$, the parabola lies above the exponential curve between the two crossings, and the exponential curve is again above from $x = 4$ onwards (M1). For example at $x = 1$ the values are $2$ and $1$, at $x = 3$ they are $8$ and $9$, and at $x = 5$ they are $32$ and $25$ (A1). So on this interval the inequality holds for
$$0 \le x \le 2 \quad\text{and}\quad 4 \le x \le 5,$$
and the diagram shows exactly two intersections.
(b) The diagram begins at $x = 0$, so it cannot say anything about the curve for $x < 0$. On the negative side the two curves behave in opposite ways: $y = 2^{x}$ falls towards zero as $x$ becomes more negative, while $y = x^{2}$ grows without bound (M1). Immediately to the left of the origin the exponential curve is still the larger of the two, because $2^{0} = 1 > 0 = 0^{2}$, but far to the left the parabola is much the larger, because $2^{-10} = 0.00098$ against $100$ (A1). A curve that starts above the other and finishes below it must cross it at least once in between, so there is at least one intersection with a negative $x$-coordinate, and the diagram is drawn on an interval that excludes it (A1). The complete solution set therefore cannot be read off the diagram.
(c) Define $f(x) = 2^{x} - x^{2}$ for $x < 0$. At $x = -1$,
$$f(-1) = 2^{-1} - 1 = -0.5 < 0,$$
while at $x = -0.5$,
$$f(-0.5) = 2^{-0.5} - 0.25 = 0.70711 - 0.25 = +0.45711 > 0,$$
so a root lies between $-1$ and $-0.5$ (M1). Repeated bisection, or a numerical solver, narrows that bracket to
$$x = -0.7666646960\ldots \qquad\text{so}\qquad x \approx -0.7667 \;(A1),$$
correct to four decimal places. To see that there is only one negative root, differentiate:
$$f'(x) = 2^{x}\ln 2 - 2x .$$
For $x < 0$ the first term is positive because $2^{x} > 0$ and $\ln 2 > 0$, and the second term $-2x$ is positive as well. Hence $f'(x) > 0$ for every $x < 0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing on the whole negative half-line and can change sign there exactly once (A1). Since $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to -\infty$ while $f(0) = 1 > 0$, that one sign change does occur, and the root is unique.
(d) Combining the three intervals, $2^{x} \ge x^{2}$ exactly when
$$-0.7667 \le x \le 2 \quad\text{or}\quad x \ge 4 \;(A1).$$
It remains to show that there is no intersection beyond $x = 4$. Consider the ratio $g(x) = \dfrac{2^{x}}{x^{2}}$ for $x \ge 5$. Differentiating,
$$g'(x) = \frac{2^{x}\,(x\ln 2 - 2)}{x^{3}},$$
and for $x \ge 5$ the factor $x\ln 2 - 2$ is at least $5(0.69315) - 2 = 1.4657 > 0$, so $g$ is strictly increasing on $x \ge 5$ (M1). At $x = 5$ the ratio is $32/25 = 1.28 > 1$, so $g(x) > 1$ for every $x \ge 5$, which means $2^{x} > x^{2}$ throughout (A1). The curves therefore do not meet again, and the largest intersection is the one at $x = 4$ (A1). The complete solution set is
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -0.7667 \le x \le 2\} \cup \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\},$$
with $-0.7667$ given to four decimal places.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for the two intersection points $(2,\,4)$ and $(4,\,16)$ read from the diagram, (M1) for comparing the two curves between and outside the crossings, (A1) for the answer $0 \le x \le 2$ together with $4 \le x \le 5$. A candidate who states only the two points without giving the intervals scores (A1) and nothing more, because the question asks for the set of values of $x$ and not for the intersections. Accept $4 \le x$ written without the upper limit of $5$ provided the candidate has made clear that the diagram only extends to $x = 5$.
(b) (M1) for the observation that the diagram begins at $x = 0$ and therefore cannot rule out anything to the left of the $y$-axis, (A1) for the correct behaviour of the two curves as $x \to -\infty$, namely $2^{x} \to 0$ and $x^{2} \to +\infty$, (A1) for the intermediate value argument that the two must therefore cross on the negative side. An answer that merely says 'the graph is not wide enough' without naming the behaviour of either curve scores (M1) only. Do not accept 'the diagram is inaccurate' or 'the scale is too small' as a substitute: the diagram is accurate on the interval it covers, and the defect is the interval, not the drawing.
(c) (M1) for a correct bracket containing the negative root, for example by evaluating $f$ at $-1$ and at $-0.5$ and observing the sign change, (A1) for $-0.7667$ to four decimal places. Accept $-0.7666$ or $-0.76666$ as intermediate working but the final answer must be rounded to four decimal places; condone $-0.7667$ obtained from any valid numerical method, including a graph plotter or a Newton iteration. (A1) for the uniqueness argument, which requires the derivative and the observation that both of its terms are positive for $x < 0$. A candidate who asserts uniqueness because 'the graphs cross only once' has used the conclusion it is meant to prove and scores no mark for it.
(d) (A1) for the correct solution set, with both the closed interval and the half-line, (M1) for a valid argument that no intersection lies beyond $x = 4$, (A1) for completing that argument, and (A1) for the statement of the set in set notation. The ratio argument is not the only acceptable one: a candidate may instead show that $2^{x} > x^{2}$ at $x = 5$ and that the difference is increasing thereafter, or may argue from the exponential eventually dominating any polynomial. Any of these earns the two marks. Follow-through: a candidate whose negative root from (c) is wrong but whose set is written consistently with it keeps the marks in (d). Forfeits: answering $0 \le x \le 2$ or $x \ge 4$, which discards the negative interval; answering $-0.7667 \le x \le 2$ only, which discards the half-line; and writing $x \ge 4$ as $4 < x$, which loses the endpoint.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.3 Wave phenomena
syllabus_ref: C.3 Wave phenomena (AHL): single-slit diffraction, theta = lambda/b, single-slit pattern modulating the double-slit pattern, multiple-slit interference
title: A fringe that the envelope removes
q_html:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda=589\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls normally on a double slit. The centres of the two slits are separated by $d=0.400\ \mathrm{mm}$ and each slit has width $b=0.100\ \mathrm{mm}$. The interference pattern is observed on a screen at a distance $D=2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ from the slits. The angles involved are small enough that $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta\approx\theta$ in radians, where convenient.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the separation of adjacent bright fringes in the interference pattern.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the distance from the centre of the pattern to the first minimum of the single-slit diffraction envelope.

    (Calculate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Show that the fourth-order bright fringe is missing from the pattern, and state which other orders would be missing if the screen were large enough to show them.

    (Show that)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine the number of bright fringes that are visible within the central maximum of the envelope.

    (Determine)
  5. [2 marks](e)

    The source is replaced by a white light source. Describe one change to the pattern, and explain it.

    (Describe)
a_html:
(a) $s=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}=\dfrac{589\times 10^{-9}\times 2.00}{0.400\times 10^{-3}}$ (M1) $=2.94\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}=2.94\ \mathrm{mm}$. (A1)

So adjacent bright fringes are $2.94\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. (A1)

(b) The first minimum of the single-slit envelope is at the smallest angle satisfying $b\sin\theta=\lambda$: (M1)

$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}=\dfrac{589\times 10^{-9}}{0.100\times 10^{-3}}=5.89\times 10^{-3}$ (A1)

The distance from the centre is $y=D\tan\theta\approx 2.00\times 5.89\times 10^{-3}=1.18\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}=11.8\ \mathrm{mm}$. (A1)

(c) A double-slit maximum of order $n$ occurs where $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$; the first single-slit minimum occurs where $b\sin\theta=\lambda$. (M1)

These coincide when $\dfrac{n\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, that is when $n=\dfrac{d}{b}$. (M1)

Here $\dfrac{d}{b}=\dfrac{0.400}{0.100}=4.0$ (A1), so the third-order condition places the minimum at $\theta$ with $\sin\theta=\dfrac{4\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{4\times 589\times 10^{-9}}{0.400\times 10^{-3}}=5.89\times 10^{-3}$, exactly the angle found in part (b). The fourth-order maximum therefore falls on a minimum of the envelope and is not visible. (A1)

More generally the missing orders are multiples of $d/b$, so orders $4,\ 8,\ 12,\ \ldots$ are missing. (A1) Order 8 would require $\sin\theta=\dfrac{8\lambda}{d}=1.18\times 10^{-2}$, which is still less than $1$, so order 8 is geometrically accessible and would also be missing. Orders beyond the first few visible ones fall outside the envelope's central region anyway.

(d) Within the central maximum of the envelope, $\left|\sin\theta\right|<\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so the allowed orders satisfy $\left|n\right|<\dfrac{d}{b}=4$. (M1)

So $n=-3,\,-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2,\,3$ are present (A1), giving seven bright fringes. (A1) Orders $n=\pm 4$ coincide exactly with the envelope minima from part (c) and are not visible.

(e) Each order becomes a continuous spectrum with the same angular spread, with red deviated most because $\theta$ increases with $\lambda$; the central maximum remains white since all wavelengths coincide there and it has no order number. (A1)(A1) Higher-order spectra overlap, so beyond the first order the colours are no longer separated cleanly.

Markscheme notes

Parts (a) and (b) are single-formula calculations; accept full marks for any self-consistent use of the small-angle approximation. In (a), the (A1) for the unit conversion is separate and should be awarded for 2.94 mm, 2.9 mm or 2.95 mm, but not for 2.94 without a unit. Part (c): the essential reasoning is the equality of the two conditions, not the arithmetic; a candidate who argues from the ratio $d/b$ alone earns (M1)(M1)(A1) and the final (A1) if the identification of order 4 is complete. Stating that 'all multiples of 4 are missing' without recognising that order 8 is accessible loses the last (A1). Part (d): the mark scheme does not require the exclusion of $n=\pm 4$ to be argued twice, provided the reasoning in (c) is present; a candidate who counts nine fringes has included the two missing orders and can earn at most the first (M1). Part (e): award one mark for a correct change and one for the reason; 'the fringes become coloured' with no reference to wavelength-dependent deviation earns only the first.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.3 Work, energy and power
syllabus_ref: A.3 Work, energy and power (work done by a force, conservation of energy, power as the rate of energy transfer, efficiency)
title: Why the conveyor motor needs twice the power you expect
q_html:
Stimulus

Gravel falls vertically from a stationary hopper onto a horizontal conveyor belt that runs at a constant speed. The gravel arrives with no horizontal velocity and is carried away at the belt's speed. In the steady state the mass of gravel delivered to the belt is $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ each second. Treat the gravel as arriving with no horizontal motion, neglect the mass and any internal friction of the belt mechanism, and consider the horizontal motion only.

The belt moves at a constant speed $v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the gravel is delivered at a constant rate of $12\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that the horizontal force the belt must exert on the gravel is $F=v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$, and calculate the value of $F$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Calculate the rate at which kinetic energy is supplied to the gravel as it is brought up to the belt's speed.

    (Calculate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Show that the power delivered by the belt's motor is twice the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy, identify where the remaining energy goes, and hence calculate the efficiency with which the motor's work becomes kinetic energy of the gravel.

    (Show that)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    The belt speed is increased to $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while the mass flow rate is unchanged. Determine the new motor power and explain why it is not simply double the original power.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) In a time interval $\Delta t$ a mass $\Delta m=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\Delta t$ of gravel is brought from rest to the belt's speed $v$. Its horizontal momentum therefore changes by $\Delta m\,v$, so the required horizontal force is

$$F=\frac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t}=v\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$$ (M1)(AG)

Numerically,

$$F=2.0\times 12=24\ \mathrm{N}$$ (A1)(A1)

(b) Each second a mass of $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ is accelerated from rest to $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the rate at which kinetic energy is supplied is

$$\frac{\Delta E_{k}}{\Delta t}=\tfrac12\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}=\tfrac12(12)(2.0)^{2}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$=24\ \mathrm{W}$$ (A1)(A1)

(c) The belt moves at constant speed, so the motor's power equals the force it exerts multiplied by the belt's speed:

$$P=Fv=(24)(2.0)=48\ \mathrm{W}$$ (M1)(A1)

The ratio is

$$\frac{P}{\Delta E_{k}/\Delta t}=\frac{48}{24}=2$$ (A1)

so the motor supplies twice the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy. The remaining $24\ \mathrm{W}$ is dissipated as heat where the gravel slides against the belt while it is being accelerated: the friction force acts over the belt's displacement, which is larger than the gravel's displacement, and the difference appears as thermal energy at the sliding contact. (A1) The efficiency is therefore

$$\eta=\frac{24}{48}=0.50=50\%.$$ (A1)

(d) Since $F=v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$, doubling $v$ doubles the force to $48\ \mathrm{N}$. The power is $P=Fv$, and both the force and the belt speed have doubled, so

$$P=48\times 4.0=192\ \mathrm{W},$$ (M1)(A1)

which is four times the original $48\ \mathrm{W}$. Equivalently $P=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}\propto v^{2}$, because the belt must accelerate twice as much momentum each second and must do so through twice the distance per second. The mass flow rate has not changed, so the factor of four comes entirely from the doubling of both quantities in $P=Fv$, not from any change in the amount of gravel handled. (A1)

The efficiency is unchanged at $50\%$ when the speed doubles, and it is in fact fixed at $50\%$ for any belt speed and any mass flow rate, because the kinetic-energy rate and the motor power are both proportional to $\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}$ and their ratio is therefore constant. It would rise above $50\%$ only if the gravel arrived already moving with the belt, so that less sliding were needed to bring it up to speed; the loss is a property of picking the mass up from rest, not of how fast the belt runs.

Markscheme notes

(a) The force must come from the rate of change of momentum, not from an energy argument. A candidate who writes $F=\tfrac12\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v=12\ \mathrm{N}$ has used the kinetic-energy rate and has made the very error the question is designed to expose; award no method mark. Accept $F=v\Delta m/\Delta t$ with $\Delta m/\Delta t=12\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.

(b) Accept $24\ \mathrm{W}$, $24\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ or $24\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s^{-1}}$. A candidate who uses $mv^{2}$ instead of $\tfrac12 mv^{2}$ obtains $48\ \mathrm{W}$ and will then report a 100% efficiency; that contradiction should prompt a re-check but earns nothing here.

(c) The essential reasoning is that the belt's force acts through the belt's displacement, not the gravel's. Simply stating 'half the energy is lost as heat' without identifying the sliding contact earns at most one mark. Award the efficiency mark for $0.50$ or $50\%$; a ratio written the other way round ($2$) with a clear statement is acceptable. Follow-through: if (a) or (b) is wrong but internally consistent, the ratio and efficiency marks remain available.

(d) The explanation must mention both that $F\propto v$ and that the belt speed is $v$, so that $P\propto v^{2}$. A candidate who says only 'because power depends on $v$ squared' earns the value mark but not the explanation mark. Accept $192\ \mathrm{W}$ and accept $190\ \mathrm{W}$.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.1 Simple harmonic motion and C.2 Wave model
syllabus_ref: C.1 Simple harmonic motion (defining equation a = -omega^2 x, period of a mass-spring oscillator, energy in SHM) and C.2 Wave model (travelling waves, the wave equation v = f lambda, phase difference and the propagation delay)
title: The coupling spring that the period ignores
q_html:
Two identical gliders, each of mass $m=0.020\ \mathrm{kg}$, rest on a frictionless horizontal air track. Each glider is held to a fixed post by a spring of stiffness $k=2.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and the two gliders are joined to each other by a coupling spring of stiffness $k_{c}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ (see the figure). The left glider carries a light piston that closes the near end of a long straight tube; the far end of the tube is lined with an absorber, so a travelling wave rather than a standing wave is set up, and when the glider moves along the track the piston drives a longitudinal compression wave along the tube. The speed of sound in the air in the tube is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Friction, the mass of the springs and the mass of the piston are all negligible.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    The two gliders are displaced by equal amounts in the same direction and released from rest. Show that the coupling spring is neither stretched nor compressed at any instant, deduce that the period of this motion is $T_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, and calculate the value of $T_{s}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    The gliders are now displaced by equal amounts in opposite directions and released from rest. Determine the period $T_{a}$ of this motion, showing how the coupling spring now contributes, and calculate the ratio $T_{s}/T_{a}$.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    In the antisymmetric motion the piston drives the wave in the tube at the frequency $f=1/T_{a}$. Calculate the frequency, the wavelength of the wave in the tube, and the phase difference between two points on the tube axis that are $0.534\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. State which of the two points is ahead in phase.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Show that $T_{s}/T_{a}=\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$, and hence determine the value of this ratio in the limits $k_{c}\to0$ and $k_{c}\to\infty$. Explain what each limit means physically for the motion of the two gliders.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) In this motion the two gliders have equal displacements in the same direction at every instant, so $x_{1}=x_{2}$ and their separation never changes; the coupling spring therefore remains at its natural length and exerts no force on either glider. (M1) Each glider is then acted on only by its own wall spring, so Newton's second law for either glider gives

$$m\ddot{x}=-kx\quad\Rightarrow\quad\ddot{x}=-\frac{k}{m}x.$$ (A1)

Comparing with the defining equation of simple harmonic motion, $a=-\omega^{2}x$, shows that $\omega_{s}=\sqrt{k/m}$ and hence

$$T_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{2.0\times10^{4}}}=2\pi\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-6}}$$ (A1)

$$T_{s}=6.28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}=6.28\ \mathrm{ms}.$$ (A1)

The coupling stiffness $k_{c}$ does not appear: in this mode the coupling spring is inert.

(b) In the antisymmetric motion $x_{1}=-x_{2}$, so the separation of the gliders changes by $2x_{1}$ and the coupling spring is stretched or compressed by twice the displacement of either glider. (M1) Its force on a glider is therefore $-k_{c}(2x_{1})$, and combining this with the wall spring gives

$$m\ddot{x}_{1}=-kx_{1}-2k_{c}x_{1}=-(k+2k_{c})x_{1},$$ (A1)

so $\omega_{a}=\sqrt{(k+2k_{c})/m}$ and

$$T_{a}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k+2k_{c}}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{2.0\times10^{4}+2(3.0\times10^{4})}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{8.0\times10^{4}}}=2\pi\sqrt{2.5\times10^{-7}}$$

$$T_{a}=3.14\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}=3.14\ \mathrm{ms}.$$ (A1)

The ratio of the two periods is

$$\frac{T_{s}}{T_{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{k+2k_{c}}{k}}=\sqrt{\frac{8.0\times10^{4}}{2.0\times10^{4}}}=2.00.$$ (A1)

The antisymmetric mode is therefore the faster of the two.

(c) The piston is driven by the glider that moves in the antisymmetric mode, so the frequency of the wave in the tube is fixed by $T_{a}$:

$$f=\frac{1}{T_{a}}=\frac{1}{3.1416\times10^{-3}}=318\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (M1)(A1)

Using the wave equation $v=f\lambda$,

$$\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{340}{318.3}=1.07\ \mathrm{m}.$$ (A1)

The phase difference between two points separated by $\Delta x=0.534\ \mathrm{m}$ is

$$\Delta\varphi=\frac{2\pi\,\Delta x}{\lambda}=\frac{2\pi(0.534)}{1.068}=3.14\ \mathrm{rad}=\pi.$$ (A1)

The two points are in antiphase. The point nearer the piston is ahead in phase: the disturbance reaches it first, and the farther point lags by the propagation delay $\Delta x/v=1.57\ \mathrm{ms}$, which is exactly half a period.

(d) Dividing the two periods,

$$\frac{T_{s}}{T_{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{k+2k_{c}}{k}}=\sqrt{1+\frac{2k_{c}}{k}}.$$ (M1)

As $k_{c}\to0$ the ratio tends to $1$, so $T_{a}\to T_{s}$. The coupling spring has gone, the two gliders are independent identical oscillators, and every possible motion is a superposition of one single frequency; the distinction between the symmetric and the antisymmetric mode therefore disappears. (A1)

As $k_{c}\to\infty$ the ratio diverges and $T_{a}\to0$. An infinitely stiff coupling spring holds the gliders a fixed distance apart, so they can no longer move in opposite directions and the antisymmetric mode is suppressed. (A1)

For any finite $k_{c}$ the ratio is greater than one, so the antisymmetric mode is always the faster of the two, while the symmetric period is completely independent of $k_{c}$. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The (M1) requires the explicit statement that equal displacements in the same direction leave the coupling spring at its natural length. A candidate who writes $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/(k+k_{c})}$ or $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/(k+2k_{c})}$ has assumed that the coupling spring acts and forfeits the mark; this is the error the question is built to expose. The two (A1)s are for obtaining $\omega_{s}=\sqrt{k/m}$ by comparison with $a=-\omega^{2}x$, and for the numerical period. Accept $6.3\ \mathrm{ms}$, $2\pi\ \mathrm{ms}$ or $6.28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(b) The (M1) is for recognising that the coupling spring's extension is twice the individual displacement; a candidate who uses $k_{c}x_{1}$ instead of $2k_{c}x_{1}$ obtains $\omega_{a}=\sqrt{(k+k_{c})/m}=1.6\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and a ratio of $1.58$, which forfeits the last two marks but should still be followed through in (c) and (d). Accept the ratio as $2$, $2.0$ or $2.00$.

(c) Follow-through from (b) is expected: if the candidate's $T_{a}$ differs, the frequency, the wavelength and the phase difference must be recomputed consistently with it and are then credited. The phase-difference mark requires the substitution $\Delta\varphi=2\pi\Delta x/\lambda$, not a quoted $\pi$; accept $3.1\ \mathrm{rad}$, $180^{\circ}$ or $\pi$. The statement of which point leads carries no separate mark, but a candidate who says the farther point leads has reversed the propagation direction and should be corrected.

(d) The (M1) requires the ratio to be written as $\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$; a candidate who states the two limits without deriving the ratio earns at most one mark. Both limits and both physical explanations are needed. Do not accept 'the ratio becomes zero' for $k_{c}\to0$; it becomes one.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.4 Standing waves and resonance
syllabus_ref: C.4 Standing waves and resonance (boundary conditions, nodes and antinodes, the harmonic series of a string fixed at both ends, resonance conditions)
title: The touch that silences the first seven harmonics
q_html:
A string of length $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ is stretched between two rigid supports with a tension $T=24\ \mathrm{N}$. Its linear mass density is $\mu=0.015\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$, and the tension may be taken as uniform along the whole string. A player lightly touches the string at a point a distance $d$ from the left support, holding that point fixed, and then sets the string vibrating; the touch forces a node at that point but does not otherwise alter the string. Only a standing wave that already has a node at the touched point can be excited.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the speed of transverse waves on the string, and calculate the frequencies of the first three standing-wave modes of the string when it is not touched.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    With the string touched at $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$, show that a standing wave can be excited only if the mode number $n$ satisfies $d=jL/n$ for some integer $j$, deduce that $n$ must be a multiple of $8$, and hence determine the lowest frequency that the touched string can produce.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the frequencies of the next two modes that the touched string can produce, and determine the total number of nodes, including the two fixed ends, in the lowest of these allowed modes. State how many of the untouched harmonics below that lowest allowed frequency are absent.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    The player now touches the string at its midpoint instead. Explain how the set of allowed modes changes, determine the new lowest frequency, and explain why every odd harmonic is now missing.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) For a stretched string the wave speed is given by $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$: (M1)

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{24}{0.015}}=\sqrt{1600}=40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$ (A1)

The standing-wave condition for a string fixed at both ends is $L=n\lambda/2$, so $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$: (M1)

$$f_{n}=\frac{n(40)}{2(0.80)}=25n\ \mathrm{Hz},$$

giving $f_{1}=25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $f_{2}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{3}=75\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (A1)

(b) A standing wave on the string has zero displacement at every node, and the nodes of the $n$th mode lie at distances $x_{j}=jL/n$ from the left support, with $j=0,1,2,\dots,n$. (M1) The touched point is held fixed, so it must be a node, and therefore $d=jL/n$ for some integer $j$. (A1) Substituting $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$n=\frac{jL}{d}=\frac{j(0.80)}{0.30}=\frac{8j}{3}.$$ (A1)

For $n$ to be an integer, $j$ must be a multiple of $3$, so $j=3,6,9,\dots$ and the mode number must be $n=8,16,24,\dots$ — a multiple of $8$. (A1) The lowest allowed mode is therefore $n=8$, with frequency

$$f=\frac{8v}{2L}=\frac{8(40)}{1.60}=200\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (A1)

(c) The next two allowed modes are $n=16$ and $n=24$: (M1)

$$f_{16}=16\times25=400\ \mathrm{Hz},\qquad f_{24}=24\times25=600\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (A1)

In the $n=8$ mode the nodes lie at $x_{j}=j(0.80)/8=0.10j\ \mathrm{m}$ for $j=0,1,\dots,8$, that is at $0.00,0.10,0.20,\dots,0.80\ \mathrm{m}$. Counting the two fixed ends, there are $9$ nodes in all. (A1) The untouched harmonics below $200\ \mathrm{Hz}$ are $25,50,75,100,125,150$ and $175\ \mathrm{Hz}$ — seven of them — and all seven are absent. (A1)

(d) Touching at the midpoint sets $d=L/2$, so $n=jL/d=2j$ and only even mode numbers survive: the allowed frequencies are $50,100,150,\dots\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (M1) The new lowest frequency is therefore the second harmonic,

$$f=\frac{2v}{2L}=\frac{2(40)}{1.60}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (A1)

Every odd harmonic has an antinode at the midpoint, so holding the midpoint fixed suppresses all of them; only the even harmonics, which already have a node there, are unaffected. (A1) In general a touch at a distance $L/p$ from one end selects the harmonics whose numbers are multiples of $p$: the midpoint touch ($p=2$) keeps the even harmonics, and the one-third touch ($p=3$) keeps every third.

Markscheme notes

(a) The first (M1) is for $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$; a candidate who writes $v=T/\mu$ or $v=\sqrt{\mu/T}$ forfeits it. Accept $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the set $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $75\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Follow-through applies: a wrong $v$ propagates consistently through (b) to (d) and those marks remain available.

(b) The essential step is that the touched point is held at zero displacement and is therefore a node. A candidate who instead treats the touch as cutting the string into two independent segments and looks for a frequency common to both will usually reach the same lowest answer here, but that is not the intended reasoning; award the method mark only if the node condition is stated. The (A1) for $n=8j/3$ must come from substituting $d=0.30$ and $L=0.80$. A candidate who assumes that a touch at three-eighths of the length gives the eighth harmonic by analogy with the familiar one-half and one-third cases earns nothing unless the condition is derived.

(c) Accept $400\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $600\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The node count must include the two fixed ends; a candidate who reports $8$ nodes has counted only the interior nodes and loses the mark. Accept the number seven or the explicit list $25$ to $175\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

(d) The (M1) is for $n=2j$, and the new lowest frequency is $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The final mark requires the reason to be stated in terms of the midpoint: odd harmonics have an antinode at the centre, while even harmonics already have a node there. 'Because the string is halved' is not sufficient, since the two halves are not independent in this situation.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.1 Structure of the atom / E.2 Quantum physics
syllabus_ref: E.1 Structure of the atom and E.2 Quantum physics (AHL): energy levels of a hydrogen-like ion E_n = -A/n^2, spectral lines from transitions between levels, ionisation energy and its scaling with Z^2, the photoelectric effect, the photoelectric equation eV_s = hf - phi, stopping voltage and work function
title: The work function that cancels in the difference
q_html:
Stimulus

A discharge tube contains a gas of a hydrogen-like ion, that is, an ion with a single electron and nuclear charge number $Z$. The energy levels of the ion are $E_{n}=-\dfrac{A}{n^{2}}$, where $A$ is a positive constant and $n$ is the principal quantum number. The light emitted by the tube is passed through a monochromator, and two spectral lines are isolated in turn and directed at the same metal photocathode inside an evacuated photocell. The two lines are identified as the $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$ transitions of the ion, and the stopping voltage is measured for each.

| Spectral line | Stopping voltage |
|---|---|
| $n=4\to2$ | $5.7\ \mathrm{V}$ |
| $n=2\to1$ | $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$ |

The work function of the cathode is $\phi$ and the electron charge is $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$.

Assume that the light from each line is monochromatic and that the photocell is ideal, so that the stopping voltage corresponds to the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. The values of the Planck constant and the speed of light are not needed.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain why the stopping voltage measures the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and state the photoelectric equation that relates the stopping voltage, the photon energy and the work function of the cathode.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the photon energies of the $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$ transitions of this ion are $\dfrac{3A}{16}$ and $\dfrac{3A}{4}$ respectively, and state which of the two measured stopping voltages corresponds to each transition.

    (Show that)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Using the two measured stopping voltages, determine the value of $A$ and the work function $\phi$ of the cathode, and explain why neither stopping voltage on its own is sufficient to find $\phi$.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the nuclear charge number $Z$ of the ion and its ionisation energy in electronvolts, and explain how the wavelengths of the two spectral lines would change if the gas were replaced by a hydrogen-like ion of larger $Z$.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) The emitted photoelectrons have a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum $K_{\max}$. (A1) The stopping voltage is the reverse potential difference that just reduces the photocurrent to zero, so it removes the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons: $eV_{s}=K_{\max}$. (A1) Energy conservation for the absorption of a single photon gives $hf=\phi+K_{\max}$, and therefore

$$eV_{s}=hf-\phi$$ (A1)

(b) The energy of the photon emitted in a transition equals the difference between the two levels involved. (M1) For $n=4\to2$,

$$hf_{1}=E_{4}-E_{2}=-\frac{A}{16}-\left(-\frac{A}{4}\right)=\frac{A}{4}-\frac{A}{16}=\frac{3A}{16}$$ (A1)

and for $n=2\to1$,

$$hf_{2}=E_{2}-E_{1}=-\frac{A}{4}-(-A)=A-\frac{A}{4}=\frac{3A}{4}$$ (A1)

Since $\dfrac{3A}{4}>\dfrac{3A}{16}$, the $n=2\to1$ line delivers the more energetic photons and must give the larger stopping voltage, $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$; the $n=4\to2$ line corresponds to $5.7\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1)

(c) Applying $eV_{s}=E_{\text{photon}}-\phi$ to each line, and working in electronvolts so that the stopping voltage in volts is numerically equal to the kinetic energy in electronvolts:

$$e(5.7)=\frac{3A}{16}-\phi \qquad\text{and}\qquad e(36.3)=\frac{3A}{4}-\phi$$ (M1)

Subtracting the first equation from the second eliminates $\phi$:

$$e(36.3-5.7)=\frac{3A}{4}-\frac{3A}{16}=\frac{12A-3A}{16}=\frac{9A}{16}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$A=\frac{16\times 30.6}{9}=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

Substituting this back into the first equation gives the work function:

$$\phi=\frac{3A}{16}-e(5.7)=\frac{3(54.4)}{16}-5.7=10.2-5.7=4.5\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

Each stopping voltage is the difference between a photon energy and the work function. A single reading is therefore one equation in two unknowns, $A$ and $\phi$, and cannot be solved; only the difference of the two readings removes $\phi$ and fixes $A$, after which $\phi$ follows from either line. (A1)

(d) For a hydrogen-like ion the energy-level constant is

$$A=13.6Z^{2}\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (M1)

so

$$Z^{2}=\frac{A}{13.6}=\frac{54.4}{13.6}=4.0\quad\Rightarrow\quad Z=2$$ (A1)

The ion is therefore $\mathrm{He}^{+}$, and its ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the electron from $n=1$ to $E=0$, namely $A=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$. (A1) Because $A\propto Z^{2}$, a larger $Z$ increases every transition energy. Since $E=hc/\lambda$, each wavelength would be shorter, so both lines would shift to shorter wavelengths, giving more energetic photons and larger stopping voltages. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The first (A1) is for the statement that the photoelectrons have a maximum kinetic energy; the second for $eV_{s}=K_{\max}$; the third for the full energy balance $eV_{s}=hf-\phi$. A candidate who writes $eV_{s}=hf+\phi$ has the sign of the work function wrong and loses the final mark. Accept 'stopping potential' for 'stopping voltage'.

(b) The (M1) is for the principle that a photon's energy equals the difference between the two levels involved. The two (A1)s are for the algebraic results $3A/16$ and $3A/4$. The final (A1) requires both the identification and a reason: because $3A/4>3A/16$, the $n=2\to1$ line gives the larger stopping voltage, $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$. A candidate who reverses the correspondence has made a physics error rather than an arithmetic slip and loses that mark.

(c) The first (M1) is for writing the two photoelectric equations, one for each line. The second (M1) is for subtracting them so that $\phi$ cancels; a candidate who substitutes one equation into the other will still reach the answer but should be given the method mark only if the algebra is shown. Accept $A$ between $54$ and $54.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\phi$ between $4.4$ and $4.6\ \mathrm{eV}$. Follow-through applies: a candidate whose $A$ is slightly off but whose $\phi$ is consistent with it keeps the final mark.

(d) The (M1) is for quoting or deriving $A=13.6Z^{2}\ \mathrm{eV}$. Accept $Z=2$ with the identification of the ion as $\mathrm{He}^{+}$. The final mark requires the direction of the shift: shorter wavelengths, larger photon energies. 'The lines would move' with no direction earns nothing.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.4 Fission
syllabus_ref: E.4 Fission (energy released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission, mass defect and binding energy, chain reactions, the role of control rods and moderators, energy production in a nuclear power plant)
title: The enrichment that cannot move the energy per fission
q_html:
A nuclear power reactor produces a steady thermal power $P = 3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ from the neutron-induced fission of uranium-235. A representative fission reaction is
$$^{235}\mathrm{U} + ^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow\ ^{141}\mathrm{Ba} + ^{92}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}.$$
The core is loaded with $1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of uranium enriched to $3.0\%$ uranium-235 by mass, the remainder being uranium-238. The chain reaction is held steady by control rods, and the fast neutrons released are slowed by a moderator before they can induce further fission.

Data (2025 data booklet): atomic mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U} = 235.0439\ \mathrm{u}$; atomic mass of $^{141}\mathrm{Ba} = 140.9144\ \mathrm{u}$; atomic mass of $^{92}\mathrm{Kr} = 91.9262\ \mathrm{u}$; mass of a neutron $= 1.008665\ \mathrm{u}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 1.661\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\,c^{-2}$; $1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.602\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that the energy released in this reaction is about $2.8\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$, and state the same energy in $\mathrm{MeV}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    The reactor operates at a constant thermal power. Determine the number of fission reactions per second and the mass of uranium-235 that undergoes fission each second.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the mass of uranium-235 consumed in one day and the mass converted to energy in one day, and explain why these two masses differ by a factor of about $10^{3}$.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the total energy that the uranium-235 in the core can release and the operating lifetime of the core at $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$. Hence explain what would change, and what would not, if the fuel were enriched to $4.5\%$ instead.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) The energy released is the mass defect of the reaction multiplied by $c^{2}$; the incident neutron is balanced by one of the three emitted neutrons, so
$$\Delta m = m_{\mathrm{U}} - m_{\mathrm{Ba}} - m_{\mathrm{Kr}} - 2m_{\mathrm{n}}$$ (M1)
$$= 235.0439 - 140.9144 - 91.9262 - 2(1.008665) = 0.18597\ \mathrm{u}$$ (A1)
$$E = \Delta m\,c^{2} = 0.18597 \times 931.5 = 173.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
$$E = 173.2 \times 1.602\times10^{-13} = 2.78\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$$ (A1)(AG)

(b) The thermal power equals the energy per fission multiplied by the fission rate, $P = R\,E$, so
$$R = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{3.0\times10^{9}}{2.775\times10^{-11}} = 1.08\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$$ (M1)(A1)
Each fission removes one uranium-235 atom of mass
$$m_{1} = 235.0439 \times 1.661\times10^{-27} = 3.904\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (M1)
so the mass consumed each second is
$$R\,m_{1} = (1.081\times10^{20})(3.904\times10^{-25}) = 4.22\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

(c) In one day the fuel consumed is
$$4.22\times10^{-5} \times 86400 = 3.65\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (A1)
while the mass converted to energy follows from $E = mc^{2}$:
$$m = \frac{P\,t}{c^{2}} = \frac{(3.0\times10^{9})(86400)}{(2.998\times10^{8})^{2}} = 2.88\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (M1)(A1)
The ratio is $3.65/(2.88\times10^{-3}) = 1.3\times10^{3}$, close to $235/0.186$: almost all of the fuel mass is carried by nucleons that survive the reaction, and only the mass defect becomes energy. (A1)

(d) The core holds $0.030 \times 1.0\times10^{5} = 3.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of uranium-235, or $N = 3.0\times10^{3}/(3.904\times10^{-25}) = 7.7\times10^{27}$ nuclei, so
$$E_{\mathrm{tot}} = N\,E = (7.7\times10^{27})(2.775\times10^{-11}) = 2.1\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)
At $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ the operating lifetime is
$$t = \frac{2.1\times10^{17}}{3.0\times10^{9}} = 7.1\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 820\ \mathrm{days}$$ (A1)
Raising the enrichment to $4.5\%$ leaves the energy per fission unchanged, since it is fixed by the mass defect, and leaves the fission rate needed for $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ unchanged; it multiplies the number of fissionable nuclei by $1.5$, so the total energy and the lifetime rise by that factor. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The (M1) requires the mass defect as reactants minus products, with the three emitted neutrons counted. A candidate who omits them from the products, or counts only two, obtains the wrong $\Delta m$ and forfeits the value marks but may still earn the conversion mark by follow-through. Accept $173\ \mathrm{MeV}$ or $2.8\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$; using $1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.60\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$ gives $2.77\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$, also accepted.

(b) The (M1) is for $P = R\,E$; a candidate who divides $E$ by $P$ has inverted it and loses the value mark. Accept $1.1\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

(c) Follow-through from (b) applies throughout. The final mark is for the explanation, not the number: the fuel consumed is the mass of the uranium nuclei, whereas only the mass defect, roughly $0.08\%$ of it, becomes energy.

(d) The (M1) is for multiplying by the enrichment fraction. Accept lifetimes between $7\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$ and $850\ \mathrm{days}$. The final mark needs both halves: the energy per fission is unchanged, and the total energy scales with the number of nuclei. Claiming the reactor becomes more powerful at a fixed control-rod setting confuses the rate with the energy per fission.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.5 Fusion and stars
syllabus_ref: E.5 Fusion and stars (fusion as the energy source of stars, energy release in fusion reactions, the equilibrium between outward radiation pressure and inward gravitational force, conditions for fusion, stellar evolution)
title: The binding energy that must be counted twelve times
q_html:
A red giant star has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and is now fusing helium into carbon through the triple-alpha process,
$$3\,^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \rightarrow\ ^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C} + \gamma.$$
During this phase the star's luminosity is $L = 3.0\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{W}$, and its core contains $1.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of helium when the burning begins. On the main sequence the same star radiated at $3.0\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{W}$ for $1.0\times10^{9}$ years. The star is in hydrostatic equilibrium: the inward gravitational force on the core is balanced by the outward pressure of the radiation produced by the fusion reactions.

Data (2025 data booklet): binding energy per nucleon of $^{4}\mathrm{He} = 7.074\ \mathrm{MeV}$; binding energy per nucleon of $^{12}\mathrm{C} = 7.680\ \mathrm{MeV}$; mass of a $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus $= 4.0026\ \mathrm{u}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\,c^{-2}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 1.661\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$; $1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.602\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$; $1\ \mathrm{year} = 3.16\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that the energy released in one triple-alpha reaction is about $7.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and explain why the binding energies per nucleon cannot be subtracted directly.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the fraction of the rest energy of the three helium nuclei that is released in one reaction is about $6.5\times10^{-4}$. Hence determine the total energy that the helium in the core can release.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine how long the core can sustain the star's present luminosity, in years. Hence show that this helium-burning phase is shorter than the main-sequence lifetime by a factor of about sixteen, and account for that factor.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Explain how the balance between the outward radiation pressure and the inward gravitational force keeps the core temperature and the fusion rate stable, and hence explain why the star's luminosity does not run away.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) The energy released is the increase in the total binding energy of the nuclei: (M1)
$$Q = B(^{12}\mathrm{C}) - 3B(^{4}\mathrm{He})$$
Each binding energy per nucleon must first be multiplied by its mass number, because the two nuclei do not contain the same number of nucleons: (M1)
$$B(^{4}\mathrm{He}) = 4(7.074) = 28.296\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad B(^{12}\mathrm{C}) = 12(7.680) = 92.16\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
$$Q = 92.16 - 3(28.296) = 92.16 - 84.888 = 7.27\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
Subtracting the per-nucleon figures directly would give $7.680 - 7.074 = 0.606\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which is the release per nucleon, not per reaction; the reaction binds twelve nucleons, so that answer is twelve times too small.

(b) The rest energy of the three helium nuclei consumed is (M1)
$$3m_{\mathrm{He}}c^{2} = 3(4.0026)(931.5) = 1.119\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
so the fraction of the fuel rest energy that appears as released energy is
$$f = \frac{7.272}{1.1185\times10^{4}} = 6.50\times10^{-4}$$ (A1)(AG)
Only about one part in $1500$ of the mass of the helium is converted. The energy reservoir is therefore
$$E = f\,Mc^{2} = (6.50\times10^{-4})(1.0\times10^{30})(2.998\times10^{8})^{2} = 5.84\times10^{43}\ \mathrm{J}$$ (A1)

(c) The time for which that reservoir can supply the luminosity is (M1)
$$t = \frac{E}{L} = \frac{5.84\times10^{43}}{3.0\times10^{28}} = 1.95\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s}$$
$$t = \frac{1.95\times10^{15}}{3.16\times10^{7}} = 6.2\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{years}$$ (A1)
The main sequence radiated $E_{\mathrm{MS}} = (3.0\times10^{27})(1.0\times10^{9})(3.16\times10^{7}) = 9.48\times10^{43}\ \mathrm{J}$, so (M1)
$$\frac{t_{\mathrm{He}}}{t_{\mathrm{MS}}} = \frac{E_{\mathrm{He}}/L_{\mathrm{He}}}{E_{\mathrm{MS}}/L_{\mathrm{MS}}}= \frac{E_{\mathrm{He}}}{E_{\mathrm{MS}}}\times\frac{L_{\mathrm{MS}}}{L_{\mathrm{He}}}= 0.616\times\frac{1}{10} = 6.2\times10^{-2}$$ (A1)
which is a phase about sixteen times shorter. The factor of sixteen splits cleanly in two: the reservoir is smaller by a factor $0.62$, because helium burning releases only $7.272/12 = 0.606\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon against about $6.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon for hydrogen, and the star is now radiating ten times faster. Neither effect alone explains the brevity of the phase; the product does.

(d) In equilibrium the energy generated in the core each second equals the energy radiated, so the core neither heats nor cools on average. (A1) If the fusion rate rises, the core temperature rises; the radiation pressure depends strongly on temperature and rises faster than the weight of the overlying layers, so the core expands. (A1) Expansion does work against gravity and lowers the temperature, which reduces the fusion rate back towards its previous value. (A1) The feedback is therefore negative, so the star settles where energy generation matches the rate at which energy can escape, and the luminosity stays stable instead of running away. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The (M1) is for identifying the energy released with the increase in total binding energy; the second (M1) is for converting each binding energy per nucleon into a total by multiplying by the mass number. A candidate who subtracts the per-nucleon values directly and reports $0.61\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for the whole reaction has made the error the question is built to expose and forfeits the last two marks. Accept $7.2$ to $7.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(b) The first (M1) is for recognising that the fraction required is $Q$ divided by the rest energy of the fuel, not by the rest energy of a single nucleus; the factor of three is the point. Accept $1.12\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for the denominator and $6.4$ to $6.6\times10^{-4}$ for the fraction. Follow-through from (a) applies, and the reservoir mark is available to a candidate whose fraction is wrong provided the multiplication by $Mc^{2}$ is correct. Accept $5.7$ to $6.0\times10^{43}\ \mathrm{J}$. A candidate who instead works out the reaction rate and the mass consumption rate and divides the core mass by it has taken a longer but equivalent route and should be credited the same marks.

(c) Accept $1.9$ to $2.0\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s}$ and $6.1$ to $6.3\times10^{7}$ years. The comparison mark is for forming the ratio of the two lifetimes as the ratio of two energy-to-luminosity quotients; the final mark is for decomposing the factor of sixteen into a reservoir term and a luminosity term. A candidate who quotes only the lower yield per nucleon, or only the higher luminosity, has given half the argument.

(d) Any two of the three links in the feedback loop earn the first two marks; the last mark requires the conclusion that the luminosity is stable. A candidate who says the star simply gets hotter without limit has not used the pressure-temperature link and forfeits the final mark.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.2 Greenhouse effect
syllabus_ref: B.2 (Greenhouse effect)
title: B.2 Greenhouse effect
q_html:
The solar constant at the Earth's orbit is $S = 1361\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, the planetary albedo is $\alpha = 0.30$, and the Stefan–Boltzmann constant is $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$. The measured mean surface temperature of the Earth is $288\ \mathrm{K}$. Treat the Earth as a sphere in a steady state, so that the mean power absorbed equals the mean power radiated to space.

  1. [4 marks](a)
