    2. B. $7.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This uses the area of the enclosing rectangle rather than the triangle, so the impulse is doubled.
    3. C. $1.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This reports the impulse itself as if it were a change in speed, omitting the division by the mass.
    4. D. $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This takes the area of only the rising part of the graph, ignoring the longer falling section.
  • (d)
    1. A. $5.06\ \mathrm{kN}$ correctThe cable must support the total weight of $460\ \mathrm{kg}$ and provide the upward acceleration, so $T=460(9.81+1.2)=5065\ \mathrm{N}$, which is $5.06\ \mathrm{kN}$.
    2. B. $4.51\ \mathrm{kN}$This is the total weight alone and ignores the acceleration entirely, as though the lift were moving at constant speed.
    3. C. $3.96\ \mathrm{kN}$This subtracts the acceleration from $g$ instead of adding it, which would be right for a lift accelerating downwards.
    4. D. $4.99\ \mathrm{kN}$This applies the acceleration to the lift but not to the passenger, treating only part of the load as being accelerated.
  • (e)
    1. A. $4v$ correctAt terminal speed the net weight balances the drag; the net weight scales as the cube of the radius while Stokes drag scales as the radius, so the terminal speed scales as radius squared and doubles in radius gives four times the speed.
    2. B. $2v$This makes the terminal speed proportional to the radius, which would follow if the driving force were also proportional to the radius.
    3. C. $8v$This scales with the cube of the radius, keeping the weight but ignoring that the drag force itself grows with radius.
    4. D. $v$This treats terminal speed as a property of the material, independent of size, which is only true if both the driving and the resisting force scale the same way.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.1 Gravitational fields
syllabus_ref: D.1 (Gravitational fields: potential, field strength, escape speed, orbital energy)
title: D.1 Gravitational fields
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on gravitational fields. Each one stands alone. The gravitational potential is taken to be zero at infinity throughout, so the potential at any finite distance from a mass is negative. $G$ is the gravitational constant.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Two point masses, each of mass $M$, are separated by a distance $2d$. What is the gravitational potential at the midpoint between them?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $-\dfrac{2GM}{d}$
    2. B. zero
    3. C. $-\dfrac{GM}{d}$
    4. D. $+\dfrac{2GM}{d}$
  2. [1 mark](b)

    The escape speed from the surface of a planet of radius $R$ is $v$. What is the escape speed from a point at a distance $2R$ from the centre of the same planet?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $0.707\,v$
    2. B. $0.500\,v$
    3. C. $1.41\,v$
    4. D. $v$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A satellite of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a planet of mass $M$. What is the total energy of the satellite?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$
    2. B. $-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$
    3. C. $+\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$
    4. D. zero
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $R$ to a circular orbit of radius $2R$ around the same planet of mass $M$. What is the change in the total energy of the satellite?

    (Determine)
    1. A. An increase of $\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$
    2. B. A decrease of $\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$
    3. C. An increase of $\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$
    4. D. No change, because the orbit is still circular.
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a uniform density. Let $g$ be the gravitational field strength at its surface. What is the gravitational field strength at a distance $R/2$ from its centre?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $\dfrac{g}{2}$
    2. B. $4g$
    3. C. $\dfrac{g}{4}$
    4. D. zero
a_html:
(a) A. Gravitational potential is a scalar, so contributions add without any direction: each mass is a distance $d$ from the midpoint and contributes $-GM/d$, giving $-2GM/d$. (A1) Option B is the signature error of this subtopic, because it is the field strength that cancels at the midpoint by symmetry, not the potential.

(b) A. Equating kinetic energy to the depth of the potential well, $\tfrac12 mv_{e}^{2}=GMm/r$, gives $v_{e}=\sqrt{2GM/r}$. At $r=2R$ this is $\sqrt{2GM/(2R)}=v/\sqrt{2}=0.707\,v$. (A1) The square root is what B misses.

(c) A. For a circular orbit $\tfrac12 mv^{2}=GMm/(2r)$, so the kinetic energy is $+GMm/(2r)$ and the potential energy is $-GMm/r$; the total is $-GMm/(2r)$. (A1) The result is negative, which is the defining feature of a bound orbit, and the factor of two is the relationship students most often misremember.

(d) A. With $E=-GMm/(2r)$, the energy changes from $-GMm/(2R)$ to $-GMm/(4R)$. The change is $-GMm/(4R)-(-GMm/(2R))=+GMm/(4R)$, an increase. (A1) The sign is the point: raising an orbit requires an input of energy even though the satellite ends up moving more slowly.

(e) A. For a uniform sphere the enclosed mass within radius $r$ is $M r^{3}/R^{3}$, so $g(r)=G(Mr^{3}/R^{3})/r^{2}=GMr/R^{3}$, which rises linearly from zero at the centre to $g$ at the surface. At $r=R/2$ it is $g/2$. (A1) B is the inverse-square law applied where it does not hold.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $-2GM/d$; a candidate who explains that the field cancels while the potential does not has demonstrated the key idea even if the sign slips. (b) Accept $0.71\,v$ or $v/\sqrt{2}$; candidates often reach for the inverse-square law here, so credit should follow the square root rather than any particular rounding. (c) The negative sign is part of the answer and a positive magnitude alone does not earn the mark. (d) Accept the modulus with a clear statement of the direction; note the well-known paradox that the satellite slows down while gaining energy, and do not penalise a candidate who flags it. (e) Accept $g/2$ or $GM/(2R^{2})$; this item depends on the uniform-density assumption, which is stated in the stem, and a candidate who objects that real planets are not uniform is right but has not answered the question as set.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. $-\dfrac{2GM}{d}$ correctPotential is a scalar, so the two contributions add: each mass is a distance $d$ away and contributes $-GM/d$, giving a total of $-2GM/d$.
    2. B. zeroThis treats the potential as though it cancelled like the field strength, but potential is a scalar and the two negative contributions add rather than oppose.
    3. C. $-\dfrac{GM}{d}$This counts only one of the two masses, ignoring that potentials from separate sources always superpose by simple addition.
    4. D. $+\dfrac{2GM}{d}$The magnitude and the addition are right but the sign is wrong; with the potential zero at infinity it is negative everywhere near a mass.
  • (b)
    1. A. $0.707\,v$ correctEscape speed is the square root of $2GM/r$, so doubling the distance from the centre divides the speed by the square root of two, giving $0.707\,v$.
    2. B. $0.500\,v$This treats the escape speed as inversely proportional to distance, missing the square root that comes from equating kinetic energy to the potential well depth.
    3. C. $1.41\,v$This has the square root the right way up but points the change in the wrong direction, as though moving outwards made escape harder.
    4. D. $v$This treats escape speed as a property of the planet alone, whereas it depends on the distance from the centre at which the escaping body starts.
  • (c)
    1. A. $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ correctThe potential energy is $-GMm/r$ and the kinetic energy is half that magnitude and positive, so the total is $-GMm/r + GMm/(2r) = -GMm/(2r)$.
    2. B. $-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$This is the gravitational potential energy alone and omits the kinetic energy the satellite has by virtue of being in orbit.
    3. C. $+\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$This is the kinetic energy on its own; the total is negative because a bound orbit has less energy than a stationary satellite at infinity.
    4. D. zeroZero total energy corresponds to the borderline escape case, not to a closed circular orbit, which is bound and therefore has negative total energy.
  • (d)
    1. A. An increase of $\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$ correctThe total energy is $-GMm/(2r)$, so it changes from $-GMm/(2R)$ to $-GMm/(4R)$, an increase of $GMm/(4R)$; energy must be supplied to lift the satellite outwards.
    2. B. A decrease of $\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong; moving to a larger orbit makes the satellite less tightly bound, so its total energy rises towards zero.
    3. C. An increase of $\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$This compares the magnitudes of the two total energies without taking their difference, so it double-counts the change.
    4. D. No change, because the orbit is still circular.The shape of the orbit does not fix its energy; a larger circular orbit has a different, less negative, total energy.
  • (e)
    1. A. $\dfrac{g}{2}$ correctInside a uniform sphere only the mass within the current radius contributes, and that mass falls as the cube of the radius, so the field rises linearly and at half the radius it is half the surface value.
    2. B. $4g$This applies the inverse-square law inside the planet, as though the whole mass were still enclosed at the centre, which it is not.
    3. C. $\dfrac{g}{4}$This gets the direction of the change right but applies the inverse-square factor anyway, rather than the linear law that holds inside a uniform sphere.
    4. D. zeroZero field at the centre is the correct result at $r=0$ for any spherical shell, but at half the radius there is still half the surface field.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.3 Motion in electromagnetic fields
syllabus_ref: D.3 (Motion in electromagnetic fields: charged particles in electric and magnetic fields)
title: D.3 Motion in electromagnetic fields
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on the motion of charged particles in electromagnetic fields. Each one stands alone. Unless a question states otherwise, any magnetic field is uniform and the particle enters it travelling at right angles to the field.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. Which statement about the particle is correct?

    (State)
    1. A. The direction of its velocity changes but the magnitude does not.
    2. B. Both the direction and the magnitude of its velocity change.
    3. C. Neither the direction nor the magnitude of its velocity changes.
    4. D. The magnitude of its velocity changes but the direction does not.
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, both moving at the same speed. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the radius of the proton's path?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $2$
    2. B. $\dfrac{1}{2}$
    3. C. $4$
    4. D. $1$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, this time with the same kinetic energy. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the radius of the proton's path?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1$
    2. B. $2$
    3. C. $\dfrac{1}{2}$
    4. D. $4$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B$. What is the period of its motion?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$
    2. B. $\dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$
    3. C. $\dfrac{2\pi q B}{m}$
    4. D. $\dfrac{2\pi m B}{q}$
  5. [1 mark](e)

    In a cyclotron, a charged particle is accelerated each time it crosses the gap between the two dees. Which statement is correct?

    (State)
    1. A. The magnetic field does no work on the particle; the increase in kinetic energy comes from the electric field in the gap.
    2. B. The magnetic field increases the kinetic energy of the particle during each half-turn.
    3. C. The time for each half-turn increases as the particle gains speed.
    4. D. The radius of the path is independent of the speed of the particle.
a_html:
(a) A. The magnetic force is $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$, which is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$ by construction, so it does no work and cannot change the speed; it only turns the velocity, producing circular motion. (A1) Every other option in this item attributes some change in speed to the field.

(b) A. Setting $qvB=mv^{2}/r$ gives $r=mv/(qB)$. An alpha particle has mass $4m_{p}$ and charge $2e$, so $r_{\alpha}/r_{p}=(4/1)\times(1/2)=2$. (A1) C, at $4$, is the mass ratio with the charge forgotten.

(c) A. Now the speed is not common, so write $r=\sqrt{2mK}/(qB)$. Then $r_{\alpha}/r_{p}=\sqrt{4}\times(1/2)=2\times0.5=1$: the paths have the same radius. (A1) The contrast with (b) is the whole point of the pair, and B is the answer to the previous question rather than this one.

(d) A. $T=2\pi r/v$ with $r=mv/(qB)$ gives $T=2\pi m/(qB)$; the speed cancels, so the period does not depend on how fast the particle is moving. (A1) B is the reciprocal, the cyclotron frequency, and is the commonest slip here.

(e) A. The magnetic field bends the path and fixes the period; only the electric field in the gap can change the kinetic energy, because only it has a component along the velocity. (A1) C is wrong for a reason worth stating explicitly: the period is independent of speed, which is what makes the cyclotron work at a fixed frequency at all.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any wording that separates the change of direction from the constancy of speed. (b) and (c) are a pair and should be marked together in the sense that a candidate who gives the same answer to both has almost certainly not noticed that the controlled quantity changed; accept $2$ and $1$ respectively, and note that an alpha particle is a helium nucleus with mass number four and charge $+2e$. (d) Accept the expression in any equivalent form; a candidate who writes the frequency instead of the period has inverted the quantity and earns nothing unless the inversion is clearly a slip in labelling. (e) Accept any statement that identifies the electric field as the source of the energy gain; credit should not be withheld from a candidate who adds correctly that the magnetic field is what keeps the particle returning to the gap. A candidate who claims that the magnetic field accelerates the particle has misunderstood the direction of the force and should not be credited even if the rest of the description is accurate.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. The direction of its velocity changes but the magnitude does not. correctThe magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion without doing any work and therefore leaves the speed unchanged.
    2. B. Both the direction and the magnitude of its velocity change.This would require the force to have a component along the velocity, which the magnetic force never does, since it is perpendicular by construction.
    3. C. Neither the direction nor the magnitude of its velocity changes.A perpendicular force is still a force, so the direction of motion must change even though the speed does not.
    4. D. The magnitude of its velocity changes but the direction does not.The opposite of the correct answer; a force perpendicular to the velocity can only turn the particle, never speed it up or slow it down.
  • (b)
    1. A. $2$ correctThe radius is $mv/(qB)$; an alpha particle has four times the proton's mass and twice its charge, so its radius is four halves, that is two, times as large.
    2. B. $\dfrac{1}{2}$This inverts the ratio, dividing the mass factor by the charge factor the wrong way round.
    3. C. $4$This uses the mass ratio alone and ignores that the alpha particle also carries twice the charge, which partly offsets its greater inertia.
    4. D. $1$This would follow only if the mass-to-charge ratios were equal, which they are not for these two particles.
  • (c)
    1. A. $1$ correctWriting the radius as the square root of $2mK$ divided by $qB$, the alpha particle's mass advantage of four is square-rooted to two and exactly cancelled by its charge factor of two, so the radii are equal.
    2. B. $2$This is the answer for equal speeds rather than equal kinetic energies, where the square root from the energy expression does not appear.
    3. C. $\dfrac{1}{2}$This applies the charge factor but forgets the square root on the mass, so the mass advantage is undercounted by a factor of two.
    4. D. $4$This uses the mass ratio on its own, ignoring both the square root and the doubled charge of the alpha particle.
  • (d)
    1. A. $\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ correctThe radius is $mv/(qB)$ and the period is the circumference divided by the speed, so the speed cancels and the period depends only on the mass, charge and field.
    2. B. $\dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$This is the frequency of the motion rather than the period; the two are reciprocals and the distinction is a single inversion.
    3. C. $\dfrac{2\pi q B}{m}$This inverts the mass-to-charge ratio inside the expression, placing the charge and field in the numerator where the mass belongs.
    4. D. $\dfrac{2\pi m B}{q}$This places the field strength in the numerator; since a stronger field bends the path more tightly, the period should shorten, not lengthen.
  • (e)
    1. A. The magnetic field does no work on the particle; the increase in kinetic energy comes from the electric field in the gap. correctThe magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and so can only bend the path, while the electric field in the gap acts along the motion and does the accelerating.
    2. B. The magnetic field increases the kinetic energy of the particle during each half-turn.A force perpendicular to the velocity does no work, so the magnetic field cannot change the kinetic energy however strong it is.
    3. C. The time for each half-turn increases as the particle gains speed.The period is $2\pi m/(qB)$ and is independent of speed, which is precisely why a fixed-frequency alternating voltage can keep accelerating the particle.
    4. D. The radius of the path is independent of the speed of the particle.The radius is proportional to the speed, which is why the particle spirals outwards as it is accelerated rather than retracing the same circle.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.2 Electric and magnetic fields
syllabus_ref: D.2 (Electric and magnetic fields)
title: D.2 Electric and magnetic fields
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on electric and magnetic fields. Each stands alone. Take $k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-2}}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $m_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}$ where needed.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A charge of $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ and a charge of $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ are fixed $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. At which point on the line joining them is the resultant electric field zero?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond the $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, on the side away from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge
    2. B. $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, between the two charges
    3. C. $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, midway between the two charges
    4. D. $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond the $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge
  2. [1 mark](b)

    What is the electric potential at a distance of $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ from an isolated point charge of $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1.2 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$
    2. B. $4.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$
    3. C. $2.4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$
    4. D. $1.2 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{V}$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of $2.5\ \mathrm{kV}$ in a vacuum. What is its final speed?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $2.97 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    2. B. $2.10 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    3. C. $4.20 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    4. D. $6.93 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A proton enters a uniform magnetic field of $0.40\ \mathrm{T}$ at $3.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, moving at right angles to the field. What is the radius of its path?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $7.8\ \mathrm{cm}$
    2. B. $12.8\ \mathrm{m}$
    3. C. $3.9\ \mathrm{cm}$
    4. D. $15.7\ \mathrm{cm}$
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Two long straight parallel wires are $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart and each carries $10\ \mathrm{A}$ in the same direction. What is the force per unit length between them?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, attractive
    2. B. $4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, repulsive
    3. C. $2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, attractive
    4. D. $8.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, attractive
a_html:
(a) A. Between opposite charges both fields point towards the negative charge, so they add and cannot cancel; the zero therefore lies outside, on the side of the smaller charge. Solving $4.0/x^{2} = 1.0/(x-0.30)^{2}$ gives $x = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, that is $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond the $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge. (A1)

(b) A. $V = kQ/r = 8.99\times10^{9} \times 4.0\times10^{-6}/0.30 = 1.20 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Potential is a scalar and falls as $1/r$, whereas field strength is a vector and falls as $1/r^{2}$; using the wrong power gives $4.0 \times 10^{5}$, which is option B and has the wrong units entirely.

(c) A. Energy conservation gives $eV = \tfrac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$, so $v = \sqrt{2 \times 1.60\times10^{-19} \times 2500/9.11\times10^{-31}} = 2.97 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) The result is about $0.10c$, so the relativistic correction is below one per cent and the classical expression is adequate here.

(d) A. The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction and not the speed, and the path is circular with $Bqv = mv^{2}/r$. Hence $r = mv/Bq = 1.67\times10^{-27} \times 3.0\times10^{6}/(0.40 \times 1.60\times10^{-19}) = 0.078\ \mathrm{m} = 7.8\ \mathrm{cm}$. (A1)

(e) A. Each wire lies in the field of the other, and $F/L = \mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}/(2\pi d) = 2\times10^{-7} \times 10 \times 10/0.050 = 4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. (A1) The force is attractive for currents in the same direction and repulsive for opposite directions, and that distinction is worth as much as the magnitude.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge stated explicitly; a candidate who gives the distance without saying which side has not answered the question. Do not credit option B on the grounds that the algebra works: recognising that the fields must oppose is the physics, and the square root introduces the spurious root precisely to test it. (b) Accept $1.19$ to $1.20 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$; note that the sign is positive because the source charge is positive, and a candidate who worries about sign here is confusing potential with field. (c) Accept $2.9$ to $3.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; relativistic correction at this speed is under one per cent and need not be applied. (d) Accept $7.8$ to $7.9\ \mathrm{cm}$ or $0.078\ \mathrm{m}$; the mark is for $r = mv/Bq$, so a candidate who writes the correct expression and then makes an arithmetic slip should be given the benefit of the doubt in bookwork terms. (e) Accept $4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ with the direction stated; the direction is half the item and should not be treated as a bonus.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond the $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, on the side away from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge correctBetween the charges both fields point towards the negative charge and cannot cancel; outside, the zero must lie on the side of the smaller charge, where $4.0/x^{2} = 1.0/(x-0.30)^{2}$ gives $x = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the larger charge.
    2. B. $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, between the two chargesThis is the algebraic root obtained by squaring without checking direction, but between opposite charges the two fields point the same way and add rather than cancel.
    3. C. $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, midway between the two chargesThe midpoint equalises the distances, not the field strengths; because the charges differ by a factor of four, the fields at the midpoint differ by the same factor.
    4. D. $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond the $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ chargeThis places the point on the correct side but at twice the correct distance, where the field from the larger charge still dominates and the two do not balance.
  • (b)
    1. A. $1.2 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$ correctPotential is a scalar given by $V = kQ/r$, so $V = 8.99 \times 10^{9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-6}/0.30 = 1.2 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$.
    2. B. $4.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$This evaluates $kQ/r^{2}$, which is the expression for field strength and has the wrong dimensions for a potential.
    3. C. $2.4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$This uses half the stated distance, as though the $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ were a diameter rather than a radius from the charge.
    4. D. $1.2 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{V}$This is a factor of ten high, the usual consequence of converting microcoulombs to coulombs incorrectly in the numerator.
  • (c)
    1. A. $2.97 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ correctThe gain in kinetic energy is $eV = \tfrac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$, so $v = \sqrt{2eV/m_{e}} = \sqrt{2 \times 1.60\times10^{-19} \times 2500/9.11\times10^{-31}} = 2.97 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
    2. B. $2.10 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This omits the factor of one half in the kinetic energy, using $eV = m_{e}v^{2}$ and losing a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.
    3. C. $4.20 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This uses a potential difference of $5.0\ \mathrm{kV}$, doubling the accelerating voltage, perhaps by counting the drop twice along the path.
    4. D. $6.93 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This substitutes the proton mass for the electron mass, giving a speed smaller by the square root of the mass ratio, about forty-three times too low.
  • (d)
    1. A. $7.8\ \mathrm{cm}$ correctThe magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, so $Bqv = mv^{2}/r$ and $r = mv/Bq = 1.67\times10^{-27} \times 3.0\times10^{6}/(0.40 \times 1.60\times10^{-19}) = 0.078\ \mathrm{m}$.
    2. B. $12.8\ \mathrm{m}$This inverts the expression to $Bq/(mv)$, producing a quantity with the wrong dimensions and a value larger by a factor of roughly $16400$.
    3. C. $3.9\ \mathrm{cm}$This uses twice the elementary charge in the denominator, as though the particle carried a charge of $+2e$ and were therefore bent twice as strongly.
    4. D. $15.7\ \mathrm{cm}$This uses twice the stated speed, doubling the numerator; the radius is proportional to momentum, so a faster particle describes a wider arc.
  • (e)
    1. A. $4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, attractive correctThe force per unit length is $\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}/(2\pi d) = 2 \times 10^{-7} \times 100/0.050 = 4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and parallel currents attract because each lies in the field of the other.
    2. B. $4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, repulsiveThe magnitude is right but the direction is reversed: repulsion occurs for antiparallel currents, not for currents in the same direction.
    3. C. $2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, attractiveThis leaves the separation as $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ rather than converting $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$, so the answer is smaller by the factor of twenty that the conversion introduces.
    4. D. $8.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, attractiveThis uses half the separation, as though the given distance were between one wire and the midpoint rather than between the two wires.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.3 Gas laws: the temperature along a straight-line change on a pressure-volume diagram
syllabus_ref: B.3 (Gas laws: the ideal gas equation, the pressure-volume, pressure-temperature and volume-temperature relationships for a fixed mass of gas, absolute temperature, and the reading of pressure-volume graphs)
title: B.3 Gas laws: the temperature along a straight-line change on a pressure-volume diagram
q_html:
The figure is a pressure-volume diagram for a fixed amount of an ideal gas taken through three successive changes. At state A the pressure is $1.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa, the volume is $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ and the temperature is 300 K. In the first change the gas expands at constant pressure to state B, where the volume is $6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$. In the second change it is compressed along the straight line shown to state C, where the pressure is $3.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa and the volume is $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$. In the third change it is cooled at constant volume back to state A. The gas behaves ideally throughout, and the molar gas constant is $R = 8.31$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this gas. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Calculate the temperature of the gas when it is at state B.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 100 K
    2. B. 1800 K
    3. C. 900 K
    4. D. 300 K
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Calculate the temperature of the gas when it is at state C.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 900 K
    2. B. 2700 K
    3. C. 300 K
    4. D. 600 K
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Calculate the amount of substance of gas, in moles, that is present in the container.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0.0267 mol
    2. B. 0.2407 mol
    3. C. 0.0401 mol
    4. D. 0.0802 mol
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Determine the greatest temperature reached by the gas at any point during the three changes.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 800 K
    2. B. 1200 K
    3. C. 900 K
    4. D. 2700 K
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Calculate the temperature of the gas at the point on the change from B to C at which its pressure is $2.50 \times 10^{5}$ Pa.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 1200 K
    2. B. 750 K
    3. C. 1130 K
    4. D. 900 K
a_html:
(a) C. For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, Charles' law gives
$V \propto T$, so $T_{B} = 300 \times (6.0\times10^{-3})/(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 900$ K.
Note that the ratio has to be taken between absolute temperatures and volumes; no
Celsius conversion is involved because both are already absolute. (A1)

(b) A. The three gas laws combine into $\tfrac{pV}{T} = \text{constant}$, so it
is the product $pV$ that settles the temperature and not either variable alone. At C,
$pV = (3.0\times10^{5})(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 600$ Pa m$^{3}$, and at A,
$pV = 200$ Pa m$^{3}$. The temperature at C is therefore
$300 \times 600/200 = 900$ K. (A1)

(c) D. Rearranging $pV = nRT$ at A,
$n = (1.0\times10^{5})(2.0\times10^{-3})/(8.31 \times 300) = 200/2493 = 0.0802$ mol.
State A is the only state whose temperature is stated, so it is the only one the
equation can be applied to directly. (A1)

(d) B. The second change is a straight line from B, at
$(V,\ p) = (6.0\times10^{-3},\ 1.0\times10^{5})$, to C, at
$(2.0\times10^{-3},\ 3.0\times10^{5})$. Its gradient is
$(3.0 - 1.0)\times10^{5}/(2.0 - 6.0)\times10^{-3} = -5.0\times10^{7}$ Pa m$^{-3}$, so
$p = 4.0\times10^{5} - 5.0\times10^{7}V$. The temperature follows $pV$, and
$pV = 4.0\times10^{5}V - 5.0\times10^{7}V^{2}$ is a downward-opening quadratic whose
stationary point satisfies $4.0\times10^{5} = 1.0\times10^{8}V$, giving
$V = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ — exactly midway along the segment. There
$p = 2.0\times10^{5}$ Pa, $pV = 800$ Pa m$^{3}$ and
$T = 300 \times 800/200 = 1200$ K. Both endpoints give only 600 Pa m$^{3}$. (A1)

(e) C. Substituting $p = 2.50\times10^{5}$ Pa into the same line gives
$V = (4.0\times10^{5} - 2.50\times10^{5})/(5.0\times10^{7}) = 3.0\times10^{-3}$
m$^{3}$, so $pV = 750$ Pa m$^{3}$ and $T = 300 \times 750/200 = 1125$ K, which is
1130 K to three significant figures. (A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 900 K. An answer of 100 K has used the volume ratio the wrong way round;
300 K treats the change as isothermal and 1800 K applies the volume ratio twice.

(b) Accept 900 K. Do not accept 2700 K, which applies the pressure ratio and the
volume ratio separately — the single product $pV$ fixes the temperature. An answer
of 600 K has read the product as a temperature. Note for the record that B and C are
at the same temperature, which is why neither of them can be the maximum.

(c) Accept 0.0802 mol. Allow answers in the range 0.0800 to 0.0804. An answer of
0.0267 mol shows the 900 K of part (a) carried into the denominator, and 0.2407 mol
shows the volume of state B carried into the numerator; 0.0401 mol is a factor of two.

(d) Accept 1200 K and no other value. This is the discriminating question of the
cluster, and a candidate who answers 900 K has simply read off the hottest labelled
state. An answer of 800 K has found the correct maximum value of $pV$ and then failed
to scale it, which is a near miss worth crediting in discussion even though it scores
nothing here. Allow 1200 K whether it is reached by differentiating the quadratic, by
completing the square or by tabulating $pV$ along the line.

(e) Accept 1130 K; accept 1125 K. An answer of 750 K has read $pV$ as a temperature,
and 1200 K is the maximum rather than the value at the stated pressure.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 100 KThis divides 300 K by the volume ratio of 3, treating temperature as inversely proportional to volume at constant pressure.
    2. B. 1800 KThis applies the volume ratio of 3 twice over, as though the pressure had also changed by that factor.
    3. C. 900 K correctAt constant pressure the volume is proportional to the absolute temperature, so tripling the volume from $2.0\times10^{-3}$ to $6.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ triples the temperature to 900 K.
    4. D. 300 KThis treats the first change as isothermal, but the pressure is held constant while the volume changes, so the temperature cannot stay fixed.
  • (b)
    1. A. 900 K correctThe product $pV$ is 600 Pa m$^{3}$ at C and 200 Pa m$^{3}$ at A, so the temperature is three times 300 K. C is as hot as B even though neither its pressure nor its volume matches B's.
    2. B. 2700 KThis applies the pressure ratio of 3 and the volume ratio of 3 separately, when only the single product $pV$ fixes the temperature.
    3. C. 300 KThis assumes the gas is back at its starting temperature, which would need $pV$ at C to equal $pV$ at A.
    4. D. 600 KThis is the product $pV = 600$ Pa m$^{3}$ at C read off directly as a temperature, with no reference to the state A.
  • (c)
    1. A. 0.0267 molThis divides by 900 K rather than 300 K, using the temperature of state B or state C in place of the one that is actually stated.
    2. B. 0.2407 molThis uses the volume of state B, $6.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$, in the numerator while keeping the temperature of state A.
    3. C. 0.0401 molThis is half the correct value, as though the molar gas constant were twice as large as it is.
    4. D. 0.0802 mol correctFrom $pV = nRT$ at A, $n = (1.0\times10^{5})(2.0\times10^{-3})/(8.31 \times 300) = 0.0802$ mol. State A is the only state whose temperature is given, so it is the one the equation has to be applied to.
  • (d)
    1. A. 800 KThis is the greatest value of the product $pV$, 800 Pa m$^{3}$, read as a temperature without scaling it against state A.
    2. B. 1200 K correctOn the straight segment from B to C the pressure is $p = 4.0\times10^{5} - 5.0\times10^{7}V$, so $pV = 4.0\times10^{5}V - 5.0\times10^{7}V^{2}$, which peaks at $V = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ where $pV = 800$ Pa m$^{3}$ and $T = 1200$ K.
    3. C. 900 KThis is the temperature at the labelled states B and C. The product $pV$ is larger between them than at either end.
    4. D. 2700 KThis multiplies the greatest pressure by the greatest volume, which is a corner the gas never occupies.
  • (e)
    1. A. 1200 KThis is the maximum temperature, which occurs at a pressure of $2.0\times10^{5}$ Pa rather than the one asked for.
    2. B. 750 KThis is the product $pV = 750$ Pa m$^{3}$ read directly as a temperature, with no scaling against state A.
    3. C. 1130 K correctPutting $p = 2.50\times10^{5}$ Pa into $p = 4.0\times10^{5} - 5.0\times10^{7}V$ gives $V = 3.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$, so $pV = 750$ Pa m$^{3}$ and $T = 300 \times 750/200 = 1130$ K.
    4. D. 900 KThis is the temperature at B and at C, not at a point between them, where the product $pV$ is larger.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.4 Standing waves: the resonant modes of a pipe closed at one end against a pipe open at both ends
syllabus_ref: C.4 (Standing waves and resonance: the boundary conditions at open and closed ends of air columns, the modes of pipes closed at one end and of pipes open at both ends, nodes and antinodes, and the relationship between wavelength and frequency)
title: C.4 Standing waves: the resonant modes of a pipe closed at one end against a pipe open at both ends
q_html:
The figure shows two organ pipes drawn to scale. Pipe P and pipe Q have the same length, 0.850 m, but pipe P is closed by a solid stopper at one end and open at the other, while pipe Q is open at both ends. The speed of sound in the air inside both pipes is 340 m s$^{-1}$. End corrections may be neglected, so a displacement antinode may be taken to lie in the plane of each open end and a displacement node at each closed end. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to these two pipes. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Calculate the lowest frequency at which the air column in pipe P resonates.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 100 Hz
    2. B. 200 Hz
    3. C. 400 Hz
    4. D. 800 Hz
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Calculate the third lowest frequency at which the air column in pipe P resonates.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 400 Hz
    2. B. 200 Hz
    3. C. 500 Hz
    4. D. 300 Hz
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Calculate the lowest frequency at which the air column in pipe Q resonates.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 100 Hz
    2. B. 50.0 Hz
    3. C. 400 Hz
    4. D. 200 Hz
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Determine the length of a pipe that is open at both ends and whose lowest resonant frequency equals the lowest resonant frequency of pipe P.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 1.70 m
    2. B. 0.850 m
    3. C. 0.425 m
    4. D. 3.40 m
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Calculate the distance between adjacent nodes of the standing wave in pipe P when it is resonating at 500 Hz.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0.170 m
    2. B. 0.340 m
    3. C. 0.680 m
    4. D. 0.850 m
a_html:
(a) A. The closed end must be a displacement node and the open end a displacement
antinode, and the shortest way to join a node to an antinode is a quarter of a
wavelength. So $\lambda = 4L = 4(0.850) = 3.40$ m and $f = v/\lambda = 340/3.40 =
100$ Hz. (A1)

(b) C. Each successive mode adds another half wavelength between the node and the
antinode, which adds $2f_{1}$ to the frequency rather than $f_{1}$. The series is
therefore $f_{1},\ 3f_{1},\ 5f_{1},\ \ldots$, that is 100, 300, 500, 700 Hz. The third
lowest of these is 500 Hz, which is the fifth harmonic. (A1)

(c) D. With both ends open, both are antinodes, and the shortest way to join an
antinode to an antinode is half a wavelength. So $\lambda = 2L = 1.70$ m and
$f = 340/1.70 = 200$ Hz, an octave above pipe P of the same length. (A1)

(d) A. The two fundamentals are $v/4L$ for the closed pipe and $v/2L$ for the open
one. Setting them equal, $v/2L_{\text{open}} = v/4(0.850)$, gives
$L_{\text{open}} = 2(0.850) = 1.70$ m. The open pipe has to be twice as long to sound
as low. (A1)

(e) B. At 500 Hz the wavelength in air is $\lambda = v/f = 340/500 = 0.680$ m. In
any standing wave the nodes are spaced half a wavelength apart, so the separation is
0.340 m. As a check, the pipe holds $0.850/0.680 = 1.25$ wavelengths, which is five
quarters — exactly what the fifth harmonic of a stopped pipe requires. (A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 100 Hz. An answer of 200 Hz has applied the open-pipe condition to a closed
pipe; 400 Hz and 800 Hz take the pipe length to be one wavelength and half a
wavelength respectively.

(b) Accept 500 Hz and no other value. This question separates the count of resonances
from the harmonic number, and 300 Hz is the answer it exists to catch: that is the
third harmonic but only the second resonance. Do not accept 400 Hz under any
circumstances — it is an even multiple of the fundamental and a stopped pipe cannot
resonate there at all.

(c) Accept 200 Hz. An answer of 100 Hz has carried the closed-pipe value across
unchanged; 50.0 Hz uses the closed-pipe condition on a pipe with no closed end.

(d) Accept 1.70 m. An answer of 0.425 m is the discriminating error: it takes the
ordering from part (c), where the closed pipe is the lower of the two at equal length,
and assumes the closed pipe must therefore be the shorter at equal pitch. It is the
other way round. An answer of 3.40 m has given the wavelength rather than the length.

(e) Accept 0.340 m. An answer of 0.680 m has given the wavelength instead of half of
it, and 0.170 m is the node-to-antinode distance.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 100 Hz correctA closed end forces a displacement node and an open end an antinode, so a quarter of a wavelength fills the pipe: $\lambda = 4L = 3.40$ m and $f = v/\lambda = 100$ Hz.
    2. B. 200 HzThis is $v/2L$, the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends, not of one closed at one end.
    3. C. 400 HzThis takes the length of the pipe to be exactly one wavelength.
    4. D. 800 HzThis takes half the length of the pipe to be one wavelength.
  • (b)
    1. A. 400 HzThis is an even multiple of the fundamental. A pipe closed at one end cannot sustain any even harmonic, so it is not a resonance at all.
    2. B. 200 HzThis is the second harmonic, which is absent from this pipe's series altogether.
    3. C. 500 Hz correctOnly the odd harmonics of 100 Hz can form, because the closed end must be a node and the open end an antinode. The series is 100, 300, 500, 700 Hz, and the third of those is 500 Hz.
    4. D. 300 HzThis is the third harmonic, $3f_{1}$, which is the second lowest resonance and not the third.
  • (c)
    1. A. 100 HzThis is the fundamental of the closed pipe; opening the far end raises the fundamental by a factor of two.
    2. B. 50.0 HzThis uses $\lambda = 4L$, the closed-pipe condition, for a pipe that has no closed end.
    3. C. 400 HzThis takes the length of the pipe to be exactly one wavelength.
    4. D. 200 Hz correctBoth ends are open, so both are antinodes and half a wavelength fills the pipe: $\lambda = 2L = 1.70$ m and $f = 340/1.70 = 200$ Hz.
  • (d)
    1. A. 1.70 m correctEquating the two fundamentals, $v/2L_{\text{open}} = v/4L_{\text{closed}}$, gives $L_{\text{open}} = 2L_{\text{closed}} = 1.70$ m.
    2. B. 0.850 mThis assumes the same fundamental needs the same length, and misses the factor of two between the two boundary conditions.
    3. C. 0.425 mThis carries the ordering across from part (c): the closed pipe is lower at a given length, so it is taken to be shorter at a given pitch. The ranking reverses.
    4. D. 3.40 mThis is the wavelength of 100 Hz sound in air, not the length of pipe that resonates at that frequency.
  • (e)
    1. A. 0.170 mThis is a quarter of a wavelength, the separation between a node and the adjacent antinode.
    2. B. 0.340 m correctAt 500 Hz the wavelength is $v/f = 340/500 = 0.680$ m, and adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so 0.340 m.
    3. C. 0.680 mThis is the wavelength; adjacent nodes are separated by half of it.
    4. D. 0.850 mThis is the length of the pipe, which is five quarters of a wavelength at this frequency.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
syllabus_ref: A.4 (Rigid body mechanics: moment of inertia, rotational dynamics, rolling without slipping)
title: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on rigid-body mechanics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-2}}$ where a numerical value is needed, and give each answer to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A solid cylinder and a thin-walled hollow cylinder have the same mass and the same outer radius. Both are released from rest and roll without slipping down the same incline. What is the ratio of the acceleration of the solid cylinder to the acceleration of the hollow cylinder?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 1.33
    2. B. 0.750
    3. C. 1.00
    4. D. 2.00
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A disc of moment of inertia $0.80\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{2}}$ rotates freely about a fixed vertical axle at $12\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. A lump of clay of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$, initially at rest, is dropped onto the disc and sticks at a point $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the axle. What is the angular speed immediately afterwards?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 9.80 rad s$^{-1}$
    2. B. 12.0 rad s$^{-1}$
    3. C. 9.60 rad s$^{-1}$
    4. D. 8.73 rad s$^{-1}$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A solid cylinder is released from rest on a rough incline and rolls down it without slipping, accelerating as it goes. What is the direction of the static frictional force that the surface of the incline exerts on the cylinder?

    (State)
    1. A. Up the incline
    2. B. Down the incline
    3. C. Zero, because the cylinder does not slip
    4. D. Perpendicular to the surface of the incline
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A light inextensible string is wound around a disc of radius $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ whose moment of inertia about its axle is $0.30\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{2}}$. The disc turns on a fixed horizontal axle with negligible friction, and a block of mass $1.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ hangs from the free end of the string. What is the tension in the string as the block descends?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 9.42 N
    2. B. 11.8 N
    3. C. 2.35 N
    4. D. 3.92 N
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A solid uniform sphere of moment of inertia $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$ about its centre rolls without slipping along level ground at a constant speed of $3.0\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$. What fraction of the sphere's total kinetic energy is rotational kinetic energy?

    (Determine)
    1. A. 0.286
    2. B. 0.400
    3. C. 0.500
    4. D. 0.714
a_html:
(a) A. For rolling without slipping the acceleration down an incline is $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/(MR^2)}$. The solid cylinder has $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$ and so accelerates at $\tfrac{2}{3}g\sin\theta$; the thin-walled hollow cylinder has $I = MR^2$ and so accelerates at $\tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$. The ratio is $\tfrac{2/3}{1/2} = \tfrac{4}{3} = 1.33$. (A1) Option B inverts it, option C assumes every rolling body behaves the same, and option D takes the ratio of the moments of inertia without the denominator.

(b) A. Angular momentum about the axle is conserved, because neither the axle force nor the weight of the clay exerts a torque about it. Initially $L = 0.80 \times 12 = 9.6\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2\ s^{-1}}$. The clay contributes $mr^2 = 0.50 \times 0.60^2 = 0.18\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2}$, so the final moment of inertia is $0.98\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2}$ and the final angular speed is $9.6/0.98 = 9.80\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. (A1) Option B ignores the clay, option C reports the angular momentum as though it were a speed, and option D adds $mr$ instead of $mr^2$.

(c) A. The weight acts through the centre of mass and the normal force passes through the contact point, so neither produces a torque about the centre. Only friction can supply the torque that increases the angular speed, and it must act up the incline to do so. (A1) Note that static friction opposes the motion the contact point *would* have, not the motion of the centre of mass.

(d) A. The string does not slip, so $a = \alpha R$. Then $mg - T = ma$ for the block and $TR = I\alpha$ for the disc, giving $T = Ia/R^2$. Hence $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + I/R^2} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 9.81}{1.2 + 4.8} = 1.96\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-2}}$, and $T = 4.8 \times 1.96 = 9.42\ \mathrm{N}$. (A1) Option B neglects the disc's inertia, option C is the resultant force rather than the tension, and option D uses $I = \tfrac{1}{2}mR^2$ with the block's mass.

(e) A. With $I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ and $\omega = v/R$, the rotational term is $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2$ and the translational term is $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2$. The rotational fraction is therefore $\dfrac{1/5}{1/5 + 1/2} = \dfrac{2}{7} = 0.286$. (A1) Option B quotes the coefficient in $I$, option C splits the energy evenly, and option D is the translational fraction.

Markscheme notes

One mark for each correct option. There is no penalty for a wrong answer under the Paper 1A rules, so every question should be attempted, and a student who cannot finish a calculation should eliminate on dimensional or limiting-case grounds and choose. In (a) condone the ratio written as $4:3$ or as $1.33$. In (b) allow follow-through from an incorrect final moment of inertia provided the conservation statement itself is explicit and correct. In (c) accept 'up the slope' or 'up the plane'; the direction must be given relative to the incline, and 'opposite to the motion' is not sufficient because the phrase is ambiguous here. In (d) accept $9.4\ \mathrm{N}$ to two significant figures, and allow an answer obtained by computing the acceleration first. In (e) accept $2/7$ or $0.29$; the fact that the answer has no unit is itself part of what is being assessed. Candidates most often lose these marks not through algebra but by applying a purely translational model to a body that is also rotating; watch for a line of working in which the moment of inertia has quietly disappeared. A calculator is available throughout, so no credit is due for an unreduced surd where a decimal was requested, and values should carry three significant figures.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 1.33 correctFor rolling without slipping the acceleration is g sin theta divided by one plus I over M R squared, giving two thirds for the solid cylinder and one half for the hollow one, and the ratio of those is four thirds.
    2. B. 0.750This inverts the ratio, comparing the hollow cylinder with the solid one rather than the other way round.
    3. C. 1.00This treats every rolling body as accelerating alike, which is only true for sliding without friction and ignores where the energy goes.
    4. D. 2.00This takes the ratio of the two moments of inertia directly, forgetting the leading term of one in the rolling acceleration formula.
  • (b)
    1. A. 9.80 rad s$^{-1}$ correctAngular momentum about the axle is conserved at 9.6 units, the clay contributes m r squared of 0.18 to the moment of inertia, and dividing gives 9.6 over 0.98.
    2. B. 12.0 rad s$^{-1}$This assumes the angular speed is unchanged, which would only follow if the clay landed exactly on the axle and added nothing to the moment of inertia.
    3. C. 9.60 rad s$^{-1}$This is the angular momentum itself quoted as if it were an angular speed, a confusion of a conserved quantity with the quantity being found.
    4. D. 8.73 rad s$^{-1}$This adds m r rather than m r squared when increasing the moment of inertia, so the clay is treated as if it sat at unit distance.
  • (c)
    1. A. Up the incline correctWeight and the normal force both give no torque about the centre of mass, so only friction can supply the torque that increases the spin, and it must point up the plane to do so.
    2. B. Down the inclineThis applies friction opposing motion rather than friction opposing the relative motion at the contact point, which is the condition static friction actually enforces.
    3. C. Zero, because the cylinder does not slipNo slipping means no kinetic friction, but static friction is present and is precisely what produces the angular acceleration of the cylinder.
    4. D. Perpendicular to the surface of the inclineThis is the direction of the normal contact force, which passes through the centre and so cannot produce any torque about it.
  • (d)
    1. A. 9.42 N correctThe tension torque spins the disc, so T equals I a over R squared, and combining with m g minus T equals m a gives an acceleration of 1.96 and hence a tension of 9.42 newtons.
    2. B. 11.8 NThis sets the tension equal to the weight of the block, which would mean zero acceleration and ignores that some energy goes into rotating the disc.
    3. C. 2.35 NThis is the resultant force on the block rather than the tension, having subtracted the tension from the weight instead of reporting it.
    4. D. 3.92 NThis substitutes the hanging block's own mass into the disc's moment of inertia, treating the disc as if it were a solid cylinder of that mass.
  • (e)
    1. A. 0.286 correctWith omega equal to v over R the rotational energy is one fifth M v squared while the translational energy is one half M v squared, so the rotational share is two sevenths.
    2. B. 0.400This quotes the coefficient two fifths from the moment of inertia as if it were already the energy fraction, skipping the conversion entirely.
    3. C. 0.500This assumes the energy splits equally between translation and rotation, which happens for no standard rolling body.
    4. D. 0.714This is the translational fraction rather than the rotational one, obtained by taking the complement and so answering the question that was not asked.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.4 Induction
syllabus_ref: D.4 (Induction: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, motional emf, self-inductance)
title: D.4 Induction
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on electromagnetic induction. Each one stands alone. In every case the magnetic field is uniform over the region stated and the resistance given is the total circuit resistance.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A rectangular coil of 200 turns and resistance $4.0\ \Omega$ has one side of length $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ inside a uniform magnetic field of $0.80\ \mathrm{T}$. The coil is pulled out of the field at a constant speed of $0.20\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$, with that side remaining perpendicular to the direction of motion. What is the current in the coil while it leaves the field?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0.40 A
    2. B. 1.60 A
    3. C. 0.020 A
    4. D. 0.0020 A
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A coil of 500 turns and area $0.020\ \mathrm{m^2}$ rotates at a steady frequency of $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.10\ \mathrm{T}$, with its axis of rotation perpendicular to the field. What is the maximum emf induced across the coil?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 314 V
    2. B. 157 V
    3. C. 50.0 V
    4. D. 1.00 V
  3. [1 mark](c)

    An inductor of inductance $0.40\ \mathrm{H}$ carries a steady current of $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$. How much energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 1.80 J
    2. B. 3.60 J
    3. C. 1.20 J
    4. D. 0.600 J
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A square loop of side $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ and resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ is pulled at constant speed completely through a region of uniform magnetic field of $0.50\ \mathrm{T}$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The region is wide enough that the loop enters and leaves separately. What total charge flows past a point in the loop?

    (Determine)
    1. A. 5.0 mC
    2. B. 2.5 mC
    3. C. 0 mC
    4. D. 10 mC
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A conducting rod of length $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ rotates at a steady angular speed of $20\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$ about one end, sweeping out a plane that is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.25\ \mathrm{T}$. What is the emf between the two ends of the rod?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0.400 V
    2. B. 0.800 V
    3. C. 2.00 V
    4. D. 0.200 V
a_html:
(a) A. Only the side of length $L = 0.050\ \mathrm{m}$ that lies across the field boundary changes the flux, so $\varepsilon = NBLv = 200 \times 0.80 \times 0.050 \times 0.20 = 1.6\ \mathrm{V}$, and $I = \varepsilon/R = 1.6/4.0 = 0.40\ \mathrm{A}$. (A1) Option B reports the emf, option C puts the coil area where the side length belongs, and option D omits the turn count.

(b) A. The flux linkage is $N\Phi = NBA\cos(\omega t)$, so $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$ with $\omega = 2\pi f = 314\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. Hence $\varepsilon_{\max} = 500 \times 0.10 \times 0.020 \times 314 = 314\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B uses $\pi f$ for $\omega$, option C uses $f$, and option D gives the flux linkage rather than its rate of change.

(c) A. $E = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.40 \times 3.0^2 = 1.80\ \mathrm{J}$. (A1) Option B omits the half, option C uses $LI$, and option D halves $LI$.

(d) A. The charge is $Q = \int I\,dt = \dfrac{1}{R}\int \varepsilon\,dt = \dfrac{|\Delta\Phi|}{R}$ over each transition. Entry gives $Ba^2/R = 0.50 \times 0.010/2.0 = 2.5\ \mathrm{mC}$ and exit gives the same again, so $Q = 5.0\ \mathrm{mC}$. (A1) This is the item that separates a student who has memorised a formula from one who knows what charge is: the *net* flux change over the whole motion is indeed zero, but the two currents flow at different times and it is their magnitudes, not their signs, that add.

(e) A. An element at distance $r$ moves at $\omega r$, so $d\varepsilon = B\omega r\,dr$ and $\varepsilon = \int_0^L B\omega r\,dr = \tfrac{1}{2}B\omega L^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times 20 \times 0.16 = 0.400\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B uses the tip speed throughout, option C is dimensionally inconsistent, and option D halves twice.

Markscheme notes

One mark per correct option, no negative marking. In (a) allow an answer reached via the rate of cutting of flux lines provided the length used is the one crossing the boundary. In (b) accept 314 V or 3.1 x 10^2 V, and condone a small discrepancy from rounding omega to 314. In (c) accept 1.8 J. In (d) do not credit an argument from the net flux change alone even if it reaches 5.0 mC by some other route, because the reasoning is what is being rewarded; equally, credit 5.0 mC reached by treating the two transitions separately as intended. In (e) accept 0.40 V and allow the integral form or the mean-speed argument. Note that in (d) the speed at which the loop is pulled does not appear in the answer at all, and that is the point of the item: the charge depends only on the change of flux linkage and on the resistance. In (e) credit the integral form and the mean-speed argument equally, but do not credit B L v applied with the tip speed, which is precisely the error option B exists to catch. In (b) the value 314 V depends on using an angular frequency in radians per second; a candidate working in degrees will reach none of the options, which is a useful diagnostic in itself.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 0.40 A correctThe emf is N B L v which is 1.6 volts, and dividing by the four ohm circuit resistance gives a current of 0.40 amperes.
    2. B. 1.60 AThis is the induced emf quoted as if it were the current, having omitted the division by the resistance of the circuit.
    3. C. 0.020 AThis uses the area of the coil where Faraday's law for a straight side needs the length, so an extra factor of the side appears.
    4. D. 0.0020 AThis omits the number of turns entirely, computing the emf for a single loop and then dividing by the resistance.
  • (b)
    1. A. 314 V correctThe flux is N B A cos omega t so the emf is N B A omega sin omega t, and N B A omega with omega equal to two pi f gives 314 volts.
    2. B. 157 VThis uses pi f in place of two pi f for the angular frequency, halving the true peak emf.
    3. C. 50.0 VThis uses the frequency in hertz directly where the angular frequency in radians per second is required.
    4. D. 1.00 VThis is the maximum flux linkage N B A rather than its rate of change, describing the flux and not the emf at all.
  • (c)
    1. A. 1.80 J correctThe stored energy is one half L I squared, which is one half times 0.40 times nine, giving 1.8 joules.
    2. B. 3.60 JThis omits the factor of one half, the same slip as using m v squared instead of one half m v squared for kinetic energy.
    3. C. 1.20 JThis computes L times I rather than L times I squared, treating the current as if it entered to the first power.
    4. D. 0.600 JThis halves L I rather than L I squared, applying the factor of one half to the wrong expression.
  • (d)
    1. A. 5.0 mC correctCharge is the integral of current, which is the total change of flux linkage divided by the resistance, and the magnitudes on entry and on exit each contribute B a squared over R.
    2. B. 2.5 mCThis counts only the entry transition and forgets that the loop leaves the field as well as entering it.
    3. C. 0 mCThis argues from the net change in flux being zero, but charge is the integral of the current, so the two transitions add in magnitude rather than cancelling.
    4. D. 10 mCThis uses twice the area of the loop in each transition, counting the field region as double the actual intercepted area.
  • (e)
    1. A. 0.400 V correctEach element moves at a speed proportional to its distance from the pivot, so the mean speed is that of the midpoint and the emf is one half B omega L squared.
    2. B. 0.800 VThis treats every element of the rod as moving at the speed of the tip, omitting the factor of one half that comes from averaging along the rod.
    3. C. 2.00 VThis uses B omega L instead of B omega L squared, which is dimensionally wrong and gives a quantity that is not an emf.
    4. D. 0.200 VThis applies a factor of one half twice, once for the mean speed and then again without justification.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.5 Current and circuits
syllabus_ref: B.5 (Current and circuits: internal resistance, non-ideal meters, power transfer)
title: B.5 Current and circuits
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions in which a circuit is altered by the act of measuring it, or by the load connected to it. In each case the supply is treated as ideal unless an internal resistance is stated explicitly.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A cell of emf $12\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $3.0\ \Omega$ is connected to a variable external resistor. What is the greatest power that can be dissipated in that external resistor?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 12 W
    2. B. 48 W
    3. C. 24 W
    4. D. 6.0 W
  2. [1 mark](b)

    For the cell in the previous question, at the external resistance that gives the greatest power in the external resistor, what fraction of the total power generated by the cell is delivered to that external resistor?

    (State)
    1. A. One half
    2. B. All of it
    3. C. Two thirds
    4. D. One quarter
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A cell of negligible internal resistance and emf $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is connected in series with a $400\ \Omega$ resistor and a $600\ \Omega$ resistor. A voltmeter of resistance $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ is connected across the $600\ \Omega$ resistor. What does the voltmeter read?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 3.21 V
    2. B. 3.60 V
    3. C. 2.77 V
    4. D. 3.86 V
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A circuit consists of a $12\ \mathrm{V}$ supply of negligible internal resistance connected to a $100\ \Omega$ resistor. An ammeter of resistance $5.0\ \Omega$ is inserted in series to measure the current. What is the percentage error in the current it reads?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 4.76%
    2. B. 5.00%
    3. C. 0%
    4. D. 95.2%
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A cell is connected to a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor and the terminal potential difference is $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$. When the same cell is connected to a $9.0\ \Omega$ resistor the terminal potential difference is $7.2\ \mathrm{V}$. What is the internal resistance of the cell?

    (Determine)
    1. A. 1.71 $\Omega$
    2. B. 0.583 $\Omega$
    3. C. 1.20 $\Omega$
    4. D. 2.57 $\Omega$
a_html:
(a) A. The power in the load is $P = \dfrac{E^2 R}{(R+r)^2}$, which is greatest when $R = r = 3.0\ \Omega$. Then $I = 12/6.0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and $P = I^2R = 4.0 \times 3.0 = 12\ \mathrm{W}$, which is also $E^2/(4r)$. (A1) Option B is $E^2/r$, the power dissipated inside the cell at short circuit, and options C and D come from dropping or doubling the factor of four.

(b) A. At $R = r$ the same current passes through both resistances, so $I^2R = I^2r$ and exactly one half of the generated power reaches the load. (A1) This is why maximum power transfer and high efficiency are different aims: option B needs an ideal cell, and options C and D correspond to $R = 2r$ and $R = r/3$ respectively.

(c) A. The voltmeter is in parallel with the $600\ \Omega$ resistor, giving $R_p = \dfrac{600 \times 2000}{2600} = 462\ \Omega$. The circuit total becomes $400 + 462 = 862\ \Omega$, so $I = 6.0/862 = 6.96\ \mathrm{mA}$ and the reading is $I R_p = 3.21\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B assumes an ideal meter, option C mixes the loaded resistance with the unloaded total, and option D loads the wrong resistor.

(d) A. True current $I_0 = 12/100 = 0.120\ \mathrm{A}$; with the ammeter in place $I = 12/105 = 0.1143\ \mathrm{A}$. The fractional error is $\dfrac{0.120 - 0.1143}{0.120} = 4.76\%$, which equals $R_A/(R + R_A) = 5.0/105$. (A1) Option B uses $R_A/R$, option C ignores the meter, and option D is the ratio of the two currents rather than the error.

(e) A. The currents are $I_1 = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_2 = 7.2/9.0 = 0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. Since $V = E - Ir$, subtracting gives $6.0 - 7.2 = -r(1.5 - 0.80)$, so $r = 1.2/0.70 = 1.71\ \Omega$ and $E = 8.57\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B inverts the gradient, option C quotes the voltage change, and option D quotes the lost volts.

Markscheme notes

One mark per correct option, no negative marking. In (a) accept 12 W reached by differentiating the power expression or by quoting the maximum power theorem, provided the condition R equals r is stated. In (b) accept 50% or one half; note that a candidate who answers (a) correctly but (b) as two thirds has applied the theorem without understanding it. In (c) accept any value between 3.20 V and 3.22 V from premature rounding of the parallel pair. In (d) accept 4.8% to two significant figures, and credit the exact form 5/105. In (e) accept 1.7 ohms, and allow a graphical solution from a V against I plot provided the gradient is taken with the correct sign. Across the cluster, a candidate who rounds the parallel resistance in (c) prematurely may report anything from 3.20 V to 3.22 V and should be credited; a comparable tolerance applies in (e). In (d) the exact form 5.0 over 105 earns the mark even when left as a fraction. Note that (a) and (b) are formally independent, so a candidate may answer either without the other, and no follow-through between them should be assumed either way.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 12 W correctPower is greatest when the load equals the internal resistance, giving a current of 2.0 amperes and hence I squared R of 12 watts.
    2. B. 48 WThis is E squared over r, the power that would be dissipated inside the cell itself at short circuit rather than in the external load.
    3. C. 24 WThis uses E squared over two r, dropping the factor of four that comes from the load and the internal resistance both being in circuit.
    4. D. 6.0 WThis uses E squared over eight r, applying the maximum power result with an extra factor of two introduced without a reason.
  • (b)
    1. A. One half correctAt maximum power the load equals the internal resistance, so equal power is dissipated in each and exactly half of what the cell generates reaches the load.
    2. B. All of itThis ignores the internal resistance altogether, which is only valid for an ideal cell with no internal dissipation.
    3. C. Two thirdsThis corresponds to a load of twice the internal resistance, which delivers more than half the power but not the maximum possible power.
    4. D. One quarterThis corresponds to a load of one third of the internal resistance, where most of the generated power is lost inside the cell.
  • (c)
    1. A. 3.21 V correctThe voltmeter and the 600 ohm resistor form a parallel pair of about 462 ohms, which then divides the 6.0 volts with the 400 ohm resistor to give 3.21 volts.
    2. B. 3.60 VThis treats the voltmeter as ideal with infinite resistance, ignoring the current it draws and the loading that results.
    3. C. 2.77 VThis combines the loaded resistance with the original unloaded total, changing one part of the circuit and not the other.
    4. D. 3.86 VThis puts the voltmeter across the 400 ohm resistor instead of the 600 ohm one, loading the wrong component of the potential divider.
  • (d)
    1. A. 4.76% correctThe true current is 0.12 amperes and the loaded current is 12 over 105, so the fractional error is the ammeter resistance over the new total of 105 ohms.
    2. B. 5.00%This uses the ammeter resistance over the original resistance alone, forgetting that adding the ammeter also increases the total resistance.
    3. C. 0%This assumes the ammeter is ideal and disturbs nothing, which is the approximation being tested rather than the situation described.
    4. D. 95.2%This reports the ratio of the measured current to the true one rather than the error, answering a different question with a correct calculation.
  • (e)
    1. A. 1.71 $\Omega$ correctThe two loads draw 1.5 and 0.8 amperes, and the internal resistance is the change in terminal voltage divided by the change in current, giving 1.2 over 0.7.
    2. B. 0.583 $\Omega$This is the reciprocal of the correct value, obtained by dividing the change in current by the change in voltage.
    3. C. 1.20 $\Omega$This quotes the change in terminal voltage as though voltage were a resistance, without dividing by the change in current.
    4. D. 2.57 $\Omega$This gives the lost volts inside the cell for the first load rather than the resistance that produced them.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.4 Thermodynamics
syllabus_ref: B.3 Gas laws (ideal gas equation), B.4 Thermodynamics (AHL): first law, work, internal energy, heat engine efficiency
title: B.4 Thermodynamics
q_html:
Stimulus

A fixed amount of monatomic ideal gas is taken round the rectangular cycle ABCDA shown in the table. Each leg is either isochoric (constant volume) or isobaric (constant pressure).

| State | $p$ / Pa | $V$ / m³ | $T$ / K |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $2.0\times10^{5}$ | $5.0\times10^{-3}$ | $300$ |
| B | $4.0\times10^{5}$ | $5.0\times10^{-3}$ | |
| C | $4.0\times10^{5}$ | $1.0\times10^{-2}$ | |
| D | $2.0\times10^{5}$ | $1.0\times10^{-2}$ | |

For a monatomic ideal gas, $U=\dfrac32 nRT$. The amount of gas is $n=0.40\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$.

The cycle runs A → B → C → D → A.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that $T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$, $T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle.

    (Calculate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Calculate the total thermal energy transferred to the gas during one complete cycle.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the efficiency of this cycle as a heat engine, and compare it with the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same maximum and minimum temperatures.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) From $pV=nRT$, with $n$ and $R$ constant, $T\propto pV$.

A → B is isochoric, so $T\propto p$: $\dfrac{T_{B}}{T_{A}}=\dfrac{p_{B}}{p_{A}}=\dfrac{4.0}{2.0}=2 \Rightarrow T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$. (M1)(A1)

B → C is isobaric, so $T\propto V$: $\dfrac{T_{C}}{T_{B}}=\dfrac{V_{C}}{V_{B}}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-2}}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=2 \Rightarrow T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$. (A1)

C → D is isochoric: $\dfrac{T_{D}}{T_{C}}=\dfrac{p_{D}}{p_{C}}=\dfrac{2.0}{4.0}=\dfrac12 \Rightarrow T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$. (A1)

(Consistency check: D → A is isobaric with $\frac{V_A}{V_D}=\frac12$, giving $T_{A}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ as stated.)

(b) Work is done only on the two isochoric-free legs:

B → C: $W=p\,\Delta V=4.0\times10^{5}(1.0\times10^{-2}-5.0\times10^{-3})=4.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3})=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

D → A: $W=p\,\Delta V=2.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3}-1.0\times10^{-2})=-1000\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

$$W_{\text{net}}=2000-1000=1000\ \mathrm{J}$$ (A1)

(Equivalently, the area of the rectangle: $(4.0-2.0)\times10^{5}\times(1.0-0.5)\times10^{-2}=1000\ \mathrm{J}$.)

(c) Heat flows in during the two legs where the temperature rises: A → B and B → C.

A → B (isochoric): $W=0$, so by the first law $Q=\Delta U$.

$$Q_{AB}=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(600-300)=1.5(0.40)(8.31)(300)=1496\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)

B → C (isobaric): $\Delta U=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(1200-600)=2992\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

$W=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ from (b), so by the first law $Q=\Delta U+W$:

$$Q_{BC}=2992+2000=4992\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$Q_{\text{in}}=1496+4992=6488\approx6.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$$

(d)

$$\eta=\frac{W_{\text{net}}}{Q_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1000}{6488}=0.154=15.4\%$$ (A1)

A Carnot engine between $T_{\max}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{\min}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ has

$$\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-\frac{T_{\min}}{T_{\max}}=1-\frac{300}{1200}=0.75=75\%$$ (M1)(A1)

So this cycle achieves only about one fifth of the Carnot efficiency. (A1) The reason is that heat is taken in over a whole *range* of temperatures — including during the isochoric leg A → B, where the gas is still relatively cool — and rejected over a range as well (C → D and D → A). A Carnot engine takes in all of its heat at the single highest temperature and rejects it all at the single lowest; any engine that absorbs heat while its temperature is changing must do worse.

Markscheme notes

(a) Credit either the ratio argument or direct substitution into $T=pV/nR$. Using $R=8.31$ and $n=0.40$ gives $T_{A}=301\ \mathrm{K}$ rather than exactly $300\ \mathrm{K}$; this is rounding in the data and must not be penalised. Award full marks for temperatures given as 600, 1200, 600 K.

(b) Award (A1) for each leg's work with the correct sign, (A1) for the net. Credit the 'area of the p–V loop' method fully if the area is correctly identified as $(p_{2}-p_{1})(V_{2}-V_{1})$.

(c) The key discrimination is *which* legs to include. Candidates who sum $\Delta U$ over the whole cycle get zero (correctly, since it returns to A) and conclude $Q_{\text{in}}=W_{\text{net}}$, which is wrong — heat is also *rejected*. Award (M1) for applying $Q=\Delta U+W$ on a heating leg. Condone 6.4–6.5 kJ given rounding.

(d) Accept 15%–16%. The Carnot comparison must use the *extreme* temperatures of the cycle (300 K and 1200 K), not the mean. The final (A1) is for an explanation in terms of heat being absorbed/rejected across a temperature range; 'real engines are always less efficient' is not sufficient.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
syllabus_ref: A.4 Rigid body mechanics (AHL): torque, moment of inertia of a disc, torque = I x angular acceleration, rotational kinetic energy
title: A flywheel, a hanging mass, and a brake
q_html:
A uniform solid disc of mass $M=2.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R=0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ is mounted on a fixed horizontal axle. A light string is wound round the rim, does not slip, and hangs vertically with a mass $m=0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ attached to its free end. The disc is released from rest and the mass falls a distance $h=0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ before it reaches the floor.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Show that the acceleration of the falling mass is $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+M/2}$ and calculate its value.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the tension in the string while the mass is falling, and explain why it is less than the weight of the mass.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the speed of the mass as it reaches the floor, and verify your answer by comparing the loss of gravitational potential energy with the total kinetic energy gained.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    After the mass lands the string goes slack. A brake then applies a constant torque of $0.24\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ about the axle. Calculate the number of complete revolutions the disc makes before it stops.

    (Calculate)
a_html:
(a) Let $T$ be the string tension and $a$ the acceleration of the mass; the string does not slip, so the angular acceleration of the disc is $\alpha=a/R$. (M1)

For the hanging mass: $mg-T=ma$ (M1)

For the disc, torque $\tau=TR$ and moment of inertia $I=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}$, so $TR=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{R}=\dfrac{1}{2}MRa$, giving $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma$. (M1)(A1)

Substituting: $mg-\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=ma$, so $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+\dfrac{M}{2}}$. (AG)

Numerically $a=\dfrac{0.80\times 9.81}{0.80+1.2}=\dfrac{7.848}{2.0}=3.92\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (A1)

(b) $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.4\times 3.924=4.71\ \mathrm{N}$. (M1)(A1)

The weight of the mass is $mg=0.80\times 9.81=7.85\ \mathrm{N}$, so $T<mg$. (A1) The tension is less than the weight because the mass is accelerating downwards: the resultant downward force $mg-T$ is what supplies its acceleration, and if $T$ equalled $mg$ the mass would not accelerate at all. Equivalently, the tension is the torque that must be provided to give the disc its angular acceleration, and that comes at the cost of part of the weight.

(c) $v^{2}=2ah=2\times 3.924\times 0.90=7.063$, so $v=2.66\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (M1)(A1)

Energy check: loss of potential energy $=mgh=0.80\times 9.81\times 0.90=7.06\ \mathrm{J}$. (M1)

The angular speed of the disc is $\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}=\dfrac{2.6577}{0.35}=7.59\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $I=\dfrac{1}{2}(2.4)(0.35)^{2}=0.1470\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}$, so the rotational kinetic energy is $\dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}(0.1470)(57.66)=4.24\ \mathrm{J}$.

Adding the translational kinetic energy of the mass, $\dfrac{1}{2}(0.80)(2.6577)^{2}=2.83\ \mathrm{J}$, gives $7.06\ \mathrm{J}$, which equals the loss of potential energy. (A1)

(d) At the moment the string goes slack the disc has $\omega=7.59\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and rotational kinetic energy $E_{k}=4.24\ \mathrm{J}$. (M1)

With a constant braking torque, the work done equals the change in rotational kinetic energy: $\tau\theta=E_{k}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{4.238}{0.24}=17.7\ \mathrm{rad}$. (M1)(A1)

$17.7\ \mathrm{rad}=\dfrac{17.66}{2\pi}=2.81$ revolutions, so the disc makes $2$ complete revolutions before stopping. (A1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the (AG) requires both equations of motion to be stated before substitution. A candidate who writes $a=g$ — treating the disc as massless or the tension as zero — earns nothing beyond the first (M1). Accept the use of $I=kMR^{2}$ with $k=1/2$ stated, and accept a solution by energy methods that differentiates an energy expression, provided the tension is still identified. Part (b): award the (A1) for the comparison only if a numerical or symbolic value of $mg$ is given. Part (c): the energy verification mark is independent of the kinematic calculation; a candidate whose kinematics slips but whose energy comparison is internally consistent still earns the final (A1). Follow-through applies from (a).
