Condonation: a candidate who writes the answer to (b) as $0.618\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ or $0.62\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ scores full marks; two or three significant figures are both acceptable here, since the forced resolution is $0.2\ \mathrm{N}$. Follow-through: a candidate whose (b) is $799\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$ and who then obtains $1.39\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in (c) is fully credited the (M1) and (A1) for the method and the arithmetic, and is expected to identify $1.18$ in the second half of (c).

Forfeits: treating the force-time record as a triangle and using $\tfrac{1}{2}F_{\max}t$; taking the sum of the forces as the impulse, which omits the time dimension entirely.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.4 The fuel-cycle arithmetic of a fission reactor carried through from the energy per fission to the mass of enriched uranium per year, and the sensitivity of the comparison with coal to the assumptions behind it
syllabus_ref: E.4 Fission, with E.3 Radioactive decay and B.1 Thermal energy transfers
title: E.4 The fuel-cycle arithmetic of a fission reactor carried through from the energy per fission to the mass of enriched uranium per year, and the sensitivity of the comparison with coal to the assumptions behind it
q_html:
A pressurised water reactor operates with a thermal power output of $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ and converts this to electrical energy with an efficiency of $33\%$. Each fission of a $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nucleus releases $202\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The reactor is refuelled with uranium enriched to $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ by mass, and the remainder is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$, which does not undergo fission in this reactor. Use $N_{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ and one year $= 3.15 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Show that the fission of all the nuclei in $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ would release about $8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ that undergoes fission in one year of continuous operation at the stated output.

    (Determine)
  3. [2 marks](c)

    Determine the mass of enriched uranium that must be loaded each year to supply that quantity of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$, and determine the mass of coal that would be needed each year to generate the same electrical energy in a station burning coal of energy content $2.4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at an efficiency of $38\%$.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate the comparison in part (c) as a measure of the environmental advantage of the reactor, referring to at least two assumptions that the comparison makes.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The number of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nuclei in $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ (M1):
$$N = \frac{1.00}{235 \times 10^{-3}}\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} = \frac{1000}{235} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 2.56 \times 10^{24}.$$

The energy released per fission is
$$202\ \mathrm{MeV} = 202 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.23 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J},$$
so
$$E = 2.56 \times 10^{24} \times 3.23 \times 10^{-11} = 8.28 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J} \approx 8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (A1).$$

(b) The electrical output is
$$P_{e} = 0.33 \times 3.0 \times 10^{9} = 9.9 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{W} \;\; (M1).$$
In one year the electrical energy delivered is
$$E_{e} = 9.9 \times 10^{8} \times 3.15 \times 10^{7} = 3.12 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (M1).$$
All of this comes from fission, so the mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ fissioned is
$$m = \frac{3.12 \times 10^{16}}{8.28 \times 10^{13}} = 377\ \mathrm{kg} \;\; (A1).$$

It is worth noting that the efficiency cancels out of nothing here: the thermal power of $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ is what the fuel must supply, so an alternative route is to use $3.0 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{W}$ directly and compute $m = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{9} \times 3.15 \times 10^{7}}{8.28 \times 10^{13}} = 1141\ \mathrm{kg}$ of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ -- but that is the mass fissioned to supply the *thermal* output, and the electrical output is what the question asks about. Working in electrical energy throughout, as above, avoids the confusion.

(c) The $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ is $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ alone. Since the fuel contains only $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ by mass (M1):
$$m_{\text{fuel}} = \frac{377}{0.040} = 9.4 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 9.4\ \mathrm{tonnes} \;\; (A1).$$
So just under ten tonnes of enriched uranium per year, of which about $9.0\ \mathrm{t}$ is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ that does not fission.

For coal, the energy must be supplied as chemical energy and the conversion is less efficient:
$$m_{\text{coal}} = \frac{3.12 \times 10^{16}}{0.38 \times 2.4 \times 10^{7}} = 3.4 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg} = 3.4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{tonnes} \;\; (A1).$$

The ratio of the two masses is $\dfrac{3.4 \times 10^{9}}{9.4 \times 10^{3}} \approx 3.6 \times 10^{5}$: the coal station consumes about three hundred and sixty thousand times the mass of fuel, each year.

(d) The comparison is a ratio of two masses and it is a real effect -- five and a half orders of magnitude is not a rounding difference -- but it is not a measure of environmental impact, and the assumptions that break the identification are worth naming.

First, the comparison counts only the fuel delivered to the station. It ignores everything upstream of that point, and the two chains are not alike. The coal figure of $3.4 \times 10^{6}$ tonnes is coal that has been mined, washed and transported, and those steps consume energy and produce emissions of their own; but the nuclear figure of $9.4$ tonnes is *enriched* uranium, and enrichment is an energy-intensive process that consumes electricity, historically generated by burning fossil fuel. A fair comparison adds the enrichment energy and the mining and milling energy to the nuclear side, and adds the transport energy to the coal side, before comparing (A1).

Second, the comparison assumes the two stations are otherwise equivalent in what they produce, and they are not. The coal station's $3.4$ million tonnes leave the plant every year as $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ -- roughly $9 \times 10^{6}$ tonnes of it, since each tonne of coal of this energy content gives about $2.6$ tonnes of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ -- which is the environmental advantage the comparison is meant to capture, and it is a genuine one. But the nuclear station produces about $9.4$ tonnes of spent fuel per year which is intensely radioactive for decades and must be stored and eventually disposed of, and the comparison assigns that waste a mass of zero (A1).

Third, the numbers themselves are conditional. The $202\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per fission and the $4.0\%$ enrichment are both stated, and both could be different; more importantly the comparison assumes continuous operation at full output for a whole year, whereas a real reactor is shut for refuelling and maintenance and runs at part load at other times, so the $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ is a lower bound on the $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ consumed per year for a station of this rating. A station with a load factor of $80\%$ would consume about $80\%$ of the fuel but also generate $80\%$ of the energy, so the ratio in (c) is unchanged -- which is worth pointing out, because it shows the ratio is robust to that particular assumption even though the absolute masses are not (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for the number of nuclei from the molar mass and Avogadro's constant, (A1) for the energy, quoted as $8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$ or $8.28 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$. A candidate who uses $235\ \mathrm{u}$ converted to kilograms ($3.90 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$) reaches the same answer by dividing rather than by using the mole, and scores full marks.

(b) (M1) for the electrical power, (M1) for the energy in one year, (A1) for $377\ \mathrm{kg}$. A candidate who obtains $1141\ \mathrm{kg}$ by using the thermal power has misread which output the question asks about and scores the first method mark and nothing else; the phrase "same electrical energy" in (c) settles it. Accept values in the range $3.7$ to $3.8 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

(c) (M1) for dividing by the enrichment fraction, (A1) for $9.4 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$; (A1) for the coal mass $3.4 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The coal calculation can use either the electrical energy (dividing by $0.38$ as well) or the thermal energy; a candidate who uses the electrical energy without dividing by the lower efficiency obtains $1.3 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and forfeits the third mark, because the whole point of the comparison is that the coal station wastes more of its input. Follow-through from (b) is allowed.

(d) (A1) for a first assumption stated and used, (A1) for a second, (A1) for the reasoning that connects the assumption to the conclusion -- that is, a candidate must say not only what the comparison ignores but whether ignoring it strengthens or weakens the claimed advantage. Naming the waste as an unaccounted cost scores the mark; listing "waste" and "emissions" and stopping does not.

Forfeits: treating the $4.0\%$ as the fraction of the uranium that fissions rather than as the fraction of the fuel that is $^{235}\mathrm{U}$; using $238$ in the molar mass because "most of the fuel is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$", which confuses the mass loaded with the mass fissioned. Condonations: answers quoted in tonnes or in kilograms are both accepted, and the ratio in (c) may be given as an order of magnitude ($\sim 10^{5}$).

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: Stopping potential against frequency for two metals
syllabus_ref: E.2 Quantum physics: the photoelectric effect, the stopping potential, Einstein's photoelectric equation, the threshold frequency and the work function, and the interpretation of a graph of stopping potential against frequency
title: Stopping potential against frequency for two metals
q_html:
A student investigates the photoelectric effect using two different metal plates X and Y in the same evacuated tube. For each metal the student illuminates the plate with light of a known frequency f and measures the stopping potential V_s, the reverse potential difference just sufficient to reduce the photocurrent to zero. The figure shows the graph of V_s against f for the two metals. Both sets of readings lie on straight lines, and the two lines are parallel to each other.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Determine the gradient of the lines in the figure, including its unit, and use it to obtain a value for the Planck constant.

    (Determine)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the threshold frequency of each metal from the figure, and hence determine the work function of each metal in electronvolts.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the two lines have the same gradient, and why their intercepts on the frequency axis are different.

    (Explain)
  4. [2 marks](d)

    Calculate the stopping potential for metal X when light of frequency 9.00 x 10^14 Hz is incident on it, and state the corresponding value for metal Y.

    (Calculate)
a_html:
(a) The graph is a straight line for each metal, so the gradient is the same at every point. Reading from the line for metal X: at $f = 10 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ the stopping potential is about 1.8 V, and the line meets the frequency axis at about $5.5 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (M1).

$$\text{gradient} = \frac{1.8 - 0}{10 \times 10^{14} - 5.5 \times 10^{14}} = \frac{1.8}{4.5 \times 10^{14}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\ s}$$ (A1)

The gradient has the unit of volts per hertz, which is V s. Since $eV_s = hf - \phi$, the gradient is $h/e$, so

$$h = e \times \text{gradient} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4.14 \times 10^{-15} = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\ s}$$ (A1)

which agrees with the accepted value.

(b) The threshold frequency is where the line meets the frequency axis, since at that frequency the stopping potential is zero and the photon energy is exactly the work function.

For metal X, $f_0 \approx 5.5 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (A1). Its work function is

$$\phi_X = h f_0 = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 5.55 \times 10^{14} = 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = \frac{3.68 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.3\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

For metal Y, $f_0 \approx 7.7 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, giving

$$\phi_Y = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 7.72 \times 10^{14}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.2\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

(c) The photoelectric equation is $eV_s = hf - \phi$, which rearranges to

$$V_s = \frac{h}{e} f - \frac{\phi}{e}$$

The gradient of the graph is therefore $h/e$ (M1). Both graphs are measurements of the same physical process on different metals, and neither $h$ nor $e$ depends on which metal is used, so the gradient is a constant of nature and must be identical for both lines. This is why the lines are parallel (A1).

The intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi/h$. This does depend on the metal, because the work function is the energy needed to remove an electron from that particular metal, and different metals hold their outer electrons more or less tightly (A1). Metal Y has the higher threshold frequency, so its work function is larger; more energy per photon is needed before any electron can escape. The intercept is therefore a property of the metal while the gradient is a property of nature.

(d) Using $V_s = (h/e)f - \phi/e$ with $f = 9.00 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$:

$$V_s(X) = 4.14 \times 10^{-15} \times 9.00 \times 10^{14} - 2.30 = 3.73 - 2.30 = 1.43\ \mathrm{V}$$ (M1) (A1)

For metal Y the same photon energy is available but the work function is larger by 0.90 eV, so

$$V_s(Y) = 3.73 - 3.20 = 0.53\ \mathrm{V}$$ (A1)

The difference between the two stopping potentials is exactly the difference of the work functions, 0.90 V, which is the vertical separation of the two parallel lines at that frequency.

Markscheme notes

Part (a): M1 for reading two points off a line, A1 for the gradient 4.1 x 10^-15 V s, A1 for the value of h. Accept any gradient from 3.9 to 4.4 x 10^-15 V s and any h from 6.2 to 7.0 x 10^-34 J s, since the graph must be read by eye. The unit must be given; a bare number scores M1 only.

Part (b): A1 for each threshold frequency read from the intercepts, A1 for one correct work function. Accept 5.4 to 5.6 x 10^14 Hz for X and 7.6 to 7.8 x 10^14 Hz for Y, with work functions 2.2 to 2.4 eV and 3.1 to 3.3 eV. A candidate who reads the intercepts from the wrong axis scores nothing here.

Part (c): M1 for identifying the gradient as h/e, A1 for the argument that h and e are constants and so the gradient cannot depend on the metal, A1 for the intercept as phi/h, which does depend on the metal. The second and third marks are independent; a candidate who says only that the lines are parallel because they are parallel scores nothing.

Part (d): M1 for the equation or for using the gradient, A1 for 1.43 V, A1 for 0.53 V. Accept 0.9 V for the difference as an alternative to the second value if both are shown to be consistent.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.3 The force needed to push a block up a ramp is greatest at an intermediate angle, while the work needed falls steadily as the ramp gets steeper
syllabus_ref: A.3 Work, energy and power: work done by a force, conservation of energy. With A.2 Forces and momentum: resolution of forces on an inclined plane, friction
title: A.3 The force needed to push a block up a ramp is greatest at an intermediate angle, while the work needed falls steadily as the ramp gets steeper
q_html:
A block of mass $m$ is pushed at constant speed up a ramp of vertical height $h$, inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the ramp is $\mu = 0.50$. The figure shows the ramp and a graph of the required force against $\theta$.

(a) Show that the force $F$, applied parallel to the ramp, that is needed to keep the block moving at constant speed is

$$F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta).$$

(b) Determine the angle $\theta$ at which this force is greatest.

(c) Show that the total work done against gravity and friction together is

$$W = mgh\,(1 + \mu\cot\theta),$$

and explain why the work becomes smaller as the ramp gets steeper even though, for angles below your answer to part (b), the required force becomes larger. Take $m = 20\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $h = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ in your numerical illustration.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Show that the force parallel to the ramp needed to keep the block moving at constant speed is $F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)$.

    (Show that)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Determine the angle $\theta$ at which the force found in part (a) is greatest.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Show that the total work done is $W = mgh(1 + \mu\cot\theta)$ and explain why it falls as the ramp steepens while the required force may rise.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) At constant speed the resultant force along the ramp is zero, so the applied force balances the component of the weight down the slope and the friction: $F = mg\sin\theta + f$ (M1). The normal reaction is $R = mg\cos\theta$ and $f = \mu R$, so

$$F = mg\sin\theta + \mu mg\cos\theta = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta) \quad \text{(A1)}.$$

(b) Differentiate with respect to $\theta$:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = mg(\cos\theta - \mu\sin\theta).$$

Setting this to zero gives $\tan\theta = \tfrac{1}{\mu} = 2$, so $\theta = 63.4^{\circ}$ (M1) (A1). For $\mu = 0.50$ the second derivative is negative there, so it is a maximum: at $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ the force is $183\ \mathrm{N}$, at $63.4^{\circ}$ it is $219\ \mathrm{N}$ and at $90^{\circ}$ it is $196\ \mathrm{N}$, so the force rises and then falls again.

(c) The distance travelled along the ramp is $s = \tfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$, so

$$W = Fs = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)\frac{h}{\sin\theta} = mgh\left(1 + \mu\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right) = mgh(1 + \mu\cot\theta) \quad \text{(M1)}.$$

As $\theta$ increases, $\cot\theta$ decreases, so $W$ falls towards its limiting value $mgh$, the work against gravity alone (A1). Numerically, $W = 1098\ \mathrm{J}$ at $30^{\circ}$, $736\ \mathrm{J}$ at $63.4^{\circ}$ and $589\ \mathrm{J}$ at $90^{\circ}$. The two quantities move in opposite directions below $63.4^{\circ}$ because they are different things: the force is what the push must match at each instant, while the work is that force multiplied by a distance that shrinks as $\tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ as the ramp steepens. Between $30^{\circ}$ and $63.4^{\circ}$ the force grows by about 20 per cent while the distance falls by about a third, and the distance wins (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for resolving along the ramp with zero resultant, (A1) for the normal reaction and the friction law. A candidate who omits friction on the grounds that the block is moving at constant speed has confused constant speed with zero friction and cannot be credited beyond the first mark.

(b) (M1) for differentiating and setting the derivative to zero; (A1) for 63.4 degrees. Stating that the answer is arctan(1/mu) without the differentiation earns the method mark only if the result is justified. The check that it is a maximum rather than a minimum may be done by citing the values at the ends of the range, which is the safer route for most candidates.

(c) (M1) for the substitution s = h over sin theta and the simplification; (A1) for the observation that cot theta decreases so the work falls monotonically; (A1) for the explanation in terms of force and distance moving in opposite directions. The third mark is for the explanation, not the arithmetic: a candidate who produces the formula and says nothing about the opposite movement has answered a different question.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.1 Kinematics: reading a velocity-time graph
syllabus_ref: A.1 (Kinematics: velocity-time graphs, displacement from the area under a graph, average velocity, acceleration as the gradient)
title: A.1 Kinematics: reading a velocity-time graph
q_html:
The figure is the velocity-time graph for an object moving in a straight line. The object accelerates uniformly from rest, then travels at a constant velocity, then decelerates uniformly until it is momentarily at rest, and then continues to accelerate in the opposite direction. The letters A, B, C and D label the four regions between the line and the time axis: A, B and C lie above the axis and D lies below it. Because the motion is along a single straight line, the sign of the velocity gives the direction of travel, and the area between the line and the axis counts as positive displacement above the axis and negative displacement below it. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this graph, each is worth one mark, and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Determine the displacement of the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph, taking account of the direction of travel.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 70.5 m
    2. B. 73.5 m
    3. C. 72.0 m
    4. D. 69.0 m
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Determine the acceleration of the object at the instant t = 11 s, at which the object is momentarily at rest.

    (Determine)
    1. A. -3.0 m s^-2
    2. B. 0 m s^-2
    3. C. -1.5 m s^-2
    4. D. +3.0 m s^-2
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Calculate the average velocity of the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 5.88 m s^-1
    2. B. 6.13 m s^-1
    3. C. 7.05 m s^-1
    4. D. 5.63 m s^-1
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Calculate the total distance travelled by the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 73.5 m
    2. B. 70.5 m
    3. C. 72.0 m
    4. D. 75.0 m
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Determine the speed of the object at the instant t = 9.5 s.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 4.5 m s^-1
    2. B. 5.6 m s^-1
    3. C. 3.0 m s^-1
    4. D. 9.0 m s^-1
a_html:
(a) A. The displacement is the signed area between the graph and the time axis. From 0 to 3.0 s the region is a triangle, $\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(9.0) = 13.5$ m; from 3.0 s to 8.0 s it is a rectangle, $(5.0)(9.0) = 45$ m; from 8.0 s to 11 s it is a triangle, $\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(9.0) = 13.5$ m; from 11 s to 12 s it is a triangle below the axis, $\frac{1}{2}(1.0)(-3.0) = -1.5$ m. Adding, $13.5 + 45 + 13.5 - 1.5 = 70.5$ m. (A1)

(b) A. The acceleration is the gradient of the graph. From 8.0 s to 12 s the graph is one straight line, so the gradient is constant over that whole interval and is $(v_{12} - v_8)/(12 - 8) = (-3.0 - 9.0)/4.0 = -3.0$ m s$^{-2}$. The velocity happens to be zero at t = 11 s, but that says nothing about the gradient: the object is passing through rest, not sitting at it. (A1)

(c) A. Average velocity is displacement divided by time, $70.5/12 = 5.875$, i.e. 5.88 m s$^{-1}$. (A1)

(d) A. Distance travelled treats every area as positive, so $13.5 + 45 + 13.5 + 1.5 = 73.5$ m. The difference between this and the answer to (a) is twice the final area, 3.0 m, which is the ground covered while moving backwards and then given up again. (A1)

(e) A. On 8.0 s to 11 s the velocity falls at 3.0 m s$^{-2}$, so $v(9.5) = 9.0 - 3.0(9.5 - 8.0) = 9.0 - 4.5 = 4.5$ m s$^{-1}$. Since the velocity is still positive there, the speed equals the velocity. (A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer. (a) Accept 70.5 m. The distractors are all arithmetic consequences of a defensible misreading, so a candidate who answers B has found the distance and a candidate who answers C has stopped the motion at t = 11 s. (b) This is the hardest question in the cluster and the one most often failed: accept only -3.0 m s$^{-2}$. An answer of 0 m s$^{-2}$ is the error the question exists to detect, because it confuses a zero value of the function with a zero value of its gradient. (c) Accept 5.88 m s$^{-1}$. An answer of 6.13 m s$^{-1}$ is the average speed and shows the candidate has not separated the two averages. (d) Accept 73.5 m. (e) Accept 4.5 m s$^{-1}$; accept -4.5 m s$^{-1}$ only if the candidate has explicitly read the gradient as positive, since the question asks for speed and the velocity at 9.5 s is positive. Where a candidate's two answers to (a) and (d) differ by exactly 3.0 m, the pair is internally consistent and both are likely to be right.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 70.5 m correctThe signed areas are 13.5 m, 45 m, 13.5 m and -1.5 m, and these sum to 70.5 m, so the object finishes 70.5 m from where it started.
    2. B. 73.5 mThis adds the final area as though it were positive, which gives the total distance travelled rather than the displacement.
    3. C. 72.0 mThis ignores the motion after t = 11 s altogether, summing only the three areas above the axis.
    4. D. 69.0 mThis subtracts the final triangle twice, treating its area as 3.0 m rather than the 1.5 m that the graph actually encloses.
  • (b)
    1. A. -3.0 m s^-2 correctThe graph is a single straight line from t = 8 s to t = 12 s, so its gradient is (-3.0 - 9.0)/4.0 = -3.0 m s^-2 throughout, including the instant at which the velocity passes through zero.
    2. B. 0 m s^-2This is the standard error of reading a velocity of zero as an acceleration of zero; the velocity is zero at that instant but it is changing.
    3. C. -1.5 m s^-2This takes half of the true gradient, which would be correct only if the deceleration lasted twice as long as it does.
    4. D. +3.0 m s^-2The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong, and the sign is the whole point: the object is decelerating, not accelerating forwards.
  • (c)
    1. A. 5.88 m s^-1 correctAverage velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, so 70.5 m divided by 12 s, which is 5.88 m s^-1.
    2. B. 6.13 m s^-1This divides the total distance travelled by the time, which gives the average speed rather than the average velocity.
    3. C. 7.05 m s^-1This divides the displacement by 10 s, as though the motion had ended when the object first came to rest.
    4. D. 5.63 m s^-1This removes the final area twice before dividing by 12 s, which is the same double subtraction that produces option D in part (a).
  • (d)
    1. A. 73.5 m correctEvery area is counted as positive, so the distance is 13.5 + 45 + 13.5 + 1.5 = 73.5 m, which is 3.0 m more than the displacement.
    2. B. 70.5 mThis is the displacement, which cancels the final 1.5 m instead of adding it, so it undercounts the ground covered by 3.0 m.
    3. C. 72.0 mThis ignores the final second of motion entirely, as though the object stopped at t = 11 s instead of reversing.
    4. D. 75.0 mThis treats the final triangle as enclosing 3.0 m rather than 1.5 m, which doubles the contribution of the last second.
  • (e)
    1. A. 4.5 m s^-1 correctFrom t = 8 s to t = 11 s the velocity falls linearly from 9.0 m s^-1 to zero, so at t = 9.5 s it has fallen by 3.0 x 1.5 = 4.5 m s^-1, leaving 4.5 m s^-1.
    2. B. 5.6 m s^-1This takes the deceleration to run from 8 s to 12 s rather than to 11 s, which spreads the same change in velocity over four seconds instead of three.
    3. C. 3.0 m s^-1This quotes the magnitude of the acceleration as though it were the speed at that instant.
    4. D. 9.0 m s^-1This keeps the velocity at its value at t = 8 s and ignores the deceleration that has already taken place by t = 9.5 s.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.1 Kinematics
syllabus_ref: A.1 (Kinematics: displacement, velocity, acceleration, projectile motion, relative velocity)
title: A.1 Kinematics
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on kinematics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ where a numerical value is needed, and give each answer to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A projectile is launched from level ground at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $40^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    2. B. $30.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    3. C. $19.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    4. D. zero
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Two projectiles are launched from the same point at the same speed, one at an angle $\theta$ and the other at $90^{\circ}-\theta$, where $\theta \ne 45^{\circ}$. Both land at the launch height. Which statement is correct?

    (Determine)
    1. A. Both have the same range, but the projectile launched at the larger angle is in the air for longer.
    2. B. Both are in the air for the same time, but the projectile launched at the larger angle travels further.
    3. C. The steeper launch has both the greater range and the greater time of flight.
    4. D. The shallower launch has the greater range and the greater time of flight.
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A ball is released from rest at the same instant that an identical ball at the same height is fired horizontally. Both balls experience air resistance with a drag force proportional to their speed. Which statement is correct?

    (Determine)
    1. A. Both balls reach the ground at the same time.
    2. B. The fired ball lands later, because the drag opposing its horizontal motion also slows its descent.
    3. C. The dropped ball lands later, because it has the lower speed and so experiences less drag.
    4. D. The fired ball lands later, because it travels along a longer path.
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A particle moves along a straight line at $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and then at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction for $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What are its average speed and its average velocity over the $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. Average speed $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    2. B. Average speed $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    3. C. Average speed $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    4. D. Average speed $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A boat whose speed in still water is $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ must cross a river $120\ \mathrm{m}$ wide in which the current flows at $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the shortest possible crossing time, and how far downstream does the boat land?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $30\ \mathrm{s}$, landing $90\ \mathrm{m}$ downstream
    2. B. $45\ \mathrm{s}$, landing $90\ \mathrm{m}$ downstream
    3. C. $30\ \mathrm{s}$, landing directly opposite
    4. D. $45\ \mathrm{s}$, landing directly opposite
a_html:
(a) A. Resolve the launch velocity: the horizontal component is $30\cos 40^{\circ}=22.98$ and the vertical component is $30\sin 40^{\circ}=19.28$. The horizontal component is constant throughout, and at the highest point the vertical component has been reduced to zero by gravity, so the speed there is simply $22.98$, i.e. $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) The near miss is C, which reports the component that has vanished rather than the one that remains.

(b) A. The range is $v^{2}\sin 2\theta/g$, and $\sin\bigl(2(90^{\circ}-\theta)\bigr)=\sin(180^{\circ}-2\theta)=\sin 2\theta$, so the two ranges are equal. The flight time is $2v\sin\theta/g$, which is larger for the larger angle. (A1) Distractor D inverts both conclusions and C gets only the time right.

(c) A. With drag $\mathbf{F}=-k\mathbf{v}$ the component equations are separate: vertically, $m\dot v_{y}=-kv_{y}-mg$ for both balls, with the same initial condition $v_{y}=0$. The horizontal motion therefore cannot influence the descent, and both land together. (A1) This is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and B, C and D are all attempts to make the longer or faster trajectory cost time.

(d) A. Distance $=8.0(3.0)+4.0(2.0)=24+8=32\ \mathrm{m}$; displacement $=24-8=16\ \mathrm{m}$. Dividing by $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$ gives an average speed of $6.4$ and an average velocity of $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) The pair is what is being tested: many candidates compute one correctly and then quote it twice.

(e) A. The crossing time is the width divided by the component of the boat's velocity perpendicular to the bank. That component is greatest, at the full $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, when the boat points straight across, so $t=120/4.0=30\ \mathrm{s}$ and the drift is $3.0\times30=90\ \mathrm{m}$. (A1) D is the trap: $45\ \mathrm{s}$ and landing opposite is a correct calculation of the *shortest path*, since the resultant speed is then $\sqrt{4.0^{2}-3.0^{2}}=2.65\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $120/2.65=45\ \mathrm{s}$, but the question asks for the shortest time.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $23.0$ or $23.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (b) The reasoning mark is implicit in the key: a candidate who states equal ranges but equal times has not earned it. (c) This is the hardest item in the cluster and the one most likely to be guessed wrong; accept any answer that identifies the independence of the components, and note that the result would be different for drag proportional to the square of the speed, where the components no longer separate and the fired ball would in fact land later. (d) Accept fractions; the unit mark is not separate here. (e) Award no follow-through from a mistaken minimum-time aim: the $45\ \mathrm{s}$ figure belongs to a different optimisation and using it for the drift gives $135\ \mathrm{m}$, which is not offered. Candidates who eliminate C and D first, on the grounds that cancelling the current must cost time, are using the strongest route to the key.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ correctAt the highest point the vertical component of the velocity is zero, so the speed is just the unchanged horizontal component $30\cos 40^{\circ}$, which is $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
    2. B. $30.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This keeps the launch speed, forgetting that the horizontal component is only part of it and that the vertical part has been removed.
    3. C. $19.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This is the vertical component $30\sin 40^{\circ}$, which is the part reduced to zero at the top rather than the part that survives.
    4. D. zeroThis treats the highest point as an instant of rest, confusing the vertical component with the whole velocity vector.
  • (b)
    1. A. Both have the same range, but the projectile launched at the larger angle is in the air for longer. correctThe range depends on $\sin 2\theta$, which takes the same value for complementary angles, while the flight time depends on $\sin\theta$, so the steeper launch stays up longer.
    2. B. Both are in the air for the same time, but the projectile launched at the larger angle travels further.This reverses the two results: the flight times differ because the vertical components differ, and the ranges do not.
    3. C. The steeper launch has both the greater range and the greater time of flight.The time claim is right but the range claim is wrong, because complementary angles share the same value of $\sin 2\theta$.
    4. D. The shallower launch has the greater range and the greater time of flight.Both claims are inverted: the shallower launch is in the air for the shorter time, and neither launch has the greater range.
  • (c)
    1. A. Both balls reach the ground at the same time. correctWhen the drag force is proportional to velocity the component equations separate, so the vertical motion is unaffected by how fast the ball is moving horizontally and both balls fall identically.
    2. B. The fired ball lands later, because the drag opposing its horizontal motion also slows its descent.Drag opposes the velocity vector, and for drag proportional to speed each component of the drag depends only on that component of the velocity.
    3. C. The dropped ball lands later, because it has the lower speed and so experiences less drag.The drag acts on each velocity component separately, so the total speed of the ball is irrelevant to how fast it falls.
    4. D. The fired ball lands later, because it travels along a longer path.Path length does not determine the fall time; only the vertical motion does, and the two vertical motions are identical.
  • (d)
    1. A. Average speed $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ correctThe distance travelled is $32\ \mathrm{m}$ and the displacement is $16\ \mathrm{m}$, so dividing each by $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$ gives $6.4$ and $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ respectively.
    2. B. Average speed $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This swaps the two definitions, dividing displacement by time to obtain a speed and distance by time to obtain a velocity.
    3. C. Average speed $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This divides distance by time twice, ignoring that the second stage partly undoes the displacement gained in the first.
    4. D. Average speed $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, average velocity $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$The velocity is right but the speed takes the unweighted mean of the two speeds instead of weighting each by the time it applies.
  • (e)
    1. A. $30\ \mathrm{s}$, landing $90\ \mathrm{m}$ downstream correctPointing the boat straight across maximises the cross-river component at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, giving $30\ \mathrm{s}$, during which the current carries the boat $90\ \mathrm{m}$ downstream.
    2. B. $45\ \mathrm{s}$, landing $90\ \mathrm{m}$ downstreamThe drift is right but the time belongs to a different aim; the crossing time is set only by the cross-river component of the boat's velocity.
    3. C. $30\ \mathrm{s}$, landing directly oppositeThis assumes the current can be cancelled at no cost, but cancelling it uses part of the boat's speed and therefore lengthens the crossing.
    4. D. $45\ \mathrm{s}$, landing directly oppositeThis is the time for the shortest path rather than the shortest time, so it correctly describes a different journey and answers a different question.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.4 Thermodynamics
syllabus_ref: B.4 (Thermodynamics: first law, internal energy, work, heat engine efficiency, second law)
title: B.4 Thermodynamics
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on thermodynamics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Throughout, take the gas to be ideal unless a question says otherwise, and remember that the first law relates the change in internal energy to both the thermal energy transferred and the work done. Use $R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ where it is needed.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A gas is compressed adiabatically. Which statement about the gas is correct?

    (State)
    1. A. Its internal energy increases by an amount equal to the work done on it.
    2. B. Its internal energy is unchanged, because no heat is transferred.
    3. C. Work is done by the gas and its internal energy falls.
    4. D. Its temperature is unchanged, because the process is adiabatic.
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A gas absorbs $500\ \mathrm{J}$ of thermal energy and expands, doing $200\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. An increase of $300\ \mathrm{J}$
    2. B. An increase of $700\ \mathrm{J}$
    3. C. A decrease of $300\ \mathrm{J}$
    4. D. An increase of $500\ \mathrm{J}$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A heat engine takes in $900\ \mathrm{J}$ from a reservoir at $600\ \mathrm{K}$ and rejects heat to a reservoir at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. It does $300\ \mathrm{J}$ of work in each cycle. What are its actual efficiency and the maximum efficiency possible between these temperatures?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $33\%$ and $50\%$
    2. B. $33\%$ and $67\%$
    3. C. $50\%$ and $33\%$
    4. D. $67\%$ and $50\%$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ from a volume $V$ to a volume $2V$. How much work is done by the gas?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}$
    2. B. $2.49\ \mathrm{kJ}$
    3. C. $1.25\ \mathrm{kJ}$
    4. D. zero
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Which of the following processes is permitted by the second law of thermodynamics?

    (Determine)
    1. A. A gas expanding into an evacuated chamber with no other change anywhere.
    2. B. Thermal energy flowing spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body with no other change.
    3. C. A heat engine converting all the thermal energy it absorbs into work over a complete cycle.
    4. D. The total entropy of an isolated system decreasing.
a_html:
(a) A. Adiabatic means $Q=0$, so the first law $\Delta U = Q - W_{\text{by}}$ becomes $\Delta U = -W_{\text{by}} = W_{\text{on}}$. Compressing the gas means work is done *on* it, so $\Delta U>0$ and the temperature rises. (A1) B confuses adiabatic with isothermal and D then inherits that confusion.

(b) A. With $W_{\text{by}}=+200\ \mathrm{J}$ and $Q=+500\ \mathrm{J}$, $\Delta U = 500-200=+300\ \mathrm{J}$. (A1) The sign convention is the whole question: B adds, C keeps the magnitude but flips the sign.

(c) A. The achieved efficiency is $\eta = W/Q_{\text{in}} = 300/900 = 0.333$. The Carnot limit depends only on the reservoir temperatures: $\eta_{C}=1-T_{C}/T_{H}=1-300/600=0.500$. (A1) The two numbers answer different questions and D, at $67\%$, comes from subtracting the achieved efficiency from one and so reporting the rejected fraction of the input as if it were the useful output.

(d) A. For an isothermal change $pV=nRT$ is constant, so $W=\int p\,dV = nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1}) = 8.31\times300\times\ln 2 = 1.73\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$. (A1) B is $nRT$ with the logarithm omitted, and C treats the pressure as falling linearly so that a mean pressure could be used.

(e) A. Free expansion into a vacuum does no work and involves no heat transfer, so $\Delta U=0$ for an ideal gas, but the entropy increases because the gas occupies a larger volume. The second law forbids the other three: B is the Clausius statement, C is the Kelvin statement, and D contradicts the entropy form directly. (A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any answer that identifies the internal energy as increasing by the work done on the gas. (b) Candidates using the opposite sign convention consistently, so that work done on the gas is positive, should still be credited if their arithmetic and conclusion match their convention. (c) Accept $33$ or $33.3\%$ and $50\%$; a candidate who quotes the Carnot value as the achieved efficiency has not distinguished the two ideas and earns nothing. (d) Accept $1.7$ to $1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}$; note that $\ln 2$ is the only place a logarithm appears in this subtopic and it is frequently forgotten. (e) Accept any correct statement of why free expansion is permitted; a candidate who says it is permitted because no heat flows has the right answer for the wrong reason, since the decisive point is that the entropy increases. Note that B and C are both statements of the second law rather than the first, so a candidate who justifies rejecting them by saying energy would not be conserved has used the wrong law and should not be credited. Candidates often find (e) the hardest item despite it requiring no calculation, because it asks which process is permitted rather than which is forbidden; three of the four options are familiar prohibitions, so the correct answer looks wrong at first reading.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. Its internal energy increases by an amount equal to the work done on it. correctAdiabatic means no heat enters or leaves, so the first law reduces to the change in internal energy being equal to the work done on the gas, and the temperature rises.
    2. B. Its internal energy is unchanged, because no heat is transferred.This confuses adiabatic with isothermal; work is still done on the gas, and that work raises the internal energy.
    3. C. Work is done by the gas and its internal energy falls.This describes an adiabatic expansion, not a compression, so both the sign of the work and the change in internal energy are reversed.
    4. D. Its temperature is unchanged, because the process is adiabatic.A constant temperature in a gas usually requires heat to flow, which is precisely what an adiabatic change forbids.
  • (b)
    1. A. An increase of $300\ \mathrm{J}$ correctWith the sign convention that work done by the gas is positive, the first law gives a change in internal energy of $500-200=300\ \mathrm{J}$.
    2. B. An increase of $700\ \mathrm{J}$This adds the work instead of subtracting it, treating work done by the gas as though it were further energy supplied to the gas.
    3. C. A decrease of $300\ \mathrm{J}$The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong; the gas absorbs more energy as heat than it loses by doing work.
    4. D. An increase of $500\ \mathrm{J}$This ignores the work term altogether and equates the change in internal energy with the heat supplied.
  • (c)
    1. A. $33\%$ and $50\%$ correctThe actual efficiency is the work output divided by the heat input, $300/900=33\%$, while the Carnot limit is one minus the ratio of the reservoir temperatures, $1-300/600=50\%$.
    2. B. $33\%$ and $67\%$The actual efficiency is right but the limit uses the ratio of temperatures the wrong way round, giving the complement of the Carnot value.
    3. C. $50\%$ and $33\%$This swaps the two quantities, reporting the Carnot limit as the achieved efficiency.
    4. D. $67\%$ and $50\%$This subtracts the achieved efficiency from one, reporting the fraction of the input energy that is rejected rather than the fraction that is converted to work.
  • (d)
    1. A. $1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}$ correctFor an isothermal change the work is $nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1}) = 8.31\times300\times\ln 2 = 1728\ \mathrm{J}$, which is $1.73\ \mathrm{kJ}$.
    2. B. $2.49\ \mathrm{kJ}$This is $nRT$ alone and omits the logarithm that comes from integrating the falling pressure over the expansion.
    3. C. $1.25\ \mathrm{kJ}$This takes half of $nRT$, treating the pressure as though it fell linearly with volume so that an average pressure could be used.
    4. D. zeroThis confuses an isothermal change with an isochoric one; a constant temperature does not mean a constant volume.
  • (e)
    1. A. A gas expanding into an evacuated chamber with no other change anywhere. correctFree expansion is irreversible and therefore allowed; the entropy of the gas increases, so the second law is satisfied rather than violated.
    2. B. Thermal energy flowing spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body with no other change.This is the Clausius statement of the second law and is forbidden; such a transfer is only possible if work is supplied, as in a refrigerator.
    3. C. A heat engine converting all the thermal energy it absorbs into work over a complete cycle.This is the Kelvin statement of the second law and is forbidden; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir.
    4. D. The total entropy of an isolated system decreasing.The entropy of an isolated system can never decrease; it stays constant for a reversible change and increases for an irreversible one.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.2 Wave model
syllabus_ref: C.2 (Wave model: reflection, refraction, superposition, interference, polarisation)
title: C.2 Wave model
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on the wave model. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Unless a question says otherwise, the frequency of a wave is fixed by its source and does not change when the wave crosses a boundary between two media.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A transverse pulse travels along a stretched string whose far end is rigidly clamped. What happens to the pulse when it reaches the clamped end?

    (State)
    1. A. It is reflected and inverted.
    2. B. It is reflected without being inverted.
    3. C. It passes into the support without reflection.
    4. D. It is inverted only if the pulse amplitude is large enough.
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A water wave of frequency $2.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$ travels from deep water, where its speed is $0.80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, into shallow water, where its speed is $0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What happens to its wavelength?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. It decreases from $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ to $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$.
    2. B. It increases from $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ to $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$.
    3. C. It stays at $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$.
    4. D. It decreases from $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ to $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$.
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Two coherent sources emit in phase. At a point P the difference in the distances from the two sources to P is $1.5\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength. What is observed at P?

    (Determine)
    1. A. A minimum, because the path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths.
    2. B. A maximum, because the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
    3. C. A maximum, because the path difference corresponds to a phase difference of $180^{\circ}$.
    4. D. Neither a maximum nor a minimum, because the condition only applies when the path difference is zero.
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Two coherent waves of amplitudes $3A$ and $A$ superpose in phase. What is the ratio of the intensity of the resultant wave to the intensity of the larger wave on its own?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1.78$
    2. B. $1.33$
    3. C. $1.11$
    4. D. $16$
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Unpolarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on a polariser. A second polariser, whose transmission axis is at $60^{\circ}$ to the first, is placed after it. What is the intensity of the light emerging from the second polariser?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $0.125\,I_{0}$
    2. B. $0.25\,I_{0}$
    3. C. $0.50\,I_{0}$
    4. D. $0.75\,I_{0}$
a_html:
(a) A. A clamped end is a fixed boundary: the displacement there must be zero at every instant, so the reflected pulse must cancel the incident one at that point, which means it is inverted. A free end gives an uninverted reflection instead. (A1) The distinction is the boundary condition, not the size of the pulse.

(b) A. Frequency is set by the source and is unchanged on crossing the boundary. With $v=f\lambda$, the deep-water wavelength is $0.80/2.0=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ and the shallow-water wavelength is $0.60/2.0=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. (A1) C is the common error: it is the frequency that is invariant, not the wavelength.

(c) A. A path difference of $1.5\lambda$ equals three half-wavelengths, an odd number, so the phase difference is $3\pi$ radians, equivalent to $\pi$, and the superposing arrivals cancel. (A1) C is the trap worth noting: it names the correct phase difference and then draws the opposite conclusion.

(d) A. Amplitudes add before squaring: the resultant is $3A+A=4A$, so the resultant intensity is proportional to $16A^{2}$ while the larger wave alone is proportional to $9A^{2}$, giving $16/9=1.78$. (A1) B omits the squaring and C treats the waves as incoherent, which would give $(9+1)/9=1.11$ and would be right only if the phase relationship were random.

(e) A. The first polariser transmits half the unpolarised intensity, giving $I_{0}/2$ of plane-polarised light. Malus' law then multiplies by $\cos^{2}60^{\circ}=0.25$, so the final intensity is $I_{0}/2\times0.25=0.125\,I_{0}$. (A1) B, at $0.25\,I_{0}$, is Malus' law applied without the initial halving.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any statement that the pulse is reflected and inverted; a candidate who adds that the reflection at a free end is not inverted shows the contrasting case and should not be penalised for the extra material. (b) Accept $0.40$ and $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$; the mark is for holding the frequency constant, so a candidate who changes the frequency and gets both wavelengths wrong earns nothing. (c) Accept any justification in terms of an odd number of half-wavelengths; note that $1.5\lambda$ and $2.5\lambda$ give the same verdict, so the answer does not depend on which odd multiple was chosen. (d) Accept $1.7$ to $1.8$, or the exact fraction $16/9$; a candidate who writes $16$ has done the hard part and then omitted the division, and should be given the benefit of the doubt only if the ratio was clearly intended. (e) Accept $0.125$ or $I_{0}/8$; the two-stage structure is the point, so a single-stage answer earns nothing.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. It is reflected and inverted. correctA fixed end cannot move, so the incident and reflected displacements must cancel there, which requires the reflected pulse to be inverted relative to the incident one.
    2. B. It is reflected without being inverted.An unchanged reflection happens at a free end, where the string is able to move; a clamped end imposes the opposite boundary condition.
    3. C. It passes into the support without reflection.The clamp is a boundary between media of very different impedance, so almost all of the pulse energy is reflected rather than transmitted.
    4. D. It is inverted only if the pulse amplitude is large enough.Inversion follows from the boundary condition and not from the amplitude, so it happens for a pulse of any size.
  • (b)
    1. A. It decreases from $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ to $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. correctThe frequency is unchanged across the boundary at $2.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so the wavelength is speed divided by frequency: $0.80/2.0=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ becomes $0.60/2.0=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$.
    2. B. It increases from $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ to $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$.This has the change in the right direction but the wrong starting values, as though the wave were travelling from shallow water into deep.
    3. C. It stays at $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$.This keeps the wavelength fixed across the boundary, confusing wavelength with frequency, which is the quantity that does stay fixed.
    4. D. It decreases from $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ to $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$.This scales the wavelength by the ratio of the speeds a second time, as though the frequency changed as well as the speed.
  • (c)
    1. A. A minimum, because the path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths. correctA path difference of $1.5\lambda$ is three half-wavelengths, an odd number, which corresponds to a phase difference of $540^{\circ}$, equivalent to $180^{\circ}$, so the arrivals cancel.
    2. B. A maximum, because the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.One and a half is not a whole number of wavelengths, so the two arrivals are not in phase and cannot reinforce.
    3. C. A maximum, because the path difference corresponds to a phase difference of $180^{\circ}$.The phase difference is stated correctly but the conclusion is inverted; a $180^{\circ}$ phase difference is precisely the condition for cancellation.
    4. D. Neither a maximum nor a minimum, because the condition only applies when the path difference is zero.Both maxima and minima occur at non-zero path differences, at whole wavelengths and odd half-wavelengths respectively.
  • (d)
    1. A. $1.78$ correctAmplitudes add first, giving a resultant of $4A$, and intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so the ratio is $16A^{2}/9A^{2}=16/9=1.78$.
    2. B. $1.33$This takes the ratio of the amplitudes rather than of the intensities, forgetting to square before comparing.
    3. C. $1.11$This adds the two intensities as though the waves were incoherent, which discards the interference term that dominates here.
    4. D. $16$This squares the resultant amplitude but forgets to divide by the intensity of the larger wave, so it is not a ratio.
  • (e)
    1. A. $0.125\,I_{0}$ correctThe first polariser halves the unpolarised intensity to $I_{0}/2$ and the second applies Malus' law, multiplying by the square of the cosine of $60^{\circ}$, giving $0.5\times0.25=0.125\,I_{0}$.
    2. B. $0.25\,I_{0}$This applies Malus' law but forgets that the first polariser halves the intensity of the unpolarised beam before the second one acts.
    3. C. $0.50\,I_{0}$This uses the cosine of $60^{\circ}$ rather than its square, which Malus' law does not do, since intensity depends on the square of the field amplitude.
    4. D. $0.75\,I_{0}$This appears to treat the angle as reducing the intensity by a simple factor of one minus the cosine, which has no basis in Malus' law.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.5 Galilean and special relativity
syllabus_ref: A.5 (Galilean and special relativity)
title: A.5 Galilean and special relativity
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on special relativity. Each stands alone, so any one of them can be attempted without the others. Unless a question says otherwise, $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the Lorentz factor is $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$. All frames referred to are inertial, and every speed quoted is measured relative to the frame named in that question rather than relative to any other object.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A spacecraft receding from Earth at $0.60c$ switches on a forward-pointing lamp. What speed does an observer on Earth measure for the light leaving the lamp?

    (State)
    1. A. $c$
    2. B. $1.60c$
    3. C. $0.40c$
    4. D. $0.60c$
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A muon has a mean lifetime of $2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ measured in its own rest frame. What mean lifetime does a laboratory observer measure for muons travelling at $0.98c$?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $11\ \mathrm{\mu s}$
    2. B. $2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}$
    3. C. $0.44\ \mathrm{\mu s}$
    4. D. $16\ \mathrm{\mu s}$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A rod of proper length $100\ \mathrm{m}$ moves lengthwise at $0.80c$ past a stationary observer. What length does that observer measure?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $60\ \mathrm{m}$
    2. B. $100\ \mathrm{m}$
    3. C. $80\ \mathrm{m}$
    4. D. $167\ \mathrm{m}$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Two spacecraft approach each other head-on, each moving at $0.75c$ relative to Earth. At what speed does the pilot of one see the other approach?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $0.96c$
    2. B. $1.50c$
    3. C. $3.43c$
    4. D. $0.75c$
  5. [1 mark](e)

    An electron has total energy $1.533\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Taking its rest energy as $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$, what is its speed?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $0.943c$
    2. B. $0.816c$
    3. C. $0.667c$
    4. D. $0.333c$
a_html:
(a) A. The second postulate fixes the speed of light at $c$ for every inertial observer, so the source's motion is irrelevant and no transformation is needed. (A1) B and C are the two Galilean habits, and they are listed because $1.60c$ and $0.40c$ are the numbers a student actually produces rather than numbers chosen at random.

(b) A. The lifetime quoted for the muon at rest is the proper time, so it is the shortest of all measured lifetimes and the laboratory value is larger: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-0.98^{2}} = 5.03$, giving $5.03 \times 2.2 = 11\ \mathrm{\mu s}$. (A1) This is the effect that lets muons created in the upper atmosphere reach sea level at all.

(c) A. The proper length is measured in the rod's own frame, and the moving observer measures $L = L_{0}/\gamma = 100/1.67 = 60\ \mathrm{m}$. (A1) The identification of which length is proper is the whole question; the division is trivial once that is settled.

(d) A. Neither spacecraft's frame is the Earth frame, so the speeds must be combined with $u' = (u+v)/(1+uv/c^{2}) = 1.50/1.5625 = 0.96c$. (A1) The denominator is what keeps the result below $c$.

(e) A. $\gamma = E/E_{0} = 1.533/0.511 = 3.00$, and inverting $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}$ gives $\beta = \sqrt{1-1/9} = 0.943$. (A1) The three distractors are all the same omission at different depths.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ written in full; no credit for any option that depends on the source speed. (b) Accept $11$ to $11.1\ \mathrm{\mu s}$; award nothing if the candidate quotes $\gamma$ correctly and then divides, since the direction of the effect is the point being tested. (c) Accept $60\ \mathrm{m}$ or $60.0\ \mathrm{m}$; a candidate who states that the transverse dimensions are unchanged shows useful extra knowledge and should not be penalised. (d) Accept $0.96c$ or $2.88 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; any answer above $c$ is wrong on principle and should be treated as evidence the transformation was not used, whichever sign error produced it. (e) Accept $0.94c$; the exact surd $\sqrt{8/9}$ is preferable but not required. Watch for candidates who convert $1.533\ \mathrm{MeV}$ to joules and then lose a factor of $10^{6}$; the ratio method avoids this entirely and is worth encouraging in feedback.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. $c$ correctThe second postulate puts the speed of light at $c$ in every inertial frame, so neither the motion of the source nor the motion of the observer changes the measured value.
    2. B. $1.60c$This is Galilean addition of the source speed and the light speed, and it is precisely the relativistic result that the second postulate rules out.
    3. C. $0.40c$This subtracts the source speed from $c$ as though the light were a material object launched from a moving platform, which is a Galilean transformation.
    4. D. $0.60c$This assigns the light the speed of its source, discarding the photon's own motion entirely rather than transforming it.
  • (b)
    1. A. $11\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ correctThe rest-frame lifetime is the proper time interval, so the laboratory measures the dilated value $\gamma \times 2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ with $\gamma = 5.03$, giving $11\ \mathrm{\mu s}$.
    2. B. $2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}$This ignores time dilation altogether and quotes the proper lifetime as though it were frame-independent.
    3. C. $0.44\ \mathrm{\mu s}$This divides by $\gamma$ instead of multiplying, which would make the moving lifetime shorter than the rest lifetime and contradicts the muon reaching the ground.
    4. D. $16\ \mathrm{\mu s}$This comes from using $1 - \beta$ rather than $1 - \beta^{2}$ inside the square root, that is, from forgetting to square the speed ratio.
  • (c)
    1. A. $60\ \mathrm{m}$ correctLength contraction divides the proper length by $\gamma = 1.67$, and the proper length is the one measured in the frame where the rod is at rest, giving $100/1.67 = 60\ \mathrm{m}$.
    2. B. $100\ \mathrm{m}$This treats length as invariant across frames, which is the Galilean answer and is only correct for dimensions perpendicular to the motion.
    3. C. $80\ \mathrm{m}$This multiplies the proper length by $\beta$ instead of by $1/\gamma$, substituting the speed ratio for the Lorentz factor.
    4. D. $167\ \mathrm{m}$This multiplies by $\gamma$ rather than dividing by it, which is the time-dilation rule applied to a length and gives a moving rod longer than its own rest length.
  • (d)
    1. A. $0.96c$ correctThe relativistic velocity transformation gives $(0.75c + 0.75c)/(1 + 0.75 \times 0.75) = 1.50c/1.5625 = 0.96c$, which never exceeds $c$ however large the two input speeds are.
    2. B. $1.50c$This is the Galilean sum of the two speeds, obtained by adding them in the Earth frame and reporting the result as a relative speed.
    3. C. $3.43c$This uses the velocity transformation with a minus sign in the denominator, which is the expression for changing from an approaching to a receding geometry and pushes the answer above $c$.
    4. D. $0.75c$This reports the speed of one spacecraft measured in the Earth frame, answering a question about a different frame than the one asked about.
  • (e)
    1. A. $0.943c$ correctThe ratio of total energy to rest energy is $\gamma = 3.00$, so $\beta = \sqrt{1 - 1/\gamma^{2}} = \sqrt{8/9} = 0.943$ and the speed is $0.943c$.
    2. B. $0.816c$This evaluates $\sqrt{1 - 1/\gamma}$, forgetting to square the Lorentz factor inside the reciprocal, a slip that survives because the result is still between zero and one.
    3. C. $0.667c$This computes $1 - 1/\gamma$ and omits the square root, treating the Lorentz factor relationship as linear rather than quadratic.
    4. D. $0.333c$This reports $1/\gamma$ as though it were the speed ratio, confusing the reciprocal of the Lorentz factor with the speed expressed as a fraction of $c$.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.5 Doppler effect
syllabus_ref: C.5 (Doppler effect)
title: C.5 Doppler effect
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on the Doppler effect. Each stands alone. Take the speed of sound in air as $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the speed of ultrasound in soft tissue as $1540\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ where those are needed. For electromagnetic radiation use $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A siren emitting $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ moves at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards a stationary observer. What frequency does the observer hear?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $548\ \mathrm{Hz}$
    2. B. $544\ \mathrm{Hz}$
    3. C. $456\ \mathrm{Hz}$
    4. D. $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$
  2. [1 mark](b)

    The same $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ siren is now stationary and the observer moves towards it at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What frequency does the observer hear?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $544\ \mathrm{Hz}$
    2. B. $548\ \mathrm{Hz}$
    3. C. $456\ \mathrm{Hz}$
    4. D. $531\ \mathrm{Hz}$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength $656\ \mathrm{nm}$ is measured in the spectrum of a galaxy at $689\ \mathrm{nm}$. What is the motion of the galaxy along the line of sight?

    (Determine)
    1. A. Receding at $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    2. B. Approaching at $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    3. C. Receding at $1.4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
    4. D. Receding at $5.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    An ultrasound probe emits $5.0\ \mathrm{MHz}$ at $60^{\circ}$ to blood flowing at $0.40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the magnitude of the Doppler shift in the reflected signal?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1.3\ \mathrm{kHz}$
    2. B. $2.6\ \mathrm{kHz}$
    3. C. $2.25\ \mathrm{kHz}$
    4. D. $0.65\ \mathrm{kHz}$
  5. [1 mark](e)

    An aircraft flies at $510\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air where the speed of sound is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the half-angle of the Mach cone it produces?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $41.8^{\circ}$
    2. B. $48.2^{\circ}$
    3. C. $33.7^{\circ}$
    4. D. No cone forms, because the aircraft is travelling below the speed of sound.
a_html:
(a) A. A moving source compresses the wavefronts ahead of it, so the wavelength in the medium is shortened while the observer samples at the usual rate: $f' = fv/(v-u_{s}) = 500 \times 340/310 = 548\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (A1) Note that the denominator contains the source speed, because it is the spacing of the crests that has changed.

(b) A. A moving observer meets unchanged wavefronts more often, so it is the numerator that changes: $f' = f(v+u_{o})/v = 500 \times 370/340 = 544\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (A1) The two answers differ by about $4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ for identical speeds, and that difference is the whole point of asking both questions: the situations are physically different even though the relative speed is the same.

(c) A. The wavelength is longer than the laboratory value, so the galaxy is receding. The redshift is $z = (689-656)/656 = 0.0503$, and since $z \ll 1$ the recession speed is $zc = 1.51 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) Direction first, magnitude second: the sign of the wavelength change carries the physics and is worth stating before any arithmetic.

(d) A. Reflection imposes the shift twice and only the along-beam component contributes, so $\Delta f = 2fv\cos 60^{\circ}/c = 2 \times 5.0\times10^{6} \times 0.40 \times 0.500/1540 = 1.30\ \mathrm{kHz}$. (A1) The factor of two is not a correction: the blood is first a moving observer and then a moving source.

(e) A. The wavelets emitted along the flight path superpose on a cone whose half-angle satisfies $\sin\theta = v_{\text{sound}}/v_{\text{source}} = 340/510 = 0.667$, giving $\theta = 41.8^{\circ}$. (A1) A faster aircraft makes the cone narrower, which is the check that rules out the cosine.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $548$ to $549\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (b) Accept $544\ \mathrm{Hz}$; if a candidate gives $548\ \mathrm{Hz}$ here, note that they have used the source formula and consider whether part (a) should also be reviewed, since the same error produces both. (c) Accept $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and require the direction; a magnitude alone is not the answer to 'what is the motion'. Accept the relativistic expression if offered, but note that it changes the third figure only. (d) Accept $1.29$ to $1.30\ \mathrm{kHz}$, and accept $1299\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Award nothing if the factor of two is missing, even if the cosine is handled correctly, because the reflection is the part of the physics that is specific to this technique. (e) Accept $42^{\circ}$ or the exact statement $\sin\theta = 2/3$; a candidate who writes $\sin\theta = 3/2$ and then notes the impossibility has understood the geometry better than one who produces $41.8^{\circ}$ by rote, and should be credited.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. $548\ \mathrm{Hz}$ correctWith a moving source the wavelength is compressed, so $f' = f\,v/(v - u_{s}) = 500 \times 340/310 = 548\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
    2. B. $544\ \mathrm{Hz}$This is the moving-observer expression $f(v+u)/v$ applied when it is the source that moves, and it is wrong because a moving source changes the wavelength rather than the rate at which crests are met.
    3. C. $456\ \mathrm{Hz}$This uses $v + u_{s}$ in the denominator, which is the receding-source case and would be right only if the siren were travelling away.
    4. D. $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$This denies any shift at all, confusing the frequency emitted by the source with the frequency arriving at the observer.
  • (b)
    1. A. $544\ \mathrm{Hz}$ correctA moving observer meets crests at a higher rate while the wavelength in the medium is unchanged, so $f' = f\,(v+u_{o})/v = 500 \times 370/340 = 544\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
    2. B. $548\ \mathrm{Hz}$This applies the moving-source formula when it is the observer that moves; the two expressions differ because only one of the two motions changes the wavelength in the medium.
    3. C. $456\ \mathrm{Hz}$This uses $v - u_{o}$ in the numerator, the receding-observer case, which would be right if the observer were moving away from the siren.
    4. D. $531\ \mathrm{Hz}$This averages the source and observer speeds as though the two cases were symmetric and the correct answer lay between them, which has no basis in the wave model.
  • (c)
    1. A. Receding at $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ correctThe wavelength is increased, so the galaxy recedes; the redshift is $z = (689-656)/656 = 0.0503$, and at this redshift $v \approx zc = 1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
    2. B. Approaching at $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This has the correct magnitude but the wrong direction: an increase in wavelength is a redshift and means recession, not approach.
    3. C. Receding at $1.4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This divides the wavelength change by the observed wavelength instead of the emitted one, which is not the definition of redshift and systematically underestimates the speed.
    4. D. Receding at $5.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$This reports the dimensionless redshift as though it were already a speed, omitting the multiplication by the speed of light.
  • (d)
    1. A. $1.3\ \mathrm{kHz}$ correctThe beam is Doppler-shifted on the way in and again on reflection, giving $\Delta f = 2 f v \cos 60^{\circ}/c = 2 \times 5.0 \times 10^{6} \times 0.40 \times 0.500/1540 = 1.3\ \mathrm{kHz}$.
    2. B. $2.6\ \mathrm{kHz}$This omits the cosine of the beam angle, which would be correct only if the beam lay along the direction of flow.
    3. C. $2.25\ \mathrm{kHz}$This uses the sine of the beam angle instead of the cosine, taking the component perpendicular to the flow, which is the component that produces no shift at all.
    4. D. $0.65\ \mathrm{kHz}$This applies the cosine twice, squaring it, as though the angle affected each leg of the round trip independently in that way.
  • (e)
    1. A. $41.8^{\circ}$ correctThe cone half-angle satisfies $\sin\theta = v_{\text{sound}}/v_{\text{source}} = 340/510 = 0.667$, so $\theta = 41.8^{\circ}$; a faster aircraft gives a smaller angle and a narrower cone.
    2. B. $48.2^{\circ}$This uses the cosine rather than the sine, which is the complementary angle and would widen the cone as the aircraft speeds up, the wrong trend.
    3. C. $33.7^{\circ}$This takes the arctangent of the speed ratio, treating the cone geometry as a right-angled triangle with the wrong pair of sides.
    4. D. No cone forms, because the aircraft is travelling below the speed of sound.The aircraft is at Mach $1.5$, which is supersonic; this option is for a candidate who compares the two speeds and reads the inequality the wrong way round.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.3 Work and power: the area under a force-distance graph against a constant friction the graph does not show
syllabus_ref: A.3 (Work, energy and power: work done as the area under a force-distance graph, the work-energy theorem, kinetic energy, and power as the product of a force and the velocity of the body on which it acts)
title: A.3 Work and power: the area under a force-distance graph against a constant friction the graph does not show
q_html:
A trolley of mass 3.0 kg starts from rest at $x = 0$ and is pushed along a straight, level track by a force whose magnitude varies with the distance $x$ exactly as shown in the figure. The force rises uniformly from zero at the start to 6.0 N at $x = 2.0$ m, stays at 6.0 N until $x = 5.0$ m, and then falls uniformly to zero at $x = 8.0$ m, where the pushing stops. Throughout the motion a constant frictional force of 2.0 N acts on the trolley, always opposing its motion; this force is not shown on the graph. The trolley may be treated as a particle. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this motion. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Determine the total work done by the applied force on the trolley over the whole 8.0 m of the motion.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 33.0 J
    2. B. 48.0 J
    3. C. 27.0 J
    4. D. 24.0 J
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Calculate the kinetic energy of the trolley at the instant it reaches $x = 8.0$ m, taking the friction into account.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 25.0 J
    2. B. 11.0 J
    3. C. 17.0 J
    4. D. 33.0 J
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Calculate the speed of the trolley at the instant it reaches $x = 8.0$ m.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 4.08 m s$^{-1}$
    2. B. 3.37 m s$^{-1}$
    3. C. 4.69 m s$^{-1}$
    4. D. 2.71 m s$^{-1}$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Determine the distance from the start at which the kinetic energy of the trolley has its greatest value.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 5.0 m
    2. B. 8.0 m
    3. C. 6.5 m
    4. D. 7.0 m
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Calculate the power developed by the applied force at the instant the trolley passes $x = 5.0$ m.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 24.0 W
    2. B. 18.3 W
    3. C. 20.2 W
    4. D. 12.2 W
a_html:
(a) A. The work done by a force that varies with distance is the area between
its graph and the distance axis, so the region has to be cut into shapes whose areas
are known. It splits into a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(6.0) = 6.0$ J, a
rectangle of area $(3.0)(6.0) = 18.0$ J and a second triangle of area
$\tfrac{1}{2}(3.0)(6.0) = 9.0$ J. Their sum is $6.0 + 18.0 + 9.0 = 33.0$ J. (A1)

(b) C. Friction acts over the whole 8.0 m and always opposes the motion, so it
does $-2.0 \times 8.0 = -16.0$ J of work. The net work is therefore
$33.0 - 16.0 = 17.0$ J. The trolley started from rest, so by the work-energy theorem
the final kinetic energy is exactly this net work, 17.0 J. (A1)

(c) B. Setting $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = 17.0$ J with $m = 3.0$ kg gives
$v = \sqrt{2(17.0)/3.0} = \sqrt{11.33} = 3.37$ m s$^{-1}$. (A1)

(d) D. The kinetic energy is the *accumulated* net work, so what matters is not
how large the applied force is but whether it exceeds the friction. While $F > 2.0$ N
the trolley keeps gaining energy; once $F < 2.0$ N it starts losing it. On the
falling branch the graph is straight from $(5.0,\ 6.0)$ to $(8.0,\ 0)$, so
$F = 6.0 - 2.0(x - 5.0) = 16.0 - 2.0x$. Setting $F = 2.0$ N gives $x = 7.0$ m. This
lies two metres beyond the point where the applied force is largest, and a metre
before the force disappears. (A1)

(e) B. Power at an instant is $P = Fv$ with both quantities evaluated at that
instant, so the speed at $x = 5.0$ m is needed first. The applied work to that point
is $6.0 + 18.0 = 24.0$ J and friction has removed $2.0 \times 5.0 = 10.0$ J, so the
kinetic energy there is 14.0 J and $v = \sqrt{2(14.0)/3.0} = 3.06$ m s$^{-1}$. Hence
$P = 6.0 \times 3.06 = 18.3$ W. (A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking and no method marks: the key is the answer.
Each distractor is the exact result of a named error, so a wrong option identifies the
error rather than being an arbitrary number.

(a) Accept 33.0 J. An answer of 48.0 J has treated the force as constant at its
maximum value; 27.0 J means the first triangle was left out; 24.0 J means a mean
force of 3.0 N was assumed, and the mean height of this graph is 33.0/8.0 = 4.1 N,
not 3.0 N.

(b) Accept 17.0 J. An answer of 33.0 J shows that the 16.0 J removed by friction was
never subtracted. An answer of 25.0 J has charged friction over half the distance
only, and 11.0 J follows from the incomplete work in part (a).

(c) Accept 3.37 m s$^{-1}$. Do not accept 4.69 m s$^{-1}$, which is the frictionless
answer. A candidate who used 25.0 J in (b) and then computes 4.08 m s$^{-1}$ here has
been consistent but earns no mark, because the value carried forward was itself wrong.

(d) Accept 7.0 m and no other value. This is the discriminating question of the
cluster. An answer of 5.0 m takes the point of greatest force for the point of
greatest energy; 8.0 m assumes the energy is still rising when the force has gone;
6.5 m treats the friction as though it were the 3.0 N mean of the falling branch.

(e) Accept 18.3 W. The commonest error is to reuse the final speed from part (c),
which gives 20.2 W; allow it only if the candidate has also used the speed at the end
in part (c), which it does not. An answer of 24.0 W has confused the work done up to
that point with the rate of doing work.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 33.0 J correctThe work is the area between the graph and the distance axis: a triangle of 6.0 J, a rectangle of 18.0 J and a second triangle of 9.0 J, giving 33.0 J.
    2. B. 48.0 JThis multiplies the greatest force, 6.0 N, by the whole distance, as though the force had been constant at its peak.
    3. C. 27.0 JThis omits the first triangle, counting only the rectangle and the falling part of the graph.
    4. D. 24.0 JThis assumes a mean force of 3.0 N over 8.0 m, which is not the mean height of this particular graph.
  • (b)
