    1. A. 25.0 JThis charges friction over only half the distance, subtracting 8.0 J rather than 16.0 J.
    2. B. 11.0 JThis follows from an applied work of 27.0 J, the value obtained when the first triangle is missed out.
    3. C. 17.0 J correctThe work done against friction is $2.0 \times 8.0 = 16.0$ J, so the net work is $33.0 - 16.0 = 17.0$ J, which is the kinetic energy gained from rest.
    4. D. 33.0 JThis is the work done by the applied force with no allowance for the 16.0 J removed by friction.
  • (c)
    1. A. 4.08 m s$^{-1}$This follows the 25.0 J obtained by charging friction over only half the distance.
    2. B. 3.37 m s$^{-1}$ correct$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = 17.0$ J with $m = 3.0$ kg gives $v = \sqrt{2(17.0)/3.0} = 3.37$ m s$^{-1}$.
    3. C. 4.69 m s$^{-1}$This uses the full 33.0 J, so it is the speed the trolley would have reached on a frictionless track.
    4. D. 2.71 m s$^{-1}$This follows the 11.0 J obtained by missing the first triangle and then subtracting the friction.
  • (d)
    1. A. 5.0 mThis is where the applied force is greatest, but the force still exceeds friction there, so the trolley is still gaining kinetic energy.
    2. B. 8.0 mBy the end the applied force has fallen to zero while friction has not, so the kinetic energy has already been falling for the last metre.
    3. C. 6.5 mThis is halfway along the falling branch, which would be right only if the friction equalled the 3.0 N mean applied force over that branch.
    4. D. 7.0 m correctThe kinetic energy is the accumulated net work, so it grows while the applied force exceeds the 2.0 N of friction and falls once it drops below it. On the falling branch $F = 16.0 - 2.0x$, which equals 2.0 N at $x = 7.0$ m.
  • (e)
    1. A. 24.0 WThis is the work done up to $x = 5.0$ m; power is a rate, not an accumulated amount.
    2. B. 18.3 W correctThe applied work to $x = 5.0$ m is 24.0 J and friction has taken 10.0 J, leaving 14.0 J, so $v = 3.06$ m s$^{-1}$ there and $P = Fv = 6.0 \times 3.06 = 18.3$ W.
    3. C. 20.2 WThis multiplies 6.0 N by the speed at the end of the motion, 3.37 m s$^{-1}$, rather than the speed at $x = 5.0$ m.
    4. D. 12.2 WThis uses a force of 4.0 N, the mean value of the applied force over the first 5.0 m, instead of its value at that instant.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.1 Simple harmonic motion: a vertical mass-spring oscillator whose equilibrium position is not the unstretched length
syllabus_ref: C.1 (Simple harmonic motion: the defining equation $a = -\omega^{2}x$, the period of a mass-spring system, amplitude, the relation between speed and displacement, and oscillations about an equilibrium position)
title: C.1 Simple harmonic motion: a vertical mass-spring oscillator whose equilibrium position is not the unstretched length
q_html:
The figure shows a light spring hanging from a fixed support. On the left the spring is drawn at its unstretched length of 0.500 m. On the right the same spring carries a mass of 0.600 kg and hangs at rest in equilibrium at a length of 0.750 m, so the static extension is 0.250 m. The mass is then pulled down a further 0.050 m below its equilibrium position and released from rest, so that it oscillates vertically about the equilibrium position with an amplitude of 0.050 m. Take $g = 9.81$ m s$^{-2}$, take the spring to be massless and to obey Hooke's law at all times, and ignore air resistance. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this oscillation. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Calculate the period of the vertical oscillation of the mass.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 2.01 s
    2. B. 1.00 s
    3. C. 1.42 s
    4. D. 0.449 s
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Calculate the greatest speed reached by the mass during the oscillation.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0.199 m s$^{-1}$
    2. B. 0.157 m s$^{-1}$
    3. C. 0.626 m s$^{-1}$
    4. D. 0.313 m s$^{-1}$
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Calculate the speed of the mass at the instant when it is 0.030 m below its equilibrium position.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0.251 m s$^{-1}$
    2. B. 0.125 m s$^{-1}$
    3. C. 0.313 m s$^{-1}$
    4. D. 0.376 m s$^{-1}$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Determine the greatest length of the spring at any point during the oscillation.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 0.750 m
    2. B. 0.850 m
    3. C. 0.800 m
    4. D. 1.000 m
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Calculate the magnitude of the net force on the mass when it is at the lowest point of the oscillation.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 0 N
    2. B. 5.89 N
    3. C. 7.06 N
    4. D. 1.18 N
a_html:
(a) B. In equilibrium the spring force balances the weight, so
$mg = ke$ and $k = (0.600)(9.81)/0.250 = 23.5$ N m$^{-1}$. Then
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.600/23.5} = 2\pi(0.1597) = 1.00$ s. Substituting
$k = mg/e$ first gives the neater form $T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}$, in which the mass has
cancelled: the period depends only on how far the spring hangs down under its own
load, and not on the load or on how far it is then pulled. (A1)

(b) D. The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi/T = 6.26$ rad s$^{-1}$ and the
greatest speed is reached at the equilibrium position, where
$v_{\max} = \omega A = 6.26 \times 0.050 = 0.313$ m s$^{-1}$. The average speed over
a quarter cycle is only 0.199 m s$^{-1}$, because the mass is slow near the ends.
(A1)

(c) A. Speed and displacement are related by $v^{2} = \omega^{2}(A^{2} - x^{2})$,
so $v = 6.26\sqrt{0.050^{2} - 0.030^{2}} = 6.26\sqrt{0.0016} = 6.26 \times 0.0400 =
0.251$ m s$^{-1}$. The displacement enters squared, so the speed at three fifths of
the amplitude is still four fifths of the maximum, not two fifths of it. (A1)

(d) C. Simple harmonic motion is motion *about the equilibrium position*, and the
amplitude is measured from there. The length of the spring therefore oscillates
between $0.750 - 0.050 = 0.700$ m and $0.750 + 0.050 = 0.800$ m. The unstretched
length of 0.500 m sets the equilibrium position but plays no part in the excursion.
(A1)

(e) D. The net force in simple harmonic motion is $F = -m\omega^{2}x$ measured
from equilibrium, and at the lowest point $x = +A = 0.050$ m, so
$|F| = kA = 23.5 \times 0.050 = 1.18$ N upwards. It is worth checking this against the
forces directly: the spring is then stretched by $0.250 + 0.050 = 0.300$ m, so it
pulls up with $23.5 \times 0.300 = 7.06$ N against a weight of 5.89 N, leaving 1.18 N.
(A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 1.00 s. Do not accept 1.42 s, which is a pendulum period built from the
0.500 m unstretched length. An answer of 0.449 s shows the amplitude being used as a
length in the same formula; the period of a simple harmonic oscillator does not
depend on the amplitude.

(b) Accept 0.313 m s⁻¹. An answer of 0.199 m s⁻¹ is the mean speed over a quarter
cycle and is the commonest wrong answer; it is worth drawing the distinction
explicitly if a candidate raises it.

(c) Accept 0.251 m s⁻¹. An answer of 0.125 m s⁻¹ shows a linear rule being used in
place of the quadrature one, which is the specific error this question tests.

(d) Accept 0.800 m. Do not accept 1.000 m. That value is right for a different
experiment — release from the natural length gives a greatest extension of twice the
static extension — and a candidate who offers it has substituted a remembered result
for the situation described.

(e) Accept 1.18 N. An answer of zero confuses a turning point with an equilibrium
point, and the confusion is worth naming: the mass is at rest for an instant precisely
because the net force is at its greatest there. An answer of 7.06 N has computed the
spring force rather than the resultant.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 2.01 sThis is twice the correct period, as though the mass completed half an oscillation in each cycle.
    2. B. 1.00 s correctIn equilibrium $mg = ke$, so $k = 23.5$ N m$^{-1}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.600/23.5} = 1.00$ s. Equivalently $T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}$, which contains neither the mass nor the amplitude.
    3. C. 1.42 sThis is $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ with the 0.500 m unstretched length, which is the period of a pendulum and not of this oscillator.
    4. D. 0.449 sThis is $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ with the 0.050 m amplitude, which has no business in either formula: the period is independent of amplitude.
  • (b)
    1. A. 0.199 m s$^{-1}$This is the amplitude divided by a quarter of the period, which is the mean speed over a quarter cycle and not the greatest speed.
    2. B. 0.157 m s$^{-1}$This is half the correct value, as though the amplitude were 0.025 m rather than 0.050 m.
    3. C. 0.626 m s$^{-1}$This is twice the correct value, using twice the amplitude as though the mass travelled the full peak-to-peak distance in a quarter period.
    4. D. 0.313 m s$^{-1}$ correct$\omega = 2\pi/T = 6.26$ rad s$^{-1}$, and the greatest speed is $v_{\max} = \omega A = 6.26 \times 0.050 = 0.313$ m s$^{-1}$.
  • (c)
    1. A. 0.251 m s$^{-1}$ correctThe speed obeys $v = \omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}$, not a linear rule: $v = 6.26\sqrt{0.050^{2} - 0.030^{2}} = 6.26 \times 0.040 = 0.251$ m s$^{-1}$.
    2. B. 0.125 m s$^{-1}$This uses $\omega(A - x)$, treating the speed as though it fell linearly with displacement. It does not; the relation is a quadrature one.
    3. C. 0.313 m s$^{-1}$This is the greatest speed, which occurs at the equilibrium position and not 0.030 m away from it.
    4. D. 0.376 m s$^{-1}$This uses $\omega(A + x)$, which would make the speed larger away from equilibrium than at it.
  • (d)
    1. A. 0.750 mThis is the equilibrium length, which the mass passes through rather than turns round at.
    2. B. 0.850 mThis adds twice the amplitude to the equilibrium length, confusing the peak-to-peak travel with the amplitude.
    3. C. 0.800 m correctThe oscillation is about the equilibrium position, so the length swings between $0.750 - 0.050$ and $0.750 + 0.050$ m; the greatest is 0.800 m.
    4. D. 1.000 mThis is the unstretched length plus twice the static extension, which is the greatest length when the mass is released from the spring's natural length. Here it is released 0.050 m below equilibrium, not from the natural length.
  • (e)
    1. A. 0 NThe mass is momentarily at rest there, but a zero velocity is not a zero net force; the net force is what turns it round.
    2. B. 5.89 NThis is the weight of the mass. The net force at the lowest point is the excess of the spring force over the weight, not the weight.
    3. C. 7.06 NThis is the force exerted by the spring alone, $k(0.250 + 0.050)$; the net force is that minus the weight.
    4. D. 1.18 N correctAt the lowest point the displacement from equilibrium is the amplitude, so the net force is $kA = 23.5 \times 0.050 = 1.18$ N directed upwards.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.3 Radioactive decay: how a constant background changes every fold-change in a measured count rate
syllabus_ref: E.3 (Radioactive decay: activity and the decay constant, the half-life, the exponential decay of activity and of the number of undecayed nuclei, and the correction of a measured count rate for background radiation)
title: E.3 Radioactive decay: how a constant background changes every fold-change in a measured count rate
q_html:
A radioactive source is placed in front of a detector. With the source in position the detector records 960 counts during a measuring interval of 120 s. With the source removed, but with the detector, its shielding and the room exactly as they were, it records 120 counts during a second interval of the same length. The detector registers 4.0% of the decays that occur in the source; the remainder are missed because the radiation is emitted in all directions and much of it never reaches the detector. The source consists of a single nuclide of half-life 12 h and emits no other radiation. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this arrangement. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Calculate the background-corrected count rate at the start of the measurements, in counts per second.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 1.00 s$^{-1}$
    2. B. 6.00 s$^{-1}$
    3. C. 7.00 s$^{-1}$
    4. D. 8.00 s$^{-1}$
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Calculate the activity of the source at the start of the measurements, in becquerels.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 70.0 Bq
    2. B. 175 Bq
    3. C. 200 Bq
    4. D. 7.00 Bq
  3. [1 mark](c)

    Calculate the count rate that the detector will record, in counts per second, 24 h after the start of the measurements.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. 2.00 s$^{-1}$
    2. B. 1.75 s$^{-1}$
    3. C. 4.00 s$^{-1}$
    4. D. 2.75 s$^{-1}$
  4. [1 mark](d)

    Determine the time, in hours, at which the count rate recorded by the detector has fallen to one half of the rate it recorded at the start of the measurements.

    (Determine)
    1. A. 14.7 h
    2. B. 12.0 h
    3. C. 6.00 h
    4. D. 24.0 h
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Calculate the number of nuclei of the nuclide present in the source at the start of the measurements.

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $6.23 \times 10^{6}$
    2. B. $2.18 \times 10^{6}$
    3. C. $1.09 \times 10^{7}$
    4. D. $1.25 \times 10^{7}$
a_html:
(a) C. Both totals have to become rates before they can be compared, and both
were taken over the same 120 s. The gross rate is $960/120 = 8.00$ s$^{-1}$ and the
background rate is $120/120 = 1.00$ s$^{-1}$, so the rate due to the source alone is
$8.00 - 1.00 = 7.00$ s$^{-1}$. (A1)

(b) B. The detector registers only 4.0% of the decays, so the corrected count rate
is 0.040 of the activity: $A = 7.00/0.040 = 175$ Bq. The activity is a property of the
source and does not depend on how well it is being watched, which is why the efficiency
has to be divided out. (A1)

(c) D. Twenty-four hours is two half-lives, so the activity falls by a factor of
four to $175/4 = 43.75$ Bq. The corrected count rate is then
$43.75 \times 0.040 = 1.75$ s$^{-1}$. But the detector cannot distinguish a decay from
a background event, so it records $1.75 + 1.00 = 2.75$ s$^{-1}$. The recorded rate has
fallen by a factor of $8.00/2.75 = 2.91$, not 4. (A1)

(d) A. The recorded rate starts at 8.00 s$^{-1}$ and has to fall to 4.00 s$^{-1}$,
which means the corrected rate must fall from 7.00 to 3.00 s$^{-1}$ — and the
background has to be removed before this can be seen. Solving
$7.00 \times 2^{-t/12} = 3.00$ gives $2^{t/12} = 7/3$, so
$t = 12\log_{2}(7/3) = 12 \times 1.222 = 14.7$ h. The recorded rate takes almost
fifteen hours to halve even though the activity halves in twelve. (A1)

(e) C. The half-life must be in seconds before it gives a decay constant in
reciprocal seconds: $\lambda = \ln 2/(12 \times 3600) = 1.60\times10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$.
Then $A = \lambda N$ gives $N = 175/1.60\times10^{-5} = 1.09\times10^{7}$ nuclei.
(A1)

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 7.00 s⁻¹. An answer of 8.00 s⁻¹ has left the background in and 1.00 s⁻¹ has
kept only the background; 6.00 s⁻¹ mixes a per-second rate with a per-minute one.

(b) Accept 175 Bq. An answer of 200 Bq shows the gross rate being used, so the
background has been treated as decays from the source. An answer of 7.00 Bq has
confused a count rate with an activity.

(c) Accept 2.75 s⁻¹. This is the discriminating question. Do not accept 2.00 s⁻¹,
which applies the decay factor to the recorded rate, and do not accept 1.75 s⁻¹, which
is the corrected rate with the background not put back.

(d) Accept 14.7 h; accept 14.6 h or 14.8 h from a rounded logarithm. An answer of
12.0 h has halved the activity rather than the recorded rate, and is the commonest
wrong answer. An answer of 6.00 h has the background acting in the wrong direction.

(e) Accept 1.09 × 10⁷. Allow answers in the range 1.08 × 10⁷ to 1.10 × 10⁷. An answer
of 2.18 × 10⁶ usually means the half-life was used in seconds without converting from
hours, giving a decay constant sixty times too large; a fifth suggests a different
slip, and is worth checking individually.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. 1.00 s$^{-1}$This is the background rate on its own, which is what has to be removed, not what is left.
    2. B. 6.00 s$^{-1}$This converts the gross count to a rate per second but the background count to a rate per minute, so the two are not in the same units when they are subtracted.
    3. C. 7.00 s$^{-1}$ correctThe gross rate is $960/120 = 8.00$ s$^{-1}$ and the background rate is $120/120 = 1.00$ s$^{-1}$, so the corrected rate is 7.00 s$^{-1}$.
    4. D. 8.00 s$^{-1}$This is the gross rate with the background left in; the detector did not stop counting when the source was taken away.
  • (b)
    1. A. 70.0 BqThis divides by 0.10 rather than 0.040, treating a 4.0% efficiency as though it were ten per cent.
    2. B. 175 Bq correctThe corrected rate of 7.00 s$^{-1}$ is 4.0% of the activity, so $A = 7.00/0.040 = 175$ Bq.
    3. C. 200 BqThis divides the gross rate by the efficiency, so the background has been counted as though it came from the source.
    4. D. 7.00 BqThis is the count rate itself. Count rate and activity differ by the detecting efficiency, which is far from unity here.
  • (c)
    1. A. 2.00 s$^{-1}$This quarters the rate that was recorded at the start. The activity quarters, but the background does not, so the recorded rate cannot.
    2. B. 1.75 s$^{-1}$This is the background-corrected rate after 24 h. The detector has no way of telling a decay from a background event, so it records both.
    3. C. 4.00 s$^{-1}$This halves the recorded rate as though 24 h were one half-life. It is two, and the background does not decay in any case.
    4. D. 2.75 s$^{-1}$ correct24 h is two half-lives, so the activity falls to $175/4 = 43.75$ Bq, giving a corrected rate of $43.75 \times 0.040 = 1.75$ s$^{-1}$. The detector still records the background on top of it, so the rate is 2.75 s$^{-1}$.
  • (d)
    1. A. 14.7 h correctThe recorded rate starts at 8.00 s$^{-1}$, so it halves at 4.00 s$^{-1}$, which means a corrected rate of 3.00 s$^{-1}$. Solving $7.00 \times 2^{-t/12} = 3.00$ gives $t = 12\log_{2}(7/3) = 14.7$ h.
    2. B. 12.0 hThis is one half-life, which halves the activity. The recorded rate is the activity plus a fixed background, so it takes longer than one half-life to halve.
    3. C. 6.00 hThis is half a half-life, as though the background made the recorded rate fall faster than the activity. It makes it fall more slowly.
    4. D. 24.0 hThis is two half-lives, which quarters the activity rather than halving the recorded rate.
  • (e)
    1. A. $6.23 \times 10^{6}$This follows from an activity of 100 Bq, which is not a value any part of this cluster produces.
    2. B. $2.18 \times 10^{6}$This is one fifth of the correct value, following from a decay constant five times too large, as if the half-life had been given in hours and used as seconds.
    3. C. $1.09 \times 10^{7}$ correct$\lambda = \ln 2/(12 \times 3600) = 1.60\times10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$, and $A = \lambda N$ gives $N = 175/1.60\times10^{-5} = 1.09\times10^{7}$.
    4. D. $1.25 \times 10^{7}$This follows from the activity of 200 Bq obtained in part (b) when the background is not subtracted.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.1 / E.2 Photons, the photoelectric effect and matter waves
syllabus_ref: E.1 (Structure of the atom), E.2 (Quantum physics)
title: E.1 / E.2 Photons, the photoelectric effect and matter waves
q_html:
Each question below is self-contained. Take the Planck constant as $6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, the speed of light in vacuum as $3.00\times10^{8}$ m per second, the elementary charge as $1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, the electron mass as $9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}$ J.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Light of wavelength 420 nm is incident on a metal surface in a darkened room. What is the energy carried by a single photon of this light, and what is that energy when it is expressed in electron-volts rather than in joules?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $4.74\times10^{-19}$ J
    2. B. $2.96$ J
    3. C. $8.36\times10^{-35}$ J
    4. D. $7.14\times10^{14}$ J
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A metal has a work function of $2.28$ eV. Light of frequency $8.00\times10^{14}$ Hz is shone on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1.66\times10^{-19}$ J
    2. B. $3.02\times10^{-19}$ J
    3. C. $8.96\times10^{-19}$ J
    4. D. $5.30\times10^{-19}$ J
  3. [1 mark](c)

    For the metal and the illumination described in the previous question, what stopping potential would be measured?

    (Determine)
    1. A. $1.04$ V
    2. B. $2.28$ V
    3. C. $3.32$ V
    4. D. $0.00$ V
  4. [1 mark](d)

    An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $150$ V. What is its de Broglie wavelength?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $1.00\times10^{-10}$ m
    2. B. $1.42\times10^{-10}$ m
    3. C. $2.34\times10^{-12}$ m
    4. D. $3.17\times10^{-12}$ m
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A laser emits $2.0$ mW of light at a wavelength of $640$ nm. How many photons does it emit each second?

    (Calculate)
    1. A. $6.4\times10^{15}$
    2. B. $6.4\times10^{18}$
    3. C. $1.0\times10^{-3}$
    4. D. $3.1\times10^{-19}$
a_html:
(a) $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{420\times10^{-9}}=4.74\times10^{-19}$ J, which is option A. (A1) Option B is the same number in electron-volts, so it catches anyone who converts and then forgets which unit they are in; option C comes from multiplying by the wavelength; option D is the frequency, one step short. (a) A

(b) $hf=6.63\times10^{-34}\times8.00\times10^{14}=5.304\times10^{-19}$ J $=3.315$ eV. Subtracting the work function gives $K_{\max}=3.315-2.28=1.035$ eV $=1.66\times10^{-19}$ J, option A. (A1) The trap in option B is subtracting $2.28\times10^{-19}$ J, which is not the same quantity as $2.28$ eV. (b) A

(c) $eV_s=K_{\max}$ in electron-volts, so $V_s=1.035$ V, option A. (A1) The rule is that one electron-volt corresponds to one volt for a singly charged particle, which is why the conversion is trivial once (b) is in eV and impossible if it is left in joules. (c) A

(d) $p=\sqrt{2\,m\,eV}=\sqrt{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.60\times10^{-19}\times150}=6.61\times10^{-24}$ kg m per second, so $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{6.61\times10^{-24}}=1.00\times10^{-10}$ m, option A. (A1) The factor of two is the discriminator here, and it is worth noting that $0.10$ nm is of the order of an atomic spacing, which is why electron diffraction works. (d) A

(e) $E=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{640\times10^{-9}}=3.11\times10^{-19}$ J, so the rate is $\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{3.11\times10^{-19}}=6.4\times10^{15}$ per second, option A. (A1) Option B is the most dangerous distractor in the cluster because the arithmetic is identical and only the prefix differs. (e) A

Markscheme notes

One mark per item and there is no negative marking, so a candidate should be advised to commit to an answer rather than leave a blank. In (a) condone $4.7$ to $4.8\times10^{-19}$ J. In (b) allow the answer in eV provided it is identified as such, and note that a candidate who works entirely in joules must convert the work function first; that conversion is where the mark is actually won or lost. In (d) allow $0.10$ nm or $1.0\times10^{-10}$ m, and credit a candidate who reaches $1.42\times10^{-10}$ m only if they show the factor of two explicitly, since otherwise the working is wrong even though the answer looks close. In (e) accept $6.4\times10^{15}$ to $6.5\times10^{15}$. It is worth telling candidates explicitly that the electron-volt is doing real work in this cluster rather than being decoration: in (b) the subtraction is only possible after the work function has been brought into the same unit as the photon energy, and in (c) the answer in volts is the answer in electron-volts, which is the sense in which the unit simplifies rather than complicates the arithmetic.

Options, and the error each distractor names

  • (a)
    1. A. $4.74\times10^{-19}$ J correctPhoton energy is $hc/\lambda$, with the wavelength converted from nanometres to metres before dividing.
    2. B. $2.96$ JThis is the correct numerical value in electron-volts, quoted with the wrong unit; it is $2.96$ eV, not $2.96$ J.
    3. C. $8.36\times10^{-35}$ JUses $E=hc\lambda$, multiplying by the wavelength instead of dividing by it.
    4. D. $7.14\times10^{14}$ JThis is the frequency in hertz; the photon energy still has to be found by multiplying by the Planck constant.
  • (b)
    1. A. $1.66\times10^{-19}$ J correctThe photon energy is $5.30\times10^{-19}$ J or $3.315$ eV, and subtracting the work function leaves $1.035$ eV, which is $1.66\times10^{-19}$ J.
    2. B. $3.02\times10^{-19}$ JSubtracts $2.28\times10^{-19}$ J rather than converting the work function; $2.28$ eV is $3.65\times10^{-19}$ J.
    3. C. $8.96\times10^{-19}$ JAdds the work function to the photon energy instead of subtracting it; the work function is the energy that must be paid to escape.
    4. D. $5.30\times10^{-19}$ JThis is the photon energy itself; the question asks for what remains after the electron has escaped.
  • (c)
    1. A. $1.04$ V correctThe stopping potential in volts is numerically equal to the maximum kinetic energy in electron-volts, $1.035$ eV.
    2. B. $2.28$ VThis is the work function in electron-volts, which sets the threshold, not the stopping potential for this frequency.
    3. C. $3.32$ VThis is the photon energy in electron-volts before the work function has been subtracted.
    4. D. $0.00$ VEmission does occur here because the photon energy exceeds the work function, so the stopping potential is not zero.
  • (d)
    1. A. $1.00\times10^{-10}$ m correctThe kinetic energy is $eV$, so the momentum is the square root of $2\,m\,e\,V$, and the wavelength is $h$ divided by that momentum.
    2. B. $1.42\times10^{-10}$ mOmits the factor of two and uses the square root of $m\,e\,V$ for the momentum.
    3. C. $2.34\times10^{-12}$ mUses the proton mass in place of the electron mass, which shortens the wavelength by the square root of the mass ratio.
    4. D. $3.17\times10^{-12}$ mTreats the accelerating potential as $150$ kV rather than $150$ V.
  • (e)
    1. A. $6.4\times10^{15}$ correctEach photon carries $hc/\lambda=3.11\times10^{-19}$ J, and dividing the power by that energy gives the emission rate.
    2. B. $6.4\times10^{18}$Reads the wavelength as $640$ micrometres rather than nanometres, making each photon a thousand times less energetic.
    3. C. $1.0\times10^{-3}$Multiplies the photon count by the elementary charge, which converts joules to electron-volts and has no place in a count.
    4. D. $3.1\times10^{-19}$This is the energy of one photon in joules; the question asks for the number emitted per second.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.3 A vehicle driven at constant power, whose driving force therefore falls as the speed rises, so that the constant-acceleration equations do not apply
syllabus_ref: A.3 Work, energy and power: power as the rate of doing work, applied to a vehicle whose engine delivers constant power, and the relationship between driving force, power and speed
title: A.3 A vehicle driven at constant power, whose driving force therefore falls as the speed rises, so that the constant-acceleration equations do not apply
q_html:
A car of mass $m = 1200\ {\rm kg}$ travels along a straight horizontal road. Its engine delivers a constant mechanical power of $P = 60\ {\rm kW}$ to the wheels, and at the speeds considered the resistive forces may be neglected in parts (a) to (d). At the instant from which times are measured the car is travelling at $10\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$. Take $g = 9.81\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}}$, though note that the road is horizontal so its value is not needed until part (e) at the earliest.
The relationship between the driving force $F$, the power $P$ and the speed $v$ is $P = Fv$.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    Calculate the driving force exerted on the car when it is travelling at $10\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$, and again when it is travelling at $20\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Show that, while the power remains constant and resistance is neglected, the acceleration of the car is inversely proportional to its speed, and calculate the acceleration at each of the two speeds in part (a).

    (Show that)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Determine the time taken for the car to accelerate from $10\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ to $20\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$, using the fact that the work done by the engine in that interval equals the increase in kinetic energy of the car.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    A student obtains a different answer to part (c) by using the constant-acceleration equation $t = (v - u)/a$ with the acceleration at $10\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$. State the value that route gives, explain why it is wrong, and determine the mean acceleration over the interval for comparison with the two values from part (b).

    (Explain)
  5. [2 marks](e)

    In reality a constant resistive force of $500\ {\rm N}$ opposes the motion. Determine the maximum speed the car can reach on the level, and state what the acceleration is at that speed.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Using $P = Fv$ with $P = 6.0 \times 10^{4}\ {\rm W}$:
$$F_{10} = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{4}}{10} = 6.0 \times 10^{3}\ {\rm N}, \qquad F_{20} = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{4}}{20} = 3.0 \times 10^{3}\ {\rm N} \;(M1)(A1).$$
The driving force halves when the speed doubles, even though the power is the same throughout.
(b) With no resistance the net force is the driving force, so $F = ma$ and
$$a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{P}{mv} \;(M1).$$
Since $P$ and $m$ are both constant, $a \propto 1/v$ as required (A1). Numerically,
$$a_{10} = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{3}}{1200} = 5.0\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}}, \qquad a_{20} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{3}}{1200} = 2.5\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}} \;(A1).$$
(c) The work done by the engine in time $t$ at constant power is $Pt$, and this equals the gain in kinetic energy:
$$Pt = \tfrac{1}{2}m\bigl(v^{2} - u^{2}\bigr) \;(M1)$$
$$t = \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}(1200)\bigl(20^{2} - 10^{2}\bigr)}{6.0 \times 10^{4}} = \frac{600 \times 300}{6.0 \times 10^{4}} = \frac{1.80 \times 10^{5}}{6.0 \times 10^{4}} = 3.0\ {\rm s} \;(M1)(A1).$$
(d) Using $t = (v-u)/a$ with $a = 5.0\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ gives
$$t = \frac{20 - 10}{5.0} = 2.0\ {\rm s} \;(A1),$$
which is too short. The constant-acceleration equations require the acceleration to be constant, and part (b) showed that it is not: the driving force is $P/v$, so as the car speeds up the force, and hence the acceleration, falls continuously from $5.0$ to $2.5\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ over the interval (M1)(A1). Because the acceleration is falling, the car spends longer at the slower end of the range than a constant-acceleration model allows, so the true time exceeds $2.0\ {\rm s}$. The mean acceleration over the interval is
$$\bar{a} = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{10}{3.0} = 3.3\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}} \;(A1),$$
which does lie between $2.5$ and $5.0\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ as it must, and is closer to the smaller of the two because the car spends more time near the lower end of the speed range.
(e) At the maximum speed the driving force has fallen to equal the resistive force, so the net force, and hence the acceleration, is zero (M1). With $F = 500\ {\rm N}$:
$$v_{\max} = \frac{P}{F} = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{4}}{500} = 120\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}, \qquad a = 0 \;(A1).$$
(This is about $430\ {\rm km\,h^{-1}}$, which is far faster than any ordinary car; the figures were chosen to make the arithmetic clean rather than realistic.)

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for using $P = Fv$, (A1) for both forces. Accept $6.0\ {\rm kN}$ and $3.0\ {\rm kN}$. A candidate who gives the same force at both speeds has assumed constant force and should be followed through into (b) but loses this mark.
(b) (M1) for combining $F = ma$ with $P = Fv$, (A1) for stating the inverse proportionality explicitly, (A1) for both accelerations. Candidates may instead note that doubling the speed halves the force and therefore halves the acceleration; this is acceptable as the demonstration of proportionality.
(c) (M1) for the energy statement $Pt = \Delta E_{k}$, (M1) for substituting with the squares of the speeds taken correctly, (A1) for $3.0\ {\rm s}$. A candidate who writes $\tfrac{1}{2}m(v-u)^{2}$ instead of $\tfrac{1}{2}m(v^{2}-u^{2})$ should be treated as having made a physics error rather than an arithmetic one and loses the second mark.
(d) (A1) for stating $2.0\ {\rm s}$, (M1) for identifying that the acceleration is not constant, (A1) for explaining the direction of the error in terms of varying acceleration, (A1) for the mean acceleration $3.3\ {\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ and the observation that it lies between the two endpoint values. Four fields; credit three. Do not accept 'the acceleration averages out' without the remark that it is the time spent at each speed that matters.
(e) (M1) for recognising that driving force equals resistive force at the maximum speed, (A1) for $120\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ and $a = 0$. Accept the speed in kilometres per hour if the conversion is shown.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Predictive maintenance on smart water meters — imbalanced data, metrics and governance
syllabus_ref: A4.2 Data preprocessing (HL only), A4.3 Machine learning approaches (HL only), A4.4 Ethical considerations, A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only)
title: Predictive maintenance on smart water meters — imbalanced data, metrics and governance
q_html:
Avonmere Water smart metering

Avonmere Water has replaced 90 000 mechanical water meters with smart meters that report consumption once an hour. The utility wants to use the data to predict pipe bursts and to identify meters that have become faulty, before either is reported by a customer. It holds six years of hourly readings together with 1 240 confirmed burst records over that period. The data science team has built a model that flags the 0.1% of meter-weeks it considers most likely to precede a burst; on historical data it identifies 70% of the bursts that actually occurred. The utility has 40 field crews and each investigation occupies a crew for one day.

You have been asked to review the proposal before it is deployed. The dataset and model figures are given in the case study.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the number of rows the utility will add per year, and the storage this requires in gigabytes if each row occupies 12 bytes. Hence state why a row-oriented operational table is unlikely to be the right home for this data.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Describe two preprocessing steps that must be applied to the raw hourly readings before any model is trained, and state the specific problem that each step addresses.

    (Describe)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why classification accuracy is a misleading measure of this model's performance, and identify the two measures you would report instead, explaining what each one tells the utility.

    (Explain)
  4. [5 marks](d)

    Using the figures given, evaluate whether the proposed model is operationally useful. Your evaluation must include a calculation of the number of false alarms the utility would face.

    (Evaluate)
  5. [5 marks](e)

    Discuss two ethical or social risks raised by deploying this model, and for each one recommend a specific governance measure that would reduce it.

    (Discuss)
a_html:
(a) The utility adds $90\,000\times24\times365=7.884\times10^{8}$ rows per year. (M1)(A1) At 12 bytes each that is $7.884\times10^8\times12=9.46\times10^{9}$ bytes, so about $9.46$ GB per year and roughly $57$ GB over the six-year history. (A1) An operational row-oriented table is the wrong home for it because the workload is not transactional: nobody retrieves one reading, and the queries the utility needs are aggregations over a meter, a street or a month. A column-oriented warehouse with a meter dimension and a date dimension lets those aggregations read only the columns they need, and keeps the operational billing system — which does need single-row access — free of a table two orders of magnitude larger than anything else in it. (R1)

(b) First, missing and impossible readings must be handled. Smart meters lose connectivity and report gaps, and some report zero for a period when the meter has failed rather than when no water was used; training on those rows teaches the model that a fault looks like normal consumption. The step is to flag gaps explicitly, distinguish a transmitted zero from a missing value, and either interpolate short gaps or mark them as a feature. (M1)(A1) Second, the readings must be aggregated into a fixed-shape window before training, because the model is asked about a meter-week and the raw data is hourly. Features such as the mean night-time flow, the variance of hourly flow, and the ratio of night flow to day flow have to be computed over each window; otherwise the model is given 168 loosely comparable numbers per row and no way to learn what a burst precursor looks like. (M1)(A1)

(c) Over six years the utility has $90\,000\times52\times6=2.808\times10^{7}$ meter-weeks and only 1240 positive cases, so a model that predicts 'no burst' every single time scores $1-\dfrac{1240}{2.808\times10^{7}}=99.996\%$ accuracy while doing nothing at all. (M1)(A1) The two measures to report are recall, the fraction of real bursts the model catches, and precision, the fraction of flagged cases that turn out to be real. (A1) Recall tells the utility how much of the damage it avoids; precision tells it how much of its field capacity it spends on nothing. Neither is visible in the accuracy figure, and at this base rate accuracy cannot distinguish a useful model from a useless one. (R1)

(d) The model flags $0.001\times2.808\times10^{7}=28\,080$ meter-weeks. At 70% recall it catches $0.70\times1240=868$ real bursts, so the number of false alarms is $28\,080-868=27\,212$. (M1)(A1)(A1) Precision is therefore $\dfrac{868}{28\,080}=3.1\%$: roughly thirty false alarms for every real burst found. (A1) With 40 crews the utility can investigate 40 sites a day, so clearing the flagged list occupies about $\dfrac{28\,080}{40}=702$ crew-days, and the list regenerates continuously. Against that, an uncaught burst costs an emergency repair, road closure and water loss that is far more expensive than a planned visit. The model is therefore not useless, but it is not deployable at this flag rate: the correct evaluation is that the utility should either raise the threshold until precision reaches a level its crews can absorb, or use the score to rank rather than to flag, sending out only as many visits per week as capacity allows and accepting lower recall. (R1)

(e) *Risk 1: unequal service by area.* Meter age, pipe material and consumption patterns all correlate with the age and income of the neighbourhood, so a model trained on historical bursts will systematically score poorer areas as riskier, and those areas will receive a disproportionate share of the investigative visits and of the blame. The governance measure is to audit the flag rate and the precision separately by deprivation decile before deployment and at fixed intervals afterwards, and to withhold deployment if the false-alarm rate in any decile is materially worse than the fleet average. (M1)(A1)(A1) *Risk 2: adverse action against customers identified as meter faults.* The same model that finds faulty meters produces a list of households whose consumption looks anomalous, and a faulty meter under-reads as often as it over-reads, so a customer may be presented with a back-bill generated by a statistical score they cannot see or contest. The governance measure is to require a physical meter test before any billing adjustment is made, to prohibit the score from being used as evidence on its own, and to publish the model's error rate on the customer-facing page. (M1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) allow 9.4 to 9.5 GB and credit the warehouse argument only if the candidate contrasts the workload rather than merely asserting that the table is big. In (b) credit any two well-chosen steps, but require the problem as well as the step; 'clean the data' earns nothing. In (c) the accuracy figure must be computed or at least quantified, not asserted. In (d) allow 27 000 to 27 500 false alarms and 3.0% to 3.2% precision, and award the highest mark only where the candidate converts the alarm count into crew-days and reaches a conclusion about deployability rather than restating the numbers. In (e) award up to three marks per risk, but note that the governance measure must be specific and testable; 'be transparent' or 'monitor the model' is not creditworthy. In (e) a candidate may raise environmental risk, the security of a customer-consumption database, or the use of the score in insurance or credit decisions. All are creditworthy provided a specific control is attached. What should not be credited is a list of harms with no control, or a control that cannot be checked, such as 'use the model fairly'.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: Emergency department triage — ADT selection, class design and cost analysis
syllabus_ref: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs (HL only), B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only), B2.4 Programming algorithms, B2.2 Data structures
title: Emergency department triage — ADT selection, class design and cost analysis
q_html:
Emergency department triage board

A hospital emergency department receives about 220 patients a day and the waiting room holds about 18 patients on average. On arrival each patient is assessed by a nurse and assigned a triage category from 1 to 5, where 1 is the most urgent. The triage board software must support four operations: adding a patient on arrival; removing and returning the most urgent patient when a doctor becomes free; escalating the category of a patient who is already waiting because their condition has deteriorated; and removing a patient who has left without being seen. The department has had an incident in which a category 3 patient waited behind a category 2 patient whose condition had in fact improved, and the board is being rewritten.

You are to design the data structure and the classes behind the new triage board. The four required operations and the operating figures are given in the case study.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Evaluate an unsorted array, an array kept sorted by category, and a binary max-heap as the underlying structure for the waiting list, referring to each of the four required operations in each case.

    (Evaluate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct Python class definitions for the two classes you would use to model a patient and the waiting list. Include the attributes, the constructor, and the signatures and a one-line comment for each of the four required operations.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    A patient who leaves without being seen cannot be removed from a heap directly, because their record may sit in the middle of the array. Justify whether the system should remove such a patient immediately or mark them as departed and skip them when they reach the front of the queue.

    (Justify)
  4. [5 marks](d)

    Using the operating figures, determine the total number of comparisons needed for one day of insertions under the unsorted-array design and under the binary-heap design, and determine which structure you would recommend for this department.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) *Unsorted array.* Adding a patient is $O(1)$, simply appending. (A1) Producing the most urgent patient requires scanning all $n$ entries, so it is $O(n)$; at $n=18$ that is 18 comparisons every time a doctor becomes free. Escalation is $O(n)$ to find the patient and then $O(1)$ to change the category. Removal of a departed patient is $O(n)$ to find and $O(n)$ to close the gap. (A1)

*Sorted array.* Producing the most urgent patient is $O(1)$, taking the head. (A1) Insertion is $O(n)$ because on average $n/2$ entries must be shifted to make room, and escalation is worse still: the patient must be found, removed and reinserted at a new position. The structure optimises exactly the operation that is already cheap and pays for it on the two that are not. (A1)

*Binary max-heap.* Producing the most urgent patient is $O(1)$ at the root and $O(\log n)$ to restore the heap after removal; insertion is $O(\log n)$. (A1) Escalation is $O(\log n)$ if the position of the patient is known, but $O(n)$ if it is not, because a heap offers no search. Removal of a departed patient has the same difficulty. The heap is therefore the best of the three for the two operations that dominate, and its weakness is that it cannot find an arbitrary entry quickly. (R1)

(b)

class Patient:
    """One patient on the triage board."""
    def __init__(self, patient_id, name, category, arrived_at):
        self.patient_id = patient_id      # unique identifier
        self.name = name
        self.category = category          # 1 (most urgent) to 5
        self.arrived_at = arrived_at      # timestamp used to break ties
        self.departed = False             # set when the patient leaves unseen

def __lt__(self, other):
# more urgent first; earlier arrival breaks ties within a category
return (self.category, self.arrived_at) < (other.category, other.arrived_at)

class TriageQueue:
"""Waiting list held in a binary heap with an id-to-index map."""
def __init__(self):
self.heap = [] # list of Patient
self.index = {} # patient_id -> position in heap

def add_patient(self, patient): # O(log n): append then sift up
...

def pop_most_urgent(self): # O(log n): take root, move last up, sift down
...

def escalate(self, patient_id, new_category): # O(log n) using the index
...

def mark_departed(self, patient_id): # O(1): flag only; skipped on pop
...
```

(M1)(A1)(A1) The two classes are related by composition: TriageQueue holds a collection of Patient objects and does not inherit from them. Encapsulation is respected because the heap array and the index map are private to TriageQueue, so no caller can corrupt the invariant that the index map and the array agree. (A1)

(c) Marking and skipping is the right choice. (A1) Immediate removal costs $O(n)$ to locate the patient and then a sift to restore the heap, and it happens eleven times a day, which is not a large cost in absolute terms. (A1) The real argument is not performance but integrity and audit: a patient who has left is still a patient who attended, and the department needs the record for its own statistics and for any later complaint about waiting times. Flagging the record and discarding it when it surfaces at the root removes the patient from clinical consideration immediately, which is what the board is for, while keeping the fact of the attendance. (M1)(A1) The only cost is that the heap retains stale entries, so the occupancy figure shown on the board must be derived by counting non-departed records rather than from the length of the array. (R1)

(d) Under the unsorted-array design each insertion is $O(1)$, so insertion costs essentially nothing; but the design is unusable because producing the most urgent patient costs 18 comparisons each time. (A1) Comparing the insertion work where it differs meaningfully: a sorted array needs on average $\dfrac{n}{2}=9$ shifts per insertion, so $220\times9=1980$ element moves per day. (M1)(A1) A binary heap needs at most $\log_2 18=4.17$ comparisons per insertion, so $220\times4.17\approx917$ comparisons per day, and removals cost at most $2\log_2 18$ each, giving about 1835 comparisons for the day's removals. (A1) I recommend the binary heap with a hash-based index from patient identifier to heap position. The absolute numbers here are small enough that any of the designs would function at this scale, so the recommendation rests on the shape of the growth rather than on today's figures: the heap keeps both insertion and removal logarithmic, and the index reduces escalation from $O(n)$ to $O(\log n)$, which is the operation the department's incident showed it gets wrong. (R1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) require all three structures to be addressed against all four operations; a candidate who discusses only insertion and removal earns at most three of the five marks. In (b) accept Java or pseudocode of equivalent quality, and accept a design with three classes if the third is justified; the marks are for attributes that support the four operations, a constructor, and composition rather than inheritance between the queue and the patient. Do not require working implementations of the heap methods, but do require signatures and a correct complexity comment for each. In (c) credit either answer provided it is justified, but the justification must engage with the audit requirement; a purely performance-based argument earns at most two marks. In (d) allow 900 to 920 comparisons for the heap and 1900 to 2000 for the sorted array, and note that the recommendation mark is awarded for reasoning about growth and about the escalation operation, not merely for repeating the arithmetic. If a candidate writes a complete working heap implementation in (b), credit it but do not award extra marks beyond the five available: the part asks for a design, and a long listing is often a way of avoiding the complexity comments that carry the marks. Conversely, a candidate who gives only signatures with no complexity annotation has answered a different question and should be capped at three.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Distributed monitoring system — architecture, transmission and schema design
syllabus_ref: A2.2 Network architecture, A2.3 Data transmissions, A2.4 Network security, A3.2 Database design
title: Distributed monitoring system — architecture, transmission and schema design
q_html:
Northreach cold chain

Northreach is a regional health authority that distributes vaccines by road. Its fleet is 140 refrigerated vehicles. Each vehicle carries four temperature probes inside the cargo compartment, and each probe is sampled every 30 seconds throughout the ten-hour delivery window. A reading consists of a probe identifier stored in one byte, a timestamp stored in four bytes, and a temperature stored in two bytes. The authority operates on 300 days each year. Regulatory rules require that any excursion above 8 degrees Celsius is detected and an alert raised within 60 seconds of the reading being taken, and that the full temperature history for any consignment can be produced as evidence for up to six years.

The authority has asked your team to design the monitoring and alerting subsystem. The parameters you need are given in the case study.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the total volume of data the fleet generates in one operating year, giving your answer in gibibytes, and state what the volume would become if each reading were instead stored as an 80-byte plain-text record.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    A junior developer proposes that each probe pushes every reading to the central server the moment it is taken, using a separate secure request per reading. Explain why this is a poor design even though the total payload is small, and explain how placing an edge device in each vehicle changes the trade-off.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Construct a relational schema, in third normal form, for the part of the system that records vehicles, consignments, probes and excursion alerts. Show the tables with their primary keys, foreign keys and a sensible attribute for each, and state the relationship between consignments and alerts.

    (Construct)
  4. [5 marks](d)

    A second proposal is that each vehicle stores readings locally and uploads the whole day's file once, when it returns to the depot. Evaluate this proposal against the regulatory requirements, considering the alert deadline, the reliability of the evidence trail, and the cost of the system.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Each probe is sampled $\dfrac{10\times3600}{30}=1200$ times per day, so each vehicle produces $4\times1200=4800$ readings per day. (M1)(A1) At 7 bytes each, the fleet produces

$$4800\times7\times140\times300=1.4112\times10^{9}\text{ bytes}$$

per year, which is $\dfrac{1.4112\times10^9}{2^{30}}=1.31$ GiB. (A1) Stored as 80-byte text the same readings occupy

$$4800\times80\times140\times300\div 2^{30}=15.0\text{ GiB},$$

roughly eleven times as much. (A1)

(b) The aggregate payload is only $140\times\dfrac{7}{30}\approx33$ bytes per second, so bandwidth is not the objection. (A1) The objection is per-request cost: each reading would carry its own transport handshake and encryption overhead, so a 7-byte reading could easily be carried inside a request of 800 bytes or more, multiplying the traffic by a factor well over a hundred and adding a fresh handshake every 30 seconds on every vehicle. (M1)(A1) Mobile coverage in a refrigerated vehicle is intermittent, and a per-reading push has no way to buffer across a dropout, so readings would simply be lost when a vehicle passes through a tunnel. (A1) An edge device in the vehicle changes the trade-off decisively: it can buffer readings locally through a coverage gap, batch them into one request every few minutes, evaluate the excursion rule locally so that an alert can be raised within seconds even with no network at all, and forward only alerts plus batched history to the centre. (R1)

(c) Four tables are needed:

VEHICLE(vehicleID PK, registration, depotID FK, commissionedDate)

CONSIGNMENT(consignmentID PK, vehicleID FK, departedAt, returnedAt, productCode)

PROBE(probeID PK, vehicleID FK, positionLabel, calibratedOn)

EXCURSION_ALERT(alertID PK, probeID FK, consignmentID FK, raisedAt, peakTemperature, durationSeconds, acknowledgedBy)

(M1)(A1)(A1) The schema is in third normal form because every non-key attribute depends on the whole of its table's key and on nothing else: probe calibration belongs to the probe, not to the alert, and the depot belongs to the vehicle, not to the consignment. (A1) The relationship between consignments and alerts is one-to-many: one consignment may generate any number of alerts, including none, and each alert belongs to exactly one consignment. (A1)

(d) The depot-upload proposal is cheap and simple, and for the storage requirement alone it would be adequate: the files arrive intact once a day and the six-year archive is straightforward to keep. (A1) It fails the alert deadline outright. A reading taken at the start of a shift would not reach the centre for up to ten hours, against a requirement of 60 seconds, and a spoiled consignment would be delivered before anyone knew. (M1)(A1) It also weakens the evidence trail: a vehicle involved in an accident, or one whose local storage fails, takes the whole day's record with it, and there is no independent copy against which a disputed reading could be checked. (A1) The correct evaluation is therefore that the proposal is acceptable only for the archive tier, not for the alerting tier. A hybrid is justified: the edge device raises alerts immediately over the mobile network, while the full-resolution history is batched opportunistically during the shift and reconciled at the depot. Alerts are small and time-critical; history is large and not. Splitting the two by their deadlines rather than by their size is the whole design. (R1) One further consideration belongs in any real design and is worth raising in an answer: the clock. Timestamps are generated on the vehicle, and if a vehicle's clock drifts then an alert can appear to precede the reading that caused it, which would undermine the evidence trail completely. Synchronising the edge device periodically and recording both the device time and the server receipt time on every alert removes that risk at negligible cost, and a candidate who spots it unprompted is thinking about the system rather than about the question.

Markscheme notes

In (a) award the method mark for the chain of multiplications even if the final conversion is wrong; allow 1.3 GiB to 1.4 GiB and 14.9 to 15.1 GiB, and condone the use of 10^9 rather than 2^30 provided the unit is stated consistently. In (b) the mark is for recognising that per-request overhead, not payload size, dominates; a candidate who simply says 'too much data' should not be credited, because the data is not large. In (c) accept any schema that reaches third normal form and states the keys; do not require the exact attribute names given here, but do require that alert data is separated from probe metadata and that both foreign keys on the alert table are present. In (d) a recommendation is required, not a list of pros and cons: award the highest mark only where the candidate separates the alerting tier from the archive tier and justifies the split by deadline rather than by volume. Candidates may reasonably propose a message queue or a publish-subscribe broker between the vehicle and the centre, and this should be credited where the alert path is separated from the bulk path. Where a candidate argues that the whole system should be edge-only with no central alerting at all, press for how a regulator would inspect the evidence; that question is usually enough to expose the gap.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2.4 Network security
syllabus_ref: A2.4 Network security, A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (binary, hexadecimal, hashing)
title: A2.4 Network security
q_html:
Wireless smart lock

A smart lock is fitted to a communal entrance. The lock is battery powered and communicates with the resident's phone over a short-range wireless link. The current protocol works as follows. The lock stores a 32-bit shared secret $S$. To unlock, the phone transmits a single frame containing the ASCII text OPEN followed by the 32-bit value $S$ in hexadecimal. The lock compares the received value with its stored $S$ and, if they match, releases the bolt. There is no encryption, no timestamp and no counter. An attacker with a $40\ \mathrm{EUR}$ software-defined radio can capture any frame transmitted within about $15\ \mathrm{m}$ and can later transmit arbitrary bytes. The lock is rated for $25$ operations per day on a $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah}$, $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. Its microcontroller can compute a keyed hash over $32$ bytes in $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ using $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$, whereas transmitting the current static frame costs $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$. The round-trip time on the wireless link is $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ and the bolt must be released within $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ of the resident's tap.

You have been asked to redesign the protocol. Use the case study to answer all four parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Describe a replay attack against the current protocol. State exactly what the attacker captures, what they transmit, why the lock accepts it, and how long the attack remains available to them.

    (Describe)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a challenge-response protocol that prevents replay. Your answer must specify what the lock sends, what the phone computes, what the phone returns, and what the lock checks.

    (Construct)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Explain how your protocol defeats the replay attack, and state clearly one attack it does not defeat. Quantify the probability that an attacker who has captured a million previous exchanges could still succeed by guessing.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether the additional cost of your protocol is acceptable for a battery-powered lock. Your answer must include a calculated comparison.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The attacker positions the receiver within range and captures one legitimate frame, which contains the literal text OPEN followed by the 32-bit secret $S$ in hexadecimal. (A1) Because the frame is not encrypted, the attacker reads $S$ directly from the captured bytes; because nothing in the frame varies, no computation is needed at all. (A1)

To unlock later, the attacker retransmits exactly the captured bytes. The lock compares them with its stored $S$, finds them identical, and releases the bolt. (A1)

The attack remains available indefinitely, or until $S$ is changed, because the accepted value never varies and there is no timestamp, counter or expiry. Capturing one frame grants permanent access. (A1)

(b) Protocol:

1. The phone sends a request frame containing HELLO and its device identifier. (A1)
2. The lock generates a fresh 64-bit random value $N$ (a nonce) using its hardware random source, stores it with a short expiry, and transmits CHALLENGE followed by $N$. (A1)(A1)
3. The phone computes $R = H(S \mathbin\| N)$, where $H$ is a keyed hash and $\|$ denotes concatenation, and returns RESPONSE followed by $R$. (A1)
4. The lock computes the same value from its stored $S$ and the $N$ it issued, compares with $R$ using a constant-time comparison, and releases the bolt only if they match and $N$ has not expired or been used before. (A1)

(c) The captured bytes are now useless because each exchange uses a different $N$. A response $R$ valid for one nonce produces a completely different hash for the next, and the phone never transmits $S$ itself, so the attacker who captures a million exchanges has a million $(N_i, R_i)$ pairs but no way to recover $S$ or to compute the response to a nonce they have not seen. (M1)(A1)

It does not defeat an active man-in-the-middle who relays a challenge to the genuine phone and returns the genuine response, because the protocol authenticates the phone to the lock but not the lock to the phone, and it does not defeat physical attacks on the lock or compromise of the phone itself. (A1)

If the attacker instead tries to guess the next nonce, the chance that a 64-bit value repeats one seen before, by the birthday bound after $10^{6}$ exchanges, is approximately (M1)

$$\frac{N^{2}}{2^{65}} = \frac{10^{12}}{3.69\times10^{19}} \approx 2.7\times10^{-8},$$

that is, about one chance in forty million. (A1)

(d) The additional cost is negligible and the protocol is clearly acceptable. (A1) The extra energy per operation is $0.90 - 0.15 = 0.75\ \mathrm{mJ}$ for the hash plus a second transmission of about $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$, so about $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$ in total. At 25 operations per day that is (M1)

$$0.90\times10^{-3} \times 25 \times 365 = 8.2\ \mathrm{J}\ \text{per year}.$$

The battery stores $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah} \times 3600\ \mathrm{s} \times 3.0\ \mathrm{V} = 25\,920\ \mathrm{J}$, so the extra drain is (A1)

$$\frac{8.2}{25\,920} \times 100\% \approx 0.032\%\ \text{of capacity per year}.$$

On latency, the protocol adds one round trip of $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ to the $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ budget, leaving $210\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the hash and the bolt mechanism against the $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ the hash actually needs. (A1) The conclusion is that the security improvement is effectively free, so there is no engineering justification for shipping the static-token version.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award the marks for capturing the frame, retransmitting it unchanged, the lock's equality check succeeding, and the indefinite lifetime of the attack. The last is the mark most often missed and is the reason the attack is severe rather than merely possible. (b) Accept any challenge-response design in which the lock supplies a fresh unpredictable value and the response depends on both that value and the shared secret. Credit equivalent constructions such as a counter-based scheme, but note that a counter requires synchronised state and ask what happens when it desynchronises. Do not credit a design in which the phone chooses the nonce unless it also signs it, since then the nonce provides no freshness guarantee to the lock. (c) The 'does not defeat' mark requires a specific named attack, not a vague statement that no system is perfectly secure; man-in-the-middle, physical tampering and phone compromise are all acceptable. For the probability, accept the birthday form $N^2/2^{65}$ or a simpler $10^6/2^{64}$ estimate, and accept any value of the order of $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-7}$. (d) The calculation must appear; a qualitative assertion that the cost is small earns nothing. Accept any reasonable energy model that uses the figures given, and credit a candidate who also notes that the hardware random source and the constant-time comparison are implementation requirements rather than automatic consequences of the design.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.4 A recursive implementation of a linear recurrence whose call count is exactly twice the answer minus one, where memoisation changes the cost class and the recursion depth sets a separate, independent limit
syllabus_ref: B2.4 Programming algorithms: recursion, and the analysis of the number of operations an algorithm performs. With B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking: identifying the procedure required to solve a problem and the efficiency of that procedure
title: B2.4 A recursive implementation of a linear recurrence whose call count is exactly twice the answer minus one, where memoisation changes the cost class and the recursion depth sets a separate, independent limit
q_html:
A service computes terms of a sequence defined by $F(1) = 1$, $F(2) = 1$ and $F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)$ for $n \ge 3$. The implementation currently in production is the following, in a language whose default recursion limit is $1000$ nested calls and whose interpreter executes about $1.0 \times 10^{7}$ function calls per second:
``
FUNCTION term(n)
IF n <= 2 THEN
RETURN 1
ELSE
RETURN term(n - 1) + term(n - 2)
END IF
END FUNCTION
`
A second implementation stores each computed value in a dictionary the first time it is needed and reads it thereafter, so that each index is evaluated once. A third implementation uses a loop and holds only the two most recent values.
Throughout, a *call* means one invocation of term`, including the invocation that answers the original request. The phrase *recursion depth* means the number of invocations that are simultaneously on the call stack at the deepest point of the computation.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the number of calls made when term(6) is evaluated, by writing down the recurrence satisfied by the call count and evaluating it from the base cases upwards. State the recurrence you used.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Let $c(n)$ be the number of calls made in evaluating term(n), and let $F$ denote the sequence itself. Show that $c(n) = 2F(n) - 1$ satisfies the recurrence from part (a) together with its base cases, and hence determine the number of calls made when term(40) is evaluated. Estimate the time this takes at the stated execution rate.

    (Show that)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    The memoised implementation makes exactly $2n - 3$ calls for $n \ge 2$. Determine the number of calls it makes for $n = 40$, determine the factor by which this reduces the work against part (b), and determine the largest value of $n$ for which the unmemoised implementation finishes within one minute.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain why the memoised implementation still fails when asked for term(2000), even though it is efficient in the number of calls. State the depth of the call stack in each implementation as a function of $n$, and state which implementation is not subject to the failure and why.

    (Explain)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    The service must answer $1.0 \times 10^{4}$ requests per day for values of $n$ up to $1500$, each request arriving independently and needing one term. Justify, with quantitative reasoning, which of the three implementations should be deployed, and state one circumstance in which your recommendation would change.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) Evaluating term(n) for n >= 3 invokes term(n - 1) and term(n - 2) as well as being an invocation itself, so the call count satisfies

$$c(n) = 1 + c(n-1) + c(n-2), \qquad c(1) = c(2) = 1 \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

the base cases holding because for n <= 2 the function returns immediately without recursing. Working upwards:

$c(3) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3$, $c(4) = 1 + 3 + 1 = 5$, $c(5) = 1 + 5 + 3 = 9$, $c(6) = 1 + 9 + 5 = 15$ (A1).

So term(6) makes 15 calls to compute the value 8.

(b) Substituting $c(n) = 2F(n) - 1$ into the recurrence, the left-hand side is $2F(n) - 1$ and the right-hand side is

$$1 + \bigl(2F(n-1) - 1\bigr) + \bigl(2F(n-2) - 1\bigr) = 2\bigl(F(n-1) + F(n-2)\bigr) - 1 = 2F(n) - 1 \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

using the definition of $F$ itself. For the base cases, $c(1) = 2(1) - 1 = 1$ and $c(2) = 2(1) - 1 = 1$, both correct (A1). Since a first-order recurrence in two variables with two base conditions has a unique solution, the closed form is established. With $F(40) = 102\,334\,155$,

$$c(40) = 2(102\,334\,155) - 1 = 204\,668\,309 \;\text{(A1)}$$

about $2.0 \times 10^{8}$ calls. At $1.0 \times 10^{7}$ calls per second that is roughly $20$ seconds for one term (A1) — and the cost grows by a factor of about $1.618$ for each increment of $n$, so each extra unit of $n$ adds about $62\%$ to the running time.

(c) For $n = 40$ the memoised version makes $2(40) - 3 = 77$ calls (A1). The reduction factor is

$$\frac{204\,668\,309}{77} \approx 2.66 \times 10^{6} \;\text{(A1)}$$

so roughly two and a half million times less work, taking a few microseconds rather than twenty seconds. For the unmemoised version, one minute allows $6.0 \times 10^{7}$ calls, which requires $2F(n) - 1 \le 6.0 \times 10^{7}$, that is $F(n) \le 3.0 \times 10^{7}$. Since $F(41) = 165\,580\,141$ and $F(42) = 267\,914\,296$ are respectively above and below $3.0 \times 10^{7}$ after dividing by two, checking directly: $c(42) = 535\,828\,591$ calls, which takes $54$ seconds, while $c(43) = 866\,988\,873$ takes $87$ seconds. The largest value computable within a minute is therefore $n = 42$ (A1).

(d) The memoised version is efficient in *calls* but not in *depth*. Each evaluation of term(n) proceeds by calling term(n - 1), which calls term(n - 2), and so on down to the base case, so the deepest point of the computation has about $n - 1$ invocations simultaneously on the stack (M1). Memoisation prevents repeated evaluation of a value; it does not shorten the chain, because the first evaluation of each index still descends the whole way to the base case before anything is stored. At $n = 2000$ the depth is about $1999$, well past the default limit of $1000$, so the interpreter raises a stack-overflow error before the answer is produced (A1). The unmemoised version has the same depth and the same problem, besides being astronomically slow. The iterative version keeps no chain at all: it holds two variables and updates them $n - 2$ times, so its stack use is constant and its depth does not depend on $n$ (A1). It is the only one of the three that is not subject to this failure.

(e) The iterative implementation should be deployed (A1). The reasoning: at $n = 1500$ the naive version needs about $2F(1500) - 1$ calls, and since $F(n) \approx \varphi^{n}/\sqrt{5}$ with $\varphi = 1.618$, $\log_{10} F(1500) \approx 1500 \times 0.2090 - 0.349 = 313$, so on the order of $10^{313}$ calls — beyond any conceivable hardware, and it would also breach the stack limit. The memoised version makes only $2(1500) - 3 = 2997$ calls, which is trivial, but at $n = 1500$ its depth is about $1499$, still beyond the default limit of $1000$, so it would fail at run time for the upper part of the requested range (M1). The iterative version uses about $1500$ loop steps and constant memory per request; at $1.0 \times 10^{4}$ requests per day that is $1.5 \times 10^{7}$ steps per day, a fraction of a second of processor time in total, and it has no stack exposure at all (A1). The recommendation would change if the language runtime guaranteed tail-call elimination or if the recursion limit were raised well above $1500$ — in that case the memoised version, or a plain iterative version with the same cost, would be equally acceptable and the choice could be made on readability alone (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) (A1) for the recurrence $c(n) = 1 + c(n-1) + c(n-2)$ with both base cases, (A1) for $c(6) = 15$ obtained by working upwards rather than by assertion. Accept a candidate who draws or describes the recursion tree and counts its nodes, provided the count is correct; a tree diagram showing 15 nodes is full evidence. Candidates who forget the +1 for the call itself get $c(6) = 25$ or similar and should lose the first mark only if the structure is otherwise right.

(b) (M1) for substituting the proposed closed form into the recurrence, (A1) for showing it satisfies the recurrence using the definition of $F$, (A1) for checking both base cases, (A1) for $204\,668\,309$, (A1) for the time estimate of about 20 seconds. Five fields; credit four. The base-case check is not optional: a recurrence of order two has a two-parameter family of solutions and matching two values is what pins one of them down. Accept a candidate who reaches the same number by direct computation of $F(40)$, provided the link to the call count is stated.

(c) (A1) for 77, (A1) for the factor $2.66 \times 10^{6}$ (accept anything between $2.6$ and $2.7$ million), (A1) for $n = 42$. Full credit requires the candidate to have *checked* both $n = 42$ and $n = 43$ against the one-minute budget rather than interpolating; a candidate who states 42 from a rough estimate alone loses the final mark. Note that the answer depends on the stated execution rate, and a candidate who says so should be credited.

(d) (M1) for identifying depth as roughly $n$ and noting that memoisation does not shorten the chain, (A1) for connecting $n = 2000$ to the limit of $1000$ and naming the failure mode, (A1) for identifying the iterative version as immune and saying why its stack use is constant. Do not accept 'memoisation fixes it' — that is the error this part exists to catch. A candidate who notes that the unmemoised version would fail on *both* counts earns credit for the observation.

(e) (A1) for choosing the iterative implementation, (M1) for quantitative reasoning about the naive version's call count at $n = 1500$, (A1) for the memoised version's stack failure above about $n = 1000$, (A1) for a circumstance that would change the recommendation. Four fields; credit three. Accept any reasonable circumstance genuinely tied to a number, such as a raised recursion limit above $1500$, a runtime with tail-call elimination, or a requirement to compute only up to $n = 900$. Do not accept vague appeals to 'readability' without a numeric trigger.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A4.3 A model whose reported accuracy of ninety-six per cent is an artefact of splitting a dataset of repeated hospital visits at the scan level rather than at the patient level
syllabus_ref: A4.3 Machine learning approaches: training, validation and test sets, and the metrics used to evaluate a classifier. With A4.4 Ethical considerations: the duties owed to those affected by a deployed model, and to the regulators who oversee it
title: A4.3 A model whose reported accuracy of ninety-six per cent is an artefact of splitting a dataset of repeated hospital visits at the scan level rather than at the patient level
q_html:
A hospital has assembled a dataset of $12\,000$ retinal scans taken from patients attending a diabetic screening clinic, labelled by whether the scan shows signs of the condition. The dataset covers $6\,400$ patients in total: $4\,800$ patients attended once, and the remaining $1\,600$ patients attended three times each, contributing $4\,800$ scans between them. Overall $25\%$ of scans are positive.
A team split the dataset at random by scan, using $80\%$ for training and $20\%$ for testing, trained a convolutional classifier, and reported the following results on the test set of $2\,400$ scans:
| split | true positives | false positives | false negatives | true negatives |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| random, by scan | $560$ | $60$ | $40$ | $1\,740$ |
| grouped, by patient | $360$ | $300$ | $240$ | $1\,500$ |
The second row was produced after a reviewer noticed the problem and repeated the evaluation with a split in which no patient appears on both sides. Both test sets contain $2\,400$ scans and both have the same prevalence of $25\%$ positive.
The hospital intends to use the model to decide which patients are recalled for further examination.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    For the random split, calculate the accuracy, the precision, the recall and the F1 score, giving each to three significant figures. Show the calculation you used for the F1 score.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Repeat all four calculations for the grouped split, and determine the percentage by which the F1 score falls between the two.

    (Calculate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain the mechanism by which grouping produces the discrepancy, and determine the expected number of scans in the test set that belong to a patient who also has at least one scan in the training set. State what fraction of the test set this represents.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The hospital's administrator notes that the grouped accuracy is still seventy-seven and a half per cent and asks whether the model is therefore useful. Evaluate this claim by comparing the grouped accuracy with the accuracy obtainable by a trivial classifier that predicts 'negative' for every scan, and by considering what the grouped precision and recall mean for a patient who is recalled unnecessarily or missed entirely.

    (Evaluate)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    Discuss what the team should report to the regulator, given that the ninety-six per cent figure has already appeared in an internal briefing, and state what change to the evaluation protocol should be made before any further claim is published.

    (Discuss)
a_html:
(a) For the random split, with 560 true positives, 60 false positives, 40 false negatives and 1740 true negatives, and a test set of 2400 scans:

$$\text{accuracy} = \frac{560 + 1740}{2400} = \frac{2300}{2400} = 0.958 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$\text{precision} = \frac{560}{560 + 60} = \frac{560}{620} = 0.903 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$\text{recall} = \frac{560}{560 + 40} = \frac{560}{600} = 0.933 \;\text{(A1)}$$

The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall:

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \times 0.903 \times 0.933}{0.903 + 0.933} = \frac{1.686}{1.837} = 0.918 \;\text{(M1)}$$

So the random split reports 95.8 per cent accuracy with an F1 of 0.918.

(b) For the grouped split:

$$\text{accuracy} = \frac{360 + 1500}{2400} = \frac{1860}{2400} = 0.775 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$\text{precision} = \frac{360}{360 + 300} = \frac{360}{660} = 0.545, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{360}{360 + 240} = \frac{360}{600} = 0.600 \;\text{(A1)}$$

$$F_1 = \frac{2 \times 0.545 \times 0.600}{0.545 + 0.600} = \frac{0.655}{1.145} = 0.571 \;\text{(A1)}$$

The F1 score falls from $0.918$ to $0.571$, a fall of

$$\frac{0.918 - 0.571}{0.918} = 0.378 \;\text{(A1)}$$

that is, about 38 per cent of the reported performance was an artefact of the split.

(c) The rows of the dataset are not independent. A patient who attended three times contributes three scans that show the same eyes, taken close together, and almost certainly carry the same label. A random split by scan places some of those scans in training and some in test, so the model is evaluated on scans of patients it was trained on (M1).
```
