It can then score well by memorising a particular patient's retina rather than by detecting the condition, and the test set ceases to measure generalisation.

```
To quantify it, consider one of the $1\,600$ repeat patients with three scans. Each scan independently lands in the test set with probability $0.2$. The expected number of that patient's scans that land in test while at least one sibling lands in training is

$$1 \times \binom{3}{1}(0.2)(0.8)^2 \;+\; 2 \times \binom{3}{2}(0.2)^2(0.8) = 0.384 + 0.192 = 0.576 \;\text{(M1)}$$

the case of all three landing in test contributing nothing, since that patient is then absent from training. Over $1\,600$ such patients the expected number of compromised test scans is

$$1600 \times 0.576 = 922 \;\text{(A1)}$$

out of $2\,400$, which is $38\%$ of the test set. Roughly two in five of the scans the model was judged on belonged to a patient it had already seen.

(d) The administrator's figure is technically correct and clinically misleading. A classifier that always predicts 'negative' would be correct on the $75\%$ of scans that are negative, giving an accuracy of $0.750$ (M1). The grouped accuracy of $0.775$ beats that by $2.5$ percentage points, so in raw accuracy terms the model adds almost nothing over never diagnosing anybody (A1). The metrics that matter are the other two. Grouped recall of $0.600$ means that two in five patients who have the condition are told they do not — a missed diagnosis, which in a screening programme is the failure that costs sight (A1). Grouped precision of $0.545$ means that nearly half of all recalls are of patients who turn out to be clear: each one costs a clinic appointment, and each one also costs the trust of a patient who was told they might be losing their sight. Taken together, an F1 of $0.571$ on a condition with a quarter prevalence is not a deployable screening tool (A1); it is a model that needs substantially more work, and the honest reading is that the ninety-six per cent figure concealed a model that barely beats doing nothing.

(e) The regulator should be told the grouped figures, and told explicitly that the earlier figure was produced by a flawed protocol rather than by a different model (A1). Concretely: the model unchanged reports $0.958$ accuracy and $0.918$ F1 under the scan-level split and $0.775$ accuracy and $0.571$ F1 under the patient-level split, and the difference is entirely attributable to $38\%$ of the test set belonging to patients present in training. Withholding that because the briefing has already circulated would mean the deployment decision is taken on a number the team knows to be wrong, and in a clinical context that is not a presentational matter but a safety one (A1). Before any further claim is published, the evaluation protocol should be changed so that splitting is done by group — all scans from a patient go to exactly one side — and, ideally, so that the whole procedure is repeated by grouped cross-validation, giving a spread of scores rather than a single number, so that the sensitivity of the result to which patients landed where is visible (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for accuracy 0.958, (A1) for precision 0.903, (A1) for recall 0.933, (M1) for the F1 calculation shown as a harmonic mean and evaluated to 0.918. Four fields; credit three. Candidates who use the arithmetic mean of precision and recall instead of the harmonic mean should be credited for the method mark only if they state that they are doing so, and lose it if they present it as F1. Accept answers given as percentages. Note that the test set size of 2400 is needed for the accuracy denominator and should come from the stem.

(b) (A1) for accuracy 0.775, (A1) for precision 0.545 and recall 0.600, (A1) for F1 0.571, (A1) for the 38 per cent fall. Candidates should be advised that the fall is to be expressed relative to the original 0.918, not as an absolute difference of 0.347, and either is accepted provided it is labelled.

(c) (M1) for identifying the non-independence of rows from the same patient as the mechanism, (M1) for setting up the expectation over one three-scan patient with the correct binomial terms, (A1) for 922 scans and the 38 per cent figure. The exclusion of the all-three-in-test case is the subtle step and should be credited specifically: a candidate who simply computes $1600 \times 3 \times 0.2 = 960$ has made a defensible approximation and may be given the mark only if they acknowledge that some of those patients appear nowhere in training. Do not accept an answer that attributes the gap to overfitting in general without naming the shared-patient mechanism.

(d) (M1) for computing the trivial baseline accuracy of 0.750, (A1) for observing that the grouped accuracy beats it by only 2.5 points, (A1) for interpreting recall 0.600 as two in five true cases missed, (A1) for interpreting precision 0.545 as nearly half of all recalls being unnecessary and drawing a conclusion about deployability. Four fields; credit four. A candidate who reaches the conclusion 'not deployable' without the baseline comparison earns at most two of these, because the baseline is what turns an opinion into an argument.

(e) (A1) for stating that the grouped figures must be reported and that the earlier figure came from a flawed protocol, (A1) for the safety framing of not correcting a circulated number, (A1) for the protocol change — grouped splitting, and preferably grouped cross-validation giving a spread. Candidates who propose retraining or collecting more data have not answered the question, which is about what to report and how to evaluate; that is worth at most one mark. Credit should be given for any clear statement that the number already in circulation must be actively corrected rather than quietly superseded.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.3 Programming constructs
syllabus_ref: B2.3 Programming constructs (sequence, selection, iteration, nested loops, loop conditions and termination, tracing the execution of a loop)
title: A loop that is linear only while the data keeps moving
q_html:
PulseTrack - steady-run detection

PulseTrack is a wearable heart-rate monitor. It samples the wearer's heart rate once per second and stores each day's readings as a list of integers.

For every reading the device reports the length of the steady run ending at that reading: the number of immediately preceding readings such that every step between consecutive readings in that run differs by no more than a tolerance of 5 beats per minute. A reading with no steady predecessor has run length 0. So for the series [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] the run lengths are [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3].

A developer wrote the function below and claims it runs in linear time: "the while loop stops as soon as it reaches a reading that differs from the one before it by more than the tolerance, and in a real recording that happens after a step or two."

The device records 86,400 readings per day, one per second for 24 hours, and runs the analysis each night on the day's readings. The analysis must finish within a few seconds.

def steady_runs(readings, tol=5):
    runs = []
    for i in range(len(readings)):
        count = 0
        j = i
        while j > 0 and abs(readings[j] - readings[j - 1]) <= tol:
            count += 1
            j -= 1
        runs.append(count)
    return runs

The readings are stored as a list of integers, one per second. The nightly analysis must finish in a few seconds on the device, and it must report the run lengths exactly.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain, by tracing the loop, what steady_runs returns for the readings [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with the default tolerance of 5.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Explain why the developer's claim that the function runs in linear time is unsound. State the property of the input that the claim assumes, and describe the input pattern on which the function performs the greatest number of steps.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Construct a Python function that returns exactly the same result as steady_runs but runs in linear time. You may not import any module and you may not use the abs function. A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm, so write the algorithm rather than a demonstration of syntax.

    (Construct)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    A colleague proposes to fix the performance by adding a limit inside the while loop so that it stops after at most 1,000 steps. Evaluate this proposal, using your answers to parts (b) and (c).

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Tracing the loop for readings = [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with tol = 5:

| i | readings[i] | comparisons in the while | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 70 | j = 0, loop does not run | 0 |
| 1 | 72 | $\lvert 72-70 \rvert = 2 \le 5 \rightarrow 1$ | 1 |
| 2 | 71 | $\lvert 71-72 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 71-70 \rvert = 1$ | 2 |
| 3 | 90 | $\lvert 90-71 \rvert = 19 > 5$ | 0 |
| 4 | 89 | $\lvert 89-90 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 89-71 \rvert = 18 > 5$ | 1 |
| 5 | 88 | $1$, then $2$, then $\lvert 88-71 \rvert = 17 > 5$ | 2 |
| 6 | 87 | $1$, then $2$, then $3$, then $\lvert 87-71 \rvert = 16 > 5$ | 3 |

The function returns [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3]. (M1) for tracing the loop as a walk backwards while consecutive differences stay within the tolerance, (A1) for the correct values, (A1) for the list as a whole, including the reset to 0 at index 3 and the growing run at the end.

(b) The claim is unsound because the number of steps the inner loop performs is not a constant — it is the length of the steady run, which is a property of the *data*, not of the code. (M1) The claim assumes that consecutive readings almost always differ by more than the tolerance, so that the loop exits after one or two steps. (A1) That assumption is false for this application: heart rate sampled once a second during steady exercise changes by far less than 5 beats per minute between consecutive samples, so long runs are the normal case and the loop walks back a long way. (A1) The greatest number of steps occurs when every consecutive difference is within tolerance — a constant series, or a slow monotonic drift. For each $i$ the loop then runs all the way back to index 0, giving $0+1+2+\dots+(n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ steps, which is quadratic rather than linear. (A1)

(c)

def steady_runs(readings, tol=5):
    n = len(readings)
    runs = [0] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        step = readings[i] - readings[i - 1]
        if -tol <= step <= tol:
            runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1
    return runs

(M1) for a single pass that keeps no inner loop. (A1) for the observation that makes it work: the steady run ending at i is either empty or it is the run ending at i - 1 extended by exactly one reading, so the answer for i can be read off the answer for i - 1. (A1) for runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1 and (A1) for initialising every entry to 0, which is what makes the run reset after a step larger than the tolerance. (A1) for using no library module and no abs, expressing the tolerance as the two-sided test -tol <= step <= tol.

The work done is $n-1$ comparisons and one assignment per reading, so the time is $O(n)$ and the extra memory is $O(n)$ for the output. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm; the translation is a for loop over the array indices and the identical recurrence, so the language is irrelevant to the reasoning.

(d) The proposal should be rejected, for three reasons.

First, it does not change the complexity. The inner loop can still run up to 1,000 steps for every reading, so the worst case is still proportional to $1000n$; capping the loop divides the running time by a constant, and a constant factor is not a change of order. (M1) With 86,400 readings a day the uncapped worst case is $86{,}400 \times 86{,}399 / 2 = 3{,}732{,}436{,}800$ inner steps, the capped version still performs up to $86{,}400 \times 1000 = 86{,}400{,}000$, and the linear version performs 86,399. (A1)

Second, and more seriously, the cap makes the result *wrong* precisely where the app matters. A steady run of 1,500 readings would be reported as 1,000, and a run of 4,000 as 1,000; the error is silent, it is always an under-report, and it is concentrated on the longest runs — which are exactly the steady states the app exists to find. (A1)

Third, the trade is unnecessary, because part (c) already gives an exact linear algorithm. Capping the loop trades a correctness guarantee for a constant factor when a change of order was available at the same cost. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept any trace, as a table or as prose. The essential marks are the mechanism (walk backwards while *each consecutive pair* is within tolerance) and the result. A candidate who compares every earlier reading against the current reading rather than against its own predecessor has misread the function and forfeits the trace marks — this is the single most common error.

(b) The two discriminating marks are the unstated assumption (that consecutive readings usually differ by more than the tolerance) and the worst-case count $n(n-1)/2$. A candidate who writes "it is actually O(n squared)" without naming the assumption earns one mark only. Accept a description of the worst case as "a constant series", "a steady recording" or "a slow drift"; require the recognition that the loop runs to index 0 each time.

(c) Accept any single-pass algorithm that returns the same list, including one that builds the list by appending rather than pre-allocating it. Do not award the linear mark to a candidate who keeps a nested loop, even a faster one — the question is about the order of growth. A candidate who uses abs despite the prohibition should be told the constraint was stated; the reasoning marks may still be awarded. A candidate who uses the csv-style two-pointer scan but does not derive the recurrence should be capped at two marks.

(d) The evaluation must distinguish a constant-factor improvement from a change of order. A candidate who says "1,000 is small enough" has missed that the cap silently corrupts the longest runs, and that those runs are the app's output. Award the final mark only when the answer connects the cap to a correctness loss rather than to performance alone.

title: A constructor that prices every team as a single seat
q_html:
Rowan Software - annual seat pricing

Rowan Software bills teams for a subscription. Every plan has a term in months and an annual fee, and the annual fee is computed once, when the plan object is created, so that invoices can be issued later without recomputing prices.

The code below defines a base class Plan and a subclass SeatPlan, whose price depends on how many seats the team has bought. A seat costs 9 pounds per month. The class attribute seats = 1 is a default for plans that have not specified a seat count.

The developer tested the class with the three tests shown, and all three pass. The service has about 900 team customers; the average team buys 20 seats and signs a 12-month term. The finance team reconciles annual fees once a year and has never queried an individual customer's monthly fee.

class Plan:
    PER_SEAT = 9                      # pounds per seat per month

    def __init__(self, months):
        self.months = months
        self.annual_fee = self.monthly_fee() * months

    def monthly_fee(self):
        return 0

class SeatPlan(Plan):
    seats = 1                         # default for plans with no seat count

    def __init__(self, seats, months):
        super().__init__(months)
        self.seats = seats

    def monthly_fee(self):
        return self.seats * Plan.PER_SEAT

# the developer's tests - all three pass
def test_one_seat():
    assert SeatPlan(1, 12).annual_fee == 108

def test_monthly_fee_scales():
    assert SeatPlan(20, 12).monthly_fee() == 180

def test_seats_are_recorded():
    assert SeatPlan(20, 12).seats == 20

The finance team has asked you to review the pricing code before the catalogue is extended. The reconciliation compares each customer's stored annual_fee with the invoice total.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain what annual_fee holds for SeatPlan(20, 12) and why it is not equal to monthly_fee() * months. Refer to the order in which the statements in SeatPlan.__init__ and Plan.__init__ run.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a corrected design in which the annual fee is always computed from the plan's own seat count and no constructor reads a field of an object that is not yet fully initialised. Use composition: a plan must hold a separate pricing object rather than inherit its price. Write the classes and state the annual fee for 20 seats over 12 months.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the annual fee that every SeatPlan caches, the fee that a 20-seat 12-month plan should be charged, and the total annual shortfall across all 900 customers. State how many of those customers are billed incorrectly.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the two ways of removing the bug - patching the inheritance hierarchy so the field is set before the superclass constructor runs, or replacing the hierarchy with composition - and recommend one for a catalogue that will soon combine seats, usage and region.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) For SeatPlan(20, 12) the attribute annual_fee holds 108. (A1) It is not 2160 because of the order in which the two constructors run. The first statement of SeatPlan.__init__ is super().__init__(months), and inside Plan.__init__ the assignment self.annual_fee = self.monthly_fee() * months calls self.monthly_fee(). (M1) Because monthly_fee is overridden, that call dispatches to SeatPlan.monthly_fee, which reads self.seats. At that moment the instance has only months in its attribute dictionary - the statement self.seats = seats has not run yet - so the lookup falls back to the class attribute seats = 1. The fee is therefore computed for a one-seat plan: $1 \times 9 = 9$ per month and $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year. (A1) Only after the superclass constructor returns is the instance attribute set to 20, and by then annual_fee has already been stored and is never recomputed; a later call to monthly_fee() correctly returns $20 \times 9 = 180$, so the live query and the cached value disagree.

(b) The defect is not that a constructor calls a method. It is that a constructor calls a method on an object that is only partly built, so the method can observe a field that does not exist yet. Composition removes the half-built object by making the pricing rule a separate, fully constructed collaborator:

class SeatPricing:
    PER_SEAT = 9
    def __init__(self, seats):
        self.seats = seats
    def monthly_fee(self):
        return self.seats * self.PER_SEAT

class Plan:
def __init__(self, months, pricing):
self.months = months
self.pricing = pricing
self.annual_fee = pricing.monthly_fee() * months

p = Plan(12, SeatPricing(20))
print(p.annual_fee) # 2160
```

(M1) for giving Plan a pricing collaborator instead of a subclass that overrides a price method. (A1) for constructing that collaborator completely before the plan uses it, so no method ever reads a field that has not been set. (A1) for computing the annual fee from the collaborator's result. (A1) for the correct value, $180 \times 12 = 2160$. (A1) for noting that Plan.__init__ still calls a method, but on a different object that is already finished, which is why the same line is now safe.

Two inheritance-preserving fixes also work and are acceptable. Assigning the subclass field before the superclass constructor runs:

class SeatPlan(Plan):
    def __init__(self, seats, months):
        self.seats = seats        # set first
        super().__init__(months)  # monthly_fee() now sees 20

and passing the already-computed fee up to the base constructor, so the base never calls an overridable method at all:

class Plan:
    def __init__(self, months, monthly_fee):
        self.months = months
        self.annual_fee = monthly_fee * months

All three produce annual_fee == 2160. (A1)

(c) During construction self.seats always falls back to the class attribute 1, so every SeatPlan caches $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year, whatever its seat count. (M1) At an average of 20 seats the correct fee is $20 \times 9 = 180$ per month, which is $180 \times 12 = 2160$ per year. (A1) The undercharge is therefore $2160 - 108 = 2052$ per customer per year. (A1) Across 900 customers the shortfall is $900 \times 2052 = 1{,}846{,}800$, and all 900 are billed incorrectly: a customer is billed correctly only if it happens to have exactly one seat, which the 20-seat average rules out. The cached fee is one twentieth of the true fee at 20 seats, which is why 108 looks like a plausible annual price for a small team rather than an obvious error. (A1)

(d) Both remedies remove the bug, so the choice is about the next change rather than this one. Patching the hierarchy - assign seats before super().__init__, or pass the fee up - is a one- or two-line change with no runtime cost, but it leaves the base constructor calling an overridable method, so the trap stays armed for the next subclass whose fields are set after super(). (M1) The composition design removes the trap: Plan depends on a SeatPricing object, so a subclass cannot observe an unset field. Its cost is one small object per plan - 900 SeatPricing objects of 48 bytes each, about 309,600 bytes once their instance dictionaries are counted, or roughly 0.31 MB - against a shortfall of 1,846,800. (A1) That is a ratio of about six to one between the money and the memory, so the memory argument is irrelevant at this scale. (A1) The decisive argument is growth: the catalogue will combine seats, usage and region, and inheritance multiplies subclasses (three independent pricing features give up to $2^3 = 8$ subclasses, and each new feature doubles that), while composition adds one collaborator per feature. Recommend adopting composition for the extended catalogue. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The mark is for the mechanism, not the number. The candidate must say that super().__init__ runs before self.seats = seats, that the call to monthly_fee() inside the base constructor dispatches to the override, and that the attribute lookup then finds the class attribute seats = 1. A candidate who writes only that the constructor uses the wrong seat count, without the order of the statements, earns at most one mark. Accept a trace table. Do not accept the claim that the class attribute is overwritten: it is not; the instance attribute is created later and shadows it only from that point on.

(b) Accept any design that removes the read of a not-yet-assigned field, including composition, assigning the field before super().__init__, or passing the computed fee into the base constructor; code in Java or another language is acceptable if the syllabus version being sat requires it. The value 2160 must appear. A candidate who keeps the original hierarchy and merely adds a recompute() call after construction has treated the symptom; award at most two marks unless they also explain why the base constructor still calls an overridable method.

(c) Follow through on any consistent seat average; the marks are for the method (a cached 108 against a correct 180 per month, times 12) and for the totals 2052 and 1,846,800. A candidate who forgets that the cached fee is 108 for every plan and uses 20 seats in both terms obtains a shortfall of zero; this forfeits the first mark. Accept all 900, or every customer with more than one seat, for the count, provided the candidate notes the one-seat exception.

(d) This is an evaluate question, so a recommendation is required; a candidate who describes both fixes without choosing earns at most two of the four marks. The memory comparison must be present for the third mark and must be tied to the 1,846,800 figure. The final mark is for the growth argument - combinatorial subclass explosion under inheritance against one collaborator per feature under composition. Do not accept composition is always better without the growth reasoning, and do not accept keep inheritance because it is shorter without acknowledging the fragile base class.

title: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs
q_html:
A weather station that samples every 16 milliseconds

A weather station records a temperature every 16 ms. Each reading is stamped with the elapsed time in milliseconds since the shift began, so during the first 128 ms the eight keys that are stored are 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112 and 128.

The readings are held in a hash table of m buckets. The hash function is h(k) = k mod m, and collisions are resolved by linear probing: a key whose bucket is already occupied is placed in the next bucket that is free, wrapping around to bucket 0 if the end of the table is reached. A lookup follows the same sequence and stops when it finds the key or reaches an empty bucket.

Two table sizes are under consideration, m = 16 and m = 17. A colleague has also suggested doubling the table to m = 32, on the grounds that a larger table must be faster.

Evaluate whether the load factor is a reliable predictor of the cost of a lookup in this table. Work in probes, where one probe examines one bucket. Assume the eight keys are inserted in increasing order, that no key is ever deleted, and that the table is empty before the first insert.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the bucket index that each of the eight keys hashes to when m = 16, and state the number of probes needed to insert each of those keys.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Determine the load factor of the table at m = 16 and at m = 17, and determine how many of the m buckets each table can ever reach with these eight keys. Give both reachable shares as percentages to two decimal places.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the number of probes needed to look up the key 128, and the number needed to establish that the key 144 is absent, in each of the m = 16 and m = 17 tables. Explain why the two load factors do not predict the difference you find.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Your colleague proposes doubling the table from m = 16 to m = 32. Determine the load factor and the reachable-bucket share at m = 32, and justify whether the proposal addresses the problem you identified in part (c).

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). Every key is a multiple of 16, because 16 = 16 x 1, 32 = 16 x 2 and so on up to 128 = 16 x 8. So for every one of the eight keys k mod 16 = 0. (M1) All eight keys hash to bucket 0. (A1)

Linear probing then places them in consecutive buckets starting at 0: the first key finds bucket 0 free and takes it, the second finds it occupied and takes bucket 1, and so on. The probes needed are therefore 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, and the total for the eight inserts is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 36. (A1)

The finished table holds 16 in bucket 0, 32 in bucket 1, 48 in bucket 2, and so on up to 128 in bucket 7. Buckets 8 to 15 are empty.

Part (b). At m = 16 the table holds 8 keys in 16 buckets, so the load factor is 8 / 16 = 0.50. (M1)(A1) At m = 17 it is 8 / 17 = 0.470588..., which is 0.47 to two decimal places. (A1)

The reachable share is a different quantity. At m = 16 only bucket 0 is ever reached, so 1 of the 16 buckets is in play: 1 / 16 = 6.25%. (M1)(A1)

At m = 17 the keys hash to 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10 and 9 — eight distinct buckets, because 17 shares no factor with the key step of 16, so each successive key lands in the bucket before the previous one. So 8 of the 17 buckets are reachable: 8 / 17 = 47.06%. (A1)

It is worth noticing that at m = 17 the reachable share and the load factor are the same number, 47.06%, because every key occupies a bucket of its own. That coincidence does not hold at m = 16, where the two quantities are 0.50 and 0.0625 — a factor of eight apart. The two quantities are equal only when no two keys collide, which is exactly the case in which there is nothing to predict.

Part (c). At m = 16 the key 128 was the eighth key inserted, so it sits at the end of a run of eight occupied buckets that begins at bucket 0. A successful search for 128 examines buckets 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7: eight probes. (M1)(A1)

The key 144 is also 0 mod 16, so it too begins at bucket 0. It must examine all eight occupied buckets and then bucket 8, which is empty, before it can conclude that the key is absent: nine probes. (A1)

At m = 17, 128 mod 17 = 9 and bucket 9 holds 128 alone, so the successful search costs one probe. And 144 mod 17 = 8, and bucket 8 is empty, so the unsuccessful search also costs one probe. (M1)(A1)

The two load factors are 0.50 and 0.47, differing by 0.03, or about 6% of either value. Yet the successful search costs eight times as much in one table as in the other, and the unsuccessful search nine times as much. A quantity that differs by 6% cannot account for a cost that differs by 700%. The load factor describes how full the table is; what governs the cost here is how the keys *distribute*, and with a key step of 16 and a table size of 16 the distribution is degenerate — every key competes for one bucket. The load factor is a correct measure of a real property that happens not to be the property that decides this question.

Part (d). At m = 32 the keys 32, 64, 96 and 128 are all 0 mod 32, and 16, 48, 80 and 112 are all 16 mod 32. So the keys occupy exactly two buckets, 0 and 16, each holding four keys. (M1)(A1)

The load factor is 8 / 32 = 0.25, exactly half of 0.50. (A1) The reachable share is 2 / 32 = 1 / 16 = 6.25%, which is unchanged from m = 16. (A1)

So the proposal does reduce the worst-case successful search from eight probes to four, and the unsuccessful search from nine to five, because each run of colliding keys is now half as long. But it does not address the defect found in part (c). The table can still reach only one sixteenth of its buckets, and it has paid for that with twice as much memory. Doubling the table halves the *consequence* of the clustering while leaving its *cause* untouched, and the cause is that the table size shares a factor with the key step. Changing the size to 17 removes that shared factor; doubling it to 32 does not, and doubling it again to 64 would not either. The general rule is that the number of buckets a key set can reach is m divided by the greatest common divisor of m and the key step, capped by the number of keys — 1 at m = 16, 2 at m = 32, 8 at m = 17.

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for recognising that every key is a multiple of 16 and therefore 0 mod 16. A1 for all eight keys in bucket 0. A1 for the probe counts 1 to 8, or for the total of 36, or for the finished table. A candidate who writes "k mod 16 = k" has not seen the divisibility and scores nothing in this part.

(b) M1 for the load factor definition, A1 for 0.50. A1 for 0.47 (accept 0.4706, accept 8/17). M1 for the idea that the reachable share is counted in buckets rather than keys. A1 for 6.25% at m = 16. A1 for 47.06% at m = 17. Do not award the last A1 for an answer that reports 100% or 8/8: the denominator is the number of buckets, not the number of keys.

(c) M1 for the correct probe count on one of the two tables, A1 for eight probes to find 128 at m = 16. A1 for nine probes to establish that 144 is absent. M1 for the corresponding m = 17 figures, A1 for both being one probe. The explanation must connect the near-equal load factors to the very different costs; a candidate who reports the numbers but says only that the tables are "different" has not answered the question and should lose the final A1.

(d) M1 for the two occupied buckets, A1 for identifying buckets 0 and 16 with four keys each. A1 for 0.25. A1 for the reachable share staying at 6.25%. The justification must separate the halved worst case from the unchanged reachable share. Accept a conclusion either way provided the two quantities are distinguished; a candidate who claims the reachable share improves has not done part (b) correctly.

title: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs
q_html:
A logger that keeps its readings in a singly linked list

A data logger keeps its most recent readings in a singly linked list. Each node holds one reading in a field called data and one pointer in a field called next that points at the following node. The last node's next pointer is None, and the whole list is reached through a single variable head that points at the first node. No node holds a pointer to the node before it.

After four readings have been logged the list is A -> B -> C -> D, where A is the node that head points at and D is the last node.

A method remove(node) is added to the class. It is called with a reference to the node that should be deleted and with nothing else: it is not given head, and it is not told where the node sits in the list.

Evaluate the design of remove(node). Assume the list is never empty when remove is called, and that no other part of the program holds a reference to the node that is deleted.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why remove(node) cannot delete node by changing the pointer that currently reaches it.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Describe the technique that remove(node) can use instead, stating what it must do to the node's data field and what it must do to its next field.

    (Describe)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine which of the four nodes A, B, C and D a correctly written remove(node) can delete in a list of four nodes, and explain what goes wrong for the node it cannot delete.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    State the single change to the node's structure that would make every node deletable in a constant number of steps, and state what that change costs.

    (State)
a_html:
Part (a). In a singly linked list the only pointer that reaches node is the next pointer of the node before it. Deleting node means changing that predecessor's next pointer so that it skips over node and points at node.next. (M1)

The method receives a reference to node itself. From node there is no pointer backwards, so the predecessor cannot be reached from the argument. The only route to the predecessor is to start at head and walk forward until some node's next pointer is node — which costs a traversal of the whole list up to that point, and which would make the reference that was passed in pointless, since the same walk would have found the node by value. (A1)

So the method holds the object that must disappear, while the thing that must change is a field of a different object it has no way to name. (A1)(A1)

Part (b). The technique is to overwrite the node with its successor and then unlink the successor, in two assignments:

node.data = node.next.data
node.next = node.next.next

The first line copies the successor's reading into the node the caller is holding, so that node's value becomes the successor's value. (M1) The second line makes the node point past its successor, so the successor is no longer reachable from anywhere in the list. (A1) The caller's reference stays valid, the list is one node shorter, and the node that is actually released is the successor rather than the node the caller named. (A1)

It is worth being explicit that the *object* the caller holds survives while the *value* it was created with does not. Any other part of the program that kept a reference to the successor is now holding a node that is no longer in the list, and any part that looks for the deleted value will find it in the node it did not nominate. (A1)

Part (c). It works for A, B and C.

For A: A.data becomes B's reading and A.next becomes C, so the list reads (B) -> C -> D. For B: B.data becomes C's reading and B.next becomes D, giving A -> (C) -> D. For C: C.data becomes D's reading and C.next becomes D.next, which is None, giving A -> B -> (D). (M1)(A1)(A1)

It fails for D. D is the last node, so D.next is None, and the first assignment evaluates None.data. In Python that raises AttributeError; in a language without exceptions it would follow a null pointer and the program would be undefined from that point on. (A1)

So three of the four nodes can be deleted and the one that cannot is the one whose successor does not exist. (A1) The failure is not a corner case in the arithmetic sense — it is the ordinary case of deleting the last item, which any logger will reach as soon as it trims its oldest reading. Note also that in a circular list no node has next equal to None, so the technique would appear to work on all four nodes; for the last node it would overwrite the head's data, corrupting the list silently instead of failing loudly, which is worse.

Part (d). Give each node a second pointer to the node before it, making the list doubly linked. (M1) Then the node can be unlinked directly by joining its two neighbours to each other, which is a constant number of pointer assignments for every node including the last one. (A1)

The cost is one extra reference per node. Four nodes need four extra references, so the node structure doubles in size for a list that holds one reading per node. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for identifying that the predecessor's next pointer is the one that must change. A1 for the observation that no backward pointer exists from the argument. A1 for the consequence: the predecessor cannot be named from node. A1 for noting that reaching it requires a traversal from head, which defeats the purpose of the argument. Accept any phrasing that distinguishes the object held from the field that must change.

(b) M1 for the copy-the-successor idea in any form. A1 for the data assignment, A1 for the next assignment. A1 for stating that the successor is the node actually released, or that the caller's reference remains valid. A candidate who describes traversing to the predecessor scores nothing here even if the traversal is correct, because part (a) established that the reference makes it unnecessary.

(c) M1 for the correct list after one removal, A1 for the list after a second, A1 for the third. A1 for identifying D as the failure. A1 for the reason: D.next is None, so the copy dereferences None. Do not award the final A1 for "the last node always fails" without the null dereference; the mark is for the mechanism. Accept a discussion of the circular case in place of the null-dereference explanation only if the null case is also stated.

(c) alternative. A candidate who answers "all four, because you can also check whether the node is the last one and traverse from head in that case" should be given full marks for the determination *and* the explanation, since the traversal is correct for that one node; award the marks and note that the constant-time claim of part (d) is what the traversal fails.

(d) M1 for the previous pointer. A1 for the constant-time unlink. A1 for the cost, expressed as one extra reference per node. Accept "a doubly linked list" as naming the change.

title: B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class
q_html:
A bike-hire class with one underlined attribute

A city bike-hire scheme is modelled by a single class, Bike. Its UML class diagram is shown in the figure. In UML an attribute or method whose name is underlined is a static member, which Java calls a class variable or class method.

A program creates three Bike objects with the identifiers B-01, B-02 and B-03. Over one day the first bike is hired twice, the second bike is hired once, and the third bike is not hired at all. The attribute hireCount records how many times a bike has been hired, and the attribute fleetSize records how many Bike objects exist. The class diagram shows which of the two is static.

Evaluate the design of the class. Where a part asks what an object reports, state the value returned by the accessor named in the class diagram. Assume the three objects are created before any of them is hired.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State the value that getHireCount() reports for each of the three objects at the end of the day, and the value that getFleetSize() reports.

    (State)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Determine the number of copies of each attribute that exist in memory once the three objects have been created, and explain how the underline in the class diagram tells you which attributes are shared.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why an object diagram cannot show the difference between a static attribute and an instance attribute, and state which diagram can.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The designer proposes to make hireCount static as well, so that the class keeps a single running total. Determine the value getHireCount() would then report for each of the three objects, and justify whether the change improves the design.

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). hireCount is not underlined, so it is an instance attribute and each object has its own copy. getHireCount() reports 2 for B-01, 1 for B-02 and 0 for B-03. (M1)(A1)

fleetSize is underlined, so it is static and there is one copy for the whole class. getFleetSize() reports 3, and it reports 3 whichever of the three objects it is called on. (A1)

Part (b). There are three copies of id, three copies of hireCount and one copy of fleetSize, making seven attribute slots in total. (M1)(A1)(A1)

The general count is the number of objects multiplied by the number of instance attributes, plus the number of static attributes: 3 x 2 + 1 = 7. (A1)

The underline is UML's notation for a static member, which Java calls a class variable. A static member belongs to the class rather than to any object, so exactly one copy exists however many objects are created, and the memory is allocated when the class is loaded rather than when an object is constructed. An attribute with no underline is an instance attribute, and a fresh copy is allocated for every object. In the diagram, fleetSize and getFleetSize() are underlined and id, hireCount, Bike(id), hire() and getHireCount() are not. (A1)

Part (c). An object diagram is a snapshot: it shows the objects that exist at one moment, the links between them, and the current value of each attribute. Two objects that share a single storage location and two objects that each hold their own copy of the same value produce exactly the same object diagram — the diagram draws one box per object with one value in it either way. (M1)(A1)

Sharing is a property of the class definition rather than of any particular set of objects, so it cannot be read off a diagram of instances. (A1)

The class diagram is the diagram that shows it, and the static underline is how. (A1) A class diagram describes the shape every object will have; the underline says that one of those members will not be duplicated when the objects are made.

Part (d). A static hireCount is a single counter belonging to the class. Every hire increments that one slot, and the total number of hires is 2 + 1 + 0 = 3. So all three objects report 3. (M1)(A1)

The change does not improve the design, because it destroys the information the attribute was there to carry. Before the change, getHireCount() answered "how many times has this bike been hired"; afterwards it answers "how many times has any bike in the fleet been hired", and the three bikes are no longer distinguishable by usage at all. A maintenance scheduler that asked which bikes were used most would now receive the same answer for every bike. (A1)

The fleet total is a reasonable quantity to keep, so the proposal is not without merit — but it is a different quantity, and it belongs under a different name such as totalHires. Renaming the existing attribute instead would leave every call site compiling while silently changing what it means, which is the failure mode that is hardest to find later. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for recognising that hireCount is an instance attribute, A1 for the three values 2, 1 and 0 in the right order. A1 for fleetSize reporting 3 and for noting that it reports 3 from any object. Do not award the final A1 for an answer that gives 3 as the value of hireCount for any object.

(b) M1 for the idea of counting copies rather than values. A1 for three copies of id, A1 for three copies of hireCount, A1 for one copy of fleetSize. A1 for the underline meaning static, or class variable, or one copy shared by the class. Accept 7 as the total with or without the general formula, provided the three parts are distinguished; a bare answer of 7 with no breakdown earns the M1 only.

(c) M1 for the snapshot idea, A1 for the observation that sharing and duplicating draw the same picture. A1 for the reason: sharing belongs to the class, not the objects. A1 for naming the class diagram. A candidate who answers "a class diagram" without saying why the object diagram fails earns the last A1 only.

(d) M1 for recognising that a static counter is one slot for the class, A1 for 3. A1 for the information-loss argument. A1 for distinguishing the fleet total from the per-bike count, or for requiring a different name. Accept a candidate who argues the change is acceptable provided they state that a different attribute is needed as well; do not accept a bare "it is better because it saves memory".

subject: CS HL

subtopic: B2.1 Programming fundamentals
syllabus_ref: B2.1 (Programming fundamentals: exception handling, the try and except regions, and the finally region)
title: B2.1 Programming fundamentals
q_html:
A function that reads one number from a file

The figure shows a function read_reading(path), written in Python, that returns the single integer stored in a text file whose path it is given.

The variable handle is assigned None before the try region. If the file opens, its first line is read and converted to an integer, and that integer is returned. If the conversion fails the function prints "bad value" and returns -1. If the file cannot be opened the function prints "cannot open" and returns -2. Whichever of those happens, the finally region then runs handle.close().

Two facts about the language matter here. FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, so a handler written for OSError also catches a missing file. And an exception raised inside a finally region replaces any value that the try or except regions were in the middle of returning.

Trace the function for each of three files and decide what the caller receives in each case. The three files are a well-formed file containing the single line 250, a malformed file whose first line is 25 0, and a path that does not exist. Assume no other code changes the value of handle.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State the value that read_reading returns for the well-formed file, and the value it returns for the malformed file.

    (State)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Determine the value the caller receives for the path that does not exist. State the order in which the regions of the function execute, and state the value the OSError handler computes before the finally region runs.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why the finally region changes the outcome on that path but leaves the outcome on the other two paths unchanged.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Describe two changes to the function that would make the caller receive -2 when the path does not exist, and justify which of the two you prefer.

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). For the well-formed file the line reads 250, int("250") is 250, and the function returns 250. (M1)(A1)

For the malformed file, int("25 0") is not a valid integer literal and raises ValueError. The ValueError handler runs, prints "bad value" and returns -1. The finally region then closes a handle that is a real file object, so the close succeeds and the caller receives -1. (A1)

Part (b). The regions execute in this order. First handle = None runs. Then the try region begins and handle = open(path) raises FileNotFoundError, so handle is never reassigned. Because FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, the OSError handler runs: it prints "cannot open" and computes the value -2. Before that value can be returned, the finally region runs handle.close(). (M1)(A1)(A1)

handle is still None, because the assignment that would have replaced it was the statement that raised. So the finally region calls None.close(), which raises AttributeError. (M1)

An exception raised inside a finally region discards the return value that was in flight. The AttributeError therefore propagates to the caller and the -2 is never delivered. The caller receives an AttributeError, not -2. (A1)

Two details are worth recording. The function still prints "cannot open" before it fails, so a log file suggests that the missing file was handled and reported, which is the opposite of what happened. And the value the handler computed, -2, is discarded rather than converted, so there is no trace of it anywhere after the call.

Part (c). On the success path, handle = open(path) completed before the read, so handle is a real file object and close() succeeds. The return value 250 stands. (M1)(A1)

On the ValueError path, open(path) also completed. The failure was in converting the line that was read, not in opening the file, so handle is again a real file object and close() succeeds. The return value -1 stands. (A1)

Only on the OSError path did the assignment fail to complete, leaving handle at its initial value of None. The finally region is therefore harmless on two paths out of three and fatal on the third, and the source line that performs the cleanup is identical in all three cases — there is nothing at that line to suggest which path the program is on. (A1)

Part (d). First change: guard the cleanup so that it does nothing when there is no handle to close, as in if handle is not None: handle.close(). (M1)

Second change: let the language manage the handle, using a context manager, as in with open(path) as handle: return int(handle.readline()), with the except regions kept around the with statement. The initial assignment of None is then not needed at all. (A1)

I prefer the second. The guard fixes this instance but leaves the pattern in place: the next resource the function acquires will need its own None check, and one that is forgotten fails in exactly the same way, silently and on a path that is rarely exercised. The context manager ties the cleanup to the resource itself, so it cannot be forgotten and cannot be reached with an unassigned handle. Its cost is that the try region has to be restructured, which is a real cost if the surrounding house style forbids the with statement, and in that case the guard is the correct minimal change. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for the successful conversion, A1 for 250. A1 for -1 with the reason that int("25 0") raises ValueError. A candidate who answers -2 for the malformed file has confused the two handlers and scores nothing in this part.

(b) M1 for recognising that the missing file reaches the OSError handler because FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError. A1 for the execution order, A1 for the value -2 being computed. M1 for the observation that handle is still None at the finally region. A1 for the conclusion that the caller receives AttributeError and not -2. Accept "the -2 is discarded" or "the finally exception replaces the return" as the final A1. A candidate who states only that an AttributeError occurs, without saying what the caller would otherwise have received, earns the M1 but not the A1.

(c) M1 for the idea that handle is a real object on the success path, A1 for close() succeeding there. A1 for the corresponding point on the ValueError path, including the reason that the failure was in the conversion rather than in the open. A1 for stating that only the OSError path leaves handle as None. Do not award the last A1 for a restatement of part (b).

(d) M1 for a None guard, A1 for a context manager or for moving the close into each handler. A1 for a justification that names a property of the preferred fix rather than merely restating it. Accept either preference provided the reasoning refers to what the change does or does not prevent; a bare "it is cleaner" earns no mark. Do not award the final A1 to a candidate who proposes catching AttributeError, since that hides the defect rather than removing it.

title: B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only)
q_html:
Sharing projectors between meeting rooms

A company has 8 meeting rooms and is buying projectors for them. Each projector costs 2 400.

Under a composition relationship each Room object creates and owns its own Projector when the room is constructed, and the projector is destroyed with the room. Under an aggregation relationship the projectors are created separately and passed to the rooms that use them, so one projector can serve more than one room. The two relationships are drawn in the figure.

Under aggregation the company buys 5 projectors. Three of them are used by two rooms each and two of them are used by one room each, which covers all 8 rooms. Every room has exactly one projector, and a projector that fails makes every room that depends on it unusable.

Evaluate the two relationships as a basis for the purchasing decision. Assume every room needs a projector, that a projector failure is equally likely to strike any of the projectors that have been bought, and that a room with no working projector cannot be used.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the capital cost of the projector fleet under each relationship, and state the saving that aggregation offers as a percentage of the composition cost.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Determine the expected number of rooms that become unusable when one projector fails, under each relationship, and express the aggregation figure as a percentage change from the composition figure.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why the two relationships give different answers in part (b) even though both use the same projectors at the same price.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Justify which relationship you would choose if the rooms must remain usable, and state what the choice costs in capital.

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). Under composition each of the 8 rooms owns its own projector, so 8 units are bought: 8 x 2 400 = 19 200. (M1)(A1)

Under aggregation 5 units are bought: 5 x 2 400 = 12 000. (A1)

The saving is 19 200 - 12 000 = 7 200, which as a fraction of the composition cost is 7 200 / 19 200 = 0.375, or 37.5%. (A1)

Equivalently, aggregation buys 5 / 8 = 62.5% of the projectors, so it saves the remaining 37.5%.

Part (b). Under composition there are 8 projectors and each serves exactly one room, so a failure takes out 1 room. (M1)(A1)

Under aggregation the five projectors serve 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 rooms. If a failure is equally likely to strike any of the five, the expected number of rooms lost is the mean of those five values: (2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1) / 5 = 8 / 5 = 1.6 rooms. (M1)(A1)

The change from 1.0 to 1.6 is an increase of (1.6 - 1.0) / 1.0 = 0.60, or 60%. (A1)

Part (c). The costs differ because the two relationships answer different questions about ownership. Composition binds one projector to one room, so the fleet must be as large as the room count. Aggregation lets one projector be referenced by several rooms at once, so the fleet only has to be large enough to cover every room rather than equal to the room count. The 8 rooms are covered by 5 units because three of the units are counted twice. (M1)(A1)

The exposure differs for the same reason read in the other direction. Under composition a projector is a part of exactly one room, so its failure is contained. Under aggregation a projector is a part of several rooms at once, so its failure is shared — and sharing is precisely what allowed the fleet to be smaller. (A1)

The two effects are not independent, and this is the point of the part. Every projector that aggregation removes from the fleet is a projector whose failure is now spread over two rooms instead of one. The 37.5% saving and the 60% increase in exposure are two descriptions of a single change: fewer failure domains, each covering more rooms. (A1)

Part (d). I would choose composition for rooms that must remain usable. (M1) It costs 19 200 rather than 12 000, an extra 7 200, and it buys the property that no single projector failure takes out more than one room. (A1)

The choice is worth stating as a rate rather than as a total. The extra 7 200 buys a reduction of 0.6 rooms of expected exposure per failure. With two failures a year, aggregation exposes 3.2 rooms a year against composition's 2.0, so the extra capital buys about 1.2 room-outages a year, which is 6 000 per outage avoided. (A1) Whether that is worth paying depends on what a room outage costs the company, which is the judgement the question asks for; the arithmetic is what makes the judgement answerable.

It is worth saying plainly what the choice does *not* buy. Composition does not remove projector failures, it only contains them: a failed projector still takes its room out of use until it is repaired or replaced. What composition buys is that the failure is not multiplied by the sharing, so the worst case a room can suffer is the failure of the one projector it owns. The purchase decision is therefore about how much the company is willing to pay to keep a single failure confined to a single room, and the two figures the item produces — 7 200 of capital and 0.6 rooms of expected exposure — are the two sides of that price.

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for 8 units under composition, A1 for 19 200. A1 for 12 000. A1 for 37.5%. Accept 0.375 or 7 200 stated as the saving with the percentage. Do not award the final A1 for a saving expressed as a fraction of the aggregation cost, which gives 60% and is the common error.

(b) M1 for recognising that each composition projector serves one room, A1 for 1.0. M1 for the mean over the five projectors, A1 for 1.6. A1 for 60%. Accept 1.6 with or without the working, provided the distribution 2, 2, 2, 1, 1 appears or is clearly implied. A candidate who divides by 8 instead of 5 and obtains 1.0 has not weighted by projector and should lose the second A1.

(c) M1 for the ownership or part-count distinction on cost, A1 for the fleet being smaller because units are counted twice. A1 for the exposure argument. A1 for the link between the two, namely that the same sharing produces both effects. A candidate who explains each effect separately but never connects them earns three of the four marks.

(d) M1 for choosing composition. A1 for 7 200 of extra capital. A1 for a justification that weighs the two quantities against each other rather than restating one of them. Accept aggregation with full marks if the candidate argues that the rooms need not all remain usable, or that the exposure is acceptable at the stated failure rate; the mark is for the weighing, not for the choice.

q_html:
A singleton holding a mutable setting

A web application runs 12 user sessions at the same time. Each session needs to know which measurement units to display, and the user can change the units at any moment.

The units are held in a class called Settings, which is written as a singleton: a private static attribute holds the one instance, a static method getInstance() returns it, and an instance attribute units holds the current unit name. Every session obtains the settings object through getInstance() and reads and writes units on it. Because there is only ever one Settings object, every session is reading and writing the same field.

In one hour the units field is changed 34 times across the 12 sessions.

Evaluate the singleton as a home for the units field. Assume the 12 sessions overlap in time, that any of them may change the units at any moment, and that a session reads the units immediately before it formats a measurement.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State what a session reads when it asks the settings object for the units, if a different session changed the units a fraction of a second earlier.

    (State)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the number of session-and-change pairs in which a session observes a change it did not make, and express that number as a percentage of all session-and-change pairs.

    (Determine)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Explain why the singleton is the right pattern for obtaining the settings but the wrong pattern for storing the units field, and state where a session's own units should be held instead.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    A colleague proposes keeping the singleton and adding a sessionId attribute, so that setUnits can ignore changes made by other sessions. Justify whether that repairs the design.

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). The session reads the most recently written value, whichever session wrote it. There is one storage location, so the last write wins, and the session has no way to tell whether the value it received is the one it set. (M1)(A1)(A1)

Part (b). Each of the 34 changes is visible to every session except the one that made it, so each change produces 12 - 1 = 11 unintended observations. The number of such session-and-change pairs is therefore 34 x 11 = 374. (M1)(A1)

The total number of session-and-change pairs is 34 x 12 = 408. (A1)

So 374 / 408 = 0.91666..., which is 91.7% to one decimal place. (A1) The 34 pairs that are not unintended are the ones in which a session observes its own change.

Part (c). The singleton is the right pattern for obtaining the settings. The units are a property of the application rather than of a session, so the value has to be reachable from anywhere in the code; constructing a fresh Settings per session would give each session a different starting value; and a single access point means the configuration is loaded once rather than repeatedly. getInstance() supplies all three without exposing a global variable. (M1)(A1)(A1)

It is the wrong pattern for storing a mutable value that belongs to a session, because one storage location cannot hold two different values at the same moment. Two sessions that want different units are not in conflict about the object — they are in conflict about the field, and no care taken at the access point can resolve that. (A1)

The units a session is using belong to that session, so they should be held in an instance attribute of the session, or passed into the formatting call as a parameter. The singleton can still hold the default units, which is a value about the application rather than about any session. (A1)

Part (d). Adding sessionId does not repair the design. It lets setUnits refuse a write that came from another session, so a session's own writes are protected from being overwritten by its neighbours. (M1)(A1)

But the field is still a single storage location. The sessionId records whose value is currently stored; it does not let two sessions each have one. If session 1 sets the units to metres and session 2 then sets them to feet, the field holds one of those two values and the other session has lost its setting. Refusing the second write does not preserve session 1's value *for* session 2 — it merely prevents session 2 from setting anything at all, so the second session is now unable to choose its units rather than able to choose them independently. (A1)

The test to apply is whether two sessions can hold two different values at the same moment. A single field cannot, whatever guard is placed on the setter, because the guard changes who is allowed to write and not how many values exist. Repairing the design means one value per session, which means moving the field out of the singleton; the singleton can keep the default and the access point. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for the last-write-wins idea, A1 for naming the most recent value, A1 for noting that the reading session cannot tell whose value it received. A candidate who answers "its own value" has missed the sharing and scores nothing in this part.

(b) M1 for 12 - 1 = 11 sessions per change, A1 for 374. A1 for 408 as the total. A1 for 91.7%. Accept 91.67% or 0.917. A candidate who computes 34 x 12 = 408 as the unintended count has confused the total with the subset and should lose the first A1.

(c) M1 for the access-point argument, A1 for reachability from anywhere in the code, A1 for a single shared initial value or a single load. A1 for the observation that one storage location cannot hold two values at once. A1 for moving the units into the session or passing them per call. Do not award the final A1 for a restatement of the problem in part (a); the mark is for naming where the value should live.

(d) M1 for stating what the guard does, A1 for recognising that it protects a session's own writes. A1 for the observation that the field remains one location. A1 for the conclusion that the second session is blocked rather than served, or for the two-values-at-once test. A candidate who concludes that the proposal repairs the design because writes are now checked scores at most two marks.

subject: CS HL

subtopic: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems

title: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
q_html:
Parcel packing cells

A fulfilment centre runs four identical packing cells. Each cell processes one parcel per cycle of 45 s. Every parcel must pass through three shared resources, each of which can serve only one cell at a time: a labelling arm, a weighbridge and a dispatch chute. A cell claims the resources one at a time as its control program reaches each stage, holds every resource it has already claimed while it waits for the next, and releases them all only when the parcel has been dispatched. The three resources are attached to the site network so that any cell can request any of them. The centre currently achieves 320 parcels per hour when nothing goes wrong. On average, once in every 40 cycles the four cells deadlock: each holds one or two resources and waits for one held by another. There is no detection, so the deadlock persists until a supervisor notices the queue, walks to the cell, and performs a manual reset taking 6 minutes, which also discards the four parcels in flight. You have been asked to review the design.

Using the case study, answer all four parts. The four cells are named C1 to C4 and the three resources are L (labelling arm), W (weighbridge) and D (dispatch chute).

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain, with reference to each of the four conditions required for deadlock, why this system deadlocks. Your answer must name all four conditions and show that each is present.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a resource-allocation scheme that makes deadlock impossible. State the rule, show that it removes at least one of the four conditions you identified, and explain what has to change in the control program of each cell.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the average throughput of the centre in parcels per hour given the current deadlock rate, and hence the percentage of capacity lost. Show your working.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    An engineer proposes instead to leave the resource requests unchanged and to add a timeout: any cell waiting more than 20 s releases everything it holds, waits 5 s and starts the parcel again. Evaluate this proposal against your scheme in (b).

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) All four Coffman conditions hold.

*Mutual exclusion:* each of L, W and D can serve only one cell at a time, so the resources are non-sharable. (A1)

*Hold and wait:* a cell that has claimed the labelling arm keeps it while it waits for the weighbridge, so processes hold resources while requesting others. (A1)

*No pre-emption:* nothing in the system can take a resource away from a cell; the only way resources are released is by the cell finishing, which is exactly what it cannot do. (A1)

*Circular wait:* with four cells and three resources a cycle is easy to form, for example C1 holds L and wants W, C2 holds W and wants D, and C3 holds D and wants L. Because each cell requests resources in whatever order its stage is reached, and the stages differ between parcels, no ordering prevents that cycle from forming. (A1)

(b) Impose a global ordering on resource acquisition: assign each resource a fixed rank, say L = 1, W = 2, D = 3, and require every cell to request resources in strictly increasing rank order, never requesting a lower-ranked resource while holding a higher-ranked one. (M1)(A1)

This removes the circular-wait condition. (A1) A cycle would require each participant to hold a resource and wait for one of lower or equal rank; since ranks strictly increase along any wait chain, the chain cannot close. Formally, in any cycle the ranks would have to satisfy $r_1 < r_2 < \dots < r_k < r_1$, which is impossible. (A1)

The control program must change in two ways: each cell must determine the full set of resources its parcel will need before claiming any of them, and must then claim them in rank order. Where a parcel genuinely needs them in a different order, the cell must claim all three up front and hold them for the whole cycle, which reduces concurrency but is safe. (A1)

(c) Without deadlock the centre does $4 \times \dfrac{3600}{45} = 320$ parcels per hour. (A1)

In 40 cycles the four cells process $4 \times 40 = 160$ parcels, taking $40 \times 45 = 1800\ \mathrm{s}$. One deadlock adds a 6-minute ($360\ \mathrm{s}$) reset, so 160 parcels take $1800 + 360 = 2160\ \mathrm{s}$. (M1)(A1)

$$\text{throughput} = \frac{160}{2160} \times 3600 = 266.7 \approx 267\ \mathrm{parcels\,h^{-1}}$$ (A1)

$$\text{loss} = \frac{320 - 267}{320} \times 100\% = 16.7\%$$

(d) The timeout does not prevent deadlock; it detects and breaks it. (A1) That is better than an indefinite hang, but it is worse than prevention in three respects. First, every near-deadlock costs 20 s of waiting plus a 5 s backoff plus the wasted work already done on the parcel, so each event costs at least 25 s of cell time against 0 s under ordering. Second, if all four cells time out together and restart together they are likely to re-form the same cycle, an effect known as livelock, which the proposal does nothing to prevent since there is no randomised backoff. (A1) Third, the parcels are discarded either way, so the material loss is unchanged. (A1)

By contrast the ordering scheme in (b) eliminates the events entirely, at the cost of holding all three resources for some parcels and so losing some concurrency. A reasonable evaluation is therefore that the timeout is an acceptable safety net to keep in place, but it should not be the primary mechanism: prevention should be used first and detection second.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award one mark for each condition correctly named and shown to be present; a candidate who names all four but does not apply them to this system earns at most two. The circular-wait mark is the one most often missed and requires an explicit example of a cycle. (b) Accept any consistent global ordering, not necessarily L-W-D, provided the rule is stated as a total order and the reasoning about cycles is given. A candidate who proposes requesting all resources at once (simultaneous acquisition) is also acceptable and should be credited equivalently, since it removes the hold-and-wait condition instead; note in that case that utilisation falls. The final mark is for identifying the change to the control program, which is the practical consequence and is frequently omitted. (c) Accept 266 to 267 parcels per hour and a loss between 16% and 17%. Award the method mark for converting the deadlock rate into an amortised time penalty; a candidate who simply subtracts 6 minutes per hour has the wrong model. (d) The key distinction is prevention versus detection, and candidates who conflate them should not earn the first mark. Credit the livelock observation even if the term is not used, provided the idea that simultaneous restart recreates the cycle is stated. There is no single right conclusion, so award the final marks for a judgement supported by the analysis given.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A4.4 Ethical considerations
syllabus_ref: A4.1 Machine learning fundamentals, A4.4 Ethical considerations, A3.1 Database fundamentals
title: A4.4 Ethical considerations
q_html:
Prioritising housing repairs

A local authority receives repair requests from tenants and must decide which to inspect within 48 hours. It has deployed a model that scores each request and flags those it predicts to be urgent. Urgent means a fault that is dangerous or that will cause rapid deterioration, such as a leaking roof or a failed heating system in winter. The authority covers two areas with very different housing stock. In the North area, of 6 000 requests in the period, 1 500 were genuinely urgent; the model flagged 1 200 as urgent and 1 080 of those were genuinely urgent. In the South area, of 2 000 requests, 400 were genuinely urgent; the model flagged 500 as urgent and 320 of those were genuinely urgent. The authority reports an overall precision of 82% and states that the model is therefore performing well. A tenant in the South area has complained that inspectors call on her neighbours repeatedly for faults that turn out to be minor, while her own leaking roof waited nine days.

Using the case study, answer all four parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why the single figure of 82% overall precision is a misleading summary of this model's performance, and state which two quantities must be reported separately for the complaint to be assessed.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct the confusion matrix for each area and calculate, for each area separately, the precision, the recall, and the proportion of non-urgent requests that were wrongly flagged.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Discuss what the two sets of figures show, including anything they do not establish. Refer to the tenant's complaint in your answer.

    (Discuss)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Justify one action the authority should take, given that it cannot simultaneously maximise both precision and recall and that inspection capacity is fixed.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) An overall figure averages over a population in which the two areas contribute very unequally, 6 000 requests from the North against 2 000 from the South, so the aggregate is dominated by the area where the model performs better. (A1) It says nothing about how the errors are distributed, and it is the distribution that the complaint is about. (A1)

The two quantities that must be reported separately are precision and recall for each area, or equivalently the false-positive rate and the false-negative rate for each area, since precision and recall alone do not determine how many non-urgent requests are wrongly flagged. (A1)(A1)

(b) *North:* flagged 1 200, of which 1 080 urgent, so 120 are not urgent. There are 1 500 urgent in total, so $1500 - 1080 = 420$ urgent requests were missed. Non-urgent requests number $6000 - 1500 = 4500$, of which 120 were wrongly flagged. (M1)(A1)

| North | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 1 080 | 420 | 1 500 |
| not urgent | 120 | 4 380 | 4 500 |
| total | 1 200 | 4 800 | 6 000 |

*South:* flagged 500, of which 320 urgent, so 180 are not urgent. There are 400 urgent in total, so $400 - 320 = 80$ were missed. Non-urgent requests number $2000 - 400 = 1600$, of which 180 were wrongly flagged. (A1)

| South | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 320 | 80 | 400 |
| not urgent | 180 | 1 420 | 1 600 |
| total | 500 | 1 500 | 2 000 |

North: precision $= 1080/1200 = 90.0\%$, recall $= 1080/1500 = 72.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 120/4500 = 2.67\%$. (A1)
South: precision $= 320/500 = 64.0\%$, recall $= 320/400 = 80.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 180/1600 = 11.25\%$. (A1)

(c) The figures support the substance of the complaint. A non-urgent request in the South is (M1)
$$\frac{11.25}{2.67} \approx 4.2$$
times as likely to be flagged as one in the North, so South tenants are much more likely to be visited for a fault that turns out to be minor, which is the nuisance she describes. (A1) At the same time the model is not uniformly worse in the South: its recall there is higher, 80% against 72%, so an urgent request in the South is more likely to be caught. That is why her own roof waiting nine days is not necessarily explained by the area statistics and may be a single unfortunate case. (A1)

What the figures do not establish is why the difference exists. The areas differ in housing stock, so the base rate of urgency differs, 25% in the North against 20% in the South, and a model trained on pooled data with one threshold will not behave identically across groups with different base rates even if it is free of bias in its inputs. The data also cannot distinguish a model that is miscalibrated from one that is correctly calibrated but operating at an inappropriate threshold, and they say nothing about whether the features used are themselves proxies for something protected. (A1)

(d) A defensible action is to set the decision threshold separately for each area so that the false-positive rates are equalised, and to publish the resulting precision and recall for both areas. (A1) This directly addresses the complaint, which is about unequal burden rather than about overall accuracy, and it is achievable within fixed inspection capacity because lowering the threshold in the North and raising it in the South reallocates roughly the same number of visits. (A1)

It must be accompanied by a stated decision about which error the authority considers more serious. If a missed urgent repair is the greater harm, the threshold should be set to favour recall and the authority must accept more minor inspections in both areas; if unnecessary visits are the greater harm, the reverse. (A1) What is not defensible is to continue reporting only the aggregate figure, because that suppresses exactly the information needed to make the choice.

Markscheme notes

(a) The mark scheme looks for the idea that an aggregate conceals distribution, and for the identification of precision and recall (or the two error rates) as the disaggregated quantities. A candidate who says only that the model is biased has asserted a conclusion the data do not yet support. (b) Award (M1) for deriving at least one cell correctly from the text, since the numbers are given as counts of flagged and correctly flagged rather than as a matrix. Accept matrices with rows and columns transposed. All six rates must appear; the wrongly-flagged proportion is the one most often omitted and is the rate the complaint is actually about. (c) The comparison mark requires the ratio. Credit the observation that South recall is higher, because it prevents the easy conclusion that the model is simply worse in the South. The 'does not establish' mark is for the point that the statistics cannot separate miscalibration from threshold choice, or for noting that different base rates alone can produce this pattern. (d) Any single action is acceptable provided it is justified against the figures and acknowledges the trade-off. Equalising false-positive rates, equalising recall, or setting thresholds from an explicit cost ratio for the two error types are all creditable. An answer that proposes collecting more data or retraining without addressing the threshold question has not engaged with the fact that the trade-off is irreducible at fixed capacity.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1 Computer fundamentals
syllabus_ref: A1.1 Computer hardware and operation (A1.1.4 the role of cache memory, A1.1.5 the machine instruction cycle, A1.1.6 the effect of clock speed and cache on performance)
title: Where the cycles actually go
q_html:
A processor whose clock speed is not the problem
