An embedded vision system processes a stream of images. Measurements on the running system give the following. Of all memory accesses, $95\%$ are satisfied by the level-1 cache in $1$ clock cycle. Of the accesses that miss in level 1, $80\%$ are satisfied by the level-2 cache, and the whole level-2 path, including the level-1 miss, takes $12$ clock cycles. An access that misses in both caches goes to main memory, and that path takes $200$ clock cycles in total. The instruction mix is fixed, and apart from memory accesses the processor completes one instruction per clock cycle.

Two upgrade proposals are on the table. Both are advertised with a large number on the box, and neither number is the one the system will actually see.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the average number of clock cycles spent on memory per instruction, showing how each level of the hierarchy contributes.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    A hardware accelerator can execute $40\%$ of the workload five times faster than the processor does now. Calculate the overall speedup of the system, and state the largest speedup that could ever be obtained by accelerating this same $40\%$, however fast the accelerator is made.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    A second proposal is to raise the clock frequency by $25\%$. The memory chips are unchanged, so their latency stays the same number of nanoseconds and therefore becomes a larger number of clock cycles. Calculate the resulting average cycles per instruction and hence the real speedup, and explain why it falls so far short of $25\%$.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate which of the two proposals is the better use of the engineering budget, referring to your answers to (b) and (c) and to one further consideration that the numbers do not capture.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Work through the hierarchy from the fastest level outwards. An access hits in level 1 with probability $0.95$ and costs $1$ cycle. It misses level 1 with probability $0.05$; of those, $0.80$ are satisfied by level 2 at $12$ cycles and $0.20$ go to main memory at $200$ cycles. (M1)(A1)
$$\text{average cycles} = 0.95(1) + 0.05\bigl[0.80(12) + 0.20(200)\bigr]$$
$$= 0.95 + 0.05\bigl[9.6 + 40\bigr] = 0.95 + 0.05(49.6) = 0.95 + 2.48 = 3.43$$ (A1)(A1)
So the processor spends about $3.43$ clock cycles per instruction, of which only $0.95$ is the level-1 access itself. The tail dominates: level-2 hits add $0.48$ cycles in total, while main-memory accesses add $2.00$ cycles, so the $1\%$ of all accesses that miss in both caches accounts for $2.00$ of the $3.43$, which is more than half the average and more than twice what the level-1 hits contribute.

(b) Amdahl's law gives the speedup as (M1)
$$S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \dfrac{f}{s}} = \frac{1}{0.60 + \dfrac{0.40}{5}} = \frac{1}{0.60 + 0.08} = \frac{1}{0.68} = 1.47$$ (A1)(A1)
The limiting case is $s \to \infty$, which gives $S_{\max} = 1/(1-0.40) = 1.67$. (A1) However fast the accelerator becomes, the remaining $60\%$ of the workload is untouched, so the system can never be more than $1.67$ times faster by this route.

(c) With the clock $25\%$ faster, a fixed nanosecond latency corresponds to $1.25$ times as many clock cycles, so the level-2 path becomes $12 \times 1.25 = 15$ cycles and the main-memory path becomes $200 \times 1.25 = 250$ cycles. (M1)
$$\text{average cycles} = 0.95(1) + 0.05\bigl[0.80(15) + 0.20(250)\bigr] = 0.95 + 0.05\bigl[12 + 50\bigr] = 0.95 + 3.10 = 4.05$$ (A1)
Execution time is cycles divided by frequency, so with the new frequency $1.25$ times the old one, (M1)
$$\frac{T_{\text{new}}}{T_{\text{old}}} = \frac{4.05/1.25}{3.43/1.00} = \frac{3.24}{3.43} = 0.945,\qquad \text{speedup} = 1.06$$ (A1)
The speedup is about $6\%$ rather than $25\%$ because the extra cycles are being spent waiting, and waiting does not get faster when the clock does. As the clock rises, the proportion of time spent stalled on memory grows, so the gap between the advertised figure and the delivered figure widens.

(d) The accelerator is the better buy on these numbers: $1.47$ against $1.06$, and the accelerator's figure is also closer to its own ceiling of $1.67$, whereas the clock increase delivers under a quarter of what its name promises. (A1)(A1) One thing the numbers do not capture is cost and risk: an accelerator is new hardware, new drivers and a new failure mode in a system that already works, while a clock change is a configuration setting. If the accelerator's development cost is more than a few times the cost of the clock change, the safer option may be worth its smaller return, and a decision that rests only on the two ratios above would be incomplete. (A1)

It is worth stating what the $3.43$ means before using it in later parts: it is an average over the whole instruction stream, so it already includes the instructions that hit in level 1 and cost almost nothing. Any proposal that changes the miss rates or the path latencies changes this average, and that is the only way an upgrade can help.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for the weighted-sum structure and (A1) for each of the three contributions; accept $3.4$ to $3.5$. A candidate who adds $1 + 12 + 200$ weighted by $0.95$, $0.04$ and $0.01$ has understood the structure but has applied the level-2 probability to all accesses rather than to level-1 misses, and should lose one of the accuracy marks. (b) Accept $1.46$ to $1.48$ and $1.67$; the ceiling mark is separate and is for understanding that the limit comes from the unaccelerated fraction. Do not credit a speedup of $5$ or of $1.40$ obtained by multiplying the fraction by the speedup. (c) Accept average cycles $4.0$ to $4.1$ and speedup $1.05$ to $1.07$; the mark is for dividing by $1.25$ as well as for recomputing the cycles, and a candidate who reports $4.05/3.43 = 1.18$ as a slowdown has forgotten the frequency change entirely. (d) Accept either proposal if it is argued from the calculations and names a non-numerical factor; the comparison must be made, not merely asserted. A candidate who computes $3.43$ correctly and then describes the main-memory contribution as small has misread their own arithmetic and should be corrected in feedback, since the tail is the dominant term and the rest of the question depends on noticing that.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2 Programming
syllabus_ref: B2.4 Programming algorithms (B2.4.1 the complexity of an algorithm, B2.4.2 searching and sorting algorithms, B2.4.3 the suitability of an algorithm for a given task)
title: The algorithm that wins on paper and loses on the machine
q_html:
Two ways to find one record

A library catalogue holds $n$ records sorted by accession number, stored contiguously in memory. Two search routines are available. Linear search examines records in order from the start of the list; in the worst case it makes $n$ comparisons. Binary search repeatedly compares against the middle of the remaining range; in the worst case it makes $\lfloor \log_{2} n \rfloor + 1$ comparisons. Profiling on this machine gives a realistic cost model rather than a comparison count: a linear-search comparison costs $3\ \mathrm{ns}$, because consecutive records are already in the cache, while a binary-search comparison costs $30\ \mathrm{ns}$, because each probe lands far from the last one and usually misses the cache. A binary search also pays a one-off $400\ \mathrm{ns}$ of setup before its first comparison.

The table appears to settle the matter. This question asks whether it does.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the worst-case number of comparisons binary search makes for each value of $n$ in the table, showing how $\lfloor \log_{2} n \rfloor + 1$ gives the stated figures, and state the complexity class of each algorithm.

    (Determine)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Using the cost model in the stimulus, calculate the worst-case time taken by each algorithm for each value of $n$ in the table. Hence determine the smallest value of $n$ for which binary search is the faster of the two, showing your method.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why the comparison counts in the table give the opposite ranking to the timings for small $n$, referring to the cost model and to the way each algorithm accesses memory.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether a programmer should implement a hybrid routine that uses linear search below the crossover value and binary search above it, giving one reason for and one reason against.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) For $n = 16$, $\lfloor\log_{2} 16\rfloor + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5$; for $n = 256$, $8 + 1 = 9$; for $n = 65\,536$, $16 + 1 = 17$; for $n = 16\,777\,216$, $24 + 1 = 25$. (A1) for the method, (A1) for the four values. Linear search is $\mathrm{O}(n)$ and binary search is $\mathrm{O}(\log n)$. (A1)

(b) Linear search takes $3n$ nanoseconds. Binary search takes $400 + 30(\lfloor\log_{2} n\rfloor + 1)$ nanoseconds. (M1)

| $n$ | linear search | binary search |
|---|---|---|
| $16$ | $48\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(5) = 550\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $256$ | $768\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(9) = 670\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $65\,536$ | $196\,608\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(17) = 910\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $16\,777\,216$ | $50\,331\,648\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(25) = 1150\ \mathrm{ns}$ |

(A1) for each column. For the crossover, note that between $n = 128$ and $n = 255$ the binary-search comparison count is fixed at $8$, so the binary-search time is constant at $400 + 30(8) = 640\ \mathrm{ns}$ across that range. (M1) Solving $3n = 640$ gives $n = 213.3$, so (M1) at $n = 213$ linear search takes $639\ \mathrm{ns}$ and binary takes $640\ \mathrm{ns}$, and at $n = 214$ linear takes $642\ \mathrm{ns}$ and binary still takes $640\ \mathrm{ns}$. The smallest $n$ for which binary search is faster is therefore $n = 214$. (A1)

(c) The comparison count measures one cost, and it is not the cost that dominates for small $n$. Binary search has a fixed setup of $400\ \mathrm{ns}$, which at $n = 16$ is more than eight times the entire cost of the linear search, and each of its comparisons costs ten times as much because the probes jump around the array and usually miss the cache. (A1)(A1) Linear search walks along the array, so after the first access every subsequent record is already in a cache line that has been fetched, and each comparison costs $3\ \mathrm{ns}$. (A1) Complexity classes describe how the time grows as $n$ becomes large, and they deliberately discard constant factors; for $n$ below a few hundred the constants here decide the outcome, and the asymptotically worse algorithm wins. (A1)

(d) In favour: the hybrid takes the better of the two routines at every size, so it is never worse than either, and the crossover is a single comparison against a constant, which is almost free. (A1) Against: it is two code paths to write, test and maintain instead of one, and the crossover of $214$ is specific to this machine's cache behaviour and this record size — on different hardware the threshold moves, so the constant becomes a tuning parameter that someone has to keep valid. (A1) Whether it is worth it depends on how often the routine runs: in a loop executed millions of times the gain is real, and in a function called once per user action it is not worth the complexity. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept the four values with or without the working; the complexity classes must be stated in big-O form. (b) Accept the table entries to two significant figures. For the crossover, credit any systematic method — tabulation, bisection or solving $3n = 640$ on the correct interval — and accept $214$; a candidate who solves $3n = 400 + 30(\log_{2} n + 1)$ treating the logarithm as continuous gets about $n = 200$ and should not be penalised provided the method is shown, since the floor function is what makes the true answer a little higher. (c) The explanation must refer to the fixed setup cost and to the per-comparison cost difference; a candidate who says only that binary search has overhead has not used the model. The cache explanation is the more valuable of the two and should be credited generously. (d) Credit a reason for and a reason against; a candidate who argues only one side cannot reach the top mark. The point that the threshold is machine-specific is the strongest objection and should be looked for. Do not accept 'binary search is O(log n) so it is always faster' as an answer to any part: the item exists to show that this is false, and a candidate who restates it has not engaged with the model at all.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.4 Programming algorithms
syllabus_ref: B2.4 (Programming algorithms: algorithm design, efficiency, and the analysis of running time)
title: The append that copies half the array
q_html:
A list that grows itself

A hospital records a reading every second. The readings are held in a structure that starts empty with room for one reading. When a reading arrives and the structure is full, the structure allocates a new region twice as large, copies every reading it already holds into the new region, and then stores the new reading. Copying one reading costs one operation.

A shift lasts 1024 seconds, so 1024 readings are appended, one per second. The monitoring software runs on a device that must respond within a fixed deadline, and the engineers have been told that the structure is cheap because "the average append costs about one operation".

You are asked to check the engineers' claim and to decide whether the structure is safe for a device with a response deadline. Work in operations, where copying one reading is one operation, and assume the first reading is appended to a structure with room for one.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State the capacities of the structure after each of the first eight appends, and identify the appends at which a copy takes place during the 1024-second shift.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Determine the total number of copy operations performed across the whole shift, and hence the average number of copy operations per append. Give your average to three decimal places.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the largest number of copy operations performed by any single append during the shift, state which append that is, and explain why the average you found in part (b) does not bound it.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    The engineers propose to keep the doubling rule but to pre-allocate room for 4096 readings before the shift begins. Justify whether that change removes the risk of missing the response deadline, and state what the change costs in operations at start-up.

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). The structure doubles when full, so the capacity sequence is 1, then 2, then 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and so on. (M1) After the first append the capacity is 1; after the second it becomes 2; after the third, 4; after the fifth, 8; after the ninth, 16. So after the first eight appends the capacities are 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8. (A1)

A copy happens when an append finds the structure already full, which is exactly the appends numbered 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65, 129, 257 and 513. (A1) There are ten such appends in the shift, and the other 1014 appends copy nothing.

Part (b). At append number 2 the structure holds one reading and copies it; at append 3 it holds two; at append 5, four; and in general the append numbered 2^k + 1 copies 2^k readings. (M1) The copy counts are therefore 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512. (A1)

The total is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 + 128 + 256 + 512 = 1023 operations. (M1)(A1)

The average per append is 1023 / 1024 = 0.999 operations, to three decimal places. (A1) So the engineers' claim is arithmetically sound: on average an append costs about one operation, and in fact slightly less.

Part (c). The largest single copy is 512 operations, performed by append number 513. (M1)(A1)

The average does not bound it because an average is a statement about a total divided by a count, and it is compatible with almost any single value in the sequence. Here the 1023 operations are concentrated in ten appends out of 1024, and one of those ten carries half of the entire total on its own. (M1) The average is a property of the run as a whole, while the deadline is threatened by one append, so the two quantities answer different questions. (A1)

It is worth being precise about why the engineers' claim and the objection to it can both be true at once. The claim is about the total cost of the shift, and it is correct: 1023 operations across 1024 appends really is about one operation each, and no arrangement of the same appends can make that total much larger. The objection is about the largest cost of any single second, and it is also correct. A quantity that describes a sum cannot also describe a maximum unless the sum happens to be spread evenly, and here it is spread as unevenly as it could be: ten appends carry the whole cost and the other 1014 carry none of it. If the device's deadline is expressed per second, then it is the maximum that must be compared with the deadline, and the average is simply the wrong statistic for the question being asked. (R1)

Part (d). Pre-allocating room for 4096 readings does remove the risk, because a shift only ever appends 1024 readings and 1024 is less than 4096, so the structure is never full during the shift and no append copies anything. (M1) The total copy work during the shift falls from 1023 operations to 0. (A1)

The change is not free. The start-up cost is that the device must obtain room for 4096 readings at once, and if it must be initialised by copying, the cost is 4096 operations in a single step, which is eight times worse than the worst append it was trying to avoid. (M1) The trade is therefore between a predictable large cost before the shift and an unpredictable large cost during it, and which is preferable depends on whether the deadline applies at start-up; a candidate may reasonably conclude either way provided the trade is stated.

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for the doubling capacity sequence. A1 for the capacities 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8 after the first eight appends. A1 for the copy appends 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65, 129, 257, 513; award this even if the capacity list is wrong, provided the two are consistent. Do not require the list to be exhaustive for full marks in (a); the exhaustive list is credited in (b).

(b) M1 for the pattern that append 2^k + 1 copies 2^k. A1 for the ten counts. M1 for summing them. A1 for 1023. A1 for 0.999 to three decimal places; accept 0.9988 or 1.0 only if the candidate's own total supports it. A candidate who reports the total as 2046 by assuming every doubling copies the *new* capacity rather than the old one scores the M1s but neither of the last two A1s.

(c) M1 for identifying that the largest copy is at the last doubling. A1 for 512 and for append 513; both are required, since 512 without the append number does not locate the event. M1 for the explanation that an average does not bound an individual value. A1 for the sharper statement that the total is concentrated in ten appends. An answer that says only "the average is not the worst case" earns the M1 but not the A1.

(d) M1 for the observation that 1024 is below 4096 so the structure never fills. A1 for the shift's copy total falling to 0. M1 for identifying the start-up cost. A1 is not available for claiming the change is free. Accept a conclusion either way provided the trade between a predictable and an unpredictable large cost is stated.

Throughout, accept 512 as "half the array" and do not require the phrase "amortised".

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A3.2 An index that makes the slow operation a hundred times faster and the system as a whole slower: two effects that have to be summed before either can be judged
syllabus_ref: A3.2 Database design: the selection of indexes and the effect of that selection on the operations the database performs. With A3.3 Database programming and B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking (identifying and evaluating the efficiency of a procedure)
title: A3.2 An index that makes the slow operation a hundred times faster and the system as a whole slower: two effects that have to be summed before either can be judged
q_html:
Meridian Freight: an index on the ORDERS table

Meridian Freight runs an order-capture system on a single relational database. The ORDERS table holds 2 000 000 rows. The system performs exactly two kinds of operation on it: a lookup, which retrieves one order by its ORDER_ID, and an insert, which adds one new order.

Measured on the production hardware, a lookup without an index performs a full scan of the table and takes 400 ms. An insert takes 5 ms. The development team creates a B-tree index on ORDER_ID; after that, a lookup takes 4 ms and an insert takes 40 ms, the extra 35 ms being the cost of maintaining the index.

The current workload is 1 000 000 operations per day, of which 5% are lookups and 95% are inserts. The service-level target is a mean operation time of at most 30 ms, measured over a whole day.

The chart shows the mean time per operation before and after the change, split into the time spent on reads and the time spent on writes. Use the data in the case study to answer the following, giving times to two decimal places and percentages to one decimal place.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the mean time per operation before the index is created and after it is created, and the percentage change in the mean.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Show that the change in the mean is the difference of two separate effects, one a saving on reads and one a penalty on writes, and calculate the size of each per operation.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the fraction of operations that would have to be reads for the index to break even, and hence state whether the index should be kept under the current workload.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The service-level target is currently a mean operation time of 30 ms. The operations team proposes to replace it with a target on the 99th percentile of individual operation times. Evaluate whether the index should be kept under each target, and recommend what Meridian should do.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Before: $0.05 \times 400 + 0.95 \times 5 = 20 + 4.75 = 24.75$ ms (M1). After: $0.05 \times 4 + 0.95 \times 40 = 0.2 + 38 = 38.20$ ms (A1). The mean therefore rises by $13.45$ ms, which is $\dfrac{13.45}{24.75} \times 100 = 54.3\%$ (A1): the index makes the average operation more than half as slow again. Over a day of 1 000 000 operations that is 24 750 s, about 6.9 hours of database work, against 38 200 s, about 10.6 hours: the same throughput costs an extra 3.7 hours.
(b) The change can be separated cleanly because each operation type appears with a known frequency. The saving on reads is $0.05 \times (400 - 4) = 0.05 \times 396 = 19.80$ ms per operation on average (M1). The penalty on writes is $0.95 \times (40 - 5) = 0.95 \times 35 = 33.25$ ms per operation on average (A1). The net change is $33.25 - 19.80 = +13.45$ ms, which is exactly the difference found in part (a) (A1). The two effects are of the same order — reads are 5% of the operations but each one saves 396 ms, writes are 95% but each one costs 35 ms — so neither can be neglected and the sign of the result is not obvious until both are computed.
(c) Let $r$ be the fraction of operations that are lookups. Without the index the mean is $400r + 5(1-r) = 5 + 395r$; with it the mean is $4r + 40(1-r) = 40 - 36r$ (M1). Break even when $5 + 395r = 40 - 36r$, so $431r = 35$ and $r = \dfrac{35}{431} = 0.0812$ (M1)(A1). The index pays for itself only when more than about $8.1\%$ of operations are lookups. The current workload runs at $5\%$, which is below that, so under the current mix the index should not be kept (A1). The margin is not thin: the observed 5% is about three fifths of the 8.1% needed, so the index fails by a comfortable distance rather than on a rounding error, and no plausible drift in the mix over a week would rescue it.
(d) Under the present target the answer is clear: the mean is 24.75 ms without the index, which meets the 30 ms target, and 38.20 ms with it, which does not — so the index turns a compliant system into a non-compliant one and should be dropped (M1). The percentile target reverses the comparison. Without the index, 5% of operations take 400 ms, so the 99th percentile is 400 ms; with the index the slowest operation is 40 ms and the 99th percentile is 40 ms (A1). Against a tail target the index is therefore a factor-of-ten improvement, and it is the only way to meet any percentile target below 400 ms (A1). The recommendation follows from which target Meridian actually cares about, and the two are not the same thing: a mean target measures throughput and a percentile target measures the experience of the unlucky operation, and an index trades the second for the first. Meridian should either keep the index and move the target to a percentile, or drop the index and accept 400 ms lookups — and if it needs both, it should look at a covering index on a narrower column set, or at batching the index maintenance, rather than at the current all-or-nothing choice (M1)(A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for a frequency-weighted mean in either case, (A1) for 24.75 ms and 38.20 ms, (A1) for +54.3%. A candidate who averages the two operation times without weighting by frequency has not modelled the workload and scores at most one.
(b) (M1) for isolating the read saving, (A1) for the write penalty, (A1) for showing that the difference of the two reproduces the answer to (a). The reconciliation is worth a mark of its own: an item of this kind is exactly where an arithmetic slip hides, and the cross-check is what catches it.
(c) (M1) for expressing the mean as a function of r in both cases, (M1) for equating them and solving, (A1) for 0.0812 (accept 8.1%), (A1) for the conclusion. Note that the break-even fraction is small — 8% — which is itself the finding: the index is not wrong in principle, it is wrong at this mix, and a candidate who concludes that indexes are harmful has over-read the result.
(d) (M1) for applying the current mean target to the two means, (A1) for computing the 99th percentile in each case (400 ms and 40 ms), (A1) for the conclusion that the ranking reverses, and (M1)(A1) for a recommendation that names the real choice — which target the organisation wants — or proposes a concrete alternative such as a narrower index or deferred maintenance. Do not credit 'it depends' on its own; the dependency must be stated.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Cache memory and average memory access time
syllabus_ref: A1.1 Computer hardware and operation (A1.1.4 the role of cache memory, A1.1.5 the machine instruction cycle, A1.1.6 the effect of clock speed and cache on performance)
title: Cache memory and average memory access time
q_html:
A design team is comparing two memory configurations for a new single-core processor. The figure shows the proposed hierarchy. Every instruction fetch and every data read or write that the processor issues is presented to the level 1 cache first. A reference that misses in level 1 is passed to the level 2 cache, and a reference that also misses there is passed to main memory. The hit rate of each cache is the proportion of the references presented to it that it satisfies, and the time given for each level is the number of processor cycles that level adds when it is consulted. Registers are not part of the calculation. The team must decide whether the level 2 cache earns the die area it occupies, because that area could be given to other parts of the processor.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the average number of cycles the processor spends on one memory reference when both caches are present. Show clearly how the level 1 hit time, the level 2 hit time and the main memory access time each contribute to your total, and state the fraction of references that reach main memory.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the average number of cycles per memory reference if the level 2 cache is removed, so that every level 1 miss is passed directly to main memory. Give your answer to three significant figures.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the contribution that main memory makes to the average in part (a) is so much smaller than its access time of 150 cycles would suggest, and why the level 2 cache makes a larger contribution than its own hit rate alone implies.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the proposal to remove the level 2 cache in order to recover its die area. Refer to your results from parts (a) and (b), and consider the effect on the processor's performance rather than only on the cost of manufacturing it.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The level 1 miss rate is $1 - 0.94 = 0.06$ (M1). Of those misses only $1 - 0.80 = 0.20$ are not satisfied by level 2, so the fraction of all references that reach main memory is $0.06 \times 0.20 = 0.012$, that is 1.2 per cent (A1).

The level 1 cache is consulted by every reference and adds 3 cycles, so its contribution is 3 cycles. The level 2 cache is consulted only by the 0.06 of references that miss in level 1 and adds 14 cycles to each of them, so its contribution is $0.06 \times 14 = 0.84$ cycles. Main memory is consulted only by the 0.012 of references that miss in both caches and adds 150 cycles to each of them, so its contribution is $0.012 \times 150 = 1.8$ cycles (A1).

The average number of cycles per reference is therefore $3 + 0.84 + 1.8 = 5.64$ cycles (A1).

(b) With no level 2 cache every level 1 miss is passed straight to main memory, so main memory is consulted by the whole 0.06 of misses and adds 150 cycles to each of them. Its contribution becomes $0.06 \times 150 = 9$ cycles (M1), and the average becomes $3 + 9 = 12.0$ cycles (A1). Removing the level 2 cache therefore raises the average from 5.64 to 12.0 cycles, a factor of $12.0 \div 5.64 = 2.13$ (A1).

(c) Main memory contributes only 1.8 cycles even though a single access costs 150 cycles, because it is reached by 1.2 per cent of references and by no others. Its 150 cycles are paid once per reference that misses in both caches, so multiplying 150 by the overall miss rate of 0.012 gives the average cost per reference; multiplying it by anything closer to 1 would charge the whole of main memory's latency to references that never reach it (M1).

The level 2 cache contributes more than its own hit rate suggests because its hit rate is conditional. The figure states that 0.80 of the references presented to level 2 are satisfied there, but only 0.06 of all references are ever presented to it, so the level 2 cache removes $0.06 \times 0.80 = 0.048$ of all references from the path to main memory (A1). Those references would otherwise have cost 150 cycles instead of 14, so the cache saves $0.048 \times (150 - 14) = 6.53$ cycles per reference; equivalently, comparing parts (a) and (b), it saves $12.0 - 5.64 = 6.36$ cycles (A1). A hit rate is a property of the cache, not of the program, and the two must be multiplied to obtain the share of references the cache actually rescues.

(d) The proposal should be rejected on performance grounds. Removing the level 2 cache raises the average memory reference from 5.64 to 12.0 cycles, an increase of 6.36 cycles on every reference the processor issues, which is a slowdown of about 2.13 times on any part of the workload that is memory-bound (A1). Because the level 2 cache is consulted on only 6 per cent of references but converts each of those from a 150-cycle main memory access into a 14-cycle access, it removes roughly 6.5 cycles per reference from the average while occupying far less die area than the level 1 cache does (A1).

The evaluation is not settled by cost alone. Die area given to level 2 could raise the level 1 hit rate instead, but part (a) shows that the level 1 hit time is paid by every reference and the level 1 miss rate is already only 0.06, so a further improvement there can remove at most 0.06 of the references from the level 2 path; the level 2 cache is currently rescuing 0.048 of them (A1). A design that removed level 2 would also make the processor's performance far more sensitive to the level 1 hit rate, because every additional level 1 miss would then cost the full 150 cycles rather than 14 (A1).

A justified answer must therefore weigh the 2.13 times slowdown against the area recovered, and should note that the decision depends on how memory-bound the intended workload is: a workload that fits in level 1 would lose little, while one that streams through data would lose most of its throughput (A1). Merely asserting that caches are fast, or that removing a component reduces cost, earns no credit.

Markscheme notes

Part (a) is marked for the conditional weights, not for the final number. Award M1 for the level 1 miss rate 0.06, then A1 for the joint miss rate 0.012, A1 for the three contributions being 3, 0.84 and 1.8 cycles, and A1 for the total 5.64.

A candidate who computes $0.94 \times 3 + 0.06 \times 14 = 3.66$ has weighted level 2 by the level 1 miss rate, which is correct, but has omitted main memory entirely; this is the commonest error and should be given M1 only.

A candidate who computes $0.94 \times 3 + 0.80 \times 14 + 0.012 \times 150$ has weighted level 2 by its own unconditional hit rate. The arithmetic is right and the reasoning is wrong; award M1 for the level 1 term and M1 for the main memory term, but no A1 for the total.

Part (b) expects 12.0 cycles and the factor 2.13. Accept 2.1. A candidate who writes 9 cycles for main memory but forgets to add the 3 cycles of level 1 hit time scores M1 only.

Part (c) needs both directions: main memory is small because it is rarely reached, and level 2 is large because its hit rate is conditional on a level 1 miss. One direction only scores M1.

Part (d) is an evaluation and must engage with the numbers. A bare recommendation with no reference to 5.64, 12.0 or 2.13 scores no more than M1. Award the remaining marks for recognising that the level 2 cache is cheap in area relative to the level 1 cache, and for noting that the answer depends on the workload.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.1 Redundancy in a block storage array: the parity block of a stripe is the exclusive OR of that stripe's data blocks, so exactly one lost block per stripe can be rebuilt, and the number of failures tolerated does not grow with the number of disks in the stripe
syllabus_ref: A1.1 Computer hardware and operation (secondary storage, and the use of redundancy across an array of disks), with A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (the exclusive OR operation and its use in a parity bit)
title: A1.1 Redundancy in a block storage array: the parity block of a stripe is the exclusive OR of that stripe's data blocks, so exactly one lost block per stripe can be rebuilt, and the number of failures tolerated does not grow with the number of disks in the stripe
q_html:
One stripe of a redundant array of independent disks

The array divides its address space into stripes and writes each stripe across several disks. A stripe consists of four data blocks followed by one parity block, and the parity block holds the bitwise exclusive OR of the four data blocks of that stripe. The array rotates the position of the parity block from stripe to stripe, so that no single disk stores the parity of every stripe. The table gives the four data blocks of one stripe as they were written.

The array divides its address space into stripes. A stripe consists of four data blocks and one parity block, and the parity block holds the bitwise exclusive OR of the four data blocks of that stripe. The position of the parity block rotates from stripe to stripe, so that no single disk holds the parity of every stripe. When the array reads a block it reads that block alone; the parity block is consulted only when a block is found to be unreadable. The table gives the four data blocks of one stripe as they were written. The figure shows that stripe together with a neighbouring stripe, and marks one unreadable block in each of the two stripes. The two unreadable blocks are in different stripes, and the controller has not yet had to rebuild two blocks that lie in the same stripe.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the parity block of the stripe given in the table, and state the fraction of the array's total block capacity that remains available for data when every stripe carries one parity block for four data blocks.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the value of the block D3 can be rebuilt from the parity block and the three surviving data blocks of the stripe, and determine the value that is rebuilt.

    (Show that)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the array can rebuild the two unreadable blocks marked in the figure at the same time, even though it could not rebuild two unreadable blocks that lay in the same stripe.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine how many simultaneous block failures the array can survive within a single stripe, and state what a second parity block in every stripe would change.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) The parity block is the exclusive OR of the four data blocks, so it is computed by combining them two at a time.

0x5A XOR 0x3C = 0x66
0x66 XOR 0xF0 = 0x96
0x96 XOR 0x27 = 0xB1

The parity block is 0xB1. The exclusive OR is associative and commutative, so the order in which the four blocks are combined does not matter.

A stripe that holds four data blocks and one parity block occupies five blocks in order to store four blocks of data. The fraction of the array's capacity available for data is therefore 4/5 = 0.80, that is eighty per cent. The remaining twenty per cent is the cost of the redundancy: one block in every five is spent on the parity and holds no data of its own.

(b) When the block D3 is unreadable, the array knows the parity block 0xB1 and the three surviving data blocks 0x5A, 0x3C and 0x27. The parity block was formed as the exclusive OR of all four data blocks, and the exclusive OR is its own inverse: a value exclusive ORed with itself gives zero, and a value exclusive ORed with zero is unchanged. Combining the parity block with the three surviving blocks therefore cancels those three and leaves the missing one.

0xB1 XOR 0x5A = 0xEB
0xEB XOR 0x3C = 0xD7
0xD7 XOR 0x27 = 0xF0

The rebuilt value is 0xF0, which is the value the table records for D3. The same computation works whichever of the four blocks is lost, because the parity block is symmetric in the four of them; a rebuild of D1 would combine 0xB1 with 0x3C, 0xF0 and 0x27 and return 0x5A.

(c) Each stripe contributes exactly one equation. For the stripe in the table the equation is D1 XOR D2 XOR D3 XOR D4 = P, in which the only unknown is the one block that has been lost, so the equation can be solved. The two unreadable blocks marked in the figure lie in different stripes, so each of the two stripes supplies its own equation, and each of those equations contains one unknown. The two equations are independent of one another, because the stripes are computed separately when the data is written, so they can be solved at the same time and the two blocks can both be rebuilt.

If two blocks of the same stripe were lost, that stripe would supply one equation containing two unknowns, and one equation in two unknowns does not determine either unknown. Every assignment of values to the two missing blocks that keeps the exclusive OR equal to the parity block would satisfy the equation equally well, so the array would have no way to tell which assignment was the original. The stripe's single equation is one constraint, and one constraint removes one unknown.

(d) A stripe with one parity block carries one equation and can therefore absorb exactly one lost block. That number does not depend on how many data blocks the stripe holds: a stripe of four data blocks and a stripe of twelve data blocks each carry one equation and each tolerate exactly one failure. Widening the stripe raises the fraction of the array available for data, since the parity overhead falls from one block in five to one block in thirteen, but it does not raise the tolerance at all. The tolerance is set by the number of parity blocks in the stripe and not by the number of disks in it, which is the point that a candidate who reasons by analogy with the disk count will miss.

A second parity block in every stripe would give each stripe two equations instead of one. Two equations in two unknowns can be solved, so such an array would tolerate two simultaneous block failures within the same stripe, and it would also be able to rebuild a block even when the parity block itself is one of the two failures. The cost is a second block of overhead: a stripe of four data blocks would then occupy six blocks, so the fraction available for data would fall from 4/5 to 4/6, that is from eighty per cent to about sixty-seven per cent.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the method of combining the blocks with the exclusive OR, one mark for the value 0xB1, and one mark for the fraction 4/5 or eighty per cent. A candidate who writes 0xB1 but gives the capacity as five quarters, or as one hundred per cent because the parity is 'not data', forfeits the third mark.

(b) One mark for stating that the exclusive OR is its own inverse or that combining the parity with the survivors cancels them, one mark for a correct sequence of combinations, one mark for the value 0xF0, and one mark for showing the check that the rebuilt value reproduces the parity block. Follow-through is allowed from a wrong parity block in (a) provided the method in (b) is sound, since a candidate who computes 0x00 in (a) and then rebuilds 0xF0 by the correct method has demonstrated the same understanding.

(c) One mark for saying that each stripe supplies its own independent equation, one mark for saying that each of those equations contains one unknown, and one mark for the contrast, that one equation in two unknowns does not determine either unknown. The phrase 'different stripes' alone earns nothing; the reason must be the independence of the equations.

(d) One mark for exactly one failure per stripe, one mark for the statement that this number is independent of the number of data blocks, and one mark for the effect of a second parity block, namely two failures per stripe at the cost of a second block of overhead. An answer that says the tolerance grows with the number of disks scores zero for this part, however well the earlier parts are done.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.2 A weighted check digit modulo a prime detects every interchange of two digits, because the change it makes to the total is a product of two factors each smaller than the modulus; an unweighted digit sum detects none, because the change is zero
syllabus_ref: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (check digits and the detection of errors in stored or transmitted data), with A2.3 Data transmissions (why an error must be detected before it can be corrected)
title: A1.2 A weighted check digit modulo a prime detects every interchange of two digits, because the change it makes to the total is a product of two factors each smaller than the modulus; an unweighted digit sum detects none, because the change is zero
q_html:
The catalogue's check on the codes it stores

A book catalogue stores ten-digit ISBN codes. Each code consists of nine identifying digits followed by a check digit. The check digit is chosen so that, with the digits weighted from ten down to one, the weighted total is a multiple of eleven. When a code is typed in, the catalogue runs a validation routine. The routine adds the ten digits together and accepts the code if that total is a multiple of ten. The routine was written by a volunteer who believed that a check digit is simply a digit chosen to make the digits add up to a round number. The table shows one record, the code as it was typed, and the routine's verdict.

The nine identifying digits of record R-4471 are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5, and the check digit is the final 2, so the code as the publisher printed it is 0306406152. The code held in the catalogue is 0306406512: the eighth and ninth digits have been interchanged somewhere between the publisher's list and the catalogue's keyboard. The catalogue's routine accepted the code, and the record has stood in the catalogue for two years. The correct rule for a ten-digit ISBN weights the first digit by ten, the second by nine, and so on down to the tenth digit weighted by one, and requires the weighted total to be a multiple of eleven. A rival scheme weights each digit by its own position, counting the first digit as position one, and requires the total to be a multiple of ten. The catalogue's routine is a third scheme again: it weights every digit by one.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the check digit that the weighted rule requires for the nine identifying digits 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5, and hence state whether the code held in the catalogue satisfies the rule.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the weighted total of the code held in the catalogue, and state what its remainder on division by eleven shows about the interchange of the two digits.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the catalogue's routine accepted a code that the weighted rule rejects, referring to the effect that interchanging two digits has on the sum of those digits.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The rival scheme that weights each digit by its position and works modulo ten is not equivalent to the weighted rule. Deduce, from the change that interchanging two digits makes to a weighted total, one interchange that the rival scheme fails to detect, and explain why the weighted rule modulo eleven cannot fail to detect any interchange of two digits.

    (Deduce)
a_html:
(a) The weighted rule weights the digits from ten down to one. For the nine identifying digits 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5 the weights are 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2, so the weighted total of the identifying digits is

10(0) + 9(3) + 8(0) + 7(6) + 6(4) + 5(0) + 4(6) + 3(1) + 2(5)
= 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 3 + 10
= 130.

The check digit carries weight one, so it must satisfy 130 + d = 0 (mod 11). Now 130 = 11 x 11 + 9, so 130 is 9 more than a multiple of eleven, and the check digit must make up the difference: d = 11 - 9 = 2. The check digit is 2, which agrees with the final digit of the publisher's code 0306406152.

The code held in the catalogue is 0306406512, which has the same ten digits in a different order. Its weighted total is 136, and 136 = 11 x 12 + 4, so the total is 4 more than a multiple of eleven. The code held in the catalogue therefore does not satisfy the rule, and the check digit it carries, 2, is not the check digit for the nine digits that precede it in that order.

(b) The weighted total of the code held in the catalogue is

10(0) + 9(3) + 8(0) + 7(6) + 6(4) + 5(0) + 4(6) + 3(5) + 2(1) + 1(2)
= 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 15 + 2 + 2
= 136.

The remainder on division by eleven is 4, and a valid code would leave a remainder of zero. The remainder is not zero, so the interchange is detected: the code held in the catalogue is not a valid ISBN under the weighted rule, and the nonzero remainder is the evidence. Comparing the two totals, the publisher's code gives 132 and the catalogue's code gives 136, so interchanging the eighth and ninth digits raised the total by 4. That increase is not an accident of these particular digits; it is the difference between the two weights, 3 and 2, multiplied by the difference between the two digits, 1 and 5.

(c) The catalogue's routine adds the ten digits together and tests whether the total is a multiple of ten. The ten digits of the publisher's code are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1, 5 and 2, which add to 27. The ten digits of the catalogue's code are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 5, 1 and 2, which also add to 27. Addition does not care about the order of its terms, so interchanging two digits leaves the sum of the digits exactly as it was. The routine therefore computes the same total for both codes, finds 27 in each case, and accepts both, because 27 has the same remainder on division by ten, namely 7, as itself.

The routine is not merely weaker than the weighted rule; it is blind to the whole class of errors to which keyboard entry is most prone. Interchanging two adjacent digits is the commonest mistake made when a long number is copied by hand, and the routine's weighting, which is to say a weight of one on every position, makes every interchange invisible. A check that cannot see the commonest error is not a check that has been weakened; it is a check that is not doing the job it was written for.

(d) Consider a weighted total in which the digit at position i carries weight w_i. Interchanging the digits at positions i and j replaces the contribution w_i d_i + w_j d_j with w_i d_j + w_j d_i, so the total changes by

(w_i d_j + w_j d_i) - (w_i d_i + w_j d_j) = (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i).

For the rival scheme the weight of a digit is its position, so w_i = i and w_j = j, and the change is (i - j)(d_j - d_i). The rival scheme accepts the corrupted code when this product is a multiple of ten. Take the digits at positions 1 and 3, and suppose they are 0 and 5. Then i - j is 1 - 3 = -2 and d_j - d_i is 5 - 0 = 5, so the change is -2 x 5 = -10, which is a multiple of ten, and the rival scheme does not notice the interchange. The interchange of a 0 and a 5 two positions apart is therefore one that the rival scheme misses. The reason the miss is possible is that ten is not prime: the factor of five that the digit difference supplies can be paired with the factor of two that the position difference supplies to make a multiple of ten.

For the weighted rule the weights are ten, nine, eight and so on down to one, and the change made by an interchange is (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i). The digits are between 0 and 9, so d_j - d_i lies between -9 and 9, and the positions are between 1 and 10, so w_i - w_j also lies between -9 and 9. Neither factor can be a multiple of eleven, because eleven is larger than nine, and neither factor is zero when the digits differ and the positions differ. Since eleven is prime, a product is a multiple of eleven only if one of its factors is, and neither factor is. The change is therefore never a multiple of eleven, so the total of a code with two digits interchanged can never be a multiple of eleven, and the interchange is always detected. Choosing a prime modulus larger than the largest possible value of either factor is what makes the guarantee hold.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the weighted total 130 of the nine identifying digits, one mark for the check digit 2 with the reasoning 130 = 9 (mod 11) so d = 2, and one mark for the verdict that the catalogue's code does not satisfy the rule. A candidate who computes 132 and then reports the code as valid has used the wrong digit order and forfeits the third mark.

(b) One mark for the total 136, one mark for the remainder 4, and one mark for the conclusion that the interchange is detected because the remainder is not zero. Accept the remainder as 4 or as -7; accept the observation that the interchange changed the total by 4 only if it is attached to the weights 3 and 2.

(c) One mark for stating that the sum of the digits is 27 in both orders, one mark for the reason, that addition does not depend on the order of its terms, and one mark for drawing the consequence, that the routine is blind to every interchange and not merely to this one. A candidate who says only that the routine 'checks the wrong thing' without referring to the invariance of the digit sum scores at most one mark.

(d) One mark for the expression (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i) or its equivalent, one mark for a correct specific interchange such as the 0 and the 5 at positions 1 and 3 with the product -10, one mark for the argument that eleven is prime and larger than both factors, and one mark for completing it, that a product is a multiple of a prime only when one factor is. Follow-through is allowed from a wrong expression in the first mark provided the prime argument is made correctly.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Two's complement overflow and exclusive OR checksums
syllabus_ref: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (A1.2.1 representation of integers in binary and hexadecimal, A1.2.2 binary encoding and its impact on storage, A1.2.3 logic gates, A1.2.4 truth tables)
title: Two's complement overflow and exclusive OR checksums
q_html:
A sensor network transmits each measurement as a three-byte frame. The first byte is the reading and the second is a calibration offset, and both are 8-bit two's complement values; the third byte is a checksum. Two frames captured from the network are shown in the figure, together with the 8-bit sum that the receiver's adder produced for each of them and the carry-out bit that the same adder produced. The receiver must reject any frame whose two signed values cannot be added without the result being misrepresented, and the engineer who wrote the receiver used the carry-out bit to make that decision.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the signed decimal value of the reading and of the offset in frame A, and state the true arithmetic sum of those two values. Show how the first bit of each byte is used in your decoding.

    (Determine)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Deduce the signed decimal value that the 8-bit sum in frame B represents, and state with a reason whether the addition of the two signed values in frame B has overflowed.

    (Deduce)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Calculate the checksum of each frame from its first two bytes, and state whether each of the two checksums in the figure is correct.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Explain why the carry-out bit cannot be used to decide whether a signed addition has overflowed. Your answer should refer to both frames and should state the condition that does detect overflow.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) In frame A the first byte is 0x7A, which in binary is 0111 1010. Its leading bit is 0, so the value is positive and the remaining bits give $64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 122$ (A1). The second byte is 0x9C, which is 1001 1100. Its leading bit is 1, so it is negative, and its magnitude is found by taking the two's complement: $1001\,1100 \to 0110\,0011 \to 0110\,0100$, which is $64 + 32 + 4 = 100$ (A1). The offset is therefore $-100$.

The true arithmetic sum of the two signed values is $122 + (-100) = 22$ (A1). Because the two values have opposite signs, the sum lies between them and no overflow is possible.

(b) In frame B the first byte is 0x6F, which is 0110 1111 with a leading bit of 0, so the reading is $+111$. The second byte is 0x32, which is 0011 0010 with a leading bit of 0, so the offset is $+50$ (M1). Their true sum is $111 + 50 = 161$, which is greater than the largest value an 8-bit two's complement number can hold, namely $+127$ (A1).

The 8-bit sum shown in the figure is 0xA1, which is 1010 0001. Its leading bit is 1, so it represents a negative number, and its magnitude is $0101\,1110 + 1 = 0101\,1111 = 95$, giving $-95$ (A1). Adding two positive values has produced a negative result, so the addition has overflowed.

(c) The checksum is the exclusive OR of the first two bytes. For frame A, $0111\,1010$ XOR $1001\,1100 = 1110\,0110$, which is 0xE6 (M1) (A1). The figure shows 0xE6, so the checksum of frame A is correct (A1).

For frame B, $0110\,1111$ XOR $0011\,0010 = 0101\,1101$, which is 0x5D (M1). The figure shows 0x5D, so the checksum of frame B is also correct (A1). This matters: the frame that overflows is not corrupt, and a receiver that relied on the checksum alone would accept it.

(d) The carry-out is the bit that leaves the most significant position of the adder, and it reports whether the unsigned sum of the two bit patterns exceeded 255. That is not the same question as whether the signed sum exceeded 127 or fell below $-128$, because the same bit patterns mean different things under the two interpretations (A1).

Frame A shows the first failure. Its bytes are 0x7A and 0x9C, whose unsigned values are 122 and 156. Their unsigned sum is 278, which exceeds 255, so the adder produces a carry-out of 1. The signed values, however, are 122 and $-100$, whose sum is 22 and fits comfortably; the carry-out is 1 while there is no overflow (A1). A receiver that rejected on the carry-out would discard a good frame.

Frame B shows the opposite failure. Its bytes are 0x6F and 0x32, whose unsigned values are 111 and 50. Their unsigned sum is 161, which does not exceed 255, so the carry-out is 0. The signed values are $+111$ and $+50$, whose sum of 161 exceeds 127, so the result stored is $-95$ and the addition has overflowed (A1). A receiver that accepted on the carry-out would accept a frame whose value is wrong by 256.

Overflow for signed addition is detected from the signs of the operands and the sign of the result, not from the carry-out: overflow occurs when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign (A1). Equivalently, it is the exclusive OR of the carry into the most significant position and the carry out of it. In frame A the signs are opposite, so no overflow is possible whatever the carry-out is; in frame B both operands are positive and the result is negative, so overflow has occurred whatever the carry-out is (A1).

Markscheme notes

Part (a): award A1 for decoding 0x7A as +122 with the leading bit used as the sign, A1 for decoding 0x9C as $-100$ by taking the two's complement of the magnitude, and A1 for the true sum 22. A candidate who reads 0x9C as 156 or as $-28$ has not applied two's complement and scores no marks on the second point.

Part (b): M1 for reading both bytes as positive, A1 for identifying that 161 exceeds +127, and A1 for decoding 0xA1 as $-95$. Accept $-95$ with or without the working.

Part (c): M1 for the exclusive OR method and A1 for each correct checksum. The marks are for the method and the values; a candidate who XORs the three bytes together, or who adds rather than XORs, scores no marks here.

Part (d): this is the discriminating part. A1 for stating that the carry-out answers the unsigned question rather than the signed one, A1 for frame A as the false-rejection case, A1 for frame B as the false-acceptance case, and A1 for the correct rule that overflow is detected from the signs of the operands and the result. A candidate who asserts that overflow occurs when the carry-out is 1 without noticing frame B scores at most A1.

Note that both checksums are correct, so the checksum cannot be used to detect the overflow either; a candidate who says the frame is corrupt has misread the question.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Choosing a translation strategy from a three-way cost model, where the compiler and the interpreter cross at a value of N that is never on the cheapest frontier
syllabus_ref: A1.4 Translation (HL only) (A1.4.1 evaluate the translation processes of interpreters and compilers, including bytecode interpreters, and the applicability of each approach to cross-platform development)
title: Choosing a translation strategy from a three-way cost model, where the compiler and the interpreter cross at a value of N that is never on the cheapest frontier
q_html:
A laboratory writes a data-reduction tool that has to run on the three operating systems its collaborators use. The team can distribute the tool in any of three forms. In form A the source is compiled ahead of time into a native executable, and one executable has to be built and tested for each of the three systems. In form B the source is shipped as it stands and translated every time the tool is run. In form C the source is compiled once, on the laboratory's own machine, into bytecode, and that single bytecode build is shipped to all three systems and executed there by a bytecode interpreter.

The figure gives the total cost of each form, in arbitrary cost units, as a function of N, the number of times the tool is executed in total across all three systems. A dashed line marks the number of executions the team currently expects. The costs are the whole cost of owning each form: translation, distribution and execution.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the value of N at which forms B and C have the same total cost, and state which of the two forms is cheaper immediately below that value and which is cheaper immediately above it. Show the equation you solved.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the value of N at which forms C and A have the same total cost. Hence state, for each of the three forms, the range of N over which that form is the cheapest of the three. Where a boundary of your range is a tie rather than a strict win, say so.

    (Determine)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    The team's current estimate is the value of N marked on the figure. Determine the total cost of each of the three forms at that estimate, and state the saving the cheapest form makes against the next cheapest. A colleague recommends form A for every project because it has the lowest cost per execution. Explain why a comparison of forms A and B on their own would have supported that recommendation at this estimate, and state the smallest number of executions at which the recommendation would actually change. Reach a judgement on which form the team should ship.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The figure gives the three cost models directly: form A is $1200 + 4N$, form B is $20N$, and form C is $240 + 8N$, all in the same cost units. Forms B and C are equal when $20N = 240 + 8N$, so $12N = 240$ and $N = 20$ (M1). At that value both cost $400$ (A1). Immediately below 20 the coefficient of $N$ is smaller for B than for C, so B is cheaper: at $N = 19$, B costs $380$ and C costs $392$. Immediately above 20, C is cheaper: at $N = 21$, B costs $420$ and C costs $408$ (A1).

(b) Forms C and A are equal when $240 + 8N = 1200 + 4N$, so $4N = 960$ and $N = 240$ (M1). At that value both cost $2160$ (A1).

The three ranges are found by taking the lower of the three costs at each N, not by listing the pairwise crossovers.

  • Form B is the cheapest for $N \leq 19$. At $N = 20$ B and C are tied at $400$.
  • Form C is the cheapest for $21 \leq N \leq 239$. At $N = 240$ C and A are tied at $2160$.
  • Form A is the cheapest for $N \geq 241$. At $N = 241$, A costs $2164$ and C costs $2168$ (A1).

Two of the three boundaries are therefore ties rather than wins (A1).

(c) At the estimate marked on the figure, $N = 100$. Form A costs $1200 + 400 = 1600$; form B costs $2000$; form C costs $240 + 800 = 1040$ (M1). Form C is the cheapest, and the saving against the next cheapest, which is form A, is $1600 - 1040 = 560$ cost units (A1).

The colleague's recommendation is not unreasonable when only A and B are considered. Forms A and B are equal when $1200 + 4N = 20N$, so $N = 75$, and A is cheaper than B for every $N$ above 75 (M1). At an estimate of 100, which is above 75, a comparison of those two forms alone therefore recommends A, and the recommendation is supported by the arithmetic of that comparison. It is still the wrong recommendation, because the question is not which of A and B is cheaper but which of the three is cheapest. At $N = 75$ form A and form B both cost $1500$, while form C costs $840$ (A1). The crossover at 75 is a genuine crossover, and it is not on the cheapest frontier: at every value of N the frontier passes through, form C is below both of the strategies that cross there. Reporting the crossover at 75 as a boundary of the answer puts a segment into the frontier that does not exist, and it does so in the direction that looks most plausible, because A really is cheaper than B above 75 (A1).

The recommendation changes at $N = 241$, which is the smallest number of executions for which form A is the cheapest of the three (A1). Below that, form C is cheaper. So the estimate would have to be wrong by more than a factor of two, in the direction of more executions, before the colleague's recommendation became the right one.

The judgement is that the team should ship form C at the current estimate (A1). Form C costs $1040$ against $1600$ for form A, a saving of $560$ cost units, or thirty-five per cent of form A's total. It also keeps the property that made form A attractive in the first place, since a single bytecode build is produced once and then runs on all three systems, so no per-system build or test effort is needed. The judgement is not unconditional: it holds while the estimate stays below 241 executions. If the tool is later executed far more often than expected, the per-execution cost of $8$ for form C against $4$ for form A becomes decisive, and form A becomes the cheaper choice. A recommendation that is not attached to the estimate it was made for is not a recommendation, it is a preference (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) 3 marks. One mark for setting $20N = 240 + 8N$ and reaching $N = 20$. One mark for stating that B is cheaper below 20 and C is cheaper above it. One mark for a justification that uses the per-execution coefficients rather than a restatement of the figure.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for solving $240 + 8N = 1200 + 4N$ to $N = 240$. One mark for the range over which C is cheapest, which must run from 21 to 239. One mark for the range over which A is cheapest, which must begin at 241 and not at 240. One mark for recognising that $N = 20$ and $N = 240$ are ties, so both boundaries are stated as equal costs rather than as wins. A candidate who writes 'A is cheapest for $N > 240$' has the right boundary and should keep the mark, provided the ranges do not overlap.

A candidate who reports three ranges taken from the three pairwise crossovers, that is B below 20, C from 21 to 75 and A above 76, has computed every crossover correctly and has still produced a frontier that does not exist. Award at most two of the four marks and read part (c) before deciding the second.

(c) 6 marks. One mark for the three totals at $N = 100$: 1600, 2000 and 1040. One mark for the saving of 560 against the next cheapest, which is A and not B. One mark for locating the A and B crossover at 75 and showing that it is above the estimate. One mark for the observation that form C undercuts both strategies at that crossover, which is what removes the segment from the frontier. One mark for the change point at 241. One mark for a judgement on form C that is attached to the estimate, and that names the condition under which it would change. A bare 'ship form C because it is cheaper' earns the first four marks and not the last two.

Accept a candidate who notes that the figure's costs are the whole cost of owning each form, so the per-system build effort is already inside form A's fixed cost and must not be added again.

A candidate who answers part (c) with 'form A, because 100 is greater than 75' has answered the two-form question. This is the trap, and it must not be credited as an evaluation of the three-form choice.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Two transfers that interleave so that the second reads the balance before the first commits, and the committed value is short by exactly the first transfer
syllabus_ref: A3.3 Database programming (A3.3.6 describe how transactions maintain data integrity in a database, including the role of atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability to ensure reliable processing of transactions, and the transaction control language commands BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK)
title: Two transfers that interleave so that the second reads the balance before the first commits, and the committed value is short by exactly the first transfer
q_html:
A savings account holds a balance of 500. Two transfers into the account are submitted at almost the same moment: one adds 100 and one adds 50. Each transfer is written as a transaction that reads the balance, computes the new balance from the value it read, writes that value back, and commits. The application does not use a lock, and the database engine is running at an isolation level that permits the two transactions to interleave.

The figure shows what the engine actually did, as an ordered list of operations. Each operation is labelled with the transaction that issued it and the moment it was issued. Nothing in the figure has been simplified: this is the whole of both transactions, and both of them commit.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Using the timeline, state the balance that each of the two transactions reads and the balance that each of them writes. Determine the balance that is left in the account once both transactions have committed, and state which of the two COMMIT statements fixes that value.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the balance that would remain if the two transfers had run one after the other, and show that both possible orders give the same result. State the amount by which the interleaved execution has lost. Name the ACID property whose role this interleaving has defeated, and name one of the other three properties that this same interleaving has not defeated, justifying each of your two answers.

    (Determine)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    A developer proposes to change nothing in the application, to rely on ROLLBACK to undo any damage, and to allow both transactions to run for longer so that they overlap more often. Evaluate that proposal. Your answer should state what ROLLBACK can and cannot recover in this timeline, identify the smallest change to the timeline that removes the loss, and reach a judgement on whether this anomaly can be prevented using transaction control commands alone.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The first SELECT is issued by the first transaction at t1 and returns 500. The second SELECT is issued by the second transaction at t3 and also returns 500, because the first transaction has not yet written anything at that moment (A1). The first transaction writes $500 + 100 = 600$ at t4, and the second writes $500 + 50 = 550$ at t6 (A1). The last COMMIT is the second transaction's, at t7, and it fixes the stored balance at 550 (A1). The first transaction's 600 is not in the database any more: the second transaction wrote over it.

(b) Run in either serial order, the arithmetic gives the same answer. First then second: the first reads 500 and writes 600, then the second reads 600 and writes $600 + 50 = 650$. Second then first: the second reads 500 and writes 550, then the first reads 550 and writes $550 + 100 = 650$ (M1). Both orders give 650, which is what makes 650 the correct result rather than merely one possible result (A1).

The interleaved execution has left 550, so the loss is $650 - 550 = 100$ (A1). That is exactly the amount the first transaction added, which is what a lost update looks like: one transaction's write is entirely overwritten by another's, and the update that is lost is the earlier one.

The property whose role has been defeated is isolation (A1). Isolation is what guarantees that the result of running transactions concurrently is the same as the result of running them in some serial order, and here the concurrent result of 550 matches neither serial order.

Atomicity has not been defeated. Each transaction did what atomicity requires: the first transaction's read and write both took effect and it committed as a unit, and the second's did the same. Atomicity is about a transaction not being half-applied, and neither transaction was half-applied; the first was applied in full and then overwritten in full by a later transaction, which is an ordering fault and not a failure of atomicity. Durability has not been defeated either: both COMMIT statements were honoured and both transactions' effects were persisted, and the persisted value is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with losing committed data. Either answer earns the mark, provided the candidate distinguishes it from isolation.

(c) ROLLBACK undoes the writes of the transaction that issues it, and only while that transaction has not yet committed. In this timeline there is nothing left for it to undo (A1). By t7 both transactions have committed, so neither can be rolled back: a rollback of the first transaction is refused because it has already committed, and a rollback of the second would remove the 550 and leave the account at 500, which is worse, not better. The value the first transaction computed, 600, was overwritten inside the second transaction's write and is no longer held anywhere the database can reach. ROLLBACK recovers a transaction that has failed; it cannot recover a value that a later committed transaction has already replaced.

Making the transactions run for longer, so that they overlap more often, makes the anomaly more likely rather than less. The loss happened because the second transaction's read fell between the first transaction's read and its COMMIT. Widening the interval between a transaction's read and its commit widens exactly the window in which another transaction can read the old value, so the proposal increases the frequency of the fault it is offered as a defence against (A1).

The smallest change to the timeline is to move the second transaction's read so that it happens after the first transaction's COMMIT, that is from t3 to after t5 (A1). If the second transaction reads after t5 it reads 600, and it then writes $600 + 50 = 650$, which is the correct result. Nothing else needs to change: both transactions keep their structure, both still commit, and no statement is rewritten. The change is a change of ordering, and it corresponds to a real mechanism, which is to make the second transaction wait until the first has finished, whether by taking a lock on the row before reading it or by raising the isolation level so that the engine takes one on the transaction's behalf (A1).

The judgement is that this anomaly cannot be prevented using transaction control commands alone (A1). The commands the guide lists are BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK, and between them they let a candidate start a transaction, finish it successfully, or abandon it. None of them constrains when another transaction may read. The fault is in the interleaving, and the interleaving is controlled by locking and by the isolation level, which are properties of how the transaction is declared and of how the engine schedules it rather than commands that a developer issues. A candidate who answers that ROLLBACK can be used to detect and retry the second transaction should be credited for the retry idea, but must also be asked to say what triggers the rollback, since nothing in this timeline fails and so nothing raises an error for the application to catch.

Markscheme notes

(a) 3 marks. One mark for both reads giving 500. One mark for the two written values, 600 and 550, each computed from the value that transaction actually read. One mark for the final committed balance of 550 and for attributing it to the second transaction's COMMIT. A candidate who answers 650 has added the transfers together without following the timeline; no marks for that part.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for showing both serial orders, 600 then 650 and 550 then 650, and stating that they agree. One mark for the loss of 100 and for identifying it as the first transaction's increment. One mark for isolation as the property defeated, with a reason that refers to the serial-order guarantee. One mark for naming atomicity or durability as preserved, with a reason. A candidate who names consistency as defeated should be credited only if the answer states the invariant that was broken, namely that the two transfers must both be reflected in the balance.

Do not accept 'atomicity is violated' for the final mark: both transactions committed as units, and the failure is in the ordering.

(c) 6 marks. One mark for stating that ROLLBACK cannot act here because both transactions have committed. One mark for stating that a rollback of the second transaction would make the balance worse rather than better. One mark for the observation that making the transactions overlap more often widens the read-to-commit window and increases the fault rate. One mark for the smallest change, which is to move the second read to after the first COMMIT, giving a write of 650. One mark for naming the mechanism, a row lock or a raised isolation level. One mark for the judgement that transaction control commands alone cannot prevent the anomaly, with the reason that none of BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK constrains when another transaction may read.

A candidate who proposes a retry loop should keep the first four marks if the reordering is also given, but must be asked what would trigger the retry, since no statement in this timeline raises an error.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Reading an append-only load table whose rows supersede one another, where the two natural wrong totals err in opposite directions
syllabus_ref: A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only) (A3.4.2 explain the primary objectives of data warehouses in data management and business intelligence, including the roles of append-only data, time-variant data and non-volatile data, and the role of data optimized for query performance)
title: Reading an append-only load table whose rows supersede one another, where the two natural wrong totals err in opposite directions
q_html:
A retail group loads its sales data into a warehouse every night. The warehouse never updates a row and never deletes one: each night's load appends new rows, and the table's whole history is still present. The same product can appear in more than one night's load, and more than one source system can report on the same product in the same night.

Two rules govern how the table is read. A row supersedes any earlier row that carries the same product and the same source, so only the newest row for a given product and source is current. Rows from different sources are not alternatives to one another and are added together, because they describe different parts of the same sale. The table is shown in the figure, together with the night on which each row was written.

The operations director has asked for the current total units and the current total revenue, and has been given two different answers by two analysts.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State the number of rows the table holds, the number of distinct products it holds, and the number of distinct combinations of product and source. Hence state how many of the rows have been superseded, and explain why an append-only table holds more rows than it holds current facts.

    (State)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the current total units and the current total revenue, applying the reading rules given above. State how many of the four rows contribute to your total, and explain for each row that does not contribute why it does not.

    (Determine)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    One analyst adds units and revenue over every row in the table. The other finds the greatest load date in the table and adds only the rows that carry it.
