Candidates who propose deleting all three problem fields outright should be credited for missing values only if they note the loss of 4 800 records.

(c) The key phrase is 'generalisation gap'. Candidates who say only 'the model is bad' earn at most one mark. Credit 'overfitting' as the diagnosis; the remedy mark accepts any two sensible actions.

(d) This is a discuss question: two issues must each be *explained*, not just named. 'It is racist' is not creditworthy; 'the model may be discriminating indirectly because postcode correlates with ethnic composition' is. The action must address the problem identified — 'retrain the model' on its own is not an action.

Additional guidance. In (b) accept mode imputation or a separate 'missing' indicator for income, provided the choice is justified. In (c) credit k-fold cross-validation or a held-out validation set as valid remedies alongside 'get more data'.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.4 Choosing between interpretation and compilation when a script runs N times
syllabus_ref: A1.4 Translation (HL only): translators, interpreters and compilers
title: A1.4 Choosing between interpretation and compilation when a script runs N times
q_html:
A greenhouse controller runs a short rule script once every sampling cycle. The script can be executed in either of two ways.

  • Interpreted. Each statement is translated every time it is met, so nothing is produced in advance. This costs $0.050$ ms per execution of the loop body and has no start-up cost.
  • Compiled. The whole script is translated once into bytecode, at a one-off cost of $6.0$ ms. The bytecode is then executed directly at $0.010$ ms per execution of the loop body.

The figure shows the total time taken by each strategy against $N$, the number of times the loop body executes.

The controller samples every $2$ minutes, and in a typical cycle the loop body executes $400$ times.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State, for each strategy, when the translation of the source code takes place and what, if anything, is produced by that translation.

    (State)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the two strategies take the same total time when $N = 150$, and determine which strategy is faster, and by how much, for a cycle in which the loop body executes $400$ times.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the total time saved over one day of continuous operation by using the compiled strategy, and express that saving as a percentage of the time the interpreted strategy would have taken.

    (Calculate)
  4. [5 marks](d)

    A developer argues that the script should always be compiled, because compiled code runs faster. Justify why this is wrong for a script that is executed only once, and determine the least value of $N$ for which compiling becomes worthwhile if a slower translator raises the one-off cost to $12.0$ ms while both per-execution times are unchanged.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) Interpreted. Translation happens at run time, every time the statement is met, and no separate translated version of the program is produced; the source is read, analysed and executed statement by statement. One mark for each of 'at run time' and 'nothing is produced', and one mark for making clear that the translation is repeated on each pass. Note also that the compiled route produces bytecode rather than native machine code, so the output is still executed by a virtual machine; what has changed is that the analysis of the source happens once rather than on every pass. This is why the translated output can be reused without the source being present, and why the advantage of compiling grows with the number of executions instead of being a fixed speed-up applied once.

Compiled. Translation happens once, before execution, and produces a separate translated version — here bytecode — which is then executed without reference to the original source. One mark for 'before execution / once' and one mark for naming bytecode as the output. Up to three marks in total across the two strategies, awarded for the pair of contrasts: when the translation happens, and what it leaves behind.

(b) Interpreted: $T_I = 0.050N$. Compiled: $T_C = 6.0 + 0.010N$. Setting them equal: $0.050N = 6.0 + 0.010N$, so $0.040N = 6.0$ and $N = 150$. At $N = 150$ both take $0.050(150) = 7.5$ ms, which confirms the crossing. For $N = 400$: $T_I = 0.050(400) = 20.0$ ms, while $T_C = 6.0 + 0.010(400) = 6.0 + 4.0 = 10.0$ ms. The compiled strategy is faster by $20.0 - 10.0 = 10.0$ ms per cycle. A sign check confirms the direction: $T_I - T_C = 0.040N - 6.0$, which is negative for $N < 150$ and positive for $N > 150$. Because $400 > 150$ the compiled route must win, and the size of the win, $0.040(400) - 6.0 = 10.0$ ms, agrees with the direct subtraction.

(c) One day is $24(60) = 1440$ minutes, and the controller samples every $2$ minutes, so there are $1440/2 = 720$ cycles per day. The saving is $10.0$ ms per cycle, so the total saved is $720 \times 10.0 = 7200$ ms $= 7.2$ s per day. As a percentage of the interpreted time: $\dfrac{20.0 - 10.0}{20.0} \times 100 = 50\%$. Note that the percentage is a property of the two strategies at $N = 400$ and does not depend on how often the controller samples. The absolute figures behind it are $720 \times 20.0 = 14\,400$ ms $= 14.4$ s per day for the interpreted route against $720 \times 10.0 = 7.2$ s for the compiled route, so the time the controller spends on this script halves. Whether that reduction matters in practice depends on what else the controller has to do inside its two-minute window, which is exactly why the percentage, rather than the absolute saving, is the figure worth quoting.

(d) The developer's argument compares only the per-execution figures, $0.010$ ms against $0.050$ ms, and ignores the one-off translation cost, which is incurred in full however few times the script runs. At $N = 1$ the interpreted route takes $0.050$ ms while the compiled route takes $6.0 + 0.010 = 6.01$ ms — about $120$ times longer. For a script executed once, compiling is therefore plainly wrong; it would also be wrong for any script whose total number of executions is below the break-even. The saving per execution is not $0.010$ ms but the difference, $0.050 - 0.010 = 0.040$ ms, and that is the figure which has to repay the translation. With a one-off cost of $12.0$ ms the condition becomes $0.040N \ge 12.0$, so $N \ge 300$: the least value is $N = 300$. This is exactly double the original break-even, as expected, because the break-even is proportional to the one-off cost. Writing the condition generally, with one-off cost $C$ and per-execution saving $s$, the requirement is $sN \ge C$, that is $N \ge C/s$; the given figures are $C = 6.0$ ms and $s = 0.040$ ms, giving $N \ge 150$. Only the ratio matters, so a change in $C$ rescales the answer directly while a change in $s$ rescales it inversely.

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept 'at run time / each time' and 'before execution / once' as the contrast. Candidates who say only that an interpreter is 'slower' without saying when translation happens earn no marks: the question asks when, not how fast. Do not require the word bytecode — 'object code', 'machine code' or 'a translated version' is acceptable, since the question stem itself names bytecode.

(b) Award one mark for each correct expression, one for solving the equality to $N = 150$ and one for the $10.0$ ms difference. A candidate who reads $N = 150$ off the figure without the algebra earns the first two only. Follow-through applies to a candidate whose arithmetic slips provided the method of equating the two totals is shown.

(c) One mark for $720$ cycles, one for $7200$ ms, one for $7.2$ s and one for $50\%$. Condone a candidate who works in seconds throughout. Do not penalise the omission of the observation that the percentage is independent of the sampling interval.

(d) Award up to two marks for the explanation, but only if the candidate identifies that the one-off cost is incurred regardless of $N$; a bare 'it is slower for one run' earns one. One mark for the $N = 1$ comparison, one for noting that the relevant saving is $0.040$ ms per execution rather than $0.010$ ms, and one for $N = 300$. The final observation — that doubling the translation cost doubles the break-even — is creditworthy as an alternative route to the same answer.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.4 An algorithm that is correct except for one class of input: the final run is never recorded
syllabus_ref: B2.4 Programming algorithms and B2.3 Programming constructs
title: B2.4 An algorithm that is correct except for one class of input: the final run is never recorded
q_html:
A programmer writes the following method to find the length of the longest run of identical adjacent values in a one-dimensional array $A$ of $N$ integers, where $N \geq 1$. The array is indexed from $0$ to $N - 1$.

LONGEST = 0
CURRENT = 1
loop I from 1 to N - 1
    if A[I] = A[I - 1] then
        CURRENT = CURRENT + 1
    else
        if CURRENT > LONGEST then
            LONGEST = CURRENT
        end if
        CURRENT = 1
    end if
end loop
return LONGEST

The programmer tests the method on the array $[3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2]$ and obtains $3$, which is correct.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Determine the value returned by the method for each of the following arrays.

    (i) $[4, 4, 4]$

    (ii) $[5]$

    (iii) $[2, 7, 7]$

    (iv) $[9, 9, 6, 6, 6]$.

    For each array, state also the value the method should return.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Identify the two classes of input for which the method returns a value that is too small, and explain, by reference to the pseudocode, why each occurs.

    (Explain)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Rewrite the method so that it returns the correct value for every array of length $N \geq 1$. Your answer must be given in the same pseudocode style, and you must state what you changed.

    (Construct)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    A second programmer suggests correcting the method by changing the first line to LONGEST = 1 and making no other change.

    Evaluate this suggestion: state whether it produces the correct answer for every array, and support your answer either by explaining why it works or by giving a specific counter-example and tracing it.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a)(i) The loop runs for $I = 1$ and $I = 2$. At $I = 1$, $A[1] = A[0]$ so $CURRENT = 2$; at $I = 2$, $A[2] = A[1]$ so $CURRENT = 3$. The loop ends with $LONGEST = 0$, so the method returns 0; the correct value is 3 (A1).

(a)(ii) The loop runs from $1$ to $0$, which is empty, so it never executes and the method returns 0; the correct value is 1, since a single element is a run of length one (A1).

(a)(iii) At $I = 1$, $A[1] = 7 \neq A[0] = 2$, so $CURRENT = 1 > LONGEST = 0$ gives $LONGEST = 1$ and $CURRENT$ resets to $1$; at $I = 2$, $A[2] = A[1]$ so $CURRENT = 2$. The loop ends and the method returns 1; the correct value is 2 (A1).

(a)(iv) At $I = 1$, $A[1] = A[0]$ so $CURRENT = 2$; at $I = 2$, $A[2] \neq A[1]$, so $LONGEST = 2$ and $CURRENT = 1$; at $I = 3$ and $I = 4$, $CURRENT$ becomes $2$ then $3$. The loop ends and the method returns 2; the correct value is 3 (A1).

(b) The two classes are:

Arrays of length 1. With $N = 1$ the loop from 1 to N - 1 runs from $1$ to $0$, which is empty, so $LONGEST$ keeps its initial value of $0$ and the method returns $0$ instead of $1$ (A1).

Arrays whose longest run ends at the final element. The variable $CURRENT$ is only ever compared with $LONGEST$ inside the else branch, that is, at the moment a run is discovered to have ended (A1). The run that is still in progress when the loop finishes is never compared with anything (A1). So whenever the longest run is the last one -- as in (i), (iii) and (iv) -- the method reports the longest run it happened to close off, or $0$ if it closed off none (A1).

The programmer's test array $[3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2]$ is misleading: its longest run of three $1$s ends at index $4$ and is closed off by the $2$ at index $5$, so the defect is invisible.

(c) One correct version compares $CURRENT$ with $LONGEST$ once more after the loop has finished:

if N = 0 then
    return 0
end if
LONGEST = 1
CURRENT = 1
loop I from 1 to N - 1
    if A[I] = A[I - 1] then
        CURRENT = CURRENT + 1
    else
        CURRENT = 1
    end if
    if CURRENT > LONGEST then
        LONGEST = CURRENT
    end if
end loop
return LONGEST

The essential change is that the comparison with $LONGEST$ is moved outside the else branch so that it happens on every iteration, including the last (A1). With that change $CURRENT$ is compared after every element is processed, so the run in progress at the end of the loop is included (A1). Initialising $LONGEST = 1$ rather than $0$ handles $N = 1$ (A1), and the guard for $N = 0$ keeps the method defined if the problem statement is ever relaxed (A1).

Alternative correct answers are acceptable, for example initialising $LONGEST = 1$ and appending a single if CURRENT > LONGEST then LONGEST = CURRENT after end loop. Credit the version a candidate gives if it is correct for $N = 1$ and for a final-run array.

(d) The suggestion does not work in general (A1). It does fix the $N = 1$ case: the loop is empty and the method returns $1$, which is correct (A1). It does nothing for the final-run case. Take $A = [4, 4, 4]$ (A1). With $LONGEST = 1$: at $I = 1$, $A[1] = A[0]$ so $CURRENT = 2$ and the else branch is not taken; at $I = 2$, $A[2] = A[1]$ so $CURRENT = 3$, again without the else branch. The loop ends and the method returns $LONGEST = 1$, but the longest run is $3$ (A1).

The lesson is that the two defects have different causes and need different fixes. The $N = 1$ case is an initialisation defect; the final-run case is a structural one, and no choice of initial value can repair an algorithm that never performs the comparison it needs.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (A1) for each row, both the returned value and the correct value. Accept a brief trace in place of an explanation. No penalty for using 1-based indexing consistently, provided the trace matches the candidate's stated convention.
(b) Award (A1) for the length-1 case with a reason that refers to the loop bounds; (A1) for noticing that the comparison is inside the else branch; (A1) for stating that the in-progress run at the end of the loop is never compared; (A1) for characterising the failing inputs as those whose longest run ends at the final element. A candidate who identifies only 'arrays ending in a run' without the length-1 case earns at most three of the four marks.
(c) Award (A1) for moving the comparison so it executes on every iteration or appending it after the loop, (A1) for handling N = 1 correctly, (A1) for a correct initialisation, (A1) for stating clearly what was changed or for presenting valid pseudocode. Do not penalise the absence of an N = 0 guard, since the question specifies N >= 1; credit it if present.
(d) Award (A1) for stating that it does not work in general, (A1) for acknowledging that it does fix N = 1, (A1) for a specific counter-example, (A1) for a correct trace of that counter-example. A candidate who says only 'it does not work' without a counter-example earns at most two marks. Accept any counter-example whose longest run is its last.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.2 Overflow in a two's-complement subtraction used as a comparison
syllabus_ref: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (binary representation of integers; two's complement; overflow)
title: A1.2 Overflow in a two's-complement subtraction used as a comparison
q_html:
An environmental control system stores each temperature reading as an eight-bit signed
integer in two's complement form, so the representable range is $-128$ to $127$. The system
compares two readings, $a$ and $b$, using the single line

if a - b < 0 then output "a is the lower reading"

and the subtraction is performed in eight bits, with no overflow detection.

(a) Explain what happens when the line is executed with $a = 100$ and $b = -50$, and state the
value the system compares with zero. \tag{3}

(b) Determine the range of values of the true difference $d = a - b$ for which the comparison
gives the correct result. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the number of ordered pairs $(a, b)$, with $a$ and $b$ each in the range
$-128$ to $127$, for which the comparison gives the wrong result, and hence the proportion of
all pairs that fail. \tag{5}

(d) State a comparison that is correct for every pair in the range, and justify it. \tag{4}

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain what happens when the line is executed with $a = 100$ and $b = -50$, and state the value compared with zero.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the range of values of the true difference $d = a - b$ for which the comparison gives the correct result.

    (Determine)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine the number of ordered pairs $(a, b)$ in the range $-128$ to $127$ for which the comparison gives the wrong result, and hence the proportion that fail.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    State a comparison that is correct for every pair in the range, and justify it.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) The true difference is $100 - (-50) = 150$ (A1). Eight-bit two's complement can only
represent $-128$ to $127$, so $150$ cannot be stored; the value wraps by subtracting $256$ and
the system obtains $150 - 256 = -106$ (M1). Since $-106 < 0$ the system reports that
$a$ is the lower reading, which is wrong: $100 > -50$ (A1).

The general rule is that a result outside the representable range has $256$ added to or
subtracted from it until it falls inside, which is exactly what modular arithmetic does. No
flag is raised and no exception is thrown, so the error is invisible at run time.

(b) The comparison is correct exactly when the subtraction does not overflow, that is when the
true difference is itself representable (M1):

$$-128 \le a - b \le 127 \tag{A1}$$

Equivalently $-128 \le d \le 127$ (A1). Outside that interval the stored value differs from the
true difference by a multiple of $256$ and, because the magnitude of the correction is larger
than the magnitude of the value being represented, the sign is reversed (A1). For example
$d = 150$ is stored as $-106$, and $d = -150$ is stored as $+106$; in both cases the sign is
wrong and so is the comparison.

(c) For a given difference $d$, the number of ordered pairs with $a - b = d$ and both values
in $[-128, 127]$ is $256 - |d|$, valid for $-255 \le d \le 255$ (M1). Summing over the correct
range from part (b),

$$N_{\text{correct}} = \sum_{d=-128}^{127} (256 - |d|) = 24512 + 256 + 24384 = 49152 \tag{A1}$$

The total number of ordered pairs is (A1)

$$N_{\text{total}} = 256 + \sum_{d=-255}^{255} (256 - |d|) - 256 = \sum_{d=-255}^{255}(256-|d|) = 65536$$

so the number that fail is (A1)

$$N_{\text{wrong}} = 65536 - 49152 = 16384 \tag{A1}$$

and the proportion is $\dfrac{16384}{65536} = 0.25$: exactly one quarter of all comparisons
give the wrong answer.

(d) Compare the signs first, and subtract only when the signs match (M1):

if (a < 0) and (b >= 0) then output "a is the lower reading"
else if (a >= 0) and (b < 0) then output "a is the higher reading"
else if a - b < 0 then output "a is the lower reading"
else output "a is the higher reading"

Justification (A1): if the signs differ, the comparison is settled by the signs alone and no
subtraction is needed, which is precisely the case in which the true difference is largest and
the subtraction most likely to overflow. If both values are non-negative then
$a - b$ lies between $-127$ and $127$; if both are negative then $a - b$ also lies between
$-127$ and $127$ (A1). In either case the result is representable, so the subtraction cannot
overflow and the test is safe (A1).

An alternative correct answer is to widen the stored type before subtracting — for example by
promoting both operands to sixteen bits — since the difference of two eight-bit values always
fits in nine bits. This is simpler but costs memory in a system that stores thousands of
readings, which is why the sign test is preferred here.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for the true difference $150$. (M1) for the wrap-around, which must be explained
as a modular reduction rather than merely asserted. (A1) for $-106$ and the conclusion that the
output is wrong.

(b) (M1) for linking correctness to the absence of overflow. (A1) for the interval
$-128 \le d \le 127$. (A1) for restating it in terms of $d$. (A1) for noting that the sign is
reversed outside the interval — a candidate who gives the interval alone has not explained why
the comparison then fails.

(c) (M1) for $256 - |d|$ as the count for a given difference. (A1) for $49152$ correct pairs.
(A1) for $65536$ total pairs. (A1) for $16384$ failing pairs. (A1) for the proportion $0.25$.
Credit any correct route to the count, including a direct enumeration argument, but the
summation must be shown rather than asserted. Condone small arithmetic slips in the partial
sums if the method is sound and the final proportion is consistent with them.

(d) (M1) for a comparison that avoids the subtraction when the signs differ. (A1) for the
justification in terms of the signs. (A1) for the bound $|a - b| \le 127$ when the signs match.
(A1) for concluding that no overflow is then possible.

Accept the alternative of promoting to a wider type, with full marks, provided the candidate
states that nine bits suffice. Do not accept "check the sign of the result", which does not
work: after the wrap the sign of the stored value is a valid sign, just the wrong one.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.4 A nested loop whose inner trip count depends on the outer index
syllabus_ref: B2.4 Programming algorithms (analysis of algorithms; efficiency of an algorithm)
title: B2.4 A nested loop whose inner trip count depends on the outer index
q_html:
A programmer writes the following routine to count the divisors of every integer up to
$N$.

COUNT = 0
for I = 1 to N
    for J = I to N step I
        COUNT = COUNT + 1
    next J
next I
output COUNT

(a) Trace the routine for $N = 6$ and state the value output. \tag{4}

(b) Show that the number of times the inner loop body executes is

$$\sum_{I=1}^{N} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor . \tag{4}$$

(c) Determine the value output when $N = 1000$, and hence determine the ratio of the number of
iterations to $N^{2}$. \tag{5}

(d) Explain why the time complexity of the routine is $\mathrm{O}(N \log N)$ rather than
$\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$. \tag{3}

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Trace the routine for $N = 6$ and state the value output.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the number of inner-loop executions is the sum from I = 1 to N of the floor of N divided by I.

    (Show that)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine the value output when $N = 1000$, and hence determine the ratio of the number of iterations to $N$ squared.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain why the time complexity is O(N log N) rather than O(N squared).

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) Tracing the outer loop (M1):

| $I$ | values taken by $J$ | inner iterations |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 | 6 |
| 2 | 2, 4, 6 | 3 |
| 3 | 3, 6 | 2 |
| 4 | 4 | 1 |
| 5 | 5 | 1 |
| 6 | 6 | 1 |

The inner counts are $6, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1$ (A1) and the total is $6 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 14$
(A1). So the routine outputs $14$ (A1). Note that only the first of the six passes runs the
full $N$ times; by the fourth pass the inner loop executes once.

(b) On the pass with outer index $I$, the inner variable $J$ takes the values
$I, 2I, 3I, \ldots$ up to $N$ (M1). The largest multiple of $I$ not exceeding $N$ is
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor \cdot I$ (A1), so the number of values taken is exactly
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor$ (A1). Summing over the $N$ passes of the outer loop
gives the stated expression (AG).

(c) Evaluating the sum for $N = 1000$ (M1):

$$\sum_{I=1}^{1000} \left\lfloor \frac{1000}{I} \right\rfloor = 7069 \tag{A1}$$

The ratio to $N^{2}$ is (M1)

$$\frac{7069}{1000^{2}} = \frac{7069}{1000000} = 0.00707 \tag{A1}$$

so the routine performs about $0.7\%$ of the iterations a quadratic algorithm would. Equally
tellings is the comparison with $N\ln N$:

$$N\ln N = 1000 \times 6.908 = 6908 \qquad \frac{7069}{6908} = 1.02 \tag{A1}$$

so the actual count is within about $2\%$ of $N\ln N$. A candidate who assumed $\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$
would predict roughly half a million iterations and would be wrong by a factor of about
seventy.

(d) From (b), the iteration count is $\sum_{I=1}^{N} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor
\le \sum_{I=1}^{N} \frac{N}{I} = N \sum_{I=1}^{N} \frac{1}{I}$ (M1). The sum on the right is
the $N$th harmonic number, $H_{N}$, which satisfies $\ln(N+1) \le H_{N} \le 1 + \ln N$ and is
therefore $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ (A1). It follows that the whole expression is
$\mathrm{O}(N\log N)$ (AG). The bound is tight rather than merely an upper limit, as the
numerical comparison in (c) shows: at $N = 1000$ the actual count of $7069$ sits about $2\%$
above $N\ln N = 6908$, and the gap between the two is the linear term that the floors and the
Euler–Mascheroni constant contribute.

It is worth being explicit about what the bound does and does not say. Replacing the floor by
$\frac{N}{I}$ can only increase the total, so the argument gives a genuine upper bound on the
running time and never an underestimate; and since the harmonic sum is also $\Omega(\log N)$,
the estimate is of the right order and not merely safe. What the argument does not do is give
a constant: $\mathrm{O}(N\log N)$ says nothing about whether the constant is $1$ or $100$, and
for small $N$ the constant can matter more than the growth rate. The numerical work in (c) is
what supplies the constant, which is why both parts are needed.

One further observation, for a candidate who wants to check the result independently: the sum
$\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$ counts the pairs $(I, J)$ with $I \mid J$ and $J \le N$, so it is
the total number of divisors possessed by all the integers from $1$ to $N$. It is therefore
also the number of times a naive divisor-counting routine would increment its counter, which
is exactly what the code in the stem is doing. Recognising that gives the answer a second
meaning and a second way to verify it.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for a systematic trace — a table, or an equivalent listing of the values taken by
$J$ for each $I$. (A1) for the inner counts $6, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1$. (A1) for the total $14$.
(A1) for the observation that only the first pass runs the full $N$ times; this is the
observation that drives the rest of the item and a bare answer of $14$ with no trace earns only
the first (A1).

(b) (M1) for identifying the values taken by $J$ as the multiples of $I$. (A1) for
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor \cdot I$ as the largest multiple. (A1) for the count.
(AG) for the summation. Allow a candidate who argues via $\lfloor (N-I)/I \rfloor + 1$ and
simplifies, but the simplification must be shown.

(c) (M1) for attempting the sum; accept a stated value obtained by computation, since summing
a thousand terms by hand is not the point. (A1) for $7069$. (M1) for dividing by $N^{2}$.
(A1) for $0.00707$. (A1) for the comparison with $N \ln N$ or with the quadratic estimate.
Accept the ratio as $0.0071$.

(d) (M1) for bounding the floor by $\frac{N}{I}$. (A1) for identifying the harmonic sum as
$\mathrm{O}(\log N)$. (AG) for the conclusion. A candidate who merely says "the inner loop does
not run $N$ times" earns the first (M1) only.

Note: do not accept an argument that the answer is $\mathrm{O}(N)$ — the harmonic sum is not
constant.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2.3 Bandwidth-delay product: when increasing the link rate changes nothing
syllabus_ref: A2.3 Data transmissions (transmission rate, bandwidth and latency; the effect of protocol overhead)
title: A2.3 Bandwidth-delay product: when increasing the link rate changes nothing
q_html:
A remote backup service transfers files between two sites. The connection has a round-trip
time of $40\ \mathrm{ms}$. The sending software uses a sliding window of $64\ \mathrm{kB}$
($65536$ bytes): it may send that much data before it must stop and wait for an
acknowledgement. The situation is shown in the diagram.

(a) Calculate the time taken to transmit one window at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$, and hence the
maximum throughput achievable with this window. \tag{3}

(b) The link is upgraded to $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$. Calculate the new transmission time for one
window and the new maximum throughput. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the window size, in bytes, that would be needed to make full use of the
$1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link. \tag{5}

(d) Explain why the upgrade produced no improvement, and state what should be changed. \tag{4}

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the time to transmit one window at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and hence the maximum throughput achievable with this window.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Calculate the new transmission time for one window at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ and the new maximum throughput.

    (Calculate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine the window size, in bytes, needed to make full use of the $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Explain why the upgrade produced no improvement, and state what should be changed.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) One window is $65536 \times 8 = 524288$ bits (A1). At $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ the
transmission time is

$$t = \frac{524288}{1.00 \times 10^{8}} = 5.24\ \mathrm{ms} \tag{A1}$$

The sender must then wait for the acknowledgement, so one window is delivered per round-trip
time and the maximum throughput is

$$\frac{524288\ \mathrm{bits}}{0.040\ \mathrm{s}} = 1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bps}
= 13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps} \tag{A1}$$

Note that this is $13.1\%$ of the link rate, even though the sender is idle for
$40 - 5.24 = 34.8\ \mathrm{ms}$ of every $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ cycle.

(b) At $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ the transmission time falls by a factor of ten (A1):

$$t = \frac{524288}{1.00 \times 10^{9}} = 0.524\ \mathrm{ms} \tag{A1}$$

The throughput is unchanged, because the amount sent per round trip has not changed (A1):

$$\frac{524288}{0.040} = 13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps} \tag{A1}$$

The sender is now idle for $39.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ of every $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ — it finishes sooner
and then waits longer, and the two effects cancel exactly.

(c) To keep the link busy the window must be at least the bandwidth-delay product (M1):

$$W = B \times \mathrm{RTT} = 1.00 \times 10^{9} \times 0.040 = 4.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bits}
\tag{A1}$$

$$W = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{7}}{8} = 5.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{bytes} = 5.0\ \mathrm{MB}
\tag{A1}$$

Compared with the existing window this is (A1)

$$\frac{5.0 \times 10^{6}}{65536} = 76.3$$

times larger (A1). Equivalently, the existing window keeps the link busy for
$\frac{5.24}{40} = 13.1\%$ of the cycle at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and for
$\frac{0.524}{40} = 1.31\%$ at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$, so the utilisation falls by a factor of ten
exactly as the rate rises by a factor of ten, and the two effects cancel precisely.

Two checks are worth applying to the answer. First, the required window scales with the
round-trip time as well as with the rate, so halving the latency would halve the window
needed — a reminder that latency and bandwidth are separate constraints and can be traded
against each other. Second, $5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$ of unacknowledged data is a large amount to have
in flight, and in practice the window would be limited by the receiving system's buffer and by
congestion control rather than by the arithmetic here; the bandwidth-delay product gives the
minimum window that makes the link usable, not a window that any real system would necessarily
grant.

(d) The upgrade improved the rate at which data is placed on the link but not the amount that
may be in flight (A1). With a windowed protocol the throughput is
$\frac{\text{window}}{\mathrm{RTT}}$ whenever the window is smaller than the bandwidth-delay
product, and the link rate does not appear in that expression at all (R1). The window here,
$64\ \mathrm{kB}$, is well below the $5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$ bandwidth-delay product of the upgraded
link, so the link is idle for $98.7\%$ of each cycle and the tenfold increase in rate is
invisible (A1).

What should be changed is the window, not the link (A1): the sending software needs a window of
about $5\ \mathrm{MB}$ to use the $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link, and with the existing $64\ \mathrm{kB}$
window there was no point buying the upgrade at all. The general diagnostic is to compute the
bandwidth-delay product before paying for bandwidth; if the window is smaller, the money is
being spent on the wrong thing.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for converting the window to $524288$ bits. (A1) for $5.24\ \mathrm{ms}$.
(A1) for $13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps}$; accept $1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bps}$. A candidate who
divides the link rate by ten or otherwise tries to include the link rate in the throughput
earns at most the first (A1).

(b) (A1) for $0.524\ \mathrm{ms}$. (A1) for the observation that the window has not changed.
(A1) for $13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps}$. (A1) for the cancellation — the sender finishes sooner and waits
longer. A candidate who reports a higher throughput here has not understood windowing and loses
the last three marks.

(c) (M1) for the bandwidth-delay product. (A1) for $4.0 \times 10^{7}$ bits. (A1) for
$5.0 \times 10^{6}$ bytes. (A1) for the ratio $76.3$. (A1) for the utilisation argument.
Accept $5\ \mathrm{MB}$ or $4.77\ \mathrm{MiB}$ provided the unit is stated.

(d) (A1) for the distinction between the rate and the amount in flight. (R1) for the
throughput expression, which must be stated as window over round-trip time. (A1) for the
quantitative comparison with the bandwidth-delay product. (A1) for identifying the window as
what should change.

Condonation: allow a candidate who says "increase the window" without the figure, provided the
reasoning about the amount in flight is present.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A3.3 One row that changes every aggregate: COUNT(*), COUNT(column), AVG, and NULL propagating through a computed column
syllabus_ref: A3.3 Database programming (SQL queries, aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING, NULL handling)
title: A3.3 One row that changes every aggregate: COUNT(*), COUNT(column), AVG, and NULL propagating through a computed column
q_html:
The orders table in a sales database

The table orders holds one row per order. customer_id identifies the customer who placed it, quantity is the number of units and unit_price is the price per unit at the time the order was taken.

The unit_price column is nullable by design: an order can be taken before the price list entry for that product exists, and the row is then stored with unit_price set to NULL while the price is confirmed later. Order 7 is the only row currently in that state.

The database engine follows the SQL standard in three respects that matter here. An aggregate function ignores NULL inputs. A NULL is not equal to anything, not even to another NULL, so it cannot be selected by an equality test. Any arithmetic expression that contains NULL evaluates to NULL, because the result of an operation on an unknown value is itself unknown.

A manager is asked three things about this table: what the average unit price is, which customers have placed more than one order, and how much each of those customers has spent. The manager writes a set of queries without reading the note on how the engine treats NULL.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(unit_price) in a query over this table, and state the value that each of the two returns.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    The manager writes SELECT SUM(unit_price) / COUNT(*) AS average_price FROM orders; and reports the result as 18.00. Determine the value that the engine's own AVG(unit_price) returns, and explain why the two expressions give different answers.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine which customers the query
    ``
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_id > 2
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
    ``
    returns, and the value it reports for each. State the result the manager intended, and identify the single clause responsible for the difference.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain why SUM(quantity * unit_price) for customer 104 returns NULL rather than 0, and state one change to the query that would make the reported total well defined for every customer.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) COUNT(*) counts rows and COUNT(unit_price) counts values, so the first returns 7 and the second returns 6. The difference is exactly one row -- order 7 -- and the gap between the two numbers is the number of NULLs in the column being counted (A1)(A1).

The two functions are not two spellings of the same count. COUNT(*) answers "how many orders are there", which is a property of the table; COUNT(unit_price) answers "for how many orders do we know the unit price", which is a property of one column. On a table with no missing prices the two agree, which is why the distinction is invisible until the first NULL arrives (M1)(A1).

(b) AVG(unit_price) returns 21.00. The engine sums the six non-NULL prices (M1):

$$10.00 + 4.00 + 99.00 + 7.50 + 2.50 + 3.00 = 126.00 \tag{M1}$$

and divides by the number of values it actually summed, which is six (A1):

$$\frac{126.00}{6} = 21.00 \tag{A1}$$

The manager's expression uses the same numerator, because SUM also ignores NULL, but divides by COUNT(*) instead (M1):

$$\frac{126.00}{7} = 18.00 \tag{A1}$$

So SUM(x) / COUNT(*) is not a way of computing the average of $x$. It is the average of $x$ diluted by every row in which $x$ is unknown. The error is systematic rather than random: whenever some values are missing and the remaining values are positive, the reported figure is too low, and the size of the error grows with the *proportion* of missing values rather than with the size of the table. The gap here is $126.00/6 - 126.00/7 = 3.00$, which is the price of one row spread across the whole report.

(c) WHERE is evaluated before grouping, so the rows it removes are gone by the time HAVING counts anything (M1). WHERE order_id > 2 keeps orders 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, which is one row for customer 101, two rows for customer 102, one row for customer 103 and one for customer 104 (M1). HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 then keeps only customer 102, whose two surviving rows contribute (A1)

$$1 \times 99.00 + 6 \times 3.00 = 117.00$$

The query therefore returns a single row, $(102,\ 117.00)$ (A1).

The manager intended the two customers who have placed more than one order, which are 101 and 102. Customer 101 has orders 1, 2 and 5, worth

$$3 \times 10.00 + 5 \times 4.00 + 4 \times 2.50 = 60.00$$

and customer 102 is worth 117.00, so the intended answer is a total of 177.00 across the two customers (M1). The clause responsible is the WHERE: a row filter and a group filter are not interchangeable when the group filter is a count, because the count is taken over whatever the row filter happened to leave behind. Deleting the WHERE clause and keeping the HAVING clause gives the intended result.

(d) For order 7 the expression quantity * unit_price is 10 * NULL, and any arithmetic expression containing NULL evaluates to NULL, so that row yields no value at all rather than the value $10 \times 0 = 0$ (M1). SUM ignores NULLs, but customer 104 has only one row, and ignoring the only value in a group leaves nothing to sum, so the aggregate over that group returns NULL rather than 0 (A1).

A change that makes the total well defined is to wrap the aggregate: COALESCE(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 0). Wrapping the product instead, SUM(COALESCE(quantity * unit_price, 0)), also returns 0 here (A1).

The two placements are not equivalent and neither is a correction. The outer form reports 0 only for a group in which *no* line has a price, and it leaves every other group untouched; the inner form treats each unpriced line as zero revenue, which quietly understates any customer who has a mix of priced and unpriced orders. Neither recovers the missing price, so the choice is a decision about what an unknown is worth in the report, and a business that needs the real figure has to obtain the price rather than choose a default for it.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for 7, (A1) for 6, (M1) for the statement that COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values, (A1) for locating the difference in the single NULL row. A candidate who says only "one ignores NULL and one does not", without saying *what* each one counts, earns the first A1 only.

(b) (M1) for the sum 126.00, (M1) for dividing by 6, (A1) for 21.00, (M1) for identifying COUNT(*) as the wrong denominator, (A1) for 18.00 and the direction of the error. A candidate who reports 21.00 with no comparison to 18.00 cannot score the last two marks, because the part asks for the reason the two differ. Follow-through: a candidate whose sum is wrong but who divides by the correct count keeps the last two marks.

(c) (M1) for WHERE running before GROUP BY, (M1) for the surviving rows per customer, (A1) for 117.00, (A1) for the single returned row. The intended result -- 101 at 60.00 and 102 at 117.00 -- is worth the final (M1) and must be distinguished from the returned result, not merely restated.

(d) (M1) for NULL propagating through quantity * unit_price, (A1) for the group having no non-NULL value left to sum, (A1) for a well-formed COALESCE change. A candidate who writes WHERE unit_price IS NOT NULL earns the third mark only if they state that this discards the row rather than repairing it.

Forfeits: treating NULL as 0 throughout, which gives 18.00 for the average and 0.00 for customer 104 and makes every part of the item consistent but wrong; claiming that AVG counts rows and SUM counts values, which inverts the rule. Condonation: a candidate who writes the average as $21.00$ or as $21$ should be given full credit, and a candidate who quotes 0.8125-type intermediate values to more figures than the data supports should not be penalised.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B4.1 Choosing an implementation for a priority queue when the number of extractions, not the complexity class, decides the winner
syllabus_ref: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs (HL only): the priority queue and the cost of different implementations
title: B4.1 Choosing an implementation for a priority queue when the number of extractions, not the complexity class, decides the winner
q_html:
A counting model for three priority-queue implementations

A priority queue stores items and always returns the one with the highest priority. Three implementations are being compared: an unsorted array, an array kept in sorted order, and a binary heap.

To make the comparison concrete, charge each operation as follows.

* An operation that only touches one end of the structure costs 1 step.
* An operation that has to work through the stored items costs $m/2$ steps on average, where $m$ is the number of items in the structure. This is the average over the position of the item being sought, and it is the convention used here so that the two array implementations are charged on the same footing.
* A binary heap costs $\log_2 m$ steps for every operation, whether it is an insertion or an extraction.

The workload holds $n = 1024$ items throughout, so $\log_2 n = 10$. The items are all inserted first, and the extractions then take place one at a time.

A student claims that the binary heap is the right implementation because its operations are $O(\log n)$ while the unsorted array's are $O(n)$, and that this settles the choice. The claim is to be tested against the counting model above, first with the full workload and then with the number of extractions reduced.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Determine the total number of steps taken by the unsorted array and by the binary heap when 1024 items are inserted and then all 1024 are extracted, and hence show that the heap performs about 25.6 times fewer steps.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the sorted array performs exactly the same total number of steps as the unsorted array on this workload, and explain why two structures with opposite cost profiles can produce the same total.

    (Show that)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    The number of extractions is now reduced from 1024 to $k$, with the 1024 insertions unchanged. Determine the largest value of $k$ for which the unsorted array is still the cheaper choice, and state the smallest value of $k$ at which the heap is cheaper.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain why the student's complexity-class argument is not by itself a sufficient reason to choose the heap for this workload.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) For the unsorted array, an insertion appends to the end and costs 1 step, and an extraction scans the array and costs $n/2 = 512$ steps (M1):

$$1024 \times 1 + 1024 \times 512 = 1024 + 524\,288 = 525\,312 \tag{M1}$$

For the heap, every operation costs $\log_2 1024 = 10$ steps, so the insertions and the extractions are charged alike (M1):

$$1024 \times 10 + 1024 \times 10 = 10\,240 + 10\,240 = 20\,480 \tag{A1}$$

The ratio is (A1)

$$\frac{525\,312}{20\,480} = 25.65$$

so the heap performs about 25.6 times fewer steps on this workload.

(b) For the sorted array, an insertion has to find the insertion point and shift the items above it, which costs $m/2 = 512$ steps, while an extraction takes the item at the front and costs 1 step (M1):

$$1024 \times 512 + 1024 \times 1 = 524\,288 + 1024 = 525\,312 \tag{M1}$$

which is the same total as the unsorted array (A1).

The two totals agree because the two structures pay the same linear cost the same number of times, in opposite phases (A1). The unsorted array does nothing to maintain order on insertion and pays for the disorder on every extraction; the sorted array pays for the order on every insertion and collects it back for free on every extraction. With $n$ insertions and $n$ extractions the two phases have equal length, so the cost simply changes place. The equality is a property of this workload and not of the structures: if the workload were 1024 insertions and 10 extractions, the sorted array would be far more expensive, and if it were 1024 insertions and 1024 extractions of a *known* minimum the unsorted array's scan could be avoided altogether.

(c) With $k$ extractions the unsorted array costs (M1)

$$1024 + 512k$$

and the heap costs (M1)

$$10\,240 + 10k$$

Setting them equal (M1):

$$1024 + 512k = 10\,240 + 10k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 502k = 9216 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k = \frac{9216}{502} = 18.36 \text{ (to 2 d.p.)}$$

Since $k$ counts extractions it must be a whole number, so the crossover lies between 18 and 19 (A1). Substituting both:

| $k$ | unsorted array | binary heap | cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | $1024 + 9216 = 10\,240$ | $10\,240 + 180 = 10\,420$ | unsorted array |
| 19 | $1024 + 9728 = 10\,752$ | $10\,240 + 190 = 10\,430$ | binary heap |

So the largest $k$ for which the unsorted array is still cheaper is 18, and the smallest $k$ at which the heap is cheaper is 19 (A1). The threshold is about 1.8% of $n$: unless the structure is drained of more than roughly one item in fifty, the array wins.

(d) The statement "$O(\log n)$ beats $O(n)$" compares how the cost of each structure *grows* as $n$ increases without bound, and it is true. It says nothing about which is cheaper at a particular $n$, and it says nothing at all when the mixture of operations is allowed to vary (M1). Here $n$ is fixed at 1024 and the number of extractions is the free variable, so the comparison has to be made at a point rather than in the limit (M1).

The reason the limit is misleading in this case is that the heap's advantage is paid for in advance. It commits 10 steps to each of the 1024 insertions, which is 10 240 steps before a single extraction has happened, whereas the unsorted array has spent only 1024. The array's expensive operation is the one that may never occur in large numbers, and the heap's expensive operation is the one that always occurs (A1). An argument from complexity classes cannot see either of those facts, because both of them are about the workload rather than about the growth rate.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for the two cost expressions, (M1) for the unsorted total, (M1) for the heap total, (A1) for the ratio 25.6. Accept 25.65 or 25.7; do not accept a bare "about 25 times" without the two totals shown, because the part asks for them.

(b) (M1) for charging the sorted array's insertion at 512 and its extraction at 1, (M1) for the total, (A1) for the equality with (a), (A1) for the explanation that the linear cost is paid the same number of times in the opposite phase. The explanation mark requires the observation that the two phases are of equal length here; a candidate who says only "the costs cancel" has not said why they cancel.

(c) (M1) for the unsorted cost expression in $k$, (M1) for the heap expression, (M1) for equating them and solving, (A1) for the non-integer value 18.36 and the observation that $k$ must be an integer, (A1) for 18 and 19 with the substitution shown. A candidate who answers "18.36 extractions" without rounding down has not answered a question about a count and loses the final mark. Follow-through applies from an incorrect (a).

(d) (M1) for the observation that the complexity class describes growth rather than a point, (M1) for identifying the number of extractions as the variable that governs, (A1) for the point that the heap pays its logarithmic cost on the insertions that may be the whole workload. A candidate who merely repeats the crossover value from (c) without saying why the asymptotic argument cannot find it earns no marks here.

Forfeits: comparing $O(\log n)$ with $O(n)$ at $n = 1024$ and concluding that the heap is 102 times faster, which is a category error rather than a rounding error; treating the heap's cost as $\log_2 n$ for the whole workload rather than per operation, which gives 10 steps in total. Condonation: a candidate who writes the heap cost as $2n\log_2 n$ but uses it consistently should be given full follow-through credit, since the model's convention is stated rather than derived.

subtopic: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic
syllabus_ref: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (A1.2.1 representation of integers in binary and hexadecimal, A1.2.2 binary encoding and its impact on storage, A1.2.3 logic gates, A1.2.4 truth tables)
title: A 12-bit temperature log and the arithmetic that breaks it
q_html:
A field temperature logger

A logger records temperature once per minute for a week. The sensing element produces a signed integer that is stored in a 12-bit two's complement register, in units of 0.0625 degrees Celsius per least significant bit. A separate summation register accumulates consecutive readings so that a rolling average can be reported, using the same 12-bit width as the readings themselves.

The logger also drives an alarm output from three inputs: P (pressure above the safe limit), T (temperature above the safe limit) and O (operator override enabled). The designer's first attempt at the alarm logic is

F = P.T + P.T' + P'.T.O

where the prime denotes NOT, the dot denotes AND and + denotes OR. The alarm output is available only at a single-frequency clock, so reducing the number of gates is worth doing.

The 12-bit register stores values in units of 0.0625 degrees Celsius per least significant bit, with the most significant bit carrying the sign.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the 12-bit two's complement representation of a reading of -37.5 degrees Celsius, giving your answer in binary and in hexadecimal.

    (Determine)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Explain why the summation register can overflow even when every individual reading is representable, and determine the minimum register width needed to sum any 16 consecutive readings without overflow.

    (Explain)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why converting a stored reading to degrees Celsius by multiplying by 0.0625 introduces no error, whereas converting it to degrees Fahrenheit does, in both cases assuming the arithmetic itself is performed exactly.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Show that F simplifies to P + T.O, and state the number of two-input gates needed for the reduced expression.

    (Show that)
a_html:
(a) One least significant bit represents $0.0625$ degrees Celsius, so the stored integer is the temperature divided by $0.0625$: $-37.5/0.0625=-600$. (M1)

To store $-600$ in 12-bit two's complement, represent $+600$ first. $600=512+64+16+8$, which is $001001011000$ in 12 bits. (A1)

Inverting every bit gives $110110100111$ and adding 1 gives $110110101000$, so $-600$ is stored as $1101\,1010\,1000$. Grouping into fours from the right: $1101$ is D, $1010$ is A, $1000$ is 8, so the answer is $\mathrm{0xDA8}$. (A1)

*Check: $1101\,1010\,1000$ is $3496$ unsigned, and $3496-4096=-600$. Correct.*

*Representable: $-600$ lies inside the 12-bit signed range $-2048$ to $+2047$, so no clamping is needed.*

(b) A 12-bit two's complement register holds values from $-2048$ to $+2047$. Each individual reading is comfortably inside this range because the largest magnitude the sensor can report is about $128$ degrees Celsius. (M1)

Overflow is a property of the accumulator, not of the sensor. Two readings of $+2047$ already sum to $4094$, which is more than the largest 12-bit signed value, so the sum wraps and a positive result can appear negative. In practice the readings are far smaller than the maximum, but the accumulator has no way of knowing that: it is only 12 bits wide, so any pair of readings above about $1023$ will overflow it. (M1)(A1)

Sixteen readings can each be as large as $2047$, so the largest possible sum is $16\times 2047=32\,752$. (M1) A 15-bit two's complement register reaches only $+16\,383$, which is not enough; a 16-bit register reaches $+32\,767$, which is. The minimum width is therefore 16 bits. (A1)

In general an accumulator summing $k$ readings of width $w$ must satisfy $2^{W-1}-1\ge k(2^{w-1}-1)$; for $w=12$ and $k=16$ the smallest satisfying width is $W=16$, which is why the answer is 16 and not 15.

(c) $0.0625=2^{-4}$. Multiplication by a power of two does not change the digits of a binary number, it only moves the binary point, so the multiplication can be performed by a shift and the result is exact. Every value the sensor can produce is mapped to an exact value in degrees Celsius. (M1)(A1)

The conversion to Fahrenheit is $F=1.8C+32$, so it requires multiplication by $1.8$, which is $9/5$. In binary, $9/5$ is the recurring fraction $1.1100110011\ldots$, which cannot be stored in a fixed number of bits. (M1) Rounding that factor introduces an error that grows with the magnitude of the reading, and because $1/5$ has a factor of 5 in the denominator it can never be represented exactly in binary. (A1)

The Celsius conversion is therefore exact by construction, while the Fahrenheit error is one of representation rather than arithmetic: using more bits shrinks the rounding error but never removes it, because the expansion of $9/5$ does not terminate.

(d) $P.T+P.T'=P.(T+T')=P.1=P$ by the distributive and complement laws. (M1)

Substituting: $F=P+P'.T.O$. (M1)

By the rule $A+A'.B=A+B$ (absorption, or the consensus theorem), with $A=P$ and $B=T.O$, this becomes $F=P+T.O$. (A1)

The reduced expression needs one AND gate for $T.O$ and one OR gate to combine it with $P$, so two two-input gates. (A1) The two inverters required by the original expression are no longer needed, so the gate count falls from five to two and the propagation delay falls as well.

A truth-table cross-check over all eight combinations of $P$, $T$ and $O$ gives identical outputs for the original expression and for $P+T.O$, confirming the simplification.

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the (M1) is for dividing by 0.0625; accept a candidate who works in the other direction by converting 37.5 to binary fractionally, provided the two's complement step is shown. Do not accept a sign-magnitude representation where two's complement was asked for. Part (b): the key discriminator is whether the candidate identifies the accumulator as the source of overflow. An answer that merely states 'the sum gets too big' without connecting this to the fixed 12-bit width earns one (M1). For the width, accept 16-bit or 'four extra bits'; do not accept 15-bit, and do not accept a candidate who computes $16 \times 2048$ and obtains $32\,768$, because that value is not achievable and the conclusion for the width happens to be the same but the reasoning is wrong. Part (c): credit any answer that identifies 0.0625 as a power of two and 1.8 as a non-terminating binary fraction. A candidate who says '1.8 is not an integer' has not addressed the question and should not receive the last (A1). Part (d): accept a truth-table proof, an algebraic proof, or a Karnaugh map. If a truth table is used it must have eight rows and all four minterms correctly placed. A candidate who writes 'F = P + TO' with no working earns one mark only.

topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
syllabus_ref: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems (A1.3.2 functions of an operating system, A1.3.3 comparison of scheduling approaches, A1.3.4 evaluation of polling and interrupt handling, A1.3.6 open-loop and closed-loop control)
title: An irrigation gateway choosing how to share its processor
q_html:
A field irrigation gateway

A solar-powered gateway controller sits in a field and manages irrigation for sixteen plots. It runs a small operating system on a single-core processor and executes four periodic tasks, described as A, B, C and D. Each task becomes ready at the same moment when the controller wakes from sleep, and their processor requirements are 5 ms, 3 ms, 8 ms and 2 ms respectively. The controller must also handle two inputs: a soil-moisture probe that is read on a fixed schedule every 30 seconds, and a rain sensor that triggers a shutdown and must be acted on within 5 milliseconds of the first drop reaching it. The device is battery-backed and mains-charged, and is connected to the farm network so that readings can be uploaded.

The four tasks A, B, C and D all become ready simultaneously when the controller wakes. Their processor requirements are 5 ms, 3 ms, 8 ms and 2 ms.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Describe how a closed-loop control system would maintain soil moisture at a target level, identifying the input, the process, the output and the feedback in your answer.

    (Describe)
  2. [6 marks](b)

    Calculate the average waiting time for the four tasks under first-come-first-served scheduling and under round-robin scheduling with a time quantum of 3 ms, then recalculate each total if every context switch costs 0.5 ms and the tasks are executed in the order A, B, C, D.

    (Calculate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the average waiting time alone is a misleading basis for choosing between the two policies, using your figures, and state which policy you would deploy.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate the use of polling for the soil-moisture probe against the use of interrupts for the rain sensor, and explain one additional operating system function that the network connection makes necessary.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) In a closed-loop system the controller measures the actual soil moisture, compares it with the target value, and uses the difference to decide how much water to release; the measurement is then repeated so that the effect of the action is observed and corrected. (M1)

Input: the reading from the soil-moisture probe, converted to a digital value. Process: the controller compares this reading with the target and computes the valve opening and the duration of watering. Output: the signal that opens the irrigation valve, and the water delivered to the plot. Feedback: the next reading from the same probe, which shows whether the moisture has reached the target and allows the next decision to be adjusted. (M1)(A1)(A1)

The feedback path is what makes the system closed-loop and is what distinguishes it from an open-loop system, which would water for a fixed time regardless of the resulting moisture level.

(b) First-come-first-served, executing in the order A, B, C, D:

| Task | Starts | Runs | Completes | Waiting time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 5 | 5 | 0 |
| B | 5 | 3 | 8 | 5 |
| C | 8 | 8 | 16 | 8 |
| D | 16 | 2 | 18 | 16 |

Average waiting time $=(0+5+8+16)/4=7.25$ ms. (M1)(A1)

Round robin with a quantum of 3 ms, queue order A, B, C, D:

| Slice | Task | Runs | Remaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A | 3 | 2 |
| 2 | B | 3 | 0 completes at 6 ms |
| 3 | C | 3 | 5 |
| 4 | D | 2 | 0 completes at 11 ms |
| 5 | A | 2 | 0 completes at 13 ms |
| 6 | C | 3 | 2 |
| 7 | C | 2 | 0 completes at 18 ms |

Waiting times are A 8 ms, B 3 ms, C 10 ms and D 9 ms, so the average is $(8+3+10+9)/4=7.50$ ms. (M1)(A1)

Both schedules take 18 ms of processing. First-come-first-served needs 3 context switches, adding 1.5 ms, for a total of 19.5 ms. Round robin needs 7 switches, adding 3.5 ms, for a total of 21.5 ms. (M1)(A1)

(c) Under round robin the average waiting time is 0.25 ms worse and the total time is 2 ms worse, so on the average the two policies are almost indistinguishable and the familiar claim that round robin is fairer is not visible. (M1)

What the average hides is the distribution. Under first-come-first-served the shortest task waits 16 ms, eight times its own running time, and a task that became ready just after a long one would wait longer still. Round robin bounds the wait for any task that is ready: with four tasks and a 3 ms quantum, no task is ever bypassed for more than three slices, so the worst case is 9 ms of other work. (A1)

For a controller whose main job is to keep the valves responding, the bounded worst case is worth more than a marginally better average, so round robin is the defensible choice, with the caveat that the context-switch cost should be reduced before the quantum is made smaller. (A1)

(d) Polling the moisture probe every 30 seconds is cheap and predictable. The probe changes slowly, the event rate is two checks per minute, and the processor overhead of reading a value on a timer is negligible; an interrupt-driven design would add hardware complexity for no benefit. (M1)(A1)

Polling the rain sensor is not acceptable. Drops arrive unpredictably and the required response is within 5 ms, so a polling loop would need a period shorter than 5 ms, consuming processor time continuously and still risking a missed event between samples. An interrupt lets the processor sleep until a drop arrives, which also suits a battery-backed device, and it guarantees the latency requirement rather than merely making it likely. (A1)

The network connection makes authentication and access control necessary: the gateway must be able to accept uploads and possibly commands from the farm network, so the operating system must identify who is allowed to talk to it and protect its memory from a malicious or faulty remote message.

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the four components must be identified in the context of this device, not defined generically; a candidate who writes 'input: a sensor' without saying which quantity is being sensed earns at most two of the four marks. Part (b): accept a correctly drawn Gantt chart as a substitute for the table. The trace marks are for the completion times and the waiting times respectively; a candidate with correct completion times but who reports waiting time as completion time minus start time should be corrected and given the trace mark only. Do not require the context-switch calculation to be presented in the same form as here, but do require an explicit count of switches; a candidate who counts 15 switches for round robin rather than 7 has counted slices rather than switches and loses the last (A1). Part (c): the essential argument is the difference between an average and a worst case; a candidate who merely repeats the average figures without discussing the shortest task's wait does not reach the explanation mark. Part (d): award the two marks for the moisture probe for the low event rate and predictability, and the mark for the rain sensor for the latency guarantee; a candidate who argues only on cost does not address the requirement. The final mark is for any plausible security function tied to the network connection, such as authentication, encryption of the upload, or memory protection from a malformed network packet.
