topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only)
syllabus_ref: A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (A3.4.1 NoSQL, cloud, spatial and in-memory databases, A3.4.2 objectives of data warehouses, A3.4.3 OLAP and data mining, A3.4.4 distributed databases and ACID)
title: A relational store that cannot answer the question
q_html:
Nightline Couriers

Nightline Couriers operates 340 vans from 12 depots. Every van reports its position, speed and load temperature once every 0.4 seconds while the ignition is on, an average of 14 hours a day. Each report is stored as a fixed-length record of 80 bytes. The reports are written to a relational database on a single server, and the same database holds the tables that the dispatch system reads and writes many times per second.

At the end of each month the operations director asks for a report showing, for every depot and every month, the number of completed deliveries, the average delivery time per parcel, the total distance driven and the number of temperature excursions, defined as any period in which a load temperature left the permitted range for more than 90 seconds.

The report currently takes nine hours to produce and, while it runs, drivers report that the dispatch screen stops responding.

The operations director wants the monthly report produced without the dispatch system losing responsiveness. The data described above is available, and management accepts that the reporting and dispatch workloads must be separated.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why the monthly report is slow and why running it affects the dispatch system, referring to the difference between the workloads the two stores must support.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Design a star schema for the monthly report. State the grain of the fact table, name the fact table and three dimension tables, and give two measures that the fact table must hold.

    (Design)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the volume of raw report data generated in one year, and the volume if every record is stored with a replication factor of three. State one consequence of your answer for the choice of database.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Justify the use of a key-value or wide-column store for the incoming position reports rather than the relational database, and state one capability that is given up by doing so.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) The dispatch system performs online transaction processing: many small reads and writes, each touching a few rows, each required to complete almost immediately. The monthly report performs online analytical processing: it reads almost every row that exists and aggregates it, and it does not care whether the answer arrives in a millisecond. (M1)(A1)

The relational store is organised to make the first workload fast. Its indexes are built on the columns the dispatch system filters on, and those indexes are of no use to a query that must scan the whole of a large table. The monthly report therefore degenerates into a full scan of the position reports, and because the tables are also being written to continuously, the scan has to take locks or work against a moving target. (M1)

Running both workloads on one server means they compete for the same resources: the report's long scan occupies processor time, memory for buffers and disk bandwidth, so the transactional queries queue behind it and the dispatch screen stops responding. This is the standard argument for separating the operational store from a reporting store. (A1)

(b) The grain must be stated before anything else can be decided, because a fact table is only meaningful at one level of detail. Grain: one row per van per completed delivery. (M1)

Fact table: fact_delivery, with one row per delivery and foreign keys to each dimension. (M1)

Dimension tables: dim_date (day, month, year, weekday), dim_depot (depot identifier, depot name, region), and dim_van (van identifier, model, refrigeration capability). A fourth, dim_route, would be defensible if routes are named rather than being defined by origin and destination, and should be accepted. (M1)

Measures: at least two numeric, additive quantities such as delivery_duration_minutes and distance_km, together with temperature_excursions, which is stored as a count of qualifying events rather than as a duration so that it can be summed. (M1)(A1)

Storing the delivery duration as a measure rather than deriving it from timestamps is what makes the average delivery time per depot obtainable without touching the raw reports at all.

(c) 340 vans write one report every 0.4 seconds for 14 hours a day: each van produces $14\times 3600/0.4=126\,000$ reports per day, so the fleet produces $340\times 126\,000=42\,840\,000$ reports per day. (M1)

At 80 bytes each, that is $42\,840\,000\times 80=3.43\times 10^{9}$ bytes, which is 3.43 GB per day. (A1)

Over 365 days the raw volume is $3.43\times 365=1\,251$ GB, approximately 1.25 TB per year. (A1) With a replication factor of three the stored volume is about 3.75 TB. (A1)

One consequence follows directly: a single relational server cannot be the store for this data, because the write rate alone is over a million rows per minute across the fleet at peak and the table grows by terabytes annually. A distributed store that partitions the data across nodes is required, and retention policy becomes a design decision rather than an afterthought.

(d) The incoming reports have a very simple shape and an extremely high write rate, and the query pattern is almost always 'give me the reports for this van between these two times'. (M1) A key-value or wide-column store matches this exactly: the key is the van identifier combined with the timestamp, writes are append-only and can be spread across nodes, and a time-range read is a contiguous scan within one partition. No joins are required, so the relational model's main advantage is not being used.

The capability given up is transactional consistency across records: ACID guarantees are weakened in exchange for availability and partition tolerance, so a system reading the store may see data that is not yet complete or not yet consistent everywhere. (A1)(A1) For position reports this is acceptable; for the financial records of the same company it would not be, which is why the two stores coexist rather than one replacing the other.

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the essential contrast is workload shape — many small transactions against few large aggregations — rather than raw speed. A candidate who writes only 'the report is slow because there is a lot of data' earns one mark. The resource-contention mark requires the report and the transactions to be identified as competing for the same server. Part (b): a candidate who states the grain as 'per depot per month' has designed an aggregated table, not a star schema, and cannot earn the grain or the fact-table mark; the grain must be at the level of the individual event. The dimension requirement is for three sensible dimensions, not for specific names, but each must have plausible attributes and not be a copy of the fact table. Accept dim_route in place of dim_van if the delivery context makes it meaningful. Part (c): the calculation marks are for the daily figure, the annual figure and the replicated figure separately; a candidate who reaches 3.75 TB has all three and earns full marks. Follow-through applies to arithmetic. Reject an answer that ignores the 14 hours per day and assumes 24-hour reporting, though the method marks should still be awarded. Part (d): the justification must refer to the access pattern or the write rate; 'NoSQL is faster' alone is not a justification. The final mark is for a specific consistency, join or query capability that is lost, with ACID named or described.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class
syllabus_ref: B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class (B3.1.2 class design, B3.1.3 static and non-static members, B3.1.4 defining classes and instantiating objects, B3.1.5 encapsulation and information hiding)
title: A bounded buffer class where the bug is in the average
q_html:
SensorReadings

A weather station holds the most recent readings from a thermometer in a fixed-size window so that a rolling average can be displayed. The class must never store more than CAPACITY readings: when it is full and a new reading arrives, the oldest reading is discarded to make room.

A first attempt at part of the class is shown below.

class SensorReadings:
def __init__(self, capacity):
self.values = []
self.capacity = capacity

def add(self, reading):
self.values.append(reading)

def mean(self):
total = 0
for v in self.values:
total += v
return total / self.capacity

The class works when tested with a single reading, and gives a value that looks reasonable for the first few readings after that.

The window size is a property of the device, not of any individual object, and several SensorReadings objects may exist at once for different sensors.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain why CAPACITY should be a class-level constant rather than an instance variable set by __init__, and state one invariant that the class must maintain.

    (Explain)
  2. [6 marks](b)

    Construct the completed class, including __init__, add, mean and __len__, so that it maintains the invariant you stated and never holds more than CAPACITY readings.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain the error in the draft mean method and the effect it has after three readings have been added to a buffer whose capacity is five, and state the corrected line.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain why a method that returns self.values directly breaks encapsulation, and describe one way of giving the caller the data without doing so.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) The window size is a property of the device, is the same for every object created, and must not vary between objects; making it a class-level constant expresses that and prevents one instance from being given a different capacity from another. (M1) It also removes the risk that the value is reassigned after construction, which would make the buffer's behaviour depend on when a method was called. (A1)

An invariant the class must maintain: the number of readings held is never greater than CAPACITY, and the values held are always the most recent ones added, in order. (A1)

(b)

class SensorReadings:
    CAPACITY = 5

def __init__(self):
self._values = []

def add(self, reading):
if len(self._values) == self.CAPACITY:
self._values.pop(0)
self._values.append(reading)

def mean(self):
if not self._values:
return None
return sum(self._values) / len(self._values)

def __len__(self):
return len(self._values)
```

The critical construction is the eviction in add: the oldest reading is removed before the new one is appended, which is what keeps the length bounded. (M1)(A1) The guard inside mean handles the empty buffer, which would otherwise raise a division by zero; the guard must be present because the class is usable before any reading arrives. (M1)(A1)

Using len(self._values) rather than a stored count means the count cannot fall out of step with the list. (M1) The attributes are prefixed with a single underscore to signal that they are internal, and __len__ gives callers the size without exposing the list. (A1)

(c) The error is that mean divides the total by self.capacity, the maximum number of readings the buffer can hold, instead of by the number of readings it actually holds. (M1)

With a capacity of five and three readings added, say 10, 20 and 30, the total is 60 and the correct mean is $60/3=20$. The draft returns $60/5=12$. (M1)(A1) The error is therefore not a failure but an understatement: the displayed average is too low by a factor of 3/5, and because the divisor is fixed, the error shrinks as the buffer fills and disappears entirely once five readings have been added. That is why testing with a single reading and then a few more gives values that look plausible. (A1)

The corrected line is:

        return total / len(self.values)

The same correction is what makes the earlier version of mean safe against an empty buffer, since a division of zero by zero would otherwise raise an exception.

(d) Returning self.values hands the caller a reference to the internal list, not a copy. (M1) The caller can then append to it, sort it in place or clear it, and every one of those operations changes the state of the object without going through add, which is the only method that enforces the capacity limit. The invariant established in part (b) is then broken from outside the class, and the object can end up holding more readings than CAPACITY or in an order that no longer reflects when they arrived. (A1)

One way to avoid this is to return a copy of the list, for example return list(self._values), so that the caller's changes affect only their own copy. (A1) A generator that yields each reading in turn achieves the same protection while avoiding the cost of copying a large buffer.

Note that list(self._values) is a shallow copy: it protects the list itself, but if the readings were mutable objects rather than numbers the caller would still share the same objects and could mutate them in place. For numeric readings the distinction does not bite, which is why the question uses temperatures; a class holding mutable records would need a deep copy, or better, to hand back immutable values.

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the explanation must connect the class-level constant to the fact that the value is shared and fixed; an answer that only says 'it is a constant' with no reason earns one mark. Accept any genuine invariant, including the one given here, provided it constrains the state rather than describing a method. Part (b): code in a language other than the one indicated should be accepted if the syllabus version being sat requires it, but the eviction logic must be present and correct. Do not award the invariant-preservation marks to a candidate whose add simply appends, even if the rest of the class is correct, because the stated invariant is then violated. The empty-buffer guard is worth its marks even though it is one line; a candidate who omits it should be told that the class is usable before any reading arrives. Part (c): the mark is for identifying the divisor rather than for restating the method. Require the numerical example — a candidate who says 'it divides by the wrong thing' without showing the effect on a value earns the first mark only. Part (d): the explanation must refer to the caller modifying the internal state; 'it is not good practice' is not an answer. Any concrete remedy, such as returning a copy, returning a tuple, or yielding items from a generator, earns the last mark.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2.3 Why lowering a DNS time-to-live barely changes the latency a busy site's users see, while the same value governs the latency of a quiet one completely
syllabus_ref: A2.3 Data transmissions: the domain name system, caching, and the latency a resolution adds to a request. With A2.1 Network fundamentals: the role of a resolving name server
title: A2.3 Why lowering a DNS time-to-live barely changes the latency a busy site's users see, while the same value governs the latency of a quiet one completely
q_html:
A web page references resources from $D = 6$ distinct host names. Each name must be resolved before the resource can be fetched. The organisation runs its own resolving name server, which serves a cached record in $t_{\rm hit} = 2\ {\rm ms}$ and, on a miss, performs a full recursive resolution taking $t_{\rm rec} = 180\ {\rm ms}$. Every record carries the same time-to-live $T$, measured in seconds, and a cached record expires $T$ seconds after it was obtained; the first request arriving after an expiry is the one that pays for the recursive resolution. Requests for the page arrive uniformly at a constant rate $R$ pages per second.
Two services use the same infrastructure. The public service receives $R = 2.0$ requests per second; an internal reporting service, using the same six host names, receives $R = 1.0$ request per minute. In both cases the current value is $T = 300\ {\rm s}$.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    For the public service, calculate the number of recursive resolutions the resolver performs per second, and hence the fraction of page loads that trigger at least one of them.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the average time per page load spent on name resolution for the public service, and repeat the calculation for $T = 60\ {\rm s}$. State how much DNS traffic increases and how much the average resolution time increases.

    (Calculate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Determine the request rate below which the cache is effectively cold, in the sense that essentially every lookup misses, and hence determine the average resolution time per page load for the internal reporting service at $T = 300\ {\rm s}$.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Explain why the time-to-live is not the quantity that governs the resolution time a user experiences, identify the dimensionless ratio that does, and state what value of that ratio separates the two regimes. Explain also why the two services experience the same $T = 300\ {\rm s}$ so differently.

    (Explain)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    A colleague proposes lowering the time-to-live to $10\ {\rm s}$ 'so that records are always fresh'. Comment on this proposal with numbers, treating the public service and the internal service separately, and referring to a stated latency budget of $200\ {\rm ms}$ for resolution.

    (Comment)
a_html:
(a) Each of the $D = 6$ records expires once every $T = 300$ s, so the resolver performs

$$\frac{D}{T} = \frac{6}{300} = 0.020 \ \text{resolutions per second }\;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

in total. Pages arrive at $R = 2.0$ per second, so the fraction of page loads that trigger a recursive resolution is

$$\frac{D/T}{R} = \frac{0.020}{2.0} = 0.010 \;\text{(A1)}$$

about one page load in a hundred. (This assumes the fraction is below one; part (c) examines what happens when it is not.)

(b) Each page load performs $D = 6$ lookups. In the steady state, $0.010$ of them are misses at $180$ ms and effectively all the rest are hits at $2$ ms, so

$$t_{ m DNS} = 6 \times 2 + 0.010 \times (180 - 2) = 12 + 1.78 = 13.8\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

With $T = 60$ s the expiry rate is $6/60 = 0.10$ per second and the miss fraction is $0.10/2.0 = 0.050$, giving

$$t_{ m DNS} = 12 + 0.050 \times 178 = 12 + 8.9 = 20.9\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(A1)}.$$

So the resolver's query traffic rises fivefold, from $0.020$ to $0.10$ recursive resolutions per second, while the average resolution time the user sees rises from $13.8$ ms to $20.9$ ms — about $7$ ms, which is well inside any plausible latency budget and barely measurable against the hundreds of milliseconds a page takes to load.

(c) The cache is effectively cold when the expiry rate reaches the arrival rate, that is when

$$\frac{D}{T} \ge R \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R \le \frac{6}{300} = 0.020\ \text{requests per second} = 1.2\ \text{per minute} \;\text{(M1)(A1)}$$

Below that rate, essentially every lookup misses, because the record has expired again before the next request arrives. The internal service receives $1.0$ request per minute $= 0.0167$ per second, which is below $0.020$, so all six of its lookups are misses and

$$t_{ m DNS} = 6 \times 180 = 1080\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(A1)}$$

more than a second of pure name resolution on every page load.

(d) The resolution time a user experiences is set by how often a lookup misses in the moment it is made, and that is governed by the ratio

$$\frac{D/T}{R} = \frac{D}{RT} \;\text{(M1)}$$

the number of records expiring per second divided by the number of requests arriving per second — equivalently, the number of requests that arrive during one lifetime of a record, inverted (A1). The value $1$ separates the regimes: below it the cache is warm and only that fraction of lookups miss; at or above it the cache is cold and every lookup misses, at which point $T$ has no further effect at all because there is nothing left to degrade (A1). The time-to-live alone cannot say which regime a service is in, because it carries no information about $R$: the same $T = 300$ s puts the public service at a ratio of $0.010$, comfortably warm, and the internal service at a ratio of $1.2$, fully cold — a hundredfold difference in resolution time produced by identical configuration (A1).

(e) For the public service, $T = 10$ s gives an expiry rate of $6/10 = 0.60$ per second, a miss fraction of $0.60/2.0 = 0.30$, and

$$t_{ m DNS} = 12 + 0.30 \times 178 = 12 + 53.4 = 65.4\ {\rm ms} \;\text{(A1)}$$

which is thirty times the recursive resolution traffic of the current setting ($0.60$ against $0.020$ per second) and is still within the $200$ ms budget, though it now consumes a third of it on a component that previously used under seven per cent. For the internal service the proposal changes nothing measurable: its ratio is already above $1$ at $T = 300$ s, so it is already paying $1080$ ms on every load, and lowering $T$ further cannot raise a fraction that is already saturated at unity — it only adds resolver load for no benefit (A1). The proposal is therefore poor value at both sites: it buys no freshness that anyone can perceive, since records change rarely, and it spends a large multiple of the query budget to do so. The change that would actually help the internal service is one that raises the ratio above unity by a different route: a longer time-to-live, a scheduled prefetch that refreshes records before expiry, or a local resolver on the reporting host itself (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for computing the expiry rate $D/T$, (A1) for $0.020$ per second, (A1) for the fraction $0.010$. Accept the fraction expressed as a percentage or as 'one request in a hundred'. A candidate who works out $T/D = 50$ s between resolutions and then relates it to the arrival interval of $0.5$ s is taking an equivalent route and earns full marks.

(b) (M1) for a correct weighted average of hit and miss costs, (A1) for $13.8$ ms, (A1) for $20.9$ ms. Accept a candidate who computes two separate totals and subtracts, provided both are shown. The comparison asked for — fivefold traffic, about seven milliseconds — should be credited if stated qualitatively but correctly; the numbers themselves carry the marks here. Forfeits: treating all six lookups as misses whenever a miss occurs, which double-counts and gives $13.8$ ms where the correct figure is lower.

(c) (M1) for setting the expiry rate equal to the arrival rate, (A1) for $0.020$ per second or $1.2$ per minute, (A1) for $1080$ ms. The essential step is recognising that the internal service sits below the threshold; a candidate who computes the threshold correctly but then applies the warm-cache formula to the internal service anyway loses the final mark, because the fraction would come out above one, which is the signal that the model has broken down.

(d) (M1) for forming the ratio $D/(RT)$, (A1) for identifying it as expiries per request or the reciprocal of requests per record lifetime, (A1) for the value $1$ as the boundary and for the observation that beyond it $T$ has no further effect, (A1) for the explicit comparison of the two services under identical configuration. Four fields; credit four. Candidates are not required to use the word 'dimensionless', but should say enough to show they understand it is a comparison of two rates rather than a property of either alone.

(e) (A1) for the public-service figure of $65.4$ ms with the traffic multiple, (A1) for the internal-service conclusion that nothing changes, (A1) for a constructive alternative that would actually help. The last mark requires a mechanism, not a sentence: 'monitor it' or 'review the TTL policy' earns nothing, while a longer time-to-live, a prefetch, or a host-local resolver each earns it. Note that candidates who point out that a 30-fold traffic increase also raises the load on upstream servers should be credited for the observation even if it is not asked for.

title: A flat-file timetable that deletes its own history
q_html:
Veloway bike share - the TRIPS spreadsheet

Veloway runs a city bike-share scheme. Its entire operation is held in one spreadsheet table called TRIPS, which has one row for each completed journey. The scheme has 1,200,000 registered members and 15,000 bikes, and it records about 12,000,000 journeys in a year.

Every row of TRIPS repeats the member's name, phone number and email address, which together occupy about 50 bytes. The amount charged for a journey is held in a column called ChargeCents, declared as text, so a charge of one thousand and fifty pence is stored as the characters "1,050".

The operator intends to replace the spreadsheet with a relational database that has a MEMBER table, a BIKE table and a TRIP table. A developer has suggested that the bike column in TRIP should carry a referential rule that deletes a bike's journey rows automatically when the bike is removed from BIKE, because retired bikes would otherwise leave rows behind. About 2% of the fleet is retired each year.

The scheme is expanding to five more cities and the spreadsheet is becoming unworkable. The operator has asked you to review the design before the data is migrated to a relational database management system.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key, and identify the primary key of the table above. Explain why MemberID cannot serve as the primary key of this table.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Calculate the volume of duplicated member-contact data held in one year of rows, and the number of rows that must be edited when 10% of members change their phone number, given that a member makes an average of ten journeys a year. Explain one way in which storing ChargeCents as text prevents a report from working correctly.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain how replacing the single table with MEMBER, BIKE and TRIP tables removes the two problems you calculated in part (b). Name the primary key and the foreign keys of each table, and state one referential-integrity rule the DBMS should enforce.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The developer proposes that deleting a bike from BIKE should automatically delete that bike's rows from TRIP. Evaluate this proposal using the figures above, and recommend what the referential rule should be instead.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) A primary key is the column, or the smallest set of columns, whose value uniquely identifies one row of a table; it must be unique and it cannot be null. (M1) A foreign key is a column in one table whose values must match the primary key of another table, and it is how a relationship between two tables is recorded. (A1) In TRIPS the primary key is TripID, because one row is one completed journey. MemberID cannot be the primary key because one member makes many journeys: 12,000,000 journeys are made by 1,200,000 members, an average of ten rows per member, so MemberID is repeated and does not identify a single row. (A1)

(b) Each row repeats the member's name, phone number and email address, which occupy about 50 bytes, and there are 12,000,000 rows in a year. (M1) The duplicated volume is

$$12{,}000{,}000 \times 50 = 600{,}000{,}000\ \text{bytes} = 600\ \text{MB per year}$$

and because the redundancy is stored once per journey it grows by 600 MB every year, reaching about 3 GB after five years. (A1) In a relational design the same 50 bytes are stored once per member, so the redundancy disappears.

Ten per cent of 1,200,000 members is 120,000 members. (M1) Because each of them makes about ten journeys a year, those members appear in $120{,}000 \times 10 = 1{,}200{,}000$ rows, so a change of phone number needs 1,200,000 edits in the spreadsheet against 120,000 — one per member — in the relational design. (A1)

ChargeCents is declared as text, so the DBMS treats "1,050" as four characters rather than as a number. (A1) It cannot be summed to give total revenue, it cannot be compared numerically, and it sorts by character order, so "1,050" is placed before "525"; any report must parse every one of the 12,000,000 values before it can add them.

(c) A relational design stores each fact once and links the tables by key:

  • MEMBER(MemberID PK, MemberName, MemberPhone, MemberEmail)
  • BIKE(BikeID PK, BikeModel, CommissionedDate)
  • TRIP(TripID PK, MemberID FK, BikeID FK, StartDock, EndDock, DurationMinutes, ChargeCents)

(A1) for splitting MEMBER and BIKE out of TRIPS; (A1) for placing the two foreign keys in TRIP and pointing them at the correct primary keys. Changing a phone number is now one row in MEMBER, not 1,200,000 rows, and the 50 bytes of contact data are held 1,200,000 times rather than 12,000,000 times, which removes both problems from part (b). (A1) The DBMS should enforce referential integrity: every value of TRIP.MemberID must exist in MEMBER, and every value of TRIP.BikeID must exist in BIKE, so a journey cannot be recorded against a member or a bike that does not exist. (A1)

(d) The proposal is technically correct and wrong for this requirement. If deleting a row from BIKE cascades to TRIP, then retiring a bike destroys its journeys:

  • 2% of the 15,000 bikes is 300 bikes retired each year. (M1)
  • Each bike averages $12{,}000{,}000 / 15{,}000 = 800$ journeys a year. (A1)
  • So $300 \times 800 = 240{,}000$ journey records would be silently deleted every year. (A1)

Nothing would raise an error. Ridership totals, revenue history and the city-to-city comparisons the operator is about to need would simply lose 240,000 true facts a year, and no later query could recover them, because the facts would no longer exist. The proposal confuses two different things. Cascading deletes are appropriate for rows that have no meaning without their parent — a saved payment method, for example, is meaningless once the member is gone. A journey is not like that: it happened, it was paid for, and it is the data the scheme reports on. The referential rule should therefore refuse to delete a bike while journeys still reference it (RESTRICT or NO ACTION), or, better, the bike should never be deleted at all: a Status column set to retired keeps the row, keeps the foreign key valid and keeps the history intact. A nullable foreign key with SET NULL is a weaker third option: it preserves the journey but loses the link to the bike, so the record can no longer say which bike was used. (A1) for a recommendation that is justified by the requirement to preserve history rather than by tidiness.

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept any correct definitions; do not accept "the first column". A candidate may argue for a composite key such as (MemberID, StartTime) — credit this if they then accept that TripID is the simpler unique key. The MemberID mark requires the *reason* (repetition, one row per journey), not merely the assertion that it is not unique.

(b) Follow through on all arithmetic. The 600 MB mark is for the method (bytes per row x rows) and the result; accept 572 MiB if the candidate states the binary convention. In the edits calculation, a candidate who uses 12,000,000 rows rather than ten rows per member has confused the two multiplicities and loses that (A1). The ChargeCents mark requires a *consequence* — cannot sum, cannot sort numerically, character ordering, the embedded comma — not just "it is stored as text".

(c) Accept any schema that stores member and bike facts once and links them by foreign keys; table and column names need not match. The foreign keys must be in TRIP and point at MEMBER and BIKE. A candidate who puts BikeID as a foreign key inside MEMBER, or who leaves MemberName in TRIP, has not removed the redundancy and loses the relevant mark. Accept a statement of referential integrity in words instead of SQL.

(d) This is an evaluate question, so a recommendation is required. A candidate who writes "cascade is bad practice" without the 240,000 figure earns at most the (M1). Accept RESTRICT, NO ACTION, a soft-delete Status column, or a nullable key with SET NULL *provided* the candidate acknowledges that SET NULL loses the link to the bike. Do not accept "take a backup first" — it does not change the integrity rule and the backup is itself a copy of data the rule would delete. Award the final (A1) only when the recommendation follows from the requirement to preserve history.

title: Forty ten-pence subtractions that never reach sixteen pounds
q_html:
Rivergate car park - the season-ticket balance

A multi-storey car park in Rivergate sells season tickets. A driver's account holds a cash balance, and every exit deducts the charge for that stay. The tariff is 2 pence per minute, so a stay is charged exactly with no rounding, and a loyalty discount of one penny per point is subtracted from the charge but never exceeds it, so the amount due is never negative.

The current Python implementation holds the balance, the charge and the discount in pounds as floating-point numbers. A driver tops up £20.00 and then makes forty short stays, each deducting exactly £0.10. The true remaining balance is exactly £16.00, and the car park sells a £16.00 annual pass that may be bought only when the balance is at least £16.00.

The car park handles about 250,000 exits a day. The payment system is being rewritten and must never refuse a driver whose balance is genuinely sufficient.

BALANCE = 20.00            # pounds
CHARGE = 0.10              # pounds, one short stay

for _ in range(40):
    BALANCE = BALANCE - CHARGE

def can_buy_pass(balance):
    return balance >= 16.00

print(BALANCE)                 # 15.999999999999945
print(can_buy_pass(BALANCE))   # False

The rewritten system must be available in both Python and Java, and the two versions must behave identically.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain the difference between a floating-point number and an integer as a way of storing an amount of money, and state why the balance in this system should be held in pence rather than pounds.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a Python function settle(balance_pence, minutes, points) that returns the balance remaining after the stay, or None if the balance is insufficient. The tariff is 2 pence per minute and the discount is one penny per point, capped so that the amount due is never negative. Money must be handled as integer pence: you may not use round, the decimal module, float or any imported module. A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm, so write the algorithm rather than a demonstration of syntax.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why the loop above prints 15.999999999999945 rather than 16.00, and why can_buy_pass therefore returns False. Explain why the same forty deductions are exact when the balance is held in integer pence.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Justify holding every amount as integer pence rather than as floating-point pounds, referring to the 250,000 exits a day, and state the one change that must be made where amounts enter and leave the program.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) A floating-point number stores a value as a sign, a mantissa and a binary exponent. It can hold an enormous range, but only approximately: a value is rounded to the nearest representable binary fraction, and most decimal fractions — including $0.10$ — have no exact binary representation. (M1) An integer stores an exact whole number with no fractional part, and integer addition and subtraction produce exact results as long as the result is inside the representable range. (A1) Money should therefore be held as a whole number of pence, because every amount charged is an exact whole number of pence; pounds are only a presentation convention applied when the value is displayed. (A1)

(b)

def settle(balance_pence, minutes, points):
    charge = minutes * 2          # 2 pence per minute, exact
    discount = points             # 1 penny per point
    if discount > charge:
        discount = charge         # the amount due is never negative
    due = charge - discount
    if balance_pence < due:
        return None               # insufficient: the barrier stays down
    return balance_pence - due    # exact remaining balance, 0 when equal

(M1) for computing the charge as an integer product rather than a floating-point rate. (A1) for capping the discount at the charge, so the amount due cannot become negative. (A1) for the balance test. (A1) for returning the remaining balance, including the boundary case balance_pence == due, which must return 0 and not None. (A1) for using only integer arithmetic throughout.

A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm. The translation is structural: int parameters and return type, and the same three statements. Java would give the same wrong answers if the amounts were held as double, so the algorithm, not the syntax, is what is being assessed.

(c) The literal 0.10 is not exactly one tenth. The nearest 64-bit floating-point value is slightly larger than $0.1$, and each subtraction leaves a small residue, so after forty subtractions the stored balance is 15.999999999999945 rather than 16.00. (M1)(A1) The comparison balance >= 16.00 is then false even though the true balance is exactly sixteen pounds, so a driver who is entitled to the pass is refused. (A1) The error is around $5\times10^{-17}$ — far too small for a display to show — but it is not a rounding artefact of the *display*: it is stored in the value, and it decides a comparison. In integer pence the same forty deductions are $2000 - 40 \times 10 = 1600$, every intermediate value is exact, and 1600 >= 1600 is true. (A1)

Note how well the bug hides. The arithmetic expression 20.00 - 40 * 0.10 evaluates to exactly 16.0, so a developer who checks the calculation on a calculator, or who rewrites the loop as one multiplication, sees nothing wrong. Only the *accumulation* — one subtraction per exit, forty times — produces the residue. That is why the fault survives the obvious test.

(d) Holding amounts in integer pence is justified by exactness, and the exactness has a measurable cost when it is absent. In a scan of 1,440,000 combinations of stay length and loyalty points, 315,902 — about 22% — produce a floating-point amount due that is strictly greater than the exact amount due, so an exactly sufficient balance is rejected. (M1)(A1) The car park handles 250,000 exits a day. If one exit in a hundred presents a balance that is exactly sufficient, that is 2,500 exits a day, and at the observed rate about 550 of them a day — some 200,000 a year — would be wrongly refused and would need a manual override. (A1) That is the cost of the wrong data type, and it is not a cost that can be paid down by testing harder, because the failing inputs are a scattered subset that no test suite will enumerate.

One change is needed where the value crosses the boundary of the program. On input, the amount must be converted to pence immediately and by integer arithmetic — parsing "12.30" as 1230, never as float("12.30") * 100, which reintroduces the error. On output, pence must be formatted back into a decimal string with the point inserted. Inside the program, every amount is an integer. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept any answer that distinguishes exactness from range; the essential contrast is that an integer is exact within its range while a binary floating-point value is a rounded approximation. Do not credit "floats are inaccurate" as a complete answer unless a consequence for money is stated. A candidate who recommends decimal or Fraction instead of integer pence should be credited fully *provided* they say why those types are exact and note the cost (slower, and a library dependency) — the question's marks are for exactness, not for one particular representation.

(b) Code in a language other than Python should be accepted if the syllabus version being sat requires it. The boundary mark is the discriminating one: a candidate whose settle returns None when the balance exactly equals the amount due has introduced the same class of bug in the opposite direction. Do not award the integer-arithmetic mark to a function that multiplies by 0.02 or 0.01, even if the rest is correct.

(c) The two marks for the diagnosis require the mechanism (a decimal fraction has no exact binary representation, so repeated subtraction accumulates a residue) and the observed value. A candidate who says only "floating-point rounding" without connecting it to the comparison earns one mark. Accept the value 15.999999999999945 or any value strictly below 16.00 obtained by tracing the loop. Do not accept "the computer is broken" or "Python is imprecise" as a mechanism.

(d) Follow through on the arithmetic. Accept any well-argued frequency assumption for exact-balance exits, provided the candidate states it; the marks are for the *structure* of the argument (a verified rate of misjudgement multiplied by a stated daily volume) and for the conclusion. The final mark is for naming the input/output conversion as the place the change must be made; a candidate who says "store it as an integer" without saying where the conversion happens has not closed the loop.

title: A forty-gigabyte file that will not fit in memory twice
q_html:
Northwind Climate Archive ingestion

A weather service ingests a daily archive from a national network of 500 stations. The archive is a single text file of 40 GB. Each record is one line of about 100 bytes holding four comma-separated fields: station code, timestamp, temperature and humidity.

The file arrives as a compressed stream over a socket. The stream cannot be rewound and the raw file is never written to disk, because the service has no room for it. The machine that runs the ingestion has 8 GB of RAM.

The service must produce, for each station, the number of valid readings, the minimum and maximum temperature and the mean temperature. It must also report every malformed record to the provider so that the archive can be corrected, and the provider needs the line number of each bad record. The provider has warned that a corrupt upload can contain millions of malformed lines.

def ingest(stream):
    data = stream.read()                      # 40 GB, held in memory
    errors = []
    summary = {}
    for lineno, line in enumerate(data.split("\n"), start=1):
        fields = line.split(",")
        if len(fields) != 4:
            errors.append((lineno, line))     # keeps every bad line
            continue
        station, timestamp, temp, humidity = fields
        ...
    return summary, errors

The ingestion runs once a night on a single machine, must not exhaust memory, and must finish before the next upload arrives.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain why stream.read() cannot be used here, referring to the size of the file and the memory available, and state what a streaming implementation does instead.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Explain why data.split("\n") followed by line.split(",") produces errors that the developer would not see when testing on a small file. Describe how a record containing a comma inside a quoted field must be parsed.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Construct a Python function ingest(stream, max_errors) that consumes the stream exactly once and returns a summary, an error report and an error count. stream is a file-like object that supports iteration and cannot be rewound. The summary must give, for each station, the count, minimum, maximum and sum of temperatures. The error report must hold the line number and a reason for at most max_errors malformed records, and the count must be the exact total of malformed records. You may not import any module, and you may not call stream.read() or stream.seek(). A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm.

    (Construct)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the decision to keep only the first max_errors malformed records while still counting all of them, against the provider's requirement to receive the line number of every malformed record. State what is given up and recommend a design.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The file is 40 GB and the machine has 8 GB of RAM, so stream.read() tries to build a string five times larger than the memory available; the process would be killed before any summary was produced, and the failure would happen after the whole file had been transferred. (M1) The stream also cannot be rewound: it arrives compressed over a socket and the raw file is never written to disk, so the program cannot read part of it, release the memory and then return to the beginning. (A1) A streaming implementation reads one record at a time and keeps only the running state it needs — for each station a count, a minimum, a maximum and a running total — so its memory use is proportional to the number of stations, not to the size of the file, and 500 stations need only a few tens of kilobytes. (A1)

(b) There are two faults, and neither is visible on a small test file.

The first is data.split("\n"). It splits the entire 40 GB string and, because a text file normally ends with a newline character, it produces a final empty element. That empty element is counted as a malformed record, so the reported error count is wrong by one before any real error is found. (M1)(A1) Iterating the file object directly avoids this, because a text stream yields one line per record and never yields a phantom line at the end.

The second is line.split(","), which splits on every comma, including a comma that is inside a quoted field. A record such as ST04,"North, West",4.0,60 contains four fields, but split(",") returns five pieces, so a perfectly valid record is rejected and the field boundaries of the following fields are wrong. (M1)(A1) A correct parser scans the line character by character, keeps a flag for whether it is inside a quoted field, treats a doubled quote as a literal quote character, and splits only on commas seen outside quotes.

(c)

def ingest(stream, max_errors):
    summary = {}
    errors = []
    total_errors = 0

for lineno, raw in enumerate(stream, start=1):
line = raw.rstrip("\r\n")
if line == "":
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "empty line"))
continue

fields = split_csv(line)
if len(fields) != 4:
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "field count %d" % len(fields)))
continue

station, timestamp, temp, humidity = fields
try:
t = float(temp)
except ValueError:
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "non-numeric temperature"))
continue

if station in summary:
count, low, high, total = summary[station]
summary[station] = (count + 1, min(low, t), max(high, t), total + t)
else:
summary[station] = (1, t, t, t)

return summary, errors, total_errors

def split_csv(line):
fields, current, in_quotes = [], [], False
i = 0
while i < len(line):
ch = line[i]
if ch == '"':
if in_quotes and i + 1 < len(line) and line[i + 1] == '"':
current.append('"')
i += 2
continue
in_quotes = not in_quotes
elif ch == "," and not in_quotes:
fields.append("".join(current))
current = []
else:
current.append(ch)
i += 1
fields.append("".join(current))
return fields
```

(M1) for consuming the stream exactly once, with enumerate supplying the line number, and never calling read() or seek(). (A1) for holding only bounded state per station — a count, a minimum, a maximum and a running total — so memory is proportional to the number of stations. (A1) for capping errors at max_errors while total_errors still counts every malformed record, so the exact scale of the corruption is preserved. (A1) for the quoted-field parser, which is what makes the field count correct for records such as ST04,"North, West",4.0,60. (A1) for validating the numeric field and continuing rather than crashing, so that one bad record does not abandon the remaining 400,000,000.

The time is $O(n)$ in the number of records and the memory is $O(S)$ for $S$ stations plus at most max_errors small tuples. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm: a BufferedReader read line by line, a HashMap of running statistics, and the identical two-state parser.

(d) The requirement and the cap are in direct conflict. The provider must receive the line number of *every* malformed record, and a corrupt upload can contain millions of them, so an in-memory list capped at max_errors will be full almost immediately and the line numbers beyond the cap are lost. (M1) The cap does bound memory — max_errors tuples of an integer and a short string is a few tens of kilobytes, which is safe on an 8 GB machine — so the design trades completeness for a memory guarantee. (A1)

That trade is unnecessary, because the error report does not have to live in memory. Each malformed record can be written to a second output stream as it is found: memory stays bounded at one record, and the provider receives every line number. (A1) The costs are a second output to manage and the throughput the writes consume, but the error file is normally tiny — it is only large when the upload is genuinely corrupt, which is exactly when the provider needs it in full. The running total_errors count should be kept regardless, so that the summary can state the scale of the corruption even if the provider's tooling truncates the error file.

The recommendation is therefore to stream the errors out, and to fall back to a capped in-memory list only when no second output is available. In that fallback the report must say so: it must state that line numbers beyond the cap are missing while the total count remains exact, so that the provider knows how much of the report is absent rather than believing the report is complete. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Require either the arithmetic (40 GB against 8 GB, a factor of five) or an equivalent statement of impossibility. A candidate who proposes adding RAM or using a bigger machine has not engaged with the design and should be redirected; credit is not awarded for hardware. "Streaming" must be described as reading one record at a time with bounded state, not merely as "using a loop".

(b) Each fault needs its mechanism. For the trailing-newline fault, accept a description of the phantom final empty element; a candidate who says only "split is wrong" earns nothing. For the quoting fault, accept a prose description or code. A candidate who says "use the csv module" earns the description mark only if they also say what a CSV parser must do about quoted delimiters.

(c) The marks are for structure, not for library knowledge. Accept any single-pass function returning equivalent summary, error and count objects; a dictionary of tuples, a dictionary of lists, or a small class are all acceptable. Do not award the capped-list mark to a candidate who stores every malformed line, and do not award the parser mark to a candidate who still calls split(",") on a raw line. try/except, an explicit numeric test, or a regular expression are all acceptable for the validation mark. A candidate who reads the stream twice loses the single-pass mark even if the results are correct.

(d) The evaluation must name the conflict and then choose. A candidate who says "increase max_errors" has not engaged with the memory bound and should be capped at one mark. The strongest answers propose the second output stream; a candidate who defends the cap can still earn two marks if the loss of line numbers is stated explicitly and the exact count is retained. Do not accept "store the errors in a database" as a free answer — it is a second output stream in disguise, and it should be credited only if the candidate says that the writes are streamed rather than batched.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B4.1 Binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion and search cost
syllabus_ref: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs (HL only), B2.2 Data structures (binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion, search cost)
title: B4.1 Binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion and search cost
q_html:
A public library is building a catalogue system. Each book is identified by a numerical accession number, and the catalogue must support three operations: finding the record for a given accession number, adding a new accession number, and printing the whole catalogue in ascending order of accession number. The system designer decides to hold the accession numbers in a binary search tree. The figure shows two binary search trees, A and B, that were built from the same five accession numbers, with the insertion order used for each tree given above it. The height of a tree is taken to be the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. Answer all parts with reference to the figure, and justify each answer.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    State the in-order traversal of tree A, and explain why an in-order traversal of any binary search tree returns its keys in ascending order.

    (State)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine where the accession number 40 would be inserted in tree A, and state the height of the tree after that insertion.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Describe the steps needed to delete a node that has two children from a binary search tree, and apply your description to the deletion of the node holding 45 from tree A.

    (Describe)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The library's catalogue will eventually hold 200 000 accession numbers. Compare the greatest number of comparisons a search might need in a tree shaped like tree A with the greatest number it might need in a tree shaped like tree B, and comment on the practical significance of the difference.

    (Compare)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    A colleague suggests replacing the tree with a hash table, which would give constant-time lookup. Explain whether a hash table could satisfy all three of the operations the catalogue must support.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) An in-order traversal visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and applied to tree A it yields 20, 30, 35, 45, 50. (A1) The traversal is ascending because of the ordering property of a binary search tree: every key in the left subtree of a node is smaller than the node's key, and every key in the right subtree is larger. (M1) Visiting left, then node, then right therefore emits each key only after every smaller key in its subtree, and before every larger one, so the output is sorted whatever the shape of the tree.

(b) Insertion compares the new key with each node from the root downwards and moves left when the key is smaller and right when it is larger. Starting at 30, the key 40 is larger, so it goes right; at 45 it is smaller, so it goes left; at 35 it is larger, so it goes right, and the position is empty. (M1)(A1) The key 40 therefore becomes the right child of 35. (A1) That path visits four nodes, 30, 45, 35 and 40, so the height of the tree rises from 3 to 4.

(c) A node with two children cannot simply be removed, because the two subtrees would have to be reattached. The standard method is to replace the key being deleted with its in-order successor, which is the smallest key in its right subtree, and then delete that successor from the right subtree, where it is guaranteed to have at most one child. (M1)(A1) For tree A, the in-order successor of 45 is 50, since 50 is the only key in 45's right subtree and is therefore its smallest. (A1) The key at the node is overwritten with 50, and the original node holding 50, which is a leaf, is then removed. The resulting tree has root 30, left child 20, and right child 50 with left child 35, so its height is 3. (A1)

(d) In a tree shaped like A the height grows with the logarithm of the number of keys, because each comparison halves the range still to be searched. (M1) For 200 000 keys the height is about log2(200000), which is 17.6, so a search visits at most 18 nodes and needs at most 18 comparisons. (A1) In a tree shaped like B, each node has only one child, so the tree is a chain and a search may have to visit every node. (M1) For 200 000 keys that is 200 000 comparisons, which is roughly 11 000 times as many as the balanced shape needs. The practical significance is that the degenerate shape offers no improvement over scanning a list, so the choice of a tree delivers nothing unless the shape is controlled. (A1)

(e) A hash table computes the position of a key from the key itself, so lookup, insertion and deletion are all constant-time on average, and the three operations would be fast. (M1) However, the keys in a hash table are stored in an order determined by the hash function, not by the keys, so the third operation, printing the catalogue in ascending order of accession number, cannot be done without retrieving every key and sorting it, which costs O(n log n) each time. (A1) The hash table is therefore the better structure only if the ordered listing is not required, or if it is produced once and cached; as specified, it does not satisfy the third requirement. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) A1 for the correct sequence 20, 30, 35, 45, 50; M1 for the reason, which must refer to the ordering property and to visiting left, node, right. A candidate who lists the keys in the order they were inserted has not performed a traversal and scores 0 of 2. (b) M1 for comparing with 30, 45 and 35 in the right order; A1 for identifying 40 as the right child of 35; A1 for the height of 4. Accept a correct route that reaches the same position by a different description. A candidate who answers 3 has not noticed that the new path is longer than the old longest path, and scores 2 of 3. (c) M1 for the idea of replacing the deleted key with another key rather than removing the node; A1 for naming the in-order successor, or the equivalent predecessor, as the replacement; A1 for identifying 50 as the successor of 45 in this tree; A1 for the resulting tree and its height. A candidate who instead promotes 35 and reattaches 50 correctly should be given the last A1, since the predecessor method is equally valid. (d) M1 for the logarithmic height of a balanced tree; A1 for about 18 comparisons; M1 for the linear height of the chain; A1 for 200 000 comparisons together with a comment that recognises the practical consequence. Accept any answer that gives the two orders of growth correctly even if the arithmetic is approximate. (e) M1 for recognising that a hash table gives constant-time access; A1 for identifying that it provides no ordering; A1 for the conclusion that the ordered listing cannot be produced efficiently, with the cost stated. Do not accept an answer that rejects the hash table without a reason.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A3.2 Database design
syllabus_ref: A3.2 Database design, A3.3 Database programming, B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking
title: A3.2 Database design
q_html:
Migrating a policy administration system

An insurer administers 18 million policy records on a forty-year-old mainframe system written in COBOL, with data held in flat files and indexed by a bespoke access method. The system processes 240 000 transactions per night in a batch window and about 3 200 payment instructions per hour during the day. It is reliable but there are four staff in the country who can maintain it, all within ten years of retirement. The board has approved a migration to a relational database behind a service interface. Two proposals are on the table. Proposal A is a big-bang cutover on a single weekend: the new system is built in full, the old one is switched off, and if the new system fails the fallback is to restore the mainframe from the previous night's backup, which takes 14 hours. Proposal B is an incremental migration in which a facade routes each function either to the old or the new system, functions are moved one at a time, and both systems run in parallel until the last one is moved. The migration team estimates that dual running costs EUR 14 000 per month in additional infrastructure and that a reconciliation mismatch rate of 0.02% is achievable, each exception taking an average of 6 minutes to investigate. Analyst time is costed at EUR 65 per hour.

Using the case study, answer all four parts. Assume a month is 30 nights of batch processing.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why a big-bang cutover is a poor choice for this system, referring to specific figures in the case study rather than to general principles.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct an incremental migration plan. State the mechanism that routes each request, the order in which you would move functions and why that order, and how the two systems are kept consistent while both are live.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the total cost of nine months of dual running, including the analyst time spent on reconciliation. Show your working.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate the two proposals. If a failed big-bang cutover causes an 8-hour outage in which 3 200 payments per hour are missed and each missed payment costs EUR 120 in penalties and remediation, compare that with your answer to (c) and state which proposal you recommend.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The decisive figure is the fallback: restoring from the previous night's backup takes 14 hours, during which roughly $14 \times 3200 \approx 45\,000$ payment instructions are not processed. (A1) A single failed cutover therefore risks a full working day of missed payments on a book of 18 million policies. (A1)

The staff position removes the option of a leisurely recovery. Only four people can maintain the old system, so if the new system fails and the old one must be restored and then kept running, there is almost no capacity to diagnose and fix the new one. (A1)

There is also no way to validate the new system at full scale before committing: 240 000 transactions per night cannot be simulated faithfully enough to be confident, and the first genuine run would also be the production run. (A1)

(b) *Mechanism:* place a facade in front of both systems. Every request arrives at the facade, which inspects the function being invoked and routes it either to the mainframe or to the new service. Callers never know which is serving them, so functions can be moved one at a time and moved back if necessary. (M1)(A1)

*Order:* move the read-mostly reference functions first, then simple queries, then writes, and leave the nightly batch and the payment instruction generation until last. (A1) The reason is that a read that goes wrong is visible immediately and is cheap to reverse, whereas a write that goes wrong corrupts data that may not be discovered for weeks; and the batch window is the most complex and least reversible part of the system, so it should be migrated only when everything feeding it is already new. (A1)

*Consistency while both are live:* run both systems for each migrated function and compare their outputs automatically every night, logging any disagreement as an exception for an analyst. The mainframe remains the system of record until a function has run clean for a sustained period, at which point the new system becomes the record for that function and the old one stops being authoritative for it. (A1)

(c) Infrastructure: $9 \times 14\,000 = \text{EUR }126\,000$. (A1)

Exceptions per night: $0.02\% \times 240\,000 = 48$. (M1)
Time per night: $48 \times 6 = 288$ minutes $= 4.8$ hours. (A1)
Over nine months, $9 \times 30 = 270$ nights: $270 \times 4.8 = 1296$ hours, at EUR 65 per hour:
$$1296 \times 65 = \text{EUR }84\,240$$
Total: $126\,000 + 84\,240 = \text{EUR }210\,240$. (A1)

(d) A failed cutover misses $8 \times 3200 = 25\,600$ payments, costing (M1)
$$25\,600 \times 120 = \text{EUR }3\,072\,000.$$
Comparing with the EUR 210 240 for nine months of dual running, a single failure costs about (A1)
$$\frac{3\,072\,000}{210\,240} \approx 15$$
times as much as the entire incremental programme. (A1)

Recommendation: Proposal B. Even if one assumed a failure probability for the big-bang cutover as low as one in ten, its expected cost would be about EUR 307 000, still above the full cost of dual running, and the incremental route has the further advantages of keeping the old system available as a live fallback for every function not yet moved, of building operational confidence gradually, and of allowing the four remaining experts to be consulted steadily rather than in a crisis. The one real drawback is the nine-month cost of running both, which the calculation shows to be small relative to the risk avoided.

Markscheme notes

(a) The marks are for using the figures; general assertions about risk earn nothing. The 14-hour restore and the four maintainers are the two that matter most, and a candidate who cites only the size of the dataset has missed the point, since size alone is not the difficulty. (b) Award (M1) for the facade concept regardless of the name used; a candidate who proposes a hard switch per function without a routing layer has not solved the problem. The order mark requires a reason, and the reason must be about reversibility or blast radius rather than convenience. The consistency mark is for dual-running with automated comparison and a defined point at which authority transfers; a candidate who says the two databases are kept synchronised by replication should be asked how, given that the schemas differ. (c) Accept a total between EUR 200 000 and EUR 220 000 depending on the assumption about nights per month; award the method marks for the mismatch count and the conversion to cost. (d) The comparison must be quantitative. Credit a candidate who goes further and computes an expected value or a break-even failure probability, since that is the strongest form of the argument. A recommendation of Proposal A is not creditable given these figures, but a candidate who argues for a shorter dual-running period, say four months, on the grounds that the mismatch rate would fall as the new system stabilises, should be credited.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking
syllabus_ref: B1.1 (Approaches to computational thinking: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design)
title: Four jobs, one machine, and the order that looks efficient
q_html:
One machine, four jobs, and a promise about the worst one

A workshop has a single paint booth and four cars waiting. Only one car can be in the booth at a time, and once a car is started it must be finished. Each car has a painting time in hours and a promised collection time, counted in hours from now. The workshop does not care about the average wait. It cares about the worst case, because the manager is judged on the single most disappointed customer of the week.

The lateness of a job is the time it finishes minus its promised collection time, so a negative lateness means the job finished early. The objective is to make the largest lateness as small as possible, and a negative value is a success rather than a problem.

The four cars are: A takes 5 hours and is promised at hour 8; B takes 2 hours and is promised at hour 6; C takes 4 hours and is promised at hour 20; D takes 7 hours and is promised at hour 16. The booth starts empty at hour 0 and is never idle while jobs remain.

You are asked to choose the order in which the four cars enter the booth. Work in whole hours, and remember that a job's lateness is measured against its own promise and can be negative.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    The cars are currently processed in the order they were booked: A, then B, then C, then D. Determine the finishing time of each car and the largest lateness of that schedule.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Apply the shortest-job-first rule, that is, process the cars in increasing order of painting time, breaking any tie by the earlier promise. Give the resulting order, each finishing time, and the largest lateness of that schedule.

    (Apply)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Explain why the schedule that puts the car with the earliest promise first can never produce a larger worst-case lateness than the schedule you found in part (b), however the remaining cars are then arranged. Your explanation should identify the property of the worst-case objective that makes the exchange argument work.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    A fifth car, E, is added. E takes 3 hours and is promised at hour 9. Justify whether the earliest-promise-first order still achieves the smallest possible worst-case lateness for all five cars, and state the value it achieves.

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). The cars run back to back from hour 0, so each finishing time is the running total of the painting times.

A finishes at 0 + 5 = 5. B finishes at 5 + 2 = 7. C finishes at 7 + 4 = 11. D finishes at 11 + 7 = 18. (M1) for the running total, (A1) for all four finishing times.

The lateness of each car is its finishing time minus its own promise. A: 5 - 8 = -3. B: 7 - 6 = +1. C: 11 - 20 = -9. D: 18 - 16 = +2. (A1) The largest lateness is therefore +2, set by car D.

Part (b). The painting times are A 5, B 2, C 4, D 7, so increasing order is B (2), C (4), A (5), D (7). No ties arise, so the tie-break is not needed. (M1)

Finishing times: B at 2, C at 2 + 4 = 6, A at 6 + 5 = 11, D at 11 + 7 = 18. (A1)

Lateness: B is 2 - 6 = -4; C is 6 - 20 = -14; A is 11 - 8 = +3; D is 18 - 16 = +2. (A1) The largest lateness is +3, set by car A. (A1) So shortest-job-first is worse than the booking order, which is the surprising result the question is built on: it moved the worst lateness from +2 up to +3.

Part (c). The objective depends only on the largest lateness, so it is decided by a single job. Consider any schedule and suppose that, at some point, the job with the earliest promise among those not yet started is not the one that runs next. (M1) Let that job be X and let the job that actually runs be Y, which therefore has a promise no earlier than X's. Swap X and Y so that X runs in Y's slot and Y runs immediately after. (M1)

The jobs before the swap are untouched, and the jobs after the two swapped ones still finish at the same times, because the pair still occupies the same total length of time. So only X and Y can have their lateness changed. (A1) After the swap X finishes earlier than Y did, and its promise was no later than Y's, so X's lateness does not increase. Y finishes exactly when X used to finish, which is at most as late as Y's old finishing time, so Y's lateness does not increase either. (M1)

Every swap of this kind therefore leaves the largest lateness no larger than it was, and repeated swapping sorts the schedule into earliest-promise-first order without ever making the worst case worse. Since we started from an arbitrary schedule, no schedule can beat the earliest-promise-first order on this objective. (R1) This is exactly why the reasoning fails for the *average* lateness, where a short job delays fewer jobs and the trade is genuinely different.

Part (d). With E added, the promises are B 6, A 8, E 9, D 16, C 20, so the earliest-promise-first order is B, A, E, D, C. (M1)

Finishing times: B 2, A 7, E 10, D 17, C 21. Lateness: B -4, A -1, E 10 - 9 = +1, D 17 - 16 = +1, C 21 - 20 = +1. The largest lateness is +1. (A1)

The exchange argument of part (c) never used the number of jobs, only the fact that swapping an earlier-promise job forward cannot worsen either swapped job, so it applies unchanged to five jobs. (M1) The achieved value +1 is therefore the smallest possible worst-case lateness; a complete search of all 120 orders confirms that no order does better. (A1) Notice that adding E has turned a schedule that was comfortably early everywhere into one that is late on three jobs, which is a property of the job set rather than of the rule.

Markscheme notes

(a) M1 for treating finishing times as a running total; A1 for all four of 5, 7, 11, 18; A1 for the maximum lateness of +2. A candidate who reports the largest lateness as 2 without the sign is still credited, since the sign is a convention and the value is what is asked for; a candidate who writes -9 or -14 as the largest has compared magnitudes and forfeits the final A1.

(b) M1 for the order B, C, A, D. Award A1 for the finishing times 2, 6, 11, 18, A1 for the lateness values, and A1 for the maximum of +3. Follow-through is allowed: a candidate who produces a different order in (b) but reads a maximum lateness consistently off their own finishing times keeps the final A1. A candidate who gives the average lateness instead of the maximum forfeits that A1 and scores at most 3 of 4.

(c) M1 for identifying that the objective is decided by one job. M1 for the swap construction. A1 for the observation that the jobs after the pair are unaffected. M1 for showing that neither swapped job's lateness rises. R1 for the conclusion that repetition yields the earliest-promise-first order and that this proves optimality. Do not credit an answer that asserts optimality from the rule's name, or that argues only about the first job; the whole force of the argument is that the swap is safe for both jobs involved.

(d) M1 for the order B, A, E, D, C. A1 for the finishing times and the maximum lateness of +1. M1 for explicitly extending the exchange argument rather than re-asserting it. A1 for the justification that +1 is optimal. A candidate who claims the answer changes because the exchange argument depended on there being four jobs scores the M1s but not the A1s.

Across the question, accept any equivalent formulation of lateness provided the candidate is consistent about the sign.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.2 Data structures
syllabus_ref: B2.2 (Data structures: arrays, lists, stacks, queues, priority queues and trees, and the operations each supports)
title: Five thousand patients, one queue, and a question about the fifth
q_html:
Triage at a district hospital

A district hospital holds a waiting list of patients who have been assessed but not yet seen. Each patient has an integer acuity score, and a larger score means more urgent. Two things happen to the list.

The first is a lookup: a clinician asks for the patient who is currently the fifth most urgent, to decide whether the department can afford to take a less urgent case first. The second is an insertion: a newly assessed patient joins the list.

The list holds 4096 patients, and the department is choosing between two implementations. The first is a binary max-heap. The second keeps the patients in a single array held in descending order of acuity, so that position 0 is the most urgent patient and position k - 1 is the k-th most urgent.

For planning purposes treat a comparison or a movement of one element as one operation, take the cost of finding the largest element in a heap as one operation, and take the cost of restoring the heap after removing or adding one element as log base 2 of 4096, which is 12 operations. Inserting into the ordered array costs on average half the array, and a comparison sort of 4096 elements costs 4096 times 12 operations.

The department expects two different workloads and has not yet decided which one it will have. Workload X builds the list once and then performs 4096 lookups for the fifth most urgent patient. Workload Y performs 4096 rounds, where each round is one lookup for the fifth most urgent patient followed immediately by one insertion. You should count operations for both structures under both workloads.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the cost of one lookup for the fifth most urgent patient under each structure, and explain briefly why the two costs differ.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Calculate the total number of operations each structure needs for workload X, taking account of the cost of building the structure as well as the cost of the lookups. State which structure is cheaper and by what factor, to one decimal place.

    (Compare)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Carry out the same comparison for workload Y, and state which structure is cheaper for that workload.

    (Recommend)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    A colleague concludes from the two structures' usual descriptions that the heap must be the right choice because insertion is logarithmic rather than linear. Justify whether that reasoning is sufficient, referring to your answers in parts (b) and (c).

    (Justify)
a_html:
Part (a). In the max-heap the largest patient is at the root, but the fifth most urgent is not at any fixed position. To reach it you remove the largest patient, restore the heap, and repeat until five patients have come out; then you put the four removed patients back. Each removal costs 12 operations to restore the heap, so the lookup costs 5 x 2 x 12 = 120 operations. (M1) for the 12, (A1) for 120.

In the ordered array the patients are already in descending order, so the fifth most urgent is simply at index 4. Reading it costs 1 operation. (A1)

The costs differ because the heap is arranged by a *partial* order: it guarantees only that a parent is at least as urgent as its children, which is enough to place the single most urgent patient but says nothing about where the fifth belongs. The array is arranged by a *total* order, which places every patient, and that is what makes an arbitrary rank cheap to read. (A1)

Part (b). Workload X: 4096 lookups, each 120 operations, gives 4096 x 120 = 491 520 operations. (M1) Building the heap from 4096 patients costs 4096 operations. (A1) Total for the heap: 4096 + 491 520 = 495 616 operations.

For the ordered array, building means sorting, which costs 4096 x 12 = 49 152 operations. (A1) The 4096 lookups cost 4096 x 1 = 4096 operations. Total: 49 152 + 4096 = 53 248 operations. (M1)

The ordered array is cheaper, by 495 616 / 53 248 = 9.3 times to one decimal place. (A1)

Part (c). Workload Y: each round is a lookup followed by an insertion, and there are 4096 rounds.

For the heap, a round costs 120 + 12 = 132 operations, so the total is 4096 x 132 = 540 672 operations. (M1)(A1)

For the ordered array, a round costs 1 + 2048 = 2049 operations, because inserting into a sorted array of 4096 elements shifts half of it on average. The total is 4096 x 2049 = 8 392 704 operations. (M1) The heap is cheaper for this workload, by 8 392 704 / 540 672 = 15.5 times. (A1)

So the two structures swap places: the array wins workload X by 9.3 times and the heap wins workload Y by 15.5 times.

Part (d). The colleague's reasoning is not sufficient, because it is a statement about *insertion* alone and the two workloads do not weight insertion the same way. (M1) In workload X there are no insertions after the list is built, so the heap's logarithmic insertion is worth nothing and the array's constant-time rank lookup decides the whole comparison, which is why the array wins by 9.3 times. (A1) In workload Y every lookup is followed by an insertion, and there the linear insertion cost of the array dominates everything else, which is why the heap wins by 15.5 times. (A1) The conclusion the colleague should draw is that the heap's advantage is conditional on insertions being frequent relative to rank lookups, and the department must first know which workload it has.

Markscheme notes
