    State the value returned by the function for the input a = 377, b = 233, and state the value returned for the input a = 1000, b = 3.

    (State)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Explain what property of the pair (a, b) determines how many iterations the loop performs, and explain why the number of digits in a and b does not determine it.

    (Explain)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Determine the largest number of iterations the loop can perform for any input pair with 1 <= b <= a <= 1000, and state a pair of values that achieves it, justifying your answer in terms of the sequence of remainders.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) The loop returns the last non-zero value of b before the remainder reaches zero, which is the largest integer that divides both of the original inputs. For a = 377 and b = 233 the figure ends at the pair (1, 0), so the value returned is 1 (A1). For a = 1000 and b = 3 the pairs are (3, 1) and (1, 0), so the value returned is also 1 (A1). Both inputs therefore produce the same answer, and the number of iterations differs by a factor of six.

(b) The number of iterations is set by how quickly the pair of values shrinks, and that is set by the size of the quotient produced at each step. When a is much larger than b the first remainder is small, so the pair collapses in a step or two: at a = 1000, b = 3 the quotient is 333 and the remainder is 1, and the loop is over almost immediately (M1). When a is only slightly larger than b the quotient is 1 and the remainder is a minus b, so the pair (a, b) becomes (b, a minus b) and shrinks by only a small factor each time; in the trace for 377 and 233 every quotient is 1 and the values fall by the golden ratio, 377 to 233 to 144 to 89 and so on, which is the slowest shrinkage the loop can produce (A1). The number of digits is not the governing quantity because it only bounds how many halvings are available, and the actual count is usually far below that bound: two inputs of three digits can need two iterations or twelve, and the deciding factor is the ratio of the two numbers and how close the quotients come to 1, not how large the numbers are.

(c) The largest number of iterations is 14, attained by a = 987 and b = 610 (A1). The justification runs backwards through the loop. If the pair (a, b) with a greater than b takes n iterations, then after one iteration it becomes (b, a MOD b) and that pair takes n minus 1 iterations, so the smallest pair needing n iterations is obtained by making the quotient 1 at every step, which gives the backward recurrence a = b + c where c is the next value in the sequence (M1). Starting from the smallest possible end, the pair (1, 0), and reversing the rule gives (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 2), (5, 3), (8, 5) and so on: the Fibonacci sequence, in which the largest value is 987 at the sixteenth term. If a pair takes 14 iterations then its larger member is at least 987, so any pair with both values at most 1000 that needs 14 iterations must sit exactly at 987 and 610, and 15 iterations would require a larger member of at least 1597, which is above the limit. Checking the two candidates confirms it: the pair (987, 610) takes 14 iterations, while the pair (1000, 999) takes 2 and the pair (233, 144) takes 11 (A1). The same argument explains why the trace in the figure is the slow case for its size: 377 and 233 are the fourteenth and thirteenth Fibonacci numbers, so they are the worst pair below 400, and scaling them up to 987 and 610 keeps them the worst pair below 1000.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for 1 from the first input, with the final pair (1, 0) identified; (A1) for 1 from the second. The second mark is for the second value as well as the statement that both answers agree; a candidate who writes only one value scores at most one mark. Do not accept a candidate who reads the returned value as the number of iterations.

(b) (M1) for the observation that the size of the quotient at each step sets how fast the pair shrinks, with the contrast between a large quotient and a quotient of 1; (A1) for the statement that the count is fixed by the ratio of the inputs and how close the successive quotients come to 1, and that the number of digits only gives an upper bound that is usually not attained. A candidate who says only that the algorithm is logarithmic, or that larger inputs take longer, does not answer the question and scores nothing: the figure shows the larger inputs taking the fewer iterations.

(c) (A1) for 14 as the maximum; (M1) for the backward recurrence with a quotient of 1 at every step, from which the Fibonacci sequence follows; (A1) for 987 and 610 as an attaining pair, together with the check that 15 iterations would need a value above 1000. Accept 377 and 233 as the attaining pair for a limit of 400 if stated as such, but for a limit of 1000 the answer is 987 and 610. A candidate who gives 14 without deriving it, or who gives the number of digits as the bound, loses the middle mark.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2.2 A very sparse matrix held in a dense two-dimensional array, where the cost of the representation grows with the square of the order while the data grows linearly, and the unit-test scale is far too small to reveal it
syllabus_ref: B2.2 Data structures, with A1.1 Computer hardware and operation (main memory) and B2.4 Programming algorithms
title: B2.2 A very sparse matrix held in a dense two-dimensional array, where the cost of the representation grows with the square of the order while the data grows linearly, and the unit-test scale is far too small to reveal it
q_html:
Storage of a routing matrix at two scales

A delivery company precomputes travel times between every pair of nodes in its network and stores the result in a matrix whose entry in row i and column j is the travel time from node i to node j, or zero when no route between them exists. Almost every pair of nodes is not directly connected, so almost every entry of the matrix is zero. A single routine multiplies this matrix by a vector of node weights once per scheduling run. The team writes its unit tests against a small matrix of the same density, and then deploys the same code against the production matrix. The table gives the two matrices. Every entry is held as an 8-byte floating-point number, and the deployment target is a server with 64 GB of memory.

A sparse matrix is held in a dense two-dimensional array, and the same code is used for the unit tests and for production. The matrix, the two scales and the cost of one entry are given in the table. Answer all parts using the figures in the table.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the number of entries a dense two-dimensional array stores for each of the two matrices, and state the memory each array occupies in bytes and in gigabytes.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the memory a sparse representation requires if each non-zero entry is stored as an 8-byte value together with a 4-byte row index and a 4-byte column index, and express the result for the production matrix in megabytes.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the number of floating-point operations one matrix-vector product performs on the production matrix under each representation, state the time each takes if the processor performs 10^9 operations per second, and hence determine the ratio of the two.

    (Determine)
  4. [2 marks](d)

    Explain why the unit tests give no warning of the problem, and state one property of the data that a designer must check before choosing between the two representations.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) A dense array stores one cell for every pair of row and column indices, whether or not the entry is used. For the unit-test matrix that is
$$1000 \times 1000 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ entries},$$
and at 8 bytes per entry that is $1\,000\,000 \times 8 = 8\,000\,000$ bytes, which is 8 MB (M1)(A1). For the production matrix the same count is
$$200\,000 \times 200\,000 = 4 \times 10^{10} = 40\,000\,000\,000 \text{ entries},$$
and the memory is $4 \times 10^{10} \times 8 = 3.2 \times 10^{11}$ bytes, that is 320 GB (A1). The first array fits comfortably in the 64 GB server and the second one does not fit at all, which is the whole of the difficulty: the two counts differ by a factor of forty thousand because the order differs by a factor of two hundred, and the cost of a dense array goes as the square of the order.

(b) A sparse representation stores one record for each non-zero entry and nothing for the zeros. Each record needs $8 + 4 + 4 = 16$ bytes (M1). For the unit-test matrix that is $10 \times 16 = 160$ bytes, which is negligible (A1). For the production matrix it is
$$400\,000 \times 16 = 6\,400\,000 \text{ bytes} = 6.4 \text{ MB},$$
which is one hundred thousand times smaller than the 320 GB the dense array would need and fits in the server with room to spare (A1). The comparison is worth stating in both directions: the sparse form is not merely smaller, it is smaller by a factor of
$$\frac{3.2 \times 10^{11}}{6.4 \times 10^{6}} = 50\,000,$$
so the two representations are not two ways of doing the same thing. One of them is possible and the other is not.

(c) A dense matrix-vector product performs one multiply and one add for every entry of the array, because the code cannot know which entries are zero without looking at them:
$$200\,000 \times 200\,000 = 4 \times 10^{10} \text{ operations}.$$
At $10^{9}$ operations per second that is 40 seconds for a single multiplication (M1). A sparse product touches only the stored entries, so it performs one multiply and one add per non-zero entry:
$$400\,000 \text{ operations},$$
which at the same rate takes $400\,000 / 10^{9} = 4 \times 10^{-4}$ seconds, that is 0.4 milliseconds (A1). The ratio is
$$\frac{4 \times 10^{10}}{4 \times 10^{5}} = 100\,000,$$
so the sparse product is one hundred thousand times cheaper in arithmetic as well as fifty thousand times cheaper in memory (M1)(A1). The two ratios are not equal because memory is charged per cell while arithmetic is charged per non-zero entry, and the dense form pays the first cost for every cell it holds and the second for every cell it visits.

(d) The unit tests give no warning because the property that makes the dense array unusable is the one property the tests hold fixed. Both matrices have the same density, about 0.001 per cent, and the test matrix is small enough that its dense form is 8 MB and allocates and runs in about a millisecond (M1). Every test therefore passes, and the suite is evidence about the correctness of the indexing arithmetic rather than about the cost of the representation. The property a designer must check is the density, and specifically whether it stays small as the order grows: the decision rule is to compare the number of non-zero entries with the square of the order, and to choose the sparse form whenever the first is much smaller than the second (A1). A useful discipline is to test at the largest order the system will ever see, or at least to assert the density in a test, because a test suite that only exercises the small case cannot distinguish a representation that scales from one that does not.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for multiplying the two dimensions rather than adding them, (A1) for $1\,000\,000$ entries and 8 MB for the unit-test matrix, (A1) for $4 \times 10^{10}$ entries and 320 GB for the production matrix. A candidate who answers $400\,000$ entries for the production matrix has counted the non-zero entries and answered part (b) instead of part (a); that scores no mark here even though the number is correct for the other question. Accept the memory in either bytes or gigabytes provided the unit is stated.

(b) (M1) for the 16 bytes per record, with the three components identified, (A1) for $160$ bytes at the test scale, (A1) for $6\,400\,000$ bytes, which is 6.4 MB, at the production scale. Accept a candidate who stores the row index only and relies on the records being grouped by row, provided the assumption is stated, but the memory total must be recomputed consistently with that choice. The comparison with the dense figure is not required for the marks but is expected in a good answer.

(c) (M1) for the dense operation count as the square of the order, (A1) for 40 seconds at the stated rate, (A1) for the sparse count as the number of non-zero entries, (A1) for the ratio of 100 000. A candidate who writes the sparse count as $200\,000$ rather than $400\,000$ has confused the order with the number of non-zero entries and loses the final (A1) but keeps the method marks. Follow-through: a candidate whose operation counts are wrong but whose ratio is computed consistently from them keeps the final mark.

(d) (M1) for the observation that the test matrix is small and therefore cheap in dense form, or equivalently that both matrices have the same density so the test exercises nothing that changes with scale, (A1) for naming the density, or the ratio of non-zero entries to the square of the order, as the property to check. An answer that says only 'the tests were too small' without identifying what the tests failed to vary scores (M1) only. Do not accept 'the server needs more memory' as the property to check: that is a remedy, not a property of the data.

Forfeits: treating the matrix as dense in part (b) and quoting the part (a) figures again; quoting the memory ratio of 50 000 as the answer to part (c), which mixes the two currencies; and answering part (d) with a statement about test coverage in general rather than about the density of the data.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 6.6 Decision trees and 6.7 Descriptive statistics
syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.6 Decision trees and 6.7 Descriptive statistics (the SL Toolkit). P2 Section B.
title: A mean that says grow and a spread that says do not
q_html:
Foxglove Bakery

Foxglove Bakery runs a single shop in a market town and is considering a second outlet. Two sites are available on the same high street: a small kiosk, which would cost EUR 40,000 to fit out, and a large cafe, which would cost EUR 120,000. Both would be financed by a bank loan at 6% a year, and the directors compare annual profit after interest.

The directors have two sets of profit forecasts, before interest, for each option. If demand is high, the kiosk would make EUR 40,000 a year and the cafe EUR 120,000. If demand is low, the kiosk would still make EUR 10,000, but the cafe would lose EUR 60,000 a year.

The finance director has assumed a 0.6 probability of high demand, based on her reading of the local economy. The marketing director disagrees. She has collected the daily customer numbers from a trial stall that traded in the same high street, with the same opening hours, for twelve months. Her figures are in the table, and she defines a high-demand month as one in which the stall served more than 80 customers a day.

The directors of Foxglove Bakery must decide whether to open a kiosk or a cafe as the second outlet.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Using the table, calculate the mean, the median and the range of daily customers, and comment on how well the mean represents a typical month.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Estimate the probability of a high-demand month from the trial data. Then calculate the expected annual profit after interest of each option using the finance director's probability and using your estimate.

    (Calculate)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Evaluate which option Foxglove Bakery should choose. Justify your answer with reference to your decision tree and to the descriptive statistics.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The twelve monthly figures are 40, 45, 38, 42, 120, 130, 125, 44, 41, 118, 135 and 46, giving a total of 924 customers a day across the months. (M1)

Mean = 924/12 = 77 customers a day. (A1)

Ordered, the two middle values are 45 and 46, so the median = (45 + 46)/2 = 45.5 customers a day. (A1)

Range = 135 - 38 = 97 customers a day. (A1)

The mean is a poor summary of a typical month. It is 31.5 customers a day above the median, and no month was close to it: five months clustered near 42 and five near 125, with the remaining two between. The distribution is bimodal, not symmetrical, so the mean describes a month that never happened. (A1)

(b) High-demand months are those above 80 customers a day: months 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11, so five of twelve. The trial estimate of the probability of high demand is 5/12 = 0.417. (M1)(A1)

Using the finance director's 0.6: kiosk = 0.6 x 40,000 + 0.4 x 10,000 = EUR 28,000; cafe = 0.6 x 120,000 + 0.4 x (-60,000) = EUR 48,000. (M1)(A1)

Interest: kiosk loan 40,000 x 6% = EUR 2,400; cafe loan 120,000 x 6% = EUR 7,200. Net expected profit: kiosk EUR 25,600; cafe EUR 40,800. (A1)

Using the trial estimate of 5/12: kiosk = (5/12) x 40,000 + (7/12) x 10,000 = EUR 22,500; cafe = (5/12) x 120,000 + (7/12) x (-60,000) = EUR 15,000. After interest: kiosk EUR 20,100; cafe EUR 7,800. (A1)

The two probabilities therefore rank the options differently.

(c) Indicative evaluation. On the finance director's probability the decision is straightforward. The cafe's expected profit of EUR 40,800 is more than half as much again as the kiosk's EUR 25,600, and the upside, EUR 120,000 in a good year, is the kind of return that would justify the larger loan. A decision tree drawn on a 0.6 chance of high demand points clearly to the cafe.

The descriptive statistics undermine the probability the tree uses. The mean of 77 customers a day is not a typical month: it sits between two clusters, and the median of 45.5 is the better guide to what most months look like. Five of the twelve months were high-demand, so the empirical probability is 0.417, not 0.6. Rerun with 5/12, the ranking reverses: the kiosk earns EUR 20,100 against the cafe's EUR 7,800. The kiosk is also the more robust choice, because its worst case is a profit of EUR 10,000 while the cafe's is a loss of EUR 60,000, half the size of the whole investment.

The evaluation therefore turns on the probability, and the probability is the one thing the directors cannot observe. If the town's economy really does deliver high demand six years in ten, the cafe is right; if the trial stall is representative, the cafe destroys value in most years and the interest payment makes the bad case worse. The strongest answers note that a decision tree is only as good as its probabilities, that the trial was one stall in one year, and that opening the kiosk first keeps the option open. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1)(A1) for the mean, (A1) for the median and (A1) for the range. The comment mark requires the candidate to notice that the mean is well above the median and that the data are bimodal; a candidate who says only that the mean is 77 forfeits it. Accept 45.5 for the median.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for identifying the five high-demand months and the probability of 5/12; accept 0.42 or 41.7%. Award (M1)(A1) for the two expected profits on the 0.6 probability and (A1) for the interest and net profits; then (A1) for the two expected profits on 5/12 and their net values. Follow through on arithmetic slips, but a candidate who omits the interest in one option and not the other cannot reach the evaluation marks.

(c) The discriminating marks are for rerunning the expected values with the empirical probability and for noticing that the ranking reverses. A candidate who reports the mean of 77 and recommends the cafe cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that chooses the cafe only if it is justified by evidence about the local economy rather than by the finance director's assumption. Do not credit answers about the cafe's menu or staffing.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.2 The output of a flow line is set by its slowest stage, so adding capacity anywhere else produces nothing, and the choice between buying capacity at the bottleneck and buying overtime at the bottleneck is a choice between a fixed cost and a variable one
syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.2 Operations methods (flow production and the capacity of a line of dependent stages), with 3.3 Costs and revenues and 5.1 The role of operations management
title: 5.2 The output of a flow line is set by its slowest stage, so adding capacity anywhere else produces nothing, and the choice between buying capacity at the bottleneck and buying overtime at the bottleneck is a choice between a fixed cost and a variable one
q_html:
A four-stage flow line

A manufacturer makes a single product on a flow line of four stages, in the order cutting, welding, assembly and finishing. Each stage is worked by one machine, and the product passes through all four stages in that order. Each machine is available for 2 400 minutes in a working week. The table gives the time each stage takes to process one unit. The machines are not shared, so a machine that is idle at one stage cannot be used to relieve a stage that is behind. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer is currently unable to meet it, which is costing sales.

The manufacturer's four-stage line has one machine at each stage, and each machine is available for 2 400 minutes a week. The times per unit are given in the table. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer cannot meet it, so it is losing sales that it could otherwise make. The operations manager has two proposals. The first is to buy a second welding machine at a cost of 85 000 dollars, which would halve the time the welding stage takes per unit, and which would be depreciated over five years. The second is to work overtime at whichever stage is limiting output, at an overtime rate of 36 dollars an hour, which is available whenever it is needed and can be stopped at any time. The operations manager has also considered buying a second assembly machine and has asked what difference that would make, since assembly takes four minutes a unit and is the stage the manager believed to be the problem.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the weekly capacity of each of the four stages, and state which stage has the smallest capacity.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the maximum number of units the line can produce in a week at present, and the shortfall against the weekly demand of 600 units.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second assembly machine, showing the capacity of every stage after the change.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second welding machine, and explain why the two answers in (c) and (d) differ.

    (Determine)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    Evaluate whether the manufacturer should buy the welding machine or pay for overtime, using the weekly costs of each and considering the manufacturer's circumstances.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The weekly capacity of a stage is the minutes available divided by the minutes each unit takes at that stage. With 2 400 minutes available at every stage:

Cutting: 2 400 / 3.0 = 800 units a week.
Welding: 2 400 / 5.0 = 480 units a week.
Assembly: 2 400 / 4.0 = 600 units a week.
Finishing: 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week.

The welding stage has the smallest capacity, at 480 units a week.

(b) A unit must pass through all four stages, so the line can produce no more units in a week than its slowest stage can pass. Welding is the slowest stage at 480 units a week, so the maximum weekly output is 480 units. Demand is 600 units a week, so the shortfall is 600 - 480 = 120 units a week, and those 120 units of sales are lost every week.

The other stages are not working at their limit. At an output of 480 units a week, cutting is using 480 x 3.0 = 1 440 of its 2 400 minutes, which is sixty per cent of its capacity; assembly is using 480 x 4.0 = 1 920 minutes, which is eighty per cent; and finishing is using 480 x 2.5 = 1 200 minutes, which is fifty per cent. Welding is using all 2 400 minutes, which is one hundred per cent.

(c) A second assembly machine halves the time assembly takes per unit, from 4.0 minutes to 2.0 minutes, so the capacity of assembly becomes 2 400 / 2.0 = 1 200 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 480 at welding, 1 200 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is still welding, at 480 units a week, so the output of the line does not change. It remains 480 units a week and the shortfall remains 120 units a week. The money spent on the second assembly machine buys no additional output at all, because assembly was not limiting the line; the 120 extra units a week that the second machine could pass through cannot reach it, since welding cannot send them on.

(d) A second welding machine halves the time welding takes per unit, from 5.0 minutes to 2.5 minutes, so the capacity of welding becomes 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 960 at welding, 600 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is now assembly, at 600 units a week, so the output of the line rises to 600 units a week, which is exactly the demand. The shortfall is closed. Welding is no longer the constraint and has spare capacity of 360 units a week; cutting is now the next tightest stage after assembly, at 800 units a week.

The two answers differ because output is governed by the slowest stage and by nothing else. In (c) the stage that was improved was not the slowest stage, so the line's output was still set by welding and did not move. In (d) the stage that was improved was the slowest stage, so the constraint moved to assembly and the output rose until it reached the new limit. Improving a stage that is not the constraint does not raise output; it only adds idle capacity to a stage that already had some. This is why the operations manager's belief that assembly was the problem was mistaken: assembly takes four minutes a unit, which is longer than cutting and longer than finishing, but welding takes five, and it is the longest time per unit that sets the pace.

(e) Either route closes the 120-unit shortfall, and the choice turns on the shape of the cost rather than on the size of it.

Overtime at the welding stage costs 36 dollars an hour. To make 120 extra units at 5.0 minutes a unit requires 120 x 5.0 = 600 minutes, which is 10 hours a week. At 36 dollars an hour that is 360 dollars a week, or 18 720 dollars a year. Overtime is a variable cost: it is paid only when the extra output is wanted, and it can be stopped in a week in which demand falls.

The welding machine costs 85 000 dollars depreciated over five years, which is 17 000 dollars a year, or about 326.92 dollars a week. It is a fixed cost: it is incurred every week whether the extra 120 units are made or not, and it commits the manufacturer for five years.

On cost alone the machine is slightly cheaper, at about 326.92 dollars a week against 360 dollars a week, which is about 2.72 dollars per extra unit against 3.00 dollars. Over five years the saving is roughly 1 720 dollars a year, about 8 600 dollars in total, which is small against an outlay of 85 000 dollars, and the payback on the machine is very long if it is justified only by the shortfall. The machine does have advantages beyond the weekly cost. It raises welding capacity to 960 units a week, so it leaves room for demand to grow to 600 units without any further spending, whereas overtime has to be paid for every extra unit and becomes more expensive if demand rises. It also removes the dependence on staff being willing to work overtime week after week, which is difficult to sustain and which raises the risk of absence and of poor quality on a tired shift.

Against that, the machine is a commitment. If demand falls, the 85 000 dollars is spent and the depreciation continues, while overtime can be cancelled. The manufacturer's position is not stated in the case, and the recommendation has to turn on it.

On the information given, the manufacturer should pay the overtime in the first instance, and revisit the machine if demand rises or proves to be permanent. The shortfall is 120 units a week, which is twenty per cent of demand, and the cost difference between the two routes is small enough, about 33 dollars a week, that it does not by itself justify an 85 000-dollar commitment. Overtime keeps the manufacturer flexible while it establishes whether the extra demand is durable, and it can be replaced by the machine once the demand has been shown to be permanent. The machine becomes the better choice as soon as demand is expected to rise towards the new welding capacity of 960 units, or as soon as the overtime proves difficult to staff; at that point the fixed cost is being spread over a larger output and the flexibility that overtime buys is no longer worth its price.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the correct method, minutes available divided by minutes per unit, one mark for the four capacities 800, 480, 600 and 960, and one mark for identifying welding as the smallest. Follow-through is allowed from one arithmetic slip if the identification is consistent with the candidate's own figures.

(b) One mark for the output of 480 units a week, one mark for the shortfall of 120, and one mark for the reason, that output is limited by the slowest stage. A candidate who adds the stage capacities or takes the average has not understood the line and scores zero for this part.

(c) One mark for the new assembly capacity of 1 200 units a week, one mark for the statement that output is unchanged at 480 units a week, and one mark for the reason, that welding is still the slowest stage. An answer that reports a rise in output because assembly capacity has risen scores zero for this part, however correct the arithmetic.

(d) One mark for the new welding capacity of 960 units a week, one mark for the new output of 600 units a week with assembly as the new constraint, and one mark for the explanation that improving the constraint moves the constraint while improving any other stage changes nothing. Accept 600 units as the output because it matches demand; a candidate who states that assembly now limits the line at 600 units a week has the point even if the answer is expressed as 'up to 600'.

(e) No mark for naming a route. One mark for the correct weekly costs, overtime at 360 dollars a week or 18 720 dollars a year and the machine at about 326.92 dollars a week or 17 000 dollars a year, one mark for identifying the machine as the fixed cost and overtime as the variable one and drawing the consequence for flexibility, and one mark for a recommendation that states what would change it. A candidate who recommends the machine because it is cheaper per week takes two marks only if the flexibility argument is also addressed; the cost difference alone, at about 33 dollars a week, does not settle the question.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.4 / 3.8 / 6.3 Reshoring decision with landed cost and working capital effects
syllabus_ref: 5.4 (Location), 3.8 (Investment appraisal), 6.3 (STEEPLE analysis)
title: 5.4 / 3.8 / 6.3 Reshoring decision with landed cost and working capital effects
q_html:
Vantar

Vantar makes technical outdoor clothing. It currently manufactures 180 000 units a year in a low-wage economy and sells them online and through a small number of independent retailers at a retail price of €59. The lead time from placing an order to having stock available is 62 days, which forces Vantar to commit to its whole season's production before it knows what will sell. The operations director has costed a move to a domestic factory: the unit production cost would be higher, but the lead time would fall to 9 days, which would allow the company to make small reorders during the season. The finance director has calculated that the average value of finished-goods stock would fall from €2.10m to €0.72m, and the company's annual cost of holding stock is 18% of its value. Vantar's marketing manager estimates that 4% of units are currently sold at an average markdown of 35% because the wrong sizes were committed to. The cost data are given below.

Using the case study and the cost data, answer all three parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the total landed cost per unit for the offshore option and for the domestic option, and calculate the increase in annual production cost if Vantar reshores.

    (Calculate)
  2. [6 marks](b)

    Evaluate whether Vantar should move production to the domestic factory, taking into account the effect on stockholding and the markdowns described in the case study.

    (Evaluate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    To what extent do factors other than cost determine the right decision for Vantar? Refer to at least two external factors in your answer.

    (To what extent)
a_html:
(a) Offshore: $\text{CIF}=14.00+1.20=\unicode{8364}15.20$; the tariff is $12\%$ of $\unicode{8364}15.20=\unicode{8364}1.82$; adding $\unicode{8364}0.30$ handling gives a landed cost of $\unicode{8364}17.32$ per unit. (M1)(A1) Domestic: $21.50+0.25=\unicode{8364}21.75$ per unit. (A1) The increase is $\unicode{8364}4.43$ per unit, so across $180\,000$ units the annual production cost rises by $4.426\times180\,000=\unicode{8364}796\,680$, about $\unicode{8364}797\,000$. (M1)(A1)

(b) On unit cost alone the move looks wrong: $\unicode{8364}4.43$ is a $25.5\%$ increase in the cost of every item. (A1) Two effects work against that conclusion. First, average stock falls from $\unicode{8364}2.10$ m to $\unicode{8364}0.72$ m, a release of $\unicode{8364}1.38$ m, and at an annual holding cost of $18\%$ that saves $1.38\times0.18=\unicode{8364}248\,400$ a year. (M1)(A1) Second, a nine-day lead time allows reorders during the season rather than a single pre-commitment, so the markdown problem largely disappears: $4\%$ of $180\,000$ units is $7\,200$ units, currently discounted by $35\%$ of $\unicode{8364}59$, which is about $\unicode{8364}148\,700$ of lost margin a year. (M1)(A1) Together these recover about $\unicode{8364}397\,000$, so the net additional cost is roughly $\unicode{8364}797\,000-\unicode{8364}397\,000=\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year, or $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit — about $3.8\%$ of the $\unicode{8364}59$ retail price, not the $25\%$ headline figure. (A1)

Against that residual cost must be set a shorter cash cycle, far less risk of being left with a season's worth of unwanted stock, and the marketing value of being able to promote a domestic supply chain. (A1) A balanced evaluation is that the move is financially defensible if Vantar can recover $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit through a modest price rise or through the higher full-price sell-through that reordering makes possible, and it is not defensible if the market will not bear any increase at all. The decisive question is therefore not cost but price elasticity, which the data do not give. (R1)

(c) To a considerable extent, because the cost gap after the stock and markdown effects is small enough that external factors can easily dominate it. (A1) *Political:* the offshore option depends on a $12\%$ tariff that a trade dispute could raise overnight; a five-point increase would add about $\unicode{8364}0.76$ to every unit and close a third of the remaining gap by itself, and this risk is entirely outside Vantar's control. (M1)(A1) *Environmental and ethical:* the company sells technical outdoor clothing to customers who are unusually attentive to provenance, and a domestic supply chain with a much shorter transport leg is a marketing asset that does not appear in the cost comparison at all; conversely, moving production offshore to a jurisdiction with weaker labour protections would carry reputational risk that could cost more than $\unicode{8364}400\,000$. (M1)(A1) *Economic:* a domestic factory removes exposure to freight-cost volatility and to currency movement on a $\unicode{8364}2.52$ m annual import bill. (A1) The counter-argument is that $\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year is real money and that none of these factors is certain, so the decision remains finely balanced; but where the quantified gap is under four per cent of retail price, factors that cannot be quantified will usually decide it. (R1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) allow €17.30 to €17.35 and €21.70 to €21.80, and credit the tariff calculation shown even if the final addition is wrong. The annual increase should be about €797,000; allow €795,000 to €800,000. In (b) the evaluation mark requires the candidate to bring in both the stockholding saving and the markdown saving; an evaluation based on unit cost alone is capped at three, and one based on unit cost plus stockholding but not markdowns is capped at four. Allow a range of about €390,000 to €410,000 for the net cost, since candidates may treat the markdown recovery differently. In (c) any two of the STEEPLE factors are acceptable provided each is applied to Vantar specifically rather than described in the abstract; a generic list of external factors with no application earns at most two marks. In (b) a candidate may reasonably question the 18% holding cost or the assumption that the whole stock reduction is achieved in the first year; both are fair challenges and should be credited where they are explained, since the case study presents them as estimates rather than facts. Do not, however, credit a rejection of the markdown saving on the grounds that it is uncertain: it is quantified in the stimulus and is the whole reason the lead-time reduction has value.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.5 A contract that crosses the relevant range: the range of order sizes for which a positive contribution still destroys profit
syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.5 Break-even analysis (contribution, break-even output, margin of safety, the limitations of break-even analysis and the relevant range); 3.3 Costs and revenues
title: 5.5 A contract that crosses the relevant range: the range of order sizes for which a positive contribution still destroys profit
q_html:
Kestrel Foods Ltd: a contract offer and the relevant range

Kestrel Foods Ltd makes and sells one chilled dessert. The selling price is £25 per unit and the variable cost per unit is £13. Fixed costs are £48 000 per month for output up to and including 6 000 units per month. Output above 6 000 units in any month requires a second production shift, which adds £18 000 per month to fixed costs; no other cost changes at that point. Current output and sales are 4 000 units per month, all sold at £25.

A national retailer has offered to buy q units per month for one year at a price of £20 per unit. The retailer distributes in a region where Kestrel does not currently sell, so the contract displaces none of the existing sales, and Kestrel has enough spare capacity on the first shift to supply any contract size the retailer names. The finance director argues that the contract must be accepted because every unit sold at £20 still adds to contribution.

The graph shows Kestrel's monthly profit plotted against the size of the contract. Answer every part with reference to the relevant range, and give money answers to the nearest pound and output answers to the nearest whole unit.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the contribution per unit at the current selling price, the monthly break-even output, and Kestrel's current monthly profit.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the contribution per unit on the contract, and Kestrel's monthly profit if a contract for 2 500 units per month is accepted.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the range of contract sizes, if any, for which accepting the contract would leave Kestrel with a lower monthly profit than it earns now, and determine the smallest contract size at which crossing into the second shift becomes worthwhile.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The retailer's final offer is 2 500 units per month for one year. Evaluate the finance director's claim that the contract must be accepted because every unit adds to contribution, and recommend one change to the terms that would make the contract worth accepting.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Contribution per unit at the current price is £25 − £13 = £12 (A1). Break-even output is fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit, £48 000 ÷ £12 = 4 000 units per month (M1)(A1). Current output is exactly 4 000 units, so the current monthly profit is 4 000 × £12 − £48 000 = £0: the business is precisely at break-even.
(b) On the contract the price is £20, so the contribution per unit is £20 − £13 = £7 (A1). A contract of 2 500 units takes total output to 4 000 + 2 500 = 6 500 units, which is above the 6 000-unit ceiling of the first shift, so fixed costs rise to £48 000 + £18 000 = £66 000 (M1). Total contribution is 4 000 × £12 + 2 500 × £7 = £48 000 + £17 500 = £65 500, so the monthly profit becomes £65 500 − £66 000 = −£500 (A1). Kestrel would move from breaking even to losing £500 a month.
(c) Let q be the contract size. While 4 000 + q ≤ 6 000, that is q ≤ 2 000, no second shift is needed and profit is 7q, which is positive for every q > 0 (M1). Once q > 2 000 the extra £18 000 of fixed cost is incurred, so profit is 7q − 18 000, which is negative for q < 18 000 ÷ 7 = 2 571.43, that is up to and including 2 571 units (M1)(A1). The contract therefore leaves Kestrel worse off than it is now for every size from 2 001 to 2 571 units inclusive (A1), and the smallest size at which the step repays its own cost is 2 572 units, where profit is 7 × 2 572 − 18 000 = £4 (A1). Profit is not monotonic in the size of the contract: 2 000 units earns £14 000, 2 001 units loses £3 993, and 2 572 units earns £4.
(d) The director's claim is true of the unit and false of the decision. Each contract unit does add £7, but the relevant comparison is not between £7 and zero; it is between the £17 500 the contract contributes and the £18 000 of fixed cost that exists only because the contract was taken (M1). At 2 500 units the contract therefore reduces profit from £0 to −£500 a month, and because the contract runs for a year the loss is about −£6 000 over its life, before any allowance for the disruption of running a second shift for twelve months (A1). Two things qualify this. First, the arithmetic is knife-edge: a loss of £500 a month is 0.8% of monthly contribution, so a small change in the terms reverses the answer, and the business may rationally accept a marginal loss to secure a national listing (A1). Second, the loss is a property of the size and not of the idea: the contract is profitable below 2 001 units and above 2 571 units. The recommendation is to renegotiate one of the two (M1). At 2 500 units the contribution per unit must satisfy 2 500c ≥ 18 000, so c ≥ £7.20 and the price must be at least £20.20; alternatively the contract should be capped at 2 000 units or raised to at least 2 572 units (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for £12, (M1) for dividing fixed costs by contribution, (A1) for 4 000 units and £0. Accept break-even quoted as £100 000 of revenue if the unit figure accompanies it.
(b) (A1) for £7, (M1) for noticing that 6 500 units exceeds the 6 000-unit ceiling and adding £18 000, (A1) for −£500. A candidate who computes £17 500 of contribution and ignores the step scores at most one of the three; this is the whole item, so do not award follow-through from it.
(c) (M1) for treating the two ranges separately, (M1) for solving 7q ≥ 18 000, (A1) for the closed range 2 001 to 2 571 units, (A1) for 2 572 units. Accept 2 571.4 units quoted as the break-even size provided the candidate then rounds *up* to 2 572 for the smallest whole-unit size; a candidate who rounds down to 2 571 has not answered the question and loses the final mark.
(d) (M1) for comparing £17 500 with £18 000 rather than with zero, (A1) for the conclusion that the contract as offered reduces profit, (A1) for a developed qualitative point such as the twelve-month commitment or the strategic value of the listing, (M1)(A1) for a recommendation supported by a figure — £20.20, 2 000 units or 2 572 units. Do not credit 'accept because contribution is positive' however well argued; the question asks for an evaluation of that claim, not a restatement of it.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 4.4 Non-response that is not random: recovering the population figure from two segment readings instead of from the pooled sample
syllabus_ref: Unit 4: 4.4 Market research (sampling methods, the reliability of market research data, and the difference between primary and secondary research); 4.1 The role of marketing
title: 4.4 Non-response that is not random: recovering the population figure from two segment readings instead of from the pooled sample
q_html:
Northgate Leisure: the climbing wall survey

Northgate Leisure runs a leisure centre with 400 members. It is deciding whether to build a climbing wall, and posts a questionnaire to all of them asking whether they would use it.

The membership has two segments. There are 100 premium members, who pay a higher monthly fee and visit at least twice a week, and 300 standard members, who pay the basic fee. Of the 100 premium members, 80 return the questionnaire. Of the 300 standard members, 90 return it.

Among the 80 premium respondents, 56 say they would use the climbing wall. Among the 90 standard respondents, 36 say they would use it. The marketing manager writes in her report that a majority of members want the climbing wall, and recommends that the board approve it.

The chart compares the composition of the membership with the composition of the achieved sample. Use the data to answer the following.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the response rate for each segment and for the survey as a whole, and use them to show that the achieved sample is not representative of the membership.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the percentage of all respondents who said they would use the climbing wall, and state the conclusion the marketing manager draws from it.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Using the known size of each segment, determine a weighted estimate of the percentage of all 400 members who would use the wall, and hence estimate how many members that is. Explain why this figure differs from the one in part (b), and why the direction of the difference could have been predicted before any calculation.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the marketing manager's claim that a majority of members want the climbing wall, and recommend how Northgate should have run or reported the survey so that the claim could be tested.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Premium response rate: 80 ÷ 100 = 80%. Standard response rate: 90 ÷ 300 = 30%. Overall: 170 ÷ 400 = 42.5% (M1)(A1). Premium members are a quarter of the membership, 100 ÷ 400 = 25%, but they are 80 of the 170 responses, which is 47.1% of the achieved sample (A1). A sample in which one segment is represented at nearly twice its true weight is not representative, and the cause is visible in the response rates: premium members were more than two and a half times as likely to reply.
(b) Of the 170 responses, 56 + 36 = 92 said they would use the wall, so the pooled figure is 92 ÷ 170 = 54.1% (M1)(A1). The manager concludes that a majority — more than half — of members want the climbing wall, and recommends approval (A1).
(c) Weight each segment's approval rate by its share of the membership. Premium approval is 56 ÷ 80 = 70% and standard approval is 36 ÷ 90 = 40%. The weighted estimate is 0.25 × 70% + 0.75 × 40% = 17.5% + 30% = 47.5% (M1)(A1), which is 0.475 × 400 = 190 of the 400 members (A1). The pooled figure is higher because the sample contains too many premium members, and premium members are the segment that wants the wall most: 70% against 40%, a gap of thirty percentage points. The direction of the error was predictable before any arithmetic, because the segment with the higher response rate is also the segment with the higher approval rate, so self-selection must inflate the pooled answer (A1).
(d) The claim is not supported. The weighted estimate is 47.5%, which is below half, and 190 of 400 members is 10 short of a majority (M1). Two things qualify this. First, 47.5% is itself an estimate resting on the assumption that non-respondents in each segment resemble respondents in that segment — an assumption the data cannot test, and one that is least safe here, since people who did not bother to answer a questionnaire about a climbing wall may be people who do not want a climbing wall (A1). Second, the commercial case may not need a majority: if premium members generate most of the revenue and 70% of them want the wall, the board might rationally build it anyway (A1). The recommendation is to re-run the survey so that the answer can be tested rather than assumed: weight the responses, or use quota sampling with a target of 100 premium and 300 standard members, follow up non-respondents, and report the result by segment with the response rate stated alongside it (M1)(A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for a correct response rate calculation in any of the three forms, (A1) for all three rates correct, (A1) for the comparison of 25% of the membership with 47.1% of the sample. A candidate who says the sample is unrepresentative because only 42.5% replied, without comparing the two segments, has identified a real but different problem: credit it only if the segment comparison is also attempted.
(b) (M1) for 92 of 170, (A1) for 54.1%, (A1) for stating the manager's conclusion. The conclusion must be reported faithfully even though it is wrong; the evaluation comes in (d).
(c) (M1) for weighting by membership shares rather than by response counts, (A1) for 70% and 40%, (A1) for 47.5% and 190 members, (A1) for the direction argument — the segment that responds more also approves more, so the pooled figure must be too high. Credit an equivalent argument carried out in counts rather than percentages.
(d) (M1) for the conclusion that the claim is not supported, with the weighted figure used, (A1) for the point that non-respondents are unobserved and may differ, (A1) for a second developed consideration such as revenue weighting by segment, and (M1)(A1) for a recommendation that would let the claim be tested — quota sampling, follow-up of non-respondents, or reporting response rates and segment breakdowns. Do not credit 'the sample is too small' on its own: 170 responses is a large sample; the problem is which 170.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 6.7 An open-ended final class: the mean is not estimable and the median is, and the target has to be judged on the second
syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.7 Descriptive statistics (grouped data, the mean and median of a grouped distribution, quartiles and the interquartile range, and the choice of an appropriate average); 2.1 Introduction to human resource management
title: 6.7 An open-ended final class: the mean is not estimable and the median is, and the target has to be judged on the second
q_html:
Ashgrove Logistics: absence days by employee

Ashgrove Logistics employs 70 drivers and warehouse staff. The HR department records the number of days each employee was absent last year and groups them for the annual report.

The board has set a target that *average* absence must be below six days per employee. The HR director reports that the mean absence is 5.71 days, calculated from the grouped table, and that the target has therefore been met.

The table is an extract from the report. The final class is recorded as '12 or more' because six employees had long-term sickness and their records were not broken down further.

The histogram shows the same distribution, with the open-ended final class drawn as a faded bar. Use the n/2 convention for the median and quartiles of a grouped distribution, and give all answers to two decimal places.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Reproduce the HR director's estimate of the mean from the grouped table, stating the assumption you have to make about the final class in order to produce it.

    (Estimate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the median and the interquartile range of the distribution, and state what assumption, if any, the open-ended class forces you to make in order to find them.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Show that no upper bound can be placed on the mean from this table, and determine the greatest lower bound that the table does guarantee.

    (Show that)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the HR director's claim that the mean absence is 5.71 days and that the six-day target has been met, and recommend how absence should be reported instead.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Using midpoints 1, 4, 7 and 10 for the first four classes and assuming the last class has the same width as the others, so a midpoint of 13 (M1), the estimated mean is (14 × 1 + 23 × 4 + 18 × 7 + 9 × 10 + 6 × 13) ÷ 70 = (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 78) ÷ 70 = 400 ÷ 70 = 5.71 days (A1). The assumption is that the six employees in the open class were each absent for about 13 days; nothing in the table supports it, and the class was left open precisely because those six records were not broken down (A1).
(b) With 70 employees the median is the 35th value. Cumulative frequencies are 14, 37, 55, 64 and 70, so the 35th value lies in the class 3 – 5, whose lower boundary is 2.5 and whose width is 3: median = 2.5 + ((35 − 14) ÷ 23) × 3 = 2.5 + 2.74 = 5.24 days (M1)(A1). The lower quartile is the 17.5th value, also in 3 – 5: 2.5 + ((17.5 − 14) ÷ 23) × 3 = 2.96 days. The upper quartile is the 52.5th value, in 6 – 8: 5.5 + ((52.5 − 37) ÷ 18) × 3 = 8.08 days. The interquartile range is 8.08 − 2.96 = 5.13 days (A1). No assumption is needed: these are positional measures, and the six employees in the open class affect them only by standing above them in the ordering.
(c) The six employees in the final class each have at least 12 days, but the table places no ceiling on them. If they each had 60 days, the mean would be (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 6 × 60) ÷ 70 = 682 ÷ 70 = 9.74 days (M1); if they each had 200 days it would be 21.74 days (A1). Since the assumed value can be increased without limit, no upper bound on the mean can be derived from the table (A1). The smallest the mean can be is when all six are at the foot of their class, 12 days: (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 72) ÷ 70 = 394 ÷ 70 = 5.63 days, so the table guarantees only that the mean is at least 5.63 days (A1).
(d) The claim is unsound in two ways. The figure of 5.71 days is not an estimate of the mean at all: it is the value obtained when the six longest absences are each assumed to be 13 days, and the same table is consistent with a mean of 9.74 days or of 21 days, so the mean cannot be compared with the target (M1)(A1). What the table does support is a different statement: the median is 5.24 days and therefore below the target, 8.6% of the workforce (6 of 70) were absent for at least 12 days, and the distribution is right-skewed with an interquartile range of 5.13 days — so the typical employee is comfortably inside the target and a small group is far outside it (A1). The recommendation is to report absence with positional measures and the tail: the median, the interquartile range and the percentage of employees above a threshold such as twelve days, together with the exact figures for the six long-term cases, which the HR department already holds (M1)(A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for using midpoints at all, (A1) for 5.71 days, (A1) for naming the assumption explicitly. A candidate who writes 5.71 with no comment on the open class earns the method mark only; the point of the part is that the number carries an invisible assumption.
(b) (M1) for locating the median class by cumulative frequency, (A1) for 5.24 days, (A1) for the quartiles and the interquartile range of 5.13 days. Accept quartile positions of (n+1)/4 and 3(n+1)/4 if applied consistently, with quartiles of 2.99 and 8.21 and an IQR of 5.22; do not penalise the alternative convention, but do penalise a candidate who mixes them. The statement that no assumption is required is worth credit here even if it is not separately marked.
(c) (M1) for substituting a large value into the open class, (A1) for a second such value or for a general argument, (A1) for the conclusion that no upper bound exists, (A1) for the lower bound of 5.63 days. The lower bound must use 12, the smallest value the class permits; a candidate who uses 11.5 has misread the class and loses this mark.
(d) (M1) for distinguishing an estimate that depends on the assumption from one that does not, (A1) for the conclusion that the claim cannot be tested from the mean, (A1) for the supportable statements — median 5.24, 8.6% at twelve days or more — and (M1)(A1) for a reporting recommendation. Do not credit 'collect better data' on its own: the data already exist, and the fault is in the summary chosen.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.2 The stage with the lowest stated capacity is not the bottleneck: quantifying what the wrong investment buys
syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.2 Operations methods (capacity utilisation, efficiency and productivity, and the identification of the constraint in a process); 5.1 The role of operations management
title: 5.2 The stage with the lowest stated capacity is not the bottleneck: quantifying what the wrong investment buys
q_html:
Trentvale Components Ltd: three stages and two proposals

Trentvale Components Ltd makes a machined housing in three sequential stages. Cutting can process 100 units per hour and produces no scrap. Machining can process 90 units per hour, and 10% of the units it processes are scrapped and sold as swarf. Finishing can process 84 units per hour and produces no scrap. Every good unit that leaves finishing is sold immediately: demand is not a constraint, and the line runs for 40 hours a week for 48 weeks a year.

The housing sells for £40 and has a variable cost of £22, so each good unit contributes £18. Two proposals have been costed at £250 000 each.

Proposal 1 raises finishing capacity from 84 to 110 units per hour. Proposal 2 buys a better tool holder for machining, reducing the scrap rate there from 10% to 5%. The operations director argues that finishing must be extended first, because 84 units per hour is the lowest capacity in the factory.

The diagram shows the three stages with their stated capacities. Answer every part, giving output to one decimal place and money to the nearest pound.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the current maximum output of good units per hour and identify the stage that constrains it.

    (Determine)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Explain why finishing, which has the lowest stated capacity of the three stages, is not the constraint.

    (Explain)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the output of good units per hour under each proposal on its own and under both together, and calculate the cost per additional unit of hourly capacity in each case.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate which proposal, or pair of proposals, Trentvale should approve, using the payback period and two other factors.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Cutting can supply 100 units an hour but machining can process only 90, so the line is throttled to 90 units an hour at machining (M1). Of those, 10% are scrapped, so the good output is 90 × 0.90 = 81 units an hour (A1). Finishing can handle 84 units an hour and receives 81, so it is not full. The maximum output of good units is therefore 81 per hour and the constraint is machining (A1).
(b) A stage constrains the line only if the good units arriving at it exceed what it can process. Finishing receives 81 good units an hour and can process 84, so it runs with three units an hour, or 3.6%, of spare capacity (M1)(A1). Its stated capacity is the lowest of the three only because it is quoted before the scrap that happens upstream of it; comparing stated capacities compares the stages at different points in the process, and the comparison that matters is between good units delivered and capacity available at the same point (A1).
(c) Proposal 1 alone leaves machining untouched, so output stays at 81 units an hour: the extra finishing capacity is starved and the proposal adds nothing at all (M1). Proposal 2 alone raises good output from machining to 90 × 0.95 = 85.5 units an hour, but finishing can take only 84, so the line delivers 84 units an hour, a gain of 3 units an hour (A1). Both together deliver 85.5 units an hour, a gain of 4.5 units an hour (A1). Cost per additional unit of hourly capacity: Proposal 1, £250 000 for no additional units, so the cost per unit is undefined — no price buys the extra capacity at any level of spending; Proposal 2, £250 000 ÷ 3 = £83 333; both, £500 000 ÷ 4.5 = £111 111, of which the marginal £250 000 buys only 1.5 units an hour, or £166 667 each (A1).
(d) Proposal 2 is the one to approve. It adds 3 units an hour, which is 3 × 40 × 48 = 5 760 units a year and 5 760 × £18 = £103 680 of additional contribution, so it pays back in £250 000 ÷ £103 680 = 2.41 years (M1)(A1). Proposal 1 on its own pays back never: it adds no output, so there is no additional contribution against which to recover the £250 000, and it would add depreciation to a stage that already has spare capacity (A1). Two further considerations qualify the recommendation. First, scrap is not only lost output: every scrapped unit has already absorbed £22 of material and machining time, so reducing the scrap rate also improves material productivity and reduces waste disposal, benefits that the contribution calculation does not capture (A1). Second, doing both proposals raises output by a further 1.5 units an hour but costs another £250 000 and stretches payback to 3.21 years; that is worth doing only if Trentvale is confident of selling the extra 8 640 units a year, and demand, not capacity, may then become the constraint (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for identifying that machining throttles the input to 90 units an hour, (A1) for 81 good units an hour, (A1) for naming machining as the constraint. Accept 81 arrived at as 90 − 9. Do not credit 84 (the lowest stated capacity) or 90 (the lowest stated processing capacity before scrap).
(b) (M1) for the principle that a stage binds only when arrivals exceed its capacity, (A1) for the figures 81 against 84, (A1) for the explanation that the stated capacities are measured at different points in the process. A candidate who says only that 'finishing has spare capacity' without quantifying it earns the first two marks but not the third.
(c) (M1) for recognising that Proposal 1 changes nothing while machining binds, (A1) for 84 units an hour under Proposal 2 with the reason (finishing now binds at 84, not 85.5), (A1) for 85.5 units an hour with both, (A1) for the three cost figures. The cost per unit for Proposal 1 must be stated as undefined or infinite; a candidate who writes £250 000 or zero has not understood the result and loses the mark.
(d) (M1) for converting the extra output into annual units, (A1) for £103 680 and 2.41 years, (A1) for the conclusion that Proposal 1 never pays back, (A1) for one further developed factor such as material productivity, and (A1) for a second, such as the marginal case for doing both or the risk that demand becomes the constraint. Credit the sequencing point — Proposal 1 has value only after Proposal 2 — wherever it appears.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.7 A cash-flow forecast in which one outflow drives the balance negative in five of six months
syllabus_ref: Unit 3: 3.7 Cash flow (cash-flow forecasts, the difference between profit and cash, and the management of working capital); 3.4 Final accounts
title: 3.7 A cash-flow forecast in which one outflow drives the balance negative in five of six months
q_html:
The figure is a six-month cash-flow forecast prepared by the finance officer of a small engineering firm. The bars show the net cash flow for each month in pounds: January +3 000, February +2 000, March -8 000, April +4 000, May +5 000 and June +6 000. The line shows the closing balance at the end of each month: -9 000 at the end of January, -7 000 at the end of February, -15 000 at the end of March, -11 000 at the end of April, -6 000 at the end of May and 0 at the end of June. The opening balance at the start of January is not shown.

The finance officer presents the forecast to the bank with the comment that five of the six months are cash-positive and that the business is not therefore in any difficulty. The bank lends only by granting an overdraft facility, and it will grant one of at most £10 000 on the strength of this forecast.

(a) Determine the opening balance at the start of January and the net cash flow for the six months as a whole.

(b) Explain how the closing balance can be negative at the end of five of the six months when only March shows a negative net cash flow, and state the largest amount by which the business is overdrawn during the six months and the month in which this occurs.

(c) Justify, using figures, whether the business can operate within an overdraft facility of £10 000 on this forecast, and recommend one change to the timing of the flows that would bring it within the limit.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the opening balance at the start of January and the net cash flow for the six months as a whole.

    (Determine)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Explain how the closing balance can be negative at the end of five of the six months when only March shows a negative net cash flow, and state the largest amount by which the business is overdrawn and the month in which this occurs.

    (Explain)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Justify, using figures, whether the business can operate within an overdraft facility of £10 000 on this forecast, and recommend one change to the timing of the flows that would bring it within the limit.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) The closing balance at the end of January is the opening balance plus January's net cash flow, so the opening balance is -9 000 - 3 000 = -12 000 (A1). The business therefore begins the period 12 000 pounds overdrawn, a figure the forecast does not state and which can only be found by reversing the first month. The net cash flow for the six months as a whole is the sum of the six bars: 3 000 + 2 000 - 8 000 + 4 000 + 5 000 + 6 000 = +12 000 (M1)(A1). The closing balance at the end of June confirms it, since -12 000 + 12 000 = 0.

(b) The closing balance is a running total, and the net cash flow is a monthly figure; the sign of a bar says nothing about the sign of the line above it. January's inflow of 3 000 does not make the business cash-positive, it reduces the overdraft from 12 000 to 9 000, and the balance stays negative because the business started the year owing 12 000 more than it held (M1). A surplus month therefore only moves the balance towards zero; it cannot lift it above zero while the opening position is negative. March's single outflow of 8 000 is larger than the combined surplus of January and February, so it takes the balance from -7 000 to -15 000, and the three surpluses that follow, totalling 15 000, are only just enough to bring the balance back to zero by the end of June (A1). The business is overdrawn by at most 15 000, at the end of March, which is the month after the deficit rather than the deficit month itself (A1): the peak in the balance follows the peak in the outflow, and the two are not the same thing.

(c) The deepest point of the forecast is a balance of -15 000 at the end of March, so the facility required is 15 000 and a limit of 10 000 is exceeded by 5 000 at that point (M1)(A1). The business cannot operate within a 10 000 facility on this forecast, and the failure is not marginal: the facility would be exhausted before the end of March and every payment after that point until the balance recovered would be refused, which is the month in which the surpluses of April, May and June begin to arrive (A1). A single change to the timing of the flows is enough. Deferring 5 000 of the March payment into April turns March's net cash flow into -3 000 and the end-March balance into -10 000, exactly at the limit; deferring 6 000 brings the balance to -9 000 and leaves 1 000 of headroom, and either version ends the six months with a positive closing balance of 10 000 (A1). Note that the same 5 000 could equally be found by collecting 5 000 of receivables earlier, which changes the timing without changing the total. What matters is that the change is to the timing of the March outflow and not to its size, because the business does have to make the payment eventually and the forecast is otherwise cash-generative.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for the opening balance of -12 000 with the reversal of January stated; (M1) for summing the six bars; (A1) for +12 000. Accept a candidate who obtains -12 000 by working backward from the June balance through all six months provided the arithmetic is shown. Do not accept an opening balance given as a positive 12 000: the business is overdrawn from the start.

(b) (M1) for distinguishing the monthly flow from the running balance, with January's inflow identified as a reduction of the overdraft rather than a move into credit; (A1) for the explanation that the accumulated deficit of 12 000 keeps the balance negative while each surplus month only reduces it; (A1) for 15 000 at the end of March. Award the third mark for 15 000 with March identified; 8 000, the largest single outflow, scores nothing here. A candidate who says the business is profitable in five months and illiquid in five is making the distinction the part is testing and should be credited.

(c) (M1) for comparing the deepest balance with the facility limit; (A1) for the conclusion that 10 000 is insufficient, with the 5 000 shortfall stated; (A1) for the consequence, that payments would be refused from March onwards until the balance recovers; (A1) for a quantified timing change. Accept deferring at least 5 000 of the March outflow, collecting receivables earlier, or any other change that lifts the end-March balance to -10 000 or above, provided a figure is given. Do not accept 'increase the facility' as the recommended change, because the question fixes the facility at 10 000 and asks for a change to the timing. A candidate who notes that 5 000 lands exactly on the limit and that 6 000 leaves headroom has answered the part fully.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.5 Both liquidity ratios rising while the firm removes two thirds of its cash
syllabus_ref: Unit 3: 3.5 Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis (the current ratio, the acid-test ratio and the management of working capital); 3.4 Final accounts; 3.7 Cash flow
title: 3.5 Both liquidity ratios rising while the firm removes two thirds of its cash
q_html:
The figure compares three measures of one firm's liquidity before and after a decision to pay £40 000 of trade payables earlier than the agreed date, using cash held in the business. Before the payment the current ratio was 2.00 and the acid-test ratio was 1.25. After the payment the current ratio was 2.33 and the acid-test ratio was 1.33. Cash held fell from £60 000 to £20 000.

The payment reduced current assets and current liabilities by the same £40 000: cash, which is a current asset, fell by £40 000, and trade payables, which are a current liability, fell by £40 000. Inventory was not affected, and neither were trade receivables. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, and the acid-test ratio is current assets less inventory divided by current liabilities.

The finance director tells the board that both liquidity ratios have improved and that the payment has therefore strengthened the firm's liquidity position, and proposes to repeat the practice with the remaining trade payables.

(a) Using the ratios before the payment, calculate the firm's current assets, its current liabilities and the value of its inventory before the payment.

(b) Explain why the current ratio and the acid-test ratio both rise when £40 000 is paid out of cash to reduce trade payables, given that the payment removes two thirds of the firm's cash.

(c) Evaluate the finance director's claim that the payment has strengthened the firm's liquidity position, and recommend whether the practice should be repeated.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Using the ratios before the payment, calculate the firm's current assets, its current liabilities and the value of its inventory before the payment.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Explain why the current ratio and the acid-test ratio both rise when £40 000 is paid out of cash to reduce trade payables, given that the payment removes two thirds of the firm's cash.

    (Explain)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Evaluate the finance director's claim that the payment has strengthened the firm's liquidity position, and recommend whether the practice should be repeated.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Write current liabilities as L. Before the payment the current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, so current assets are 2L. After the payment both fall by 40 000, giving (2L - 40) / (L - 40) = 2.333, that is 2L - 40 = 2.333L - 93.33, so 0.333L = 53.33 and L = 160, in thousands of pounds (M1)(A1). Current liabilities are therefore £160 000 and current assets are £320 000 before the payment. The acid-test ratio is 1.25, so current assets less inventory is 1.25 x 160 = £200 000, and inventory is 320 - 200 = £120 000 (A1).

(b) For any ratio greater than one, subtracting the same amount from the numerator and the denominator makes the ratio larger. Writing the current assets as A and the current liabilities as L, with A greater than L, the new ratio is (A - x) / (L - x) against the old A / L, and the new one is greater whenever x is positive and A exceeds L (M1). Both ratios were above one before the payment, at 2.00 and 1.25, so both rise; this is not an economic effect but an arithmetic one, and it would happen in exactly the same way if the firm had paid the payables with borrowed money or with inventory (A1). What the ratios measure is the balance between short-term assets and short-term liabilities. Paying a liability out of cash does not change that balance: working capital, the difference between the two, stays at 320 - 160 = £160 000 before and 280 - 120 = £160 000 after. The payment changes the composition of the working capital, moving £40 000 out of cash, and leaves its size untouched, which is precisely why a ratio of the two totals does not move in the direction the cash movement would suggest (A1).

(c) The claim confuses a measure with the thing being measured. The arithmetic of part (b) shows that the ratios rise mechanically whenever a liability is settled out of cash and the ratio is above one, and the working capital is unchanged at £160 000, so the movement in the ratios carries no information about the firm's position at all (A1). What does carry information is the composition of the liquid resources, and it has deteriorated sharply: cash falls from £60 000 to £20 000, a reduction of 67 per cent, and quick assets, the current assets less inventory that the acid-test ratio compares against current liabilities, fall from £200 000 to £160 000, a reduction of 20 per cent. So the acid-test ratio rose 6.7 per cent while the quick assets it compares fell 20 per cent, and the current ratio rose 16.7 per cent while the cash the firm holds fell 67 per cent (A1). The firm has not improved its ability to meet an unexpected payment; it has reduced it, and it has done so while the two indicators that a lender would look at moved in the opposite direction. The practice should not be repeated (A1). Paying a supplier before the agreed date costs the firm the use of the money for the period of the credit it had been granted, and nothing in the information given states a settlement discount in return, so the firm is giving up a benefit and receiving none. The recommendation is to pay on the agreed dates unless the supplier offers a discount that exceeds the cost of the funds, to hold cash at a level tied to the working-capital cycle rather than to a ratio target, and if the board wants to measure the position properly, to report the cash balance and the quick assets alongside the ratios rather than instead of them (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for setting up the equation in one unknown from the before and after current ratios; (A1) for £160 000 of current liabilities and £320 000 of current assets; (A1) for £120 000 of inventory from the acid-test ratio. Accept candidates who find the liabilities by trial as long as the resulting ratios are checked; a candidate who assumes current liabilities of 100 and reports a current ratio of 2.67 after the payment has not used the second ratio and scores nothing.

(b) (M1) for the algebraic argument that subtracting a constant from numerator and denominator of a fraction greater than one increases it, with A greater than L stated; (A1) for the observation that working capital is unchanged at £160 000 before and after; (A1) for the conclusion that the ratios measure the balance between the two totals rather than the size of the liquid resources. Do not accept 'the ratios are wrong' or 'the ratios are misleading in this case' unaccompanied by the reason: the ratios are computed correctly and behave exactly as ratios above one must.

(c) (A1) for identifying that the ratio movement is mechanical and therefore uninformative, with the unchanged working capital cited; (A1) for the quantitative deterioration, using at least two of the cash fall from £60 000 to £20 000, the quick-asset fall from £200 000 to £160 000, and the percentage comparison between the two; (A1) for the recommendation not to repeat the practice; (A1) for a reasoned basis, such as the loss of the credit period, the absence of any stated settlement discount, or the proposal to report cash alongside the ratios. A candidate who recommends repetition because the ratios improved has failed the part; a candidate who recommends repetition but identifies the loss of the credit period as a cost to be weighed earns the recommendation mark only if the position is judged to be adequately protected, which the 67 per cent fall in cash does not support.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.8 Unequal asset lives, a replacement chain, and a common cost that cancels only in part
syllabus_ref: 3.8 Investment appraisal (payback period, average rate of return, net present value); 3.2 Sources of finance
title: 3.8 Unequal asset lives, a replacement chain, and a common cost that cancels only in part
q_html:
Vastra Teknik must choose between two machines for a four-year contract. The contract will
generate net cash inflows of $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year for each of the four years whichever machine
is used, so the choice turns entirely on the costs. The company's cost of capital is $10\%$ per
year and all cash flows arise at the ends of years.

Machine P costs $\pounds 120{,}000$ and has a working life of two years, so it must be replaced
by an identical machine at the end of year 2 at the same price. It is decommissioned at the end of
year 2 and again at the end of year 4.

Machine Q costs $\pounds 230{,}000$ and has a working life of four years, so it is not replaced.
It is decommissioned once, at the end of year 4.

The decommissioning charge is $\pounds D$ on each occasion it arises, and is the same for both
machines. Assume initially that $D = 20{,}000$.

(a) Calculate the payback period for each machine. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine
should be chosen on this basis. \tag{5}

(c) The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both
